exp.0:2:
It says that if someone wanted to offer a burnt offering from the herd, they had to bring a male without defect. A burnt offering was one that was burned whole on the altar. Without defect means without any flaw. The phrase about giving it of one's own will indicates that the person gave it freely, though some translators understand that it was so that it would be accepted by God. The offering had to be brought to the entrance of the tabernacle, before the Lord.

Here God himself speaks. He calls Moses from the tabernacle and gives him instructions for the people of Israel. These rules taught how to approach a holy God, and they showed the seriousness of sin and the need for atonement.

For today: God values what is given to him sincerely and with our best. We can ask ourselves whether we give him our time, affection, and service willingly, or only to fulfill an obligation.
exp.0:3:
It says the person who brought the animal for the burnt offering was to lay his hand on its head. In this way the animal was accepted on his behalf, that is, to cover his sin and restore his relationship with God. A burnt offering was an offering that was burned whole on the altar.

God speaks to Moses from the tabernacle and gives him instructions for the people of Israel. He wanted to teach them how to draw near to Him with reverence. Placing the hand on the animal probably showed that it was his offering and that he was presenting it in his own place, though scholars explain its exact meaning in several ways.

Today we do not offer animals, but we can learn that drawing near to God requires sincerity and personal devotion. Christians see in Christ the sacrifice that covers sin once and for all. We can pray with humility, acknowledging our need and trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.0:6:
This verse says that the priests, descendants of Aaron, were to light a fire on the altar and arrange the wood on top of it. The altar was the place where sacrifices were offered to God.

God speaks to Moses from the tabernacle and gives instructions about the burnt offering, an offering that was burned up completely. Here the work of the priests is described: it mattered not only that the sacrifice was made, but also that everything was prepared with care and order. Some understand that the original fire came from God (Leviticus 9:24), although this text only speaks of the priests putting it in place.

For today: God values that we serve him with preparation and diligence. Before we pray, teach, or serve in the church, we can take a moment to prepare ourselves with seriousness and humility.
exp.0:10:
It says that when someone offered a sheep, a lamb, or a goat as a burnt offering, he had to kill it on the north side of the altar, in the presence of the Lord. Then the priests, Aaron's sons, took the blood and splashed it against the altar on all its sides.

God speaks to Moses from the tent of meeting and gives instructions to the people of Israel about how to approach Him. The blood held a central place because it represented a life given. Leviticus 17:11 says that the blood made atonement. That is why only the priests handled it. It is not known for certain why the north side was specified; scholars do not agree.

For today: approaching God is not something casual. Christians see in Jesus the complete sacrifice (Hebrews 10:10), so we can come to God with reverence and with confidence, grateful for what it cost.
exp.0:11:
This verse says that the burnt offering, already slaughtered, is cut into pieces. The head and the fat that covers the entrails are set apart with the other pieces. Then the priest arranges them on the burning wood of the altar. The sentence about the arranging of the pieces explains that they are placed in order and with care.

God speaks to Moses from the tabernacle and gives Israel instructions for drawing near to Him. The burnt offering was burned whole, and it expressed total surrender and the need for forgiveness. Before this verse, the worshiper presents an animal without defect, and the blood is sprinkled on the altar. Christians often see in this a shadow of the sacrifice of Christ, though the original text speaks directly of worship in Israel.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we give God everything, not just a part. Offering Him today a task, a fear, or a decision, with care and sincerity, is a way of worshiping Him.
exp.0:12:
The person who brings the animal is to wash its inner parts and its legs with water. Then the priest places all of it on the altar and burns it. This is called a burnt offering, an offering that is consumed completely. The verse that it is an offering burned entirely, where the whole animal goes up in smoke, is the meaning of the phrase, and the phrase about it being a pleasing aroma expresses that God receives the offering with favor.

God speaks to Moses from the tent of meeting and gives Israel instructions on how to draw near to Him. The burnt offering was a voluntary offering that expressed complete surrender. The washing shows that it was done with care and reverence. Christians often see here a shadow of the sacrifice of Christ, although the text itself speaks of worship in Israel.

God deserves our best, not what we have left over. Today we can offer Him our lives with sincerity and care, and place in His hands our time, work, and decisions.
exp.0:13:
It says that if someone wants to present a burnt offering to God and has no livestock, they may bring birds: turtledoves or young pigeons. A burnt offering was a sacrifice that was burned whole on the altar. "The Lord" is the name of God, and an offering is what is presented as a gift or act of worship.

God speaks to Moses from the tent of meeting, giving Israel instructions on how to draw near to Him. Earlier the bull and the lamb or young goat are mentioned. This option of birds made room for those with fewer resources, so no one was excluded from worshiping. Some see here a special care of God for the poor.

For today: God does not measure our devotion by the size of the offering, but by a sincere heart. Offer Him today whatever you have, your time, your prayer, or your service, without being ashamed that it is little.
exp.0:15:
When offering a bird, the priest was to remove its crop, the pouch where the bird keeps its food, along with its feathers. All of this was thrown beside the altar on the east side, by the place where the ashes were kept. Some scholars believe the Hebrew text refers to the crop together with its contents, which is why not all translations say the same thing.

God speaks to Moses from the tabernacle and gives him instructions for the people of Israel. Birds were the offering of those who did not have a bull or a lamb. Even so, God asked for order, care, and respect, because the people were drawing near to a holy God.

For today: God receives what we can give, whether much or little, but He wants us to give it with reverence and sincerity. Come near to Him with what you have, without carelessness and without shame.
exp.1:1:
The person who brings this grain offering carries his handful of fine flour to the priests, the descendants of Aaron. The priest takes a handful of the flour with the oil, along with all the frankincense, and burns it on the altar. That portion is called the memorial, and it is an offering of a sweet aroma to God.

God speaks to Moses to teach the people of Israel how to worship him. This offering was different from the animal sacrifices, since it was a gift of thanksgiving from the fruit of one's labor. Scholars explain the exact meaning of the memorial in several ways, but it is understood as a portion that represents the whole offering before God.

Today we can give God the best of what we have, with gratitude and not out of obligation. It can be our time, our work, or our resources, offered with a sincere heart.
exp.1:3:
This verse describes how the grain offering was to be prepared if someone brought it baked in an oven. It could be cakes made of fine flour, without yeast, mixed with oil, or thin, flat breads, without yeast, spread with oil.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel, and the priests receive them. This offering expressed gratitude and devotion to God with the fruit of daily labor. Yeast is commonly understood as a symbol of corruption, and oil is often related to the Spirit and consecration, though this is interpreted in different ways.

Today we can offer God the best of our everyday lives: our work, our time, and our care for our family. Let us do it with a sincere heart, without hypocrisy, grateful for what He has given us.
exp.1:4:
It says that if someone wants to bring God an offering of grain cooked on a pan (a flat plate or sheet for baking), they must use fine flour, that is, flour of the finest and best quality. It must not contain yeast, and the dough is mixed with oil. The word "offering" here means a gift presented to God.

God speaks to Moses, and this book explains how the people of Israel were to draw near to Him. Grain offerings were a way of giving thanks and dedicating to God part of the fruit of daily labor. The instructions vary according to how the offering was cooked, but they always call for the best and for no yeast. Scholars discuss the exact meaning of the yeast; many see it as a symbol of corruption or of something that puffs up.

For today: God cares about the everyday. We can offer Him our work and our time with sincerity and with the best we have, not with what we have left over.
exp.1:6:
This verse describes a third way of presenting the grain offering. If someone wanted to prepare it in a pan (a deep pot or vessel for cooking), it had to be made with the finest flour, the best and most refined quality, mixed with oil. The word "offering" here simply means the gift brought to God.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. These were voluntary offerings of thankfulness and devotion. People could give according to what they had or what they cooked at home, and the priest would place a portion on the altar. Some interpreters see in the oil a picture of the Spirit or of God's blessing, though the text here does not explain this.

Today we can learn that God values the best we give, even in the simple and everyday. Offering Him our time, work, or resources with care is a way of worshiping Him.
exp.1:7:
This verse says that the person must bring to the Lord the grain offering, made of fine flour and oil, and present it to the priest. Then the priest brings it to the altar, that is, he draws it near or carries it up to the altar. The word "presented" in this verse is the word for the offering being handed over.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses gives these instructions to Israel. This offering was a way of worshiping and giving thanks with the fruit of daily labor. The verses that follow say that one part was burned on the altar and the rest was for the priests. In this way God cared for those who served him.

For today: what we give to God is not given in secret, but with order, humility, and gratitude. We can offer him our work, time, and resources with a thankful heart, and support those who serve in the church.
exp.1:11:
This verse says that the offerings of firstfruits, that is, the first fruits of the harvest, were brought to the Lord, but they were not burned on the altar as a pleasing aroma. The phrase about a pleasing scent speaks of a smell that is pleasing to God. Earlier, the burning of leaven and honey was forbidden, and this verse seems to refer to those products.

God speaks to Moses to teach Israel how to worship him with the grain offering. The priests received a portion, and what was burned followed clear rules. Some understand that leaven and honey were associated with fermentation or corruption, but the text does not fully explain this, so there are several interpretations.

For today: let us give God the first and the best, not what is left over. And let us do it with obedience and gratitude, trusting that he cares more about a sincere heart than about an eye-catching appearance.
exp.1:14:
What it says: God commands that, on the offering of roasted heads of grain from the first fruits, oil and frankincense be placed. In this older text, the word for this kind of gift means a grain offering, not an ordinary gift. The first fruits were the first part of the harvest.

Context: God speaks to Moses to teach the people of Israel how to bring their offerings. This grain offering expressed thanksgiving for the harvest. Oil and frankincense are mentioned often in worship; oil is commonly seen as a sign of blessing or of the Spirit, and frankincense as prayer and adoration, although the text does not explain this here.

For today: When you give God the first and best of what you have, do it with a grateful heart and in a spirit of prayer, not as a mere obligation.
exp.2:0:
This verse begins to explain the peace offering. If someone wanted to offer an animal from the herd, meaning a cow or a bull, it could be a male or a female, but it had to be without defect. The peace offering was an offering of fellowship or thankfulness, and the phrase "before the LORD" means in his presence, at the place of worship.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel on how to draw near to him. This sacrifice was voluntary and, according to the following texts, part of the meat was shared in a meal before God. Many understand it as an expression of fellowship and thanksgiving, although the details are interpreted in various ways.

For today: when we give something to God, whether time, service, or gratitude, let us give it sincerely and with the best we have, not with what is left over. Christians believe that Christ opened the way for us to come to God.
exp.2:2:
This verse says that the person bringing the peace offering must present to God, burned on the altar, the fat that covers the intestines and all the fat that is on the inner parts. "Fat" here is the animal's fat. An offering made by fire is one that was burned on the altar. A peace offering was an offering of fellowship or thanksgiving.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel on how to draw near to Him. In this sacrifice, part was burned for God and the rest was shared as food. Many understand that the fat, the best part of the animal, symbolizes giving God what is most valuable, though the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: when we give thanks to God or share with Him, let us do it with our best, not with leftovers. It can be time, attention, help to others, or sincere gratitude, offered from the heart.
exp.2:3:
It says that from the animal offered as a peace offering, the two kidneys had to be taken away, along with the fat that covers them and the fat that is on the flanks, together with the caul, which is the fatty membrane that covers the liver. All of this was set apart to be presented to God.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel on how to draw near to Him. The peace offering expressed fellowship and thankfulness. The fat was the best part of the animal, and it was given to God. Some think it symbolizes giving what is most valuable; the text gives no further explanation.

For today: let us give God our best, not our leftovers. It can be our time, attention, or sincere gratitude. He invites us to live at peace with Him, and responding with a generous heart is a way of worshiping Him.
exp.2:4:
This verse says that the priests, descendants of Aaron, would burn the fatty parts of the animal on the altar. They would place them on top of the burnt offering, which was already burning on the wood. The fat is the animal's fat, and an offering of a sweet savour means an offering that is pleasing to God.

God speaks to Moses and gives instructions to the people of Israel about the peace or fellowship sacrifice. The one who presented it expressed gratitude and fellowship with God. The fat was considered the best part, and it was given to God. Scholars explain the exact symbolism in several ways, but they all agree that it meant giving the best.

For today: we can give God the best of our time, affection, and resources, not the leftovers. Today we no longer offer animals, but we still give thanks and serve with a sincere heart.
exp.2:5:
This verse says that if someone wants to bring a sheep or a young goat as a peace offering to the Lord, it may be a male or a female, but it must be without blemish, that is, without defect or sickness. The peace offering, or fellowship offering, is the one referred to here, and the verse makes clear that the animal must be offered as described.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. He had already spoken about cattle; now he includes those who had smaller flocks. In this way, the peace offering was within reach of people with different means, and it was always to be given with reverence and the best one could bring.

For today: when we give something to God, whether our time, our service, or our money, it should not be merely what we have left over, but something offered with sincerity and gratitude. He looks at the heart, and he desires a relationship of peace with us.
exp.2:7:
This verse describes the steps followed by the person who brought a lamb as a peace offering. First, he laid his hand on the head of the animal. Then he killed it, that is, cut its throat, at the entrance of the tabernacle. Finally, the priests, the sons of Aaron, sprinkled the blood around the altar.

God speaks to Moses and gives instructions for the people of Israel, who had recently come out of Egypt. The peace offering expressed fellowship and thankfulness toward God. Laying the hand on the animal showed that it was that person's offering. The blood, according to the same book, represents life (Leviticus 17:11).

For today: draw near to God with sincerity, not out of routine. Make your thankfulness something personal, something that costs you. And remember that Christ, according to the New Testament, opened the way for us to that fellowship with God.
exp.2:8:
This verse describes which parts of the animal the person offering the peace sacrifice was to burn. The fat was offered, the entire tail cut off close to the backbone (the spine), the fat that covers the entrails, and all the fat that lies over the inner organs. An offering made by fire is an offering burned on the altar. The peace offering refers to the offering of fellowship or thanksgiving.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel on how to draw near to Him. The person placed his hand on the animal, the blood was poured out, and the best part was given to God. The fat was considered the choicest portion. Many understand this sacrifice as an expression of fellowship and gratitude with God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we give God our best and not the leftovers. We can give Him the first of our time, attention, and gratitude, living in peace and fellowship with Him.
exp.2:16:
God gave a permanent rule: the people of Israel were not to eat fat (the hard fat that surrounds the animal's organs) or blood. A law that remains in force from generation to generation is what is meant by the rule being permanent. Their homes are the places where they lived, that is, their houses, wherever they were.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, at the end of the instructions about the peace offering. Shortly before, he said that the fat belongs entirely to the Lord, since it was burned on the altar as an offering. Blood was also considered sacred, because it represented life (Leviticus 17:11). This law was part of the covenant with Israel, and Christians understand it in different ways today.

For today: God deserves our best and our first. We can ask ourselves what valuable things in our lives we are setting aside for Him with gratitude and respect.
exp.3:3:
This verse describes what the anointed priest had to do when he sinned. He would bring the young bull to the entrance of the tabernacle, before the Lord. He would lay his hand on the animal's head and then kill it, that is, cut its throat. The tabernacle of the congregation was the sacred tent where God met with his people.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct Israel. The priest represented the people before God, so his sin was serious and affected everyone. Laying the hand on the animal is usually understood as a way of identifying with it, as if the sin passed to the victim. Scholars explain this gesture in several ways.

For today: do not minimize your sin or hide it. Come before God with sincerity and confess. Christians see in Christ the complete sacrifice that offers true forgiveness.
exp.3:5:
It says that the priest would dip his finger in the blood of the bull and sprinkle it seven times before God, toward the veil, the curtain that separated the holy place from the most holy place. To sprinkle is to splash, and the sanctuary is the sacred place where God met with his people.

God speaks to Moses and gives instructions for the sacrifice for the sin of the anointed priest, whose error could affect the whole people. The blood represented a life given, and the number seven is often associated with completeness, though scholars explain it in different ways. Sin was taken seriously, but God also offered a way to forgiveness.

For today: do not minimize your sin or hide it. Come before God with sincerity, trusting that he offers cleansing. Christians see in Christ the fulfillment of this poured-out blood.
exp.3:8:
This verse continues the instructions for the sin offering. It calls for the two kidneys to be taken from the bull, along with the fat that lies on them and on the flanks, and also the caul, the fatty membrane that covers the liver. All of this was set apart to be burned on the altar.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct Israel. Here the subject is the anointed priest who had sinned without intending to, and this affected the whole people. The fat was regarded as the best part and was offered to God. Scholars explain the symbolism in several ways, so it is wise not to claim more than the text itself says.

For today: when you fail, do not downplay your mistake or hide it. Come before God with honesty and offer your best in repentance, trusting in the forgiveness that Christ offers fully.
exp.3:9:
This verse says that the fatty parts of the calf offered for sin were to be removed in the same way as they were from the ox of the sacrifice of peace offerings. Then the priest would burn them on the altar of the burnt offering. The fat is the part set apart as God's portion, and the peace offering was the offering of fellowship with God.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel. Here the subject is the calf offered for the sin of the anointed priest, whose failure affected the whole people. The fat was considered the best part and was given to God. The same procedure is used as in another offering, which shows a clear order.

For today: when you recognize a fault, do not minimize it or hide it. Draw near to God with sincerity and offer Him the best of yourself in repentance. Christians believe that Christ fulfilled that sacrifice for us, and because of this we can approach with confidence.
exp.3:10:
This verse describes what was left of the bull after its fat and kidneys were offered on the altar: the skin, the flesh, the head, the legs, the entrails, and the dung. None of this was eaten or burned on the altar. The peace offering was a different offering, and it is mentioned here only as a comparison.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to Israel. This passage concerns the sin offering for the anointed priest, when he sinned without meaning to. Because his wrong affected the whole people, the bull was taken outside the camp to a clean place and burned completely (v. 12). This shows how serious sin is and that it had to be removed entirely.

For today: we should not make light of sin or hide it. We can come to God with honesty, trusting that Christ, according to the New Testament, bore our guilt and cleanses us completely.
exp.3:14:
This verse says that the leaders of the people, called the elders of the congregation, would lay their hands on the head of a young bull, a calf, before the Lord. Afterward they would kill it, that is, put it to death, also in the presence of the Lord. "Before the Lord" refers to the entrance of the tabernacle, where God dwelt among his people.

God gives these instructions to Moses. He speaks of a sin committed by the whole nation without their realizing it. Even though it was unintentional, it was still guilt. The elders represented everyone. Many understand that laying on of hands was a way of identifying the people with the animal that died in their place, although the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: do not minimize sin because it was done without your realizing it. Ask God to show you your faults, and remember that Christ offered the complete sacrifice for us.
exp.3:15:
This verse says that the anointed priest, that is, the high priest, carried part of the bullock's blood into the inside of the tabernacle. The tabernacle of the congregation is the sacred tent where God was present with his people. A bullock is a young bull, and atonement means covering over or cleansing sin.

Here God speaks through Moses, giving instructions to the people of Israel. This is the case in which the whole congregation sinned without realizing it. When they discovered it, they were to acknowledge it and offer a sacrifice. The blood represented a life given up, and it showed that sin is serious and that God provided a way to forgiveness.

For today: do not take sin lightly, not even the sin you commit without realizing it. Ask God to show you your faults, and trust in Christ, whose blood cleanses us completely (Hebrews 9:12-14).
exp.3:16:
It says the priest would dip his finger in the blood of the bull and sprinkle it seven times before the veil, the curtain that separated the holy place from the most holy place, where the ark was. The word for sprinkling in this verse means to splash or scatter drops. The name of God in this verse is the LORD.

God gives these instructions to Moses for Israel. Here the whole congregation had sinned without realizing it, and the elders represented them by laying their hands on the bull. The blood showed that sin is serious and that atonement was needed. The number seven often points to something complete, though some interpret it in other ways.

Today, Christians see in Christ the fulfillment of these sacrifices (Hebrews 9:11-14). This invites us to take sin seriously, but also to draw near to God with confidence, thankful that Jesus has already paid the price.
exp.3:17:
This verse describes what the priest did with the blood of the bull. He put some of it on the horns of the altar that was inside the tabernacle, before the Lord. Then he poured out the rest at the bottom of the altar of the burnt offering, near the entrance. The tabernacle of the congregation was the sacred tent where God met with his people.

God speaks to Moses to teach what to do when the anointed priest sinned without meaning to. Because his sin affected the whole people, the rite was more solemn. The blood represented life given up, and the horns of the altar were a place of great importance for atonement.

For today: sin is serious and it has a cost. Christians believe Christ paid that cost with his blood. That is why we can approach God with sincerity, acknowledging our faults and trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.3:24:
The priest would dip his finger in the blood of the animal offered for the sin. He would put it on the horns of the altar, which were the points that stood out at its corners. The rest of the blood he would pour out at the bottom of the altar. The burnt offering was the offering that was burned whole, and atonement means the payment or cleansing for sin.

God gave these instructions to Moses for Israel. This passage is about a leader who sinned without meaning to and then realized it. Even unintentional mistakes needed to be acknowledged and dealt with before God. Leviticus 17:11 says that the life is in the blood.

For today: do not minimize sin, even when it was done through carelessness. Bring it before God with sincerity. Christians believe that Jesus, through his sacrifice, offers complete forgiveness, and so we can come near with confidence.
exp.3:25:
It says that the priest was to burn all the fat of the male goat on the altar, just as the fat of the peace offering was burned. "Fat" here refers to the animal's fat, considered the best part. "Atonement" means covering or cleansing sin. So the priest made atonement for that person, and God granted forgiveness.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel. This passage deals with sin committed unintentionally, and here it refers to that of a ruler (v. 22). God showed that every sin is serious, even when it is unintended, and that He Himself offered a way to be forgiven through the sacrifice.

For today: let us not minimize our faults, even when we commit them without meaning to, nor live with constant guilt. Christians believe that Christ is the final and sufficient sacrifice (Hebrews 10:10-12). We can come to God with honesty, confess, and receive His forgiveness with confidence.
exp.3:27:
If a common person realizes that they have sinned without meaning to, they are to bring as an offering a female goat, without any flaw.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about the offerings. Earlier, the text explained what a priest or leader was to do when they sinned; now it speaks of anyone among the people. The law shows that God takes sin seriously, even unintentional sin, and that he provides a way to be forgiven.

For today: when God shows you a fault, do not ignore it or excuse it. Acknowledge it promptly and come to God with humility. Christians believe that Christ fulfilled that sacrifice, so we can draw near with confidence.
exp.3:29:
This verse describes what the priest did with the blood of the goat offered for sin. He would take some of it on his finger and put it on the "horns" of the altar, which were the points that stuck out at its corners. The rest of the blood he poured out at the base of the altar. The "burnt offering" was the offering that was burned whole.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. Here he speaks of an ordinary person who sinned without meaning to and later realized it. That person had to acknowledge the wrong and bring an offering. The blood showed that sin is serious and that forgiveness had a cost. According to the New Testament, this is fulfilled in the sacrifice of Christ.

Today we can take our wrongs seriously, without excusing them or sinking into guilt. Acknowledge them before God with sincerity, and receive with gratitude the forgiveness that Jesus has already secured with his blood.
exp.3:31:
This verse speaks of a person who decides to bring a lamb as an offering for their sin. In this case, it had to be a female, and without blemish, that is, without any fault or physical flaw.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. Here it explains what to do when someone from the people sinned without meaning to. There were different options, depending on the person and what they could afford, and this is one of them. Something valuable was required, and sin was taken seriously, yet God also offered a clear way to be forgiven.

For today: God still takes sin seriously, but he always opens a path of forgiveness. Christians see in Christ the perfect lamb who fulfills what these sacrifices pointed toward. Today we can draw near to God with sincerity, acknowledge our failings, and receive his forgiveness with gratitude.
exp.3:34:
This verse says that the priest will take away all the fat from the animal, just as was done with the sacrifice of the peace offerings, and will burn it on the altar as an offering to God. With this, the priest makes an atonement, that is, he covers over or repairs the guilt, and the person is forgiven for his sin.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about the offerings. This passage deals with sin committed without intention by a person from the people. The sacrifice showed that sin is serious and that God himself provided a way to be forgiven. Christians often see here a shadow of Christ, as the letter to the Hebrews explains.

For today: when you know you have failed, do not hide or make excuses. Go to God with sincerity, trusting that He forgives. And if something cannot be made right just by asking forgiveness, also seek to repair the harm with the person you offended.
exp.4:3:
It says that if someone makes a rash oath, committing with their lips to do something wrong or something good, and does not realize what they promised, they are guilty when they later understand it.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel, within the laws about sin offerings. It shows that God takes seriously even faults committed without awareness. Afterward, the person was to confess and bring an offering to be forgiven.

For today: let us take care with our words and promises, because they carry weight before God. If we discover that we spoke without thinking or failed without intending to, we should not ignore it. Let us acknowledge it with humility, confess it, and seek God's forgiveness.
exp.4:6:
It says that if a person does not have the money to bring a lamb, they may offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons. One of them was presented as the offering for sin, and the other as a burnt offering, a gift that was burned whole on the altar as a surrender to God.

God speaks through Moses to Israel, in the laws about the offerings. Earlier, the person was asked to confess the sin and bring a ewe lamb or a goat. Here God makes an allowance: forgiveness did not depend on how wealthy the person was, but on coming near to Him with humility.

For today: God does not set up barriers of money or social standing to forgive us. We can come near with simplicity, confess our failure and trust in His mercy, without thinking that we must have something great to offer Him.
exp.4:7:
This verse says that the person brings the two birds to the priest. He offers first the one that is for the sin offering, that is, to cover the sin. He twists its head against the neck to take its life, but without tearing it completely off.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel. This law is for the one who sinned but did not have the means to bring a lamb or a goat. God provides a simpler option, so that the poor could also be forgiven. The blood and the sacrifice showed that sin is serious and has a cost.

For today: God does not place unfair barriers in the way of our coming near to Him. We can acknowledge our faults with sincerity and trust in His mercy, without feeling that we do not have enough to present ourselves before Him.
exp.4:10:
It says that if a person did not have enough money to buy two turtledoves or two young pigeons, he could bring as his offering for sin a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour (about two liters, though estimates vary). This offering had no oil and no frankincense, because it was for dealing with sin, not a festive offering. An atonement means the sacrifice that covers or cleanses guilt.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about sin offerings. The animals were offered according to what each person could afford. Here God makes provision for the poorest, so that no one would be left without a way to forgiveness. Since there was no blood, many see here a special exception, and the text still says that forgiveness did come.

For today: God does not put grace out of anyone's reach. If some sin weighs on you, do not think you lack what it takes to come near to Him. Today we come trusting in Christ, and we can draw near with humility and sincerity.
exp.4:12:
This verse says that the priest will make atonement for the person who sinned, and that the person will be forgiven. What is left of the grain offering will belong to the priest, just as happened with the grain offering. "Atonement" means covering or repairing sin. The grain offering was the offering of grain or flour. The part left over is what remained after the handful was burned.

God speaks to Moses and gives instructions for the people of Israel. This passage deals with offerings for sins committed without intending to, or through carelessness. God allowed the poor to offer only flour when they could not afford birds, so that no one was left without a way to forgiveness.

For today: God wants forgiveness to be within reach of everyone, regardless of their situation. If you carry a burden of guilt today, you can come to God with simplicity and sincerity. Christians believe that Jesus is the one who offers that complete forgiveness.
exp.4:14:
This verse speaks of someone who, without realizing it, commits a trespass against the holy things of the Lord, such as the offerings or tithes that belonged to the sanctuary. The person was to bring a ram without blemish from the flock, valued in shekels of silver according to the shekel of the sanctuary.

God speaks to Moses to teach Israel how to live near a holy God. Even faults made without bad intent mattered, because what was sacred had to be respected. That is why the person was required to make up for the harm and seek forgiveness.

For today: when you discover that you have failed, even if it was unintentional, do not ignore it. Acknowledge it before God, make right the harm you can, and trust in his forgiveness.
exp.4:15:
This verse says that a person who sinned unintentionally against the holy things, meaning what belonged to God, such as offerings or tithes, had to return what he had taken or failed to give. In addition, he had to add a fifth part, that is, twenty percent more. All of this was handed over to the priest. The word "atonement" refers to covering guilt so as to be at peace with God. The priest made it with the ram, and the person was forgiven.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel. He wants to teach that sin committed by mistake also counts, and that repairing the harm is part of repentance. Many understand that this sacrifice points to Christ, although the text itself speaks of the law of Israel.

Today, if we fail God or others, even without bad intent, it is good to acknowledge it, repair what we can, and ask forgiveness with humility.
exp.4:18:
This verse closes the teaching about the guilt offering. It says that the sin is a real offense, a true breach of what is owed, and that the person who truly commits it has wronged the Lord himself, offending God directly. A breach here means a violation of a law that was broken.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel. In this section, a sin committed through ignorance still required an offering and forgiveness. The unblemished ram was presented to the priest as atonement. Some scholars see in this a shadow of what Christ would later accomplish, although the text itself does not say so.

For today: do not minimize your faults because you did not know better or because you did not mean it. Ask God to show you what you cannot see in yourself, and trust in his forgiveness, which is always available to anyone who comes near with humility.
exp.5:1:
This verse speaks of someone who sins and fails God by deceiving their neighbor. The text mentions denying something another person entrusted to them or left in their hands, stealing, or cheating and taking advantage of someone through abuse or fraud.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions about the guilt offering. It is part of the law given to Israel. An important point is that God counts these wrongs against a neighbor as sins against Himself. The verses that follow say the stolen thing had to be returned and the wrong repaired.

For today: if you owe someone something, whether money, a favor, or the truth, do not hide it. Speak with that person, return what is due, and ask for forgiveness. Settling accounts with people is also part of walking well with God.
exp.5:3:
This verse says that when someone recognizes that they have sinned and is guilty, they must give back what they took unjustly. It may be something stolen, something obtained through deceit or through oppression, something that was left with them in trust for safekeeping, or something lost that they found and kept.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to the people of Israel. In this passage, sinning against a neighbor through deceit or lies is also considered sinning against the LORD. For that reason, besides giving back what was taken, they had to add a fifth part and bring a guilt offering.

For today: if we have harmed someone, asking forgiveness is not enough if we are able to repair the harm. Giving back what we owe, or correcting what we did wrong, shows a sincere repentance.
exp.5:8:
God tells Moses to instruct Aaron and his sons, the priests, about the law of the burnt offering. This sacrifice was burned whole on the altar, all night until morning. In addition, the fire on the altar was to be kept burning.

The Lord speaks to Moses just after the rules about offenses and atonement. Now God gives practical instructions to the priests for offering the burnt offering, which expressed total surrender to God. Israel was in the wilderness, learning to live before a holy God.

For today: the fire that was never allowed to go out reminds us of constancy. We can seek God regularly, praying and reading his Word every day, not only when we feel like it, and give him our whole day faithfully.
exp.5:9:
It says the priest was to dress in his linen garments, including linen breeches or undergarments as well. At dawn, when the fire had already consumed the burnt offering, he would gather the ashes from the altar and place them beside the altar itself.

God speaks to Moses and tells him to give these instructions to Aaron and his sons, the priests. The fire on the altar was to be kept burning all night. Removing the ashes was a humble task, but it was done with care and reverence, because it concerned a holy place.

For today: God values faithful service, even in small tasks that are little seen. We can do the simple things of each day with reverence and a good attitude, as if we were doing them for the Lord.
exp.5:10:
What it says: After removing the ashes from the altar, the priest was to take off the linen garments he wore for service and put on other clothes. Wearing those other clothes, he carried the ashes outside the camp of Israel to a clean place, that is, a set-apart and pure spot where they could be deposited.

Context: God speaks to Moses and tells him to instruct Aaron and his sons about the burnt offering, the offering that was burned whole. These regulations ensured that the service was orderly and reverent. Interpreters explain the change of clothing in various ways, but all agree that it distinguished the most sacred work from ordinary tasks.

For today: God cares about the small and humble details of service. We can serve him with reverence even in simple tasks, such as cleaning, tidying, or helping without being seen, doing them with care and gratitude.
exp.5:11:
This verse says that the fire on the altar was never to go out. Every morning the priest put fresh wood on it, arranged the burnt offering (the offering that was burned whole) on top, and burned the fat of the peace offerings, which were offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving. The fat of the animal is what is meant here.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes the instructions on to Aaron and his sons, the priests. In context, God explains how the altar is to be cared for, from removing the ashes to keeping the fire lit. Many understand this to express that access to God was to remain always open. The text does not explain all the details of its meaning.

For today: just as the priest tended the fire each morning, we can set aside time each day for prayer and the Word, before the day takes hold of us. Simple consistency keeps our relationship with God alive.
exp.5:12:
It says that the fire on the altar was to be kept burning all the time, never allowed to go out. Every morning the priest put fresh wood on it, arranged the burnt offering (the offering that was burned completely) and burned the fat (the fat) of the peace offerings.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to Aaron and his sons, the priests. These rules governed worship in the tabernacle. Many understand that the constant fire showed that access to God was always available. Some add that it also pointed to the need to care for what is holy with faithfulness.

For today: keep your life of prayer and your relationship with God steady. It does not depend only on emotions; it is maintained through simple, daily habits, like the wood laid each morning.
exp.5:13:
This verse begins the instructions about the offering, which is the grain or flour offering. The word "offering" here means a gift or an offering to God. It says that the priests, the descendants of Aaron, were to bring it before the Lord, in front of the altar.

God speaks to Moses so that he may teach Israel and the priests how to worship. This offering of flour, oil and incense expressed thankfulness and devotion to God. One part was burned, and the rest was eaten by the priests in a holy place. In this way God cared for those who served him.

For today: God does not want an offering made without thought. We can give him what is ordinary, such as our work, our time and our gratitude, with order and reverence, remembering that he gladly receives what we offer from the heart.
exp.5:14:
Here God explains how the grain offering was made. The priest would take a handful of fine flour mixed with oil, along with all the frankincense that was on it. Then he would burn it on the altar as a representative portion that stood for the whole offering before God. A pleasing aroma to the Lord is what the burning produced. This means the smoke would be a fragrance pleasing to the Lord.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Aaron and his sons, the priests. Israel needed clear rules to worship God in an orderly way. The priest burned one part for God, and the rest was food for the priests, as the following verses say.

For today: God is pleased when we give him our best, with a sincere and grateful heart. You can offer him your time, your work, or your prayer with that attitude today, without waiting for it to be perfect.
exp.5:15:
This verse says that what remained of the grain offering, after a handful had been burned on the altar, belonged to Aaron and his sons, the priests. They were to eat it without yeast, that is, without leavened bread, and in a place set apart for God: the court of the tabernacle.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses gives these instructions to Israel. The priests did not receive an inheritance of land as the other tribes did, so God gave them this portion for their support. The text calls it a most holy thing, and for that reason it was to be eaten with care and reverence.

For today: God cares for those who serve others in his name. We can support with generosity those who serve in the church, and also live with reverence, remembering that what is given to God is precious to him.
exp.5:16:
This verse says that the grain offering was not to be baked with yeast. God gave it to the priests as their share of the offerings burned on the altar. The grain offering is the offering of fine flour, and the sin offering and the guilt offering were other sacrifices, also called most holy. In this way it is taught that this portion is very sacred.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions about the offerings. After a handful is burned on the altar, what was left was eaten by Aaron and his sons in the court, a holy place. The text does not state here the reason for forbidding yeast. Some think it was a symbol of corruption, but the text does not explain it.

For today: what is dedicated to God deserves respect and sincerity. We can think about how we serve, give, and worship, and take care that it is done with a clean and grateful heart, without deceit.
exp.5:19:
Aaron and his sons were to bring an offering to God on the day they were anointed as priests: a tenth of an ephah (a measure of grain, roughly 20 to 22 liters by common estimates) of fine flour. It was offered every day, half in the morning and half in the evening. The offering was a gift to God, and the word for it means something that is continual and steady, never stopping.

God speaks to Moses, giving instructions for the priests. This offering marked the start of their service, and it taught them to depend on God and to dedicate their work to him each day. Scholars debate whether it was a daily offering of the high priest or only the offering for the day of his anointing; the text allows both readings.

For today: God values steadiness. We can begin and end the day by offering God our work, our strength, and our thankfulness in prayer, without waiting for a special occasion.
exp.5:22:
It says that every grain offering that a priest presented had to be burned completely on the altar. The priests could not eat any part of it, as they could with the offerings of the people (Leviticus 6:16-18).

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to Aaron and his sons. These are instructions for worship in the tabernacle. When the priest offered for himself, he could not benefit from what he offered. Many understand that this shows his giving to God had to be complete, holding nothing back.

For today: when we serve God, let us do it with a sincere heart, without seeking personal advantage or applause. Offering God our best, with humility, is a way of worshiping him.
exp.5:25:
This verse says that the priest who presents the sin offering must eat part of it. He had to eat it in a holy place, in the court of the tabernacle. Atonement means covering over or removing the guilt of sin.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Aaron and his sons, the priests. Israel was learning to live near a holy God. That is why the sin offering was treated as most holy, with care and order. Some think that eating the meat showed the priest taking part in bearing the guilt of the people, though the text does not fully explain this.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but He also offers forgiveness. We can approach Him with reverence and sincerity, without minimizing our failings, trusting in His mercy.
exp.5:27:
This verse says that the pot in which the meat of the sin offering was cooked had to be handled with great care. If it was made of clay, it was broken, because clay is porous and soaks up whatever is cooked in it. If it was made of metal, it was scoured and rinsed with water. Scoured means rubbed hard to clean it thoroughly.

God speaks to Moses, and he passes the instructions on to Aaron and his sons, the priests. In this part of the law about offerings, what was dedicated to God was most holy. For that reason, nothing that touched that meat could afterward be used as common. Many understand that this shows how serious God's holiness is and how grave sin is.

For today: let us treat with respect what belongs to God, such as his Word, his church, and our time of prayer. And let us ask him to cleanse our hearts thoroughly, not only on the outside.
exp.5:28:
This verse says that any male from the priestly family could eat the meat of the sin offering. It was called "most holy" because it was set apart for God and had to be treated with great respect.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Aaron and his sons. These rules explained how to handle the sin offering. The priests ate their portion in the holy place, and the utensils used had to be cleaned or broken with care. This taught that sin is serious and that what God sets apart for himself must be treated carefully.

For today: treat with reverence what belongs to God, such as his Word, prayer, and fellowship with other believers. And remember with gratitude that Christ, according to the New Testament, offered the complete sacrifice for our sins.
exp.5:29:
It says that when a sin offering was made and its blood was brought inside the tent of meeting, to make atonement in the holy place, that meat was not to be eaten. It had to be burned completely in the fire. "Atonement" is the sacrifice that covers sin, and "to make atonement" means to restore peace with God.

God speaks to Moses to instruct the priests. Shortly before, it was said that the priests ate the common sin offering. Here an exception is noted: when the blood was brought into the sanctuary, as in the more serious cases, the priests did not eat any of it. Scholars explain this difference in several ways, but the text emphasizes the holiness and the seriousness of sin.

Today we can remember that sin is serious, and that God, in great mercy, provided the way to forgive it. We can come near to Him with humility and gratitude, without taking His forgiveness lightly.
exp.6:1:
This verse says that the animal offered for guilt had to be slaughtered in the same place where the burnt offering, the offering burned completely, was slaughtered. "Slaughter" here means killing by cutting the throat. Sprinkling the blood all around the altar means splashing it around the altar.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes the instructions on to Israel. These instructions are addressed to the priests and the people, and they explain how the guilt offering was presented. It was used when someone had wronged God or their neighbor. That it was done in the same place shows that sin was taken very seriously, and that there was one orderly way to approach God.

For today: let us not take our faults lightly. We can come to God with sincerity, and Christians believe that Jesus, with his blood, made the complete sacrifice for our guilt (Hebrews 9:14). Let us live thankful and ready to make amends for the harm we have done.
exp.6:2:
This verse gives an instruction about the guilt offering. The person bringing the animal was to present its fat: the tail (this refers to the broad fat tail of certain sheep) and the fat that covers the entrails. That fat was considered the best part of the animal.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses is to pass the instructions on to Israel. The guilt offering was used when someone had wronged God or their neighbor and needed to make amends for the harm done. The verses that follow say that the priest burned that fat on the altar as an offering to the LORD.

For today: God deserves our best, not what we have left over. When we recognize a fault, we can come to Him with sincerity and devotion. Christians believe that Christ offered the perfect sacrifice for our sins, so we can come with confidence and also give Him the best of our lives.
exp.6:5:
This verse says that only the men of the priestly family could eat the meat of the guilt offering. They were to eat it in the holy place, that is, in the area of the sanctuary that God had set apart. The phrase "most holy" means that it was something dedicated to God in a special way, and it was not to be treated as ordinary food.

God spoke to Moses, and Moses passed these instructions on to Israel. After the parts that belonged to God were burned on the altar, the rest of the animal provided food for the priests. In this way God cared for those who served in the sanctuary, and at the same time he taught that guilt and forgiveness are serious matters.

For today: God deserves that we treat with reverence what he has set apart. We can approach him with gratitude and respect, remembering that forgiveness cost a great deal and that, for Christians, Christ offered it once for all.
exp.6:6:
This verse says that the guilt offering follows the same rule as the sin offering. The meat belonged to the priest who had made atonement, that is, the one who presented the offering to restore the relationship with God. "Atonement" means covering over or repairing a wrong.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about the sacrifices. Here it explains what part the priests received for their service. The meat was most holy, and only the male priests ate it in the holy place. In this way, those who served in the sanctuary were provided for.

For today: God cares for those who serve and takes forgiveness seriously. We can support with generosity those who teach and care for us spiritually. And when we fail, we should come to God with honesty, trusting in the forgiveness that Christ offers.
exp.6:7:
This verse says that when a priest offers another person's burnt offering, the skin of the animal sacrificed belongs to him. A burnt offering was an offering that was burned whole on the altar. The skin was not burned, so it remained part of the priest's portion.

God speaks to Moses and gives Israel instructions about the offerings. The verses nearby explain which parts of each offering were for the priests. In this way, those who served in the sanctuary and had no inheritance of land received their provision from what the people brought to God.

For today: God cares for those who serve others in his name. We can support, with gratitude and generosity, those who teach us and care for us spiritually, and those who serve can trust that God provides.
exp.6:8:
This verse says that the grain offerings (the "offering" was a gift of flour or bread) that were baked in an oven, cooked in a frying pan, or prepared in a pan belonged to the priest who presented them.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to Israel. In these instructions, the Lord explains how the offerings were to be shared out. The priests had no inheritance of land, so God provided for their support through what the people brought to Him.

For today: God cares for those who devote themselves to serving Him, and He invites us to be generous toward them. We can support our pastor, our church, or those who serve, with gratitude and joy, knowing that we give first to the Lord.
exp.6:9:
This verse says that every grain offering, whether mixed with oil or dry, belonged to all the priests, the descendants of Aaron, and was shared equally among them. The word "offering" in the verse is the sense of this passage, and mixing with oil is the sense of the wording that follows.

God speaks to Moses and gives instructions about the offerings. The priests had no inheritance of land as the other tribes did, so God provided for them with a portion of what the people brought. What is described here was for their support while they served in the sanctuary.

For today: God cares that those who serve receive what they need to live. We can support pastors, missionaries, and the servants of our church with generosity and respect. And those who serve can trust that God looks after them, and do so without envy or favoritism.
exp.6:12:
This verse says that, along with the unleavened cakes, the person offering thanks to God was also to present loaves made with leaven. In this translation, the offering is called the sacrifice of thanksgiving within the peace offerings.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel on how to worship him. The peace offering was a shared meal, a moment of joy and gratitude. Some scholars note that leavened bread was a common part of everyday meals, and that here it was not burned on the altar. Others explain this in different ways, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: giving thanks to God is a natural part of a life of faith. We can thank him simply, both for the extraordinary and for the ordinary, such as our daily bread, and share that gratitude with others.
exp.6:13:
This verse says that from each kind of bread the person brought, they were to set aside one portion as a wave offering for the Lord. That portion then belonged to the priest who sprinkled the blood of the sacrifice of peace. The peace offering was the offering of fellowship, and the offering that was lifted up was a portion raised and given to God.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. The person who offered thanks brought bread along with the sacrifice, and one part went to support the priest who served. It shows that giving thanks was something concrete and shared, not only a feeling.

For today: when God blesses you, don't keep your thanks only in your heart. Set aside something concrete, such as time, money, or help, to bless those who serve and to share your joy with others.
exp.6:14:
It says that the meat of the peace offering, offered as thanks to God, had to be eaten on the same day it was presented. Nothing could be kept for the next day. Peace offerings are fellowship offerings, and "thanksgiving" means giving thanks.

God speaks to Moses and gives instructions to Israel about the offerings. This sacrifice was a shared meal with God, with the priest, and with the family or guests. The verses that follow allow more time for vow offerings or freewill offerings. Why the thank offering had a shorter limit is not explained here; some think that it made thanksgiving something to celebrate soon and with others.

For today: do not put gratitude off until later. Thank God today, in a concrete way, and share your joy with someone else.
exp.6:15:
If someone brings a peace offering as a vow or as a freewill gift, the meat was to be eaten on the same day as the offering. Whatever was left over could be eaten the next day.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Israel about the offerings. The peace offering was shared in a meal of fellowship before God. The thank offering had a stricter rule: only on the same day. Scholars explain the time limit in several ways, such as showing respect for what is holy or preventing the meat from spoiling. The text does not give an explicit reason.

For today: when we give something to God, whether a promise or a gesture of love, it is good to do so with order and reverence. Fulfill what you promised promptly, and do not let it grow cold.
exp.6:17:
This verse says that the meat of the peace offering had to be eaten within the days allowed. If someone ate it on the third day, God would not accept that person's offering, and it would not be counted in his favor.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses to Israel, to teach how to offer these sacrifices. The shared meal before God was to be done with order and respect. The text does not explain in detail the reason for the third day; some think it prevented carelessness with the meat, others that it protected the holiness of what was offered.

For today: come near to God with sincerity and reverence, not with empty habit. Give Him your best attention and your time, not the leftovers.
exp.6:22:
God tells Moses to instruct the Israelites not to eat the fat, that is, the hard fat of oxen, sheep, and goats. These are the animals that could be offered in sacrifice.

It is the LORD who speaks to Moses, within the instructions about the offerings. The fat of these animals was burned on the altar as a portion for God (Leviticus 3:16-17). That is why it was not for human consumption. Disobedience carried a serious penalty: to be cut off from the people, a phrase that some interpret as exclusion and others as a judgment of God.

For today: the best and the first belongs to God. We can ask ourselves what things we have kept for ourselves that we should give to him with gratitude and reverence, such as our time, our money, or our attention.
exp.6:25:
This verse forbids eating blood. The word "dwellings" in the verse means the places where the people lived, that is, wherever they lived. The command applied to the blood of birds and of animals, with no exception for where it was eaten.

God speaks to Moses so that he may tell Israel, within the laws about offerings. Blood was set aside for the altar. Later, in Leviticus 17:11, it is explained that the life is in the blood and that God gave it to make atonement, so the blood served as a reminder that forgiveness costs a life. Christians understand that this points to Christ, although the ceremonial law was given to Israel.

For today: value what God calls holy. When you take the Lord's Supper or remember the cross, do so with gratitude and reverence, and do not treat forgiveness as something ordinary.
exp.6:30:
This verse says that the priest was to burn the fat of the animal, that is, the suet, on the altar. The breast of the animal, however, was not burned. It was given to Aaron and his sons, the priests, as their portion to eat.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct the Israelites on how to present this sacrifice. It was a voluntary offering, made with thankfulness and fellowship with God. The fat was burned for God, and the breast, which was waved before Him, then passed to the priests, who served in the sanctuary. Many understand that this showed that God took care of those who served Him.

For today: let us give God our best with thankfulness, and generously support those who serve others in the church. Sharing what God gives us is also a way of worshiping Him.
exp.6:36:
This verse sums up all the laws about the offerings found in the earlier chapters. It names the burnt offering (an offering completely burned), the grain offering, the sin offering, the trespass offering, the consecrations (the offering made when the priests were set apart), and the peace offering (the fellowship offering). The word "peace" refers to peace or fellowship with God.

God speaks through Moses, and Leviticus 7 closes this section of instructions. The people and the priests needed to know how to approach God in the way He had prescribed. The following verse says that these laws were given at Mount Sinai.

For today: God shows us that drawing near to Him is a serious matter, but it is also possible. Christians believe that Christ fulfilled what these offerings pointed to. Today we can pray with confidence, confess our sins, and give thanks, knowing that God receives us.
exp.7:1:
God tells Moses to gather what is needed to consecrate the priests: Aaron and his sons, the special garments, the anointing oil, a young bull for the sin offering (atonement), two rams, and a basket with bread made without yeast (unleavened bread). The word "basket" here refers to a small basket.

The LORD speaks, and Moses listens so that he may obey. Israel was at the foot of Sinai and already had the tabernacle. Now God establishes how the priestly service would begin. Before serving, Aaron and his sons needed to be set apart and purified, and the people would witness it.

For today: drawing near to God does not depend on our own merits, but on the way He Himself provides. Christians see in Christ the complete atonement. We can serve Him with humility, with gratitude, and obey Him with care, as Moses did.
exp.7:6:
Moses dressed Aaron, the high priest, in the sacred garments, one by one: the coat, the sash, the robe, and the ephod. The ephod was a special garment, something like a long, embroidered apron. It had its own belt, which fastened it closely to the body. Moses fastened the belt around him, that is, tied the garment at his waist.

Moses acts in front of the whole congregation and follows what God commanded him. Aaron and his sons had just been washed with water. This was the ceremony in which Aaron began his service as priest. None of this was Moses' own idea; everything was done just as the LORD had commanded.

For today: God cares about the details when it comes to drawing near to Him. We do not wear those garments today, but we can approach God with reverence, humility and obedience, never taking Him lightly, trusting that Christ is our High Priest.
exp.7:7:
Moses put on Aaron the breastplate, which is the chest piece, a square piece with twelve stones that the high priest wore over his chest. Inside it he placed the Urim and Thummim. It is not known for certain what they were; the Bible does not describe them, but they were used to inquire of God's will.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting how Moses consecrated Aaron and his sons as priests. Each garment was put on just as the LORD had commanded. Everything happens at the beginning of the service in the tabernacle, and it is emphasized that nothing was done by human whim.

For today: God cares about how we draw near to Him. We can serve Him with humility and obedience, remembering that Jesus, our High Priest, represents us before the Father.
exp.7:8:
He put the turban, that is the mitre, on Aaron's head. On the front he placed a plate of gold, which the text calls the holy crown. According to Exodus 28:36, it had an inscription on it. The passage repeats that everything was done as the Lord had commanded.

This is the account of Aaron's consecration as high priest. Moses acts according to the instructions God gave him on the mountain. Aaron does not take the office on his own; it is God who sets him apart and clothes him. With the mitre the priestly garments are complete, and right after this comes the anointing with oil.

For today: God values holiness and obedience to what He says. We can ask Him that our minds and our lives belong to Him, and remember that Jesus, our great high priest, brings us near to God.
exp.7:9:
Moses takes the anointing oil and pours it on the tabernacle and on everything that was in it. Anointing means applying oil to set something apart for God, and to sanctify means to make something holy, that is, to set it apart for sacred use.

The book narrates the ceremony in which Aaron and his sons are consecrated as priests. Moses acts following what God commanded him. Earlier he dressed Aaron in the priestly garments, and after anointing the tabernacle, he anoints Aaron himself. First the place and its objects are set apart, and then the people who would serve there.

For today: what is dedicated to God is not used in just any way. We can intentionally set apart our time, our home, and our work, offering them to God and asking him to use them for his purpose, not only for ours.
exp.7:12:
This verse tells that Moses presented Aaron's sons, that is, the priests who would serve alongside their father. He put the tunics on them, tied the sashes around their waists, and placed upon them the caps, which are simple hats or head coverings. Everything was done just as God had commanded.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, and Moses acts as the one who directs the ceremony. God was setting apart Aaron and his sons for holy service. Earlier, the altar and Aaron had already been anointed. Now the sons receive their priestly clothing, and afterward the sin offering will follow.

For today: God cares about the details of how we serve him. We can serve him with humble obedience, without inventing our own path. Doing what he asks, even when it seems small, is a way of honoring him.
exp.7:13:
Moses presents the bull that would serve as the sin offering. The word for this offering can also be understood as covering or cleansing guilt. Aaron and his sons lay their hands on the head of the animal, a gesture that many understand as identifying themselves with it and symbolically transferring their guilt to it.

The book narrates this as part of the ordination of the priests. Moses acts following what God had commanded him. Before serving the people, Aaron and his sons had to be cleansed of their own sin. They too needed forgiveness.

For today: no one draws near to God on the basis of their own merits, not even those who serve in the church. Christians see in this sacrifice a shadow of Christ, who takes away sin once and for all. Today you can come before God with humility, acknowledging your need and trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.7:14:
Moses slaughters the calf that is offered for sin. With his finger he puts blood on the horns of the altar, all around, and in this way he cleansed the altar, that is, he made it clean. He pours the rest of the blood out at the bottom of the altar. With this he set it apart for God, that is, he made it holy, so that atonement could be made and the relationship with Him restored.

This takes place at the ordination of Aaron and his sons as priests. The text narrates it, though God does not speak directly here, and it repeats that everything is done as the LORD commanded. Before serving the people, even the altar and the priests needed to be made clean. The blood shows that sin is serious and has a cost.

For today: do not take lightly your need for forgiveness. Christians see in Christ the blood that reconciles us to God, so approach Him with humility and gratitude, and serve others with a clean heart.
exp.7:19:
This verse describes how Moses prepares the ram of the burnt offering. He cuts it into pieces and burns on the altar the head, the pieces, and the fat, that is, the animal's fat. It was customary to set the fat aside as the choicest part for God.

This is not a speech by a character; it is the account of the ceremony in which Aaron and his sons are consecrated as priests. Moses acts as the LORD had commanded. By placing their hands on the head of the ram, the priests identified themselves with the offering. Many understand that the burnt offering, burned entirely, expressed total surrender to God.

For today: God values a complete surrender, not a half-hearted one. Today you can ask yourself what part of your life you have kept back from him and, simply, offer it to him in prayer.
exp.7:23:
Moses calls Aaron's sons forward and puts some of the blood of the ram on the tip of the right ear of each of them, on the thumb of their right hand, and on the great toe of their right foot. Then he sprinkles the blood on the altar all around.

God had commanded that Aaron and his sons be set apart as priests, and Moses leads the ceremony. The blood marked them as set apart for the service of God. The ear, the hand, and the foot are usually understood as a sign that their whole being, for hearing, doing, and walking, was dedicated to God, although the text does not give a detailed explanation.

For today: we can ask God that what we hear, what we do, and the paths we take belong to him. Each day, ask yourself: what will I listen to, do, and walk toward today to honor him?
exp.7:24:
This verse describes which parts of the animal Moses took to present to God. They were the fat, the thick tail, the fat of the entrails, the caul above the liver (the membrane or lobe that covers the liver), the two kidneys with their fat, and the right shoulder (the foreleg on the right side). These were the best parts of the ram of consecration.

Here the narrator speaks, and Moses acts following God's instructions. He is consecrating Aaron and his sons as priests. After the blood on the ear, thumb, and toe, the best of the animal is offered. Many understand that the fat represented what was most valuable, but the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: God deserves the best, not the leftovers. We can give Him our time, our strength, and our heart with sincerity, and not only what we have left over.
exp.7:25:
This verse tells that Moses took three things from the basket of unleavened bread: one unleavened cake, a cake of oiled bread, and one wafer, which was a kind of thin, flat pastry or cracker. He placed them on the fat of the animal and on the right shoulder, which is the animal's front leg, the shoulder of the animal.

This takes place during the ordination of Aaron and his sons as priests. Moses leads the ceremony following what God had commanded him. The unleavened bread and the oil accompanied the offering, and then everything was presented to God and burned on the altar.

For today: serving God implies complete devotion. Just as the priests offered their best and presented it with order and reverence, we can give God the best of our time and our heart, leaving nothing half-done.
exp.7:26:
He put all of it into the hands of Aaron and his sons, and had them wave the pieces before the Lord as a wave offering. Moses did this with the parts of the ram and the unleavened bread he had set apart.

This is part of the ceremony by which Aaron and his sons were set apart as priests. Moses carries out the rite as God had commanded him. By placing everything in their hands, they take part: they receive the service God entrusts to them. Scholars explain the waving gesture in various ways, but it is generally understood as presenting the offering to God.

Serving God begins with open hands. Before we do anything for Him, we receive what He gives us. Today we can begin the day by offering God our work, our time, and our strength, asking Him to use them for good.
exp.7:28:
Moses took the breast and waved it back and forth before the Lord as a wave offering. He says that this ram was the ram of the ordination, that is, the animal used to set the priests apart for God. The breast was Moses' portion. Everything was done just as God had commanded.

The writer describes the ceremony in which Aaron and his sons were set apart as priests. Moses acted as the mediator, following the instructions God had given him. Waving the offering was a gesture that presented the portion to God, and then God gave it for Moses' use. Scholars explain the gesture in different ways, but all of them see in it surrender and obedience.

For today: God values obedience in what seems small. We can do what He asks of us faithfully, without taking away from it or adding to it.
exp.7:29:
Moses took some of the anointing oil and some of the blood that was on the altar, and sprinkled them on Aaron, his sons, and their garments. Setting them apart for God, for his service, is what the sanctifying meant, and the garments were the holy clothing the priests wore.

Here the narrator tells what Moses did, following God's commands. Israel was beginning its life of worship in the tabernacle, and Aaron and his sons were being consecrated as priests in a ceremony lasting several days. The blood speaks of sin being forgiven through a sacrifice, and the oil is usually understood as a sign that God sets apart and equips people to serve him, though the text does not explain this in detail here.

For today: God does not call us because we are perfect, but sets us apart through his forgiveness. Today you can give him your day and your work, and serve him with gratitude for having been cleansed.
exp.7:31:
It says that what remained of the flesh and of the bread from the consecration was not to be kept or eaten afterward, but burned with fire.

Moses speaks to Aaron and his sons during the ceremony in which they are set apart as priests. They had already eaten the flesh and the bread near the entrance of the tent of meeting. What had been used for something holy was not to be treated as ordinary food. Burning it was a way of caring for what was sacred and closing the act with reverence. The texts do not explain every detail, so it is better not to invent reasons.

For today: God deserves that we treat with respect what is dedicated to Him. We can serve with seriousness and gratitude, without making ordinary what God calls holy.
exp.7:32:
Moses tells Aaron and his sons that they must not leave the entrance of the tabernacle for seven days. That time completes their consecration, that is, the process by which they are set apart to serve God as priests.

Moses speaks in line with what God commanded him. He had already washed, clothed, and anointed the priests, and sacrifices had been offered. Now they had to remain there, obeying carefully. The text says this was necessary so that they would not die, which shows the seriousness of approaching a holy God.

For today: serving God is not only about doing tasks, but also about giving time to be in his presence. Set aside quiet moments to pray, listen, and obey, before rushing to your responsibilities.
exp.7:33:
