It says that everything Moses did that day in the ceremony of consecration was not his own idea, but a command from God. The word "atonement" means covering or cleansing sin so that a person can draw near to God. What was done was done so that Aaron and his sons would be cleansed and set apart.

Moses speaks to Aaron and his sons at the end of the first day of the ceremony that prepared them to serve as priests. He tells them they must stay seven days by the entrance of the tent of meeting and obey everything, because serving before a holy God was a serious matter. Many Christians see here a shadow of the work of Christ, although the text itself does not say so.

For today: come near to God as He Himself has directed, not in your own way. Today we trust in the work of Jesus and respond with humble and steady obedience.
exp.8:1:
Moses tells Aaron to take a young calf from the herd for the sin offering, which was for sin, and a ram for the burnt offering, which was burned whole on the altar. Both animals had to be without blemish, meaning with no physical flaw. He was to present them before the Lord, that is, in the presence of the Lord.

This takes place on the eighth day, when the consecration of Aaron and his sons as priests comes to an end. Moses passes on God's instructions. Before serving the people, Aaron himself had to offer a sacrifice for his own sin, because he too needed forgiveness.

For today: before serving others or leading them, it is good to come near to God with humility, acknowledging our failings. Christians believe that Christ is the perfect offering who allows us to draw near with confidence.
exp.8:2:
Moses was to speak to the people and ask them to bring offerings: a male goat for the sin offering (to deal with sin), and a calf and a lamb of one year old, without blemish, for the burnt offering (an offering that was burned whole as a complete surrender to God). "Without blemish" means without any flaw. The command to speak is an order: you shall say.

Moses speaks here by command of God. It was the eighth day, when Aaron and his sons were beginning their service as priests. Before God revealed himself, all the people had to take part: first acknowledging sin and then giving themselves to God. The sacrifices pointed to the need for forgiveness and for drawing near to him with reverence.

Today we can learn that drawing near to God begins with humility and sincerity. Christians believe that Christ is the perfect offering for our sin, so we live grateful, giving him the best of ourselves.
exp.8:3:
Leviticus 9:4 tells the people to bring a bullock and a ram as peace offerings, to be offered before the Lord, along with a grain offering mixed with oil. This verse says that, in addition to the sin offering and the burnt offering, the people were to bring a bullock and a ram as a peace offering (an offering of fellowship, of thankfulness, and of friendship with God). There was also a grain offering mixed with oil. The word "offer" here means to present something as a sacrifice, and the phrase "the Lord will appear" means that God would make his presence visibly known.

Moses speaks to Aaron and the elders of Israel on the eighth day, when Aaron and his sons begin to serve as priests. First the sin was dealt with, then total dedication to God, and then fellowship. Everything prepared the people to see the glory of the Lord.

For today: before seeking the presence of God, it is good to prepare ourselves with humility, acknowledging our failings, surrendering our lives to him, and giving him thanks. He desires to be near us.
exp.8:8:
Aaron's sons, who were priests, brought him the blood of the sacrificed calf. Aaron dipped his finger in that blood and put it on the horns of the altar (the raised corners shaped like horns), and he poured out the rest at the bottom of the altar.

We are on the eighth day of the priests' consecration. Moses tells Aaron to make atonement first for himself and then for the people, just as God commanded. The blood represented a life given to cover sin. Scholars understand the detail of the horns in different ways, but they all agree that it pointed to the seriousness of sin and the need for forgiveness.

For today: Aaron first recognized his own need before God. We can do the same, approaching with humility, confessing our faults, and trusting in the forgiveness that Christ offers.
exp.8:9:
This verse says that Aaron burned on the altar the fat, the kidneys, and the fatty part of the liver of the animal he offered for sin. The fat and the kidneys are named as the portions burned, and the verse adds that everything was done just as the Lord had commanded Moses.

The book describes how the service in the tabernacle began. Aaron, the first priest, offers a sacrifice for his own sin first, before offering for the people. The narrator stresses that he obeyed what God had ordered, without adding to or changing anything.

For today: God values sincere and humble obedience. Before serving others, it is wise to acknowledge our own faults. Christians believe that Jesus, our high priest, offered the final and sufficient sacrifice for us.
exp.8:11:
Aaron killed the animal for the burnt offering, which was an offering burned whole on the altar. His sons, who were helping as priests, brought him the blood, and he sprinkled it around the altar.

It is the day when Aaron and his sons officially begin their service as priests, after seven days of consecration. The text follows the instructions that God gave through Moses. First Aaron offered the sin offering, and now he offers the burnt offering. The narrator is the author of the book, traditionally identified with Moses.

For today: this passage shows that drawing near to God requires seriousness, obedience, and recognizing that sin is serious. Christians believe that Jesus fulfilled this system through his own sacrifice. We can thank him and live by giving God our whole life, not just a part.
exp.8:12:
Here it is told that the sons of Aaron handed Aaron the burnt offering, already cut into pieces, along with the head. Aaron burned it all on the altar. A "burnt offering" was an offering that was burned whole.

This takes place on the eighth day, when Aaron begins his service as priest. The text is Moses' account of how the sacrifices were offered. First the sin offering was made, and then the burnt offering, which expressed total surrender to God. Christians often see here a shadow of Christ, although the passage itself does not say so.

For today: God does not want a half-hearted surrender. Today we can offer him our whole day, with work, family and decisions, and not just a moment on Sunday.
exp.8:16:
He presented the grain offering, which the text calls the meat offering. He took a handful of it and burnt it on the altar. He did this in addition to the burnt sacrifice of the morning, which was the daily offering that was burned whole.

It is the eighth day of the consecration of the priests. Moses has given the instructions, and Aaron begins to serve as priest for the first time, offering sacrifices for himself and for the people. The account stresses that everything was done just as the LORD had commanded.

For today: God values sincere and orderly obedience. We can serve him with humility, doing things with care and gratitude, knowing that he deserves the best of us.
exp.8:18:
This verse describes the fatty parts of the bull and the ram that were set apart in the peace offering. "Fat" is the animal's fat. The fat covering the liver is the thin fatty layer over the liver. The text also mentions the broad fat tail of the ram, and the fat covering the inner organs and the kidneys.

Aaron offers sacrifices for the people for the first time, after being consecrated, as Moses had instructed him. According to Leviticus, the fat was burned on the altar as the best part, and the breasts were waved before God. The text does not explain all the reasons, but the fat was understood as the best part, given to God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we give God the best of our time, attention and affection, and not merely what is left over. A simple way is to begin the day with a few minutes of prayer before other hurries.
exp.8:19:
Leviticus 9:20 describes a moment of worship on the day Aaron and his sons begin their work as priests. The fat from the animal is placed on the breasts of the offering, and then Aaron burns that fat on the altar. The breast of the animal is the part that is placed here, and it is then lifted up before the LORD, as the next verse describes.

This is the day the priests take up their service, and the account presents these actions as something the LORD had already commanded through Moses. The fat was regarded as the best part of the animal, and burning it on the altar was a way of giving it to God. The gestures with the breast are explained in different ways by readers, but the central idea stays the same: God receives what is best.

For today, we can ask ourselves whether we give God the best of our time, attention, and affection, or only what is left over. Offering Him our first and finest, with gratitude and simplicity, is one way of worshiping Him.
exp.8:21:
Aaron lifts up his hands toward the people and blesses them. Then he comes down from the altar, where he had finished offering three sacrifices: the sin offering (for sin), the burnt offering (an offering completely burned) and the peace offering (an offering of fellowship and thanksgiving).

It is the eighth day of the consecration of the priests. The text tells what happens: Aaron, as high priest, completes the offerings for himself and for the people for the first time, just as the LORD commanded Moses. After this comes the glory of God and the fire on the altar.

For today: the blessing comes after forgiveness and dedication. Before asking for blessing, it is good to draw near to God with humility, acknowledge our faults and offer him thanks. For Christians, Christ is the one who makes that way to God complete.
exp.8:22:
Moses and Aaron entered the tent of meeting, which was the tent where God met with his people. Then they came out and blessed the people, and the glory of the Lord, that is, his bright and powerful presence, was seen by everyone.

It is the eighth day of the ordination of the priests. Aaron had already offered the sacrifices that God commanded. The narrator reports that everything was done as God had ordered, and then God responded by showing himself. Right after this, fire comes from the Lord and consumes the offering. The text does not explain in detail what they did inside the tabernacle; it only mentions it.

For today: God draws near when we seek him with obedience and humility. Before asking for things, we can approach him with reverence, and then go out to bless others with good words.
exp.8:23:
It says that God himself sent a fire that appeared before him and completely consumed the offering that was on the altar, including the fat. The whole burnt offering was one that was burned entirely. When the people saw this, they shouted in joy and worship, and they fell facedown on the ground in reverence.

This is part of the account in Leviticus 9. Moses tells how Aaron and his sons began their service as priests, eight days after their consecration. They had offered the sacrifices just as God had commanded. The fire showed that God accepted that worship and was present with his people. Some scholars also see it as a sign that he approved the new priesthood.

For today: when we recognize what God has done for us, the natural response is gratitude and respect. We can set aside a moment this week to thank him with humility, without rushing.
exp.9:1:
This verse tells that fire came out from the presence of God and killed Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron.

The episode takes place when the priesthood was just beginning. Nadab and Abihu, who were priests, offered incense in their own way, without God's command. Afterward, Moses reminds Aaron of what God had said: that those who draw near to him must treat him as holy. Aaron stayed silent, in sign of his grief. The Bible does not detail exactly what the mistake consisted of; some think of the fire that was used, others of the timing or of the attitude.

For today: draw near to God with reverence and obedience, seeking to please him according to his Word and not only according to what seems right to you.
exp.9:2:
Moses reminds Aaron of what God had said: that God would be treated as holy by those who draw near to him (the phrase used in the source means those close to him, the ones who serve in his presence), and that he would be honored before all the people. When Aaron's two sons died, Aaron said nothing: he did not protest or defend himself.

Moses is the one speaking, and he quotes God's words. Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's sons and priests, had just offered strange fire, something God had not commanded, and they died. The text does not explain all the details of their wrongdoing, and some think their condition or attitude may also have played a part. Aaron's silence is understood as grief, respect, or acceptance, but the Bible does not clarify it further.

For today: draw near to God with reverence and obedience, not on your own terms. And when you face something painful that you do not understand, sometimes the wisest thing is to be silent before him and trust.
exp.9:3:
Moses calls Mishael and Elzaphan, cousins of Aaron, sons of his uncle Uzziel. He asks them to come near and carry the bodies of Nadab and Abihu from in front of the sanctuary, taking them outside the camp. Carrying them out is what "carry" means here; the camp is the camp of Israel; the sanctuary is the holy place of the tabernacle.

Moses speaks just after God burned Aaron's two sons for offering strange fire (Lev. 10:1). Aaron kept silent in the face of his grief. Because Aaron and his sons were consecrated, they could not make themselves unclean by touching the bodies, so Moses asked other Levite relatives for help.

For today: God deserves reverence, and at the same time he cares for those who suffer. When someone is going through grief, we can help in practical and quiet ways, doing what that person cannot do.
exp.9:4:
It says that Mishael and Elzaphan drew near and carried the bodies of Nadab and Abihu out of the camp. They carried them still wearing their priestly tunics, just as Moses had commanded. The phrase "carried them" simply means that they took them away, and "camp" refers to the camp of Israel.

Moses is the one who gives the command, and the narrator reports that it was carried out. Nadab and Abihu, sons of Aaron, had died for offering to God a fire that he had not commanded them to offer. It was a time of great grief and also of great seriousness, because God wanted his holiness to be taken seriously. Aaron's cousins took charge of the bodies so that the priests would not become defiled.

For today: God deserves to be treated with reverence, and obeying him is not optional. At the same time, we see the value of quietly helping someone who is suffering a loss, as these relatives did.
exp.9:6:
It says that Aaron and his sons Eleazar and Ithamar were not to leave the entrance of the tent of meeting (the tabernacle), or they would die. The reason is that the anointing oil, with which they had been set apart to serve God, was upon them. And they obeyed what Moses said.

Moses speaks just after God had struck down Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's sons, for offering a fire that God had not commanded. Although it was a moment of grief, the priests on duty were not to leave their place or observe the usual mourning rites. God was asking them to show that their sacred duty came first.

For today: when we go through pain, we can weep honestly and still trust God and keep obeying Him, knowing that He sustains those who serve Him.
exp.9:8:
It says that Aaron and his sons, who were the priests, were not to drink wine or cider (a fermented drink, usually made from fruit) when they went into the tabernacle of the congregation, which was the tent where God met with his people. If they did, they would die. This command was to be kept always, from generation to generation.

God himself speaks to Aaron. This comes right after Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's sons, died for offering strange fire before the LORD. The Bible does not say for certain that they were drunk, although many think this command is connected to that. The purpose was so that they could tell the holy from the common and teach the people.

For today: when we serve God or worship him, let us do it with a clear mind and an attentive heart, and avoid anything that distracts us or takes away good judgment.
exp.9:9:
This verse says that the priests had to be able to tell clearly between what is holy (set apart for God) and what is common (ordinary, everyday), and between what is unclean (what kept a person from drawing near to God under the law) and what is clean. It is the reason for the command just before it: to think clearly.

God speaks to Aaron shortly after his sons Nadab and Abihu died for offering strange fire before the Lord. God commands that the priests drink no wine or strong drink (fermented drink) when they serve in the tabernacle. The text does not say that they had drunk; some think so, but that is an interpretation. What is clear is that serving God required a clear mind, so that they could then teach the people.

For today: ask God for wisdom, and guard against whatever clouds your judgment, so that you can tell what pleases Him and live clearly before Him.
exp.9:11:
Moses speaks to Aaron and to his two sons who were still living, Eleazar and Ithamar. He tells them to take what remains of the grain offering brought to the Lord and to eat it without leaven, beside the altar. The word "offering" here refers to the gift brought to God, and the phrase "most holy" refers to something set apart for God in a special way.

This happens right after Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's sons, died for offering unauthorized fire. Moses insists that the service continue in obedience, even in the middle of grief. The priests' portion was to be eaten in a holy place, as God had commanded.

For today: even when we are sad or confused, we can keep drawing near to God with reverence and obedience, without taking lightly what He calls holy. He sustains those who serve Him with humility.
exp.9:12:
Moses tells Aaron and his remaining sons that they must eat the portion of the offering that belongs to them in a holy place.

This happens right after Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's sons, died for offering fire that God had not commanded them. Aaron and his surviving sons were in mourning and discouraged. Moses calmly reminds them how to obey God in holy service, and that God also provides for them.

For today: God cares for those who serve Him and also expects us to honor Him as He asks. We can draw near to Him with reverence, obeying His Word, and trust that He provides.
exp.9:13:
This verse says that Aaron and his family were to eat the breast of the wave offering and the raised thigh in a clean place. Those portions were their share of the peace offerings that the people brought.

Moses speaks right after the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's sons who offered strange fire. The surviving priests were in mourning, and Moses clearly reminds them how they were to eat what God gave them, without neglecting what is holy. Even the whole family, sons and daughters, could take part.

For today: God cares for those who serve him, and he also invites us to receive his blessings with reverence. We can do this by giving thanks before we eat and by living each day with a heart attentive to him.
exp.9:14:
This verse says that, together with the fat that was burned on the altar, the priests were to bring the heave shoulder (the animal's front leg) and the breast. These parts were lifted up and waved, that is, moved back and forth, as an offering presented to God. Afterward, those portions became the lasting share of Aaron and his sons.

Moses speaks with Aaron and his sons after the deaths of Nadab and Abihu. He reminds them how to eat their portion of the offerings. He wants them to follow God's instructions carefully, even in the middle of grief and fear.

For today: obeying God in the simple and everyday things is a way of showing respect. We can ask him for help to take it seriously even when we are tired or sad.
exp.9:18:
Aaron answers Moses that on that same day his sons had presented their sin offering and their burnt offering before God, but that terrible things had happened to him. Then he asks whether it would have been pleasing to God for him to eat of the sin offering on such a day.

Aaron speaks after his sons Nadab and Abihu died for offering strange fire before God. Moses had rebuked him because the flesh of the sin offering was not eaten in the holy place, as it was commanded. Aaron explains his decision out of grief. The text does not give every detail of what he thought, and some understand that he acted out of reverence and mourning.

Today we can learn that God looks at the heart and not only at outward obedience. We also see humility: Aaron explains honestly, and Moses listens and is satisfied.
exp.9:19:
This verse says that Moses heard Aaron's explanation and was content.

Moses had rebuked Eleazar and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron, because they did not eat the flesh of the sin offering, as they had been commanded. This happened on the same day that Nadab and Abihu, their brothers, died for offering strange fire. Aaron answered that, with such grief and reverence, eating that offering did not seem right to him before God. The text does not explain every detail, but Moses accepted his reason.

Today, before judging someone, it is wise to listen calmly. When a person explains their reasons with sincerity and respect for God, we can respond with humility and grace.
exp.10:2:
God says that the Israelites could eat land animals that had two marks: a divided hoof, meaning split in two, and chewing the cud, that is, bringing back up food already swallowed to chew it again. If an animal had only one of the two marks, it could not be eaten. The phrase "you may eat" is a permission, and "split" here means divided.

Here the LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron so that they may pass these instructions on to the people. It was part of the law given to Israel to live as a people set apart for God. The exact reason for these rules is debated: some see a lesson about holiness and Israel's distinctiveness; others see health or cultural reasons. The text emphasizes obedience and separation.

For today: God cares about the details of everyday life, even what we eat. We can ask ourselves how to honor him in ordinary things, with gratitude and simple obedience.
exp.10:3:
It says that, although some animals chew the cud (chew their food again), they could not be eaten unless they also had a divided hoof. The camel chews the cud but does not have a divided hoof, so they were to regard it as unclean. This word does not necessarily mean dirty, but rather not fit to be eaten or for use by God's people. Nevertheless here means but.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron so that they may teach Israel. These rules were part of the law given to Israel as a people set apart for God. It teaches that they were to distinguish between the clean and the unclean. Scholars explain the exact reason for each animal in various ways, and the Bible does not detail it.

For today: although Christians do not live under these food rules, we can learn to obey God attentively, even in everyday matters, and to live differently for Him.
exp.10:7:
God tells his people not to eat the flesh of certain animals, such as the pig and the hare, and not to touch their carcasses. The word "unclean" in this verse means that the people would regard these animals as impure, not fit for the use of the people. "Unclean" does not necessarily mean dirty, but set apart from what was permitted for Israel.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, and through them to Israel, after bringing the people out of Egypt. These laws taught the people to distinguish between what is clean and what is unclean, and to live as a people set apart for God. Scholars explain the reasons in various ways: health, identity, symbolism. The text itself stresses holiness (Leviticus 11:44-45).

Today Christians are not under these dietary rules, since Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). But we can learn to ask ourselves what habits or influences draw us closer to God, and which ones pull us away from living for Him with attention and reverence.
exp.10:16:
This verse follows a list of birds that God declared unclean for eating. It mentions the owl, the cormorant (a bird that dives into the water), and the ibis. The exact identification of these birds is uncertain, and ancient and modern translators do not always agree on the names.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron so that they may teach the people of Israel. These laws about clean and unclean animals helped Israel live as a people set apart for God, reminding them that He is holy. Scholars offer several explanations for the reasons behind each animal, but the text emphasizes holiness and obedience.

Today we do not follow these dietary rules, because they were fulfilled in Christ (Acts 10:15; Mark 7:19). Even so, we can learn that God cares about our whole life, even the everyday things. Ask yourself: is there some small habit I can surrender to him today to honor him?
exp.10:18:
This verse continues a list of birds that God forbade the people of Israel to eat. It names the heron (probably the stork or some similar bird), the lapwing (another bird of uncertain identity, perhaps a plover), the hoopoe and the bat. Scholars are not sure exactly which animal each Hebrew word names, and for that reason the translations vary. The bat appears in the list because it flies, although today we classify it as a mammal.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives them instructions for all Israel. These laws about clean and unclean animals helped the people live as a people set apart for God. Scholars discuss the exact reasons: some think of health, others of symbolism or of separation from other nations.

For today: God is interested in the details of everyday life, even in what we eat. We can ask ourselves whether we also hand over our small decisions to him, and live with gratitude and obedience in ordinary things.
exp.10:24:
It says that if someone carries or lifts the dead body of certain unclean animals, they must wash their clothes and will be unclean until evening. The word "unclean" does not mean sinful; it means ceremonially not fit to draw near to worship.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel, newly formed as a nation. He gives them rules about clean and unclean animals and about contact with death. These rules taught them that God is holy and that they were to live differently. Scholars also mention possible reasons of hygiene or symbolism, but the text stresses above all holiness.

For today: it reminds us that God invites us to live with care and reverence. We can pause to ask him to cleanse our hearts after a burdened day, and trust that Christ purifies us.
exp.10:26:
This verse says that any animal with four legs that walks on "paws" (that is, on the soles of its feet, like cats, bears, or dogs) is considered unclean, meaning ceremonially impure. Anyone who touches its dead body becomes unclean until the evening, that is, until that day is over.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel. These laws about clean and unclean animals were part of the covenant with the people and helped them live as a people set apart for God (Leviticus 11:44-45). Scholars explain the reason for each rule in various ways, and the Bible does not spell out every reason.

For today: God cares about every detail of daily life. We can ask ourselves which habits draw us closer to Him and which ones make us unclean inside, and bring them to Him sincerely, trusting that Christ cleanses us.
exp.10:31:
It says that if the dead body of one of these small animals falls onto an object, that object becomes unclean. This includes wooden utensils, clothing, leather, or sacks, that is, anything used for work. It must be put into water. It remains unclean until evening, and after that it is clean.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel. These laws taught that God is holy and that his people were to live set apart, with order and reverence. Scholars discuss the exact reasons for each rule: hygiene, symbolism, or separation from other nations. The text emphasizes holiness.

For today: God cares about the details of our daily life. We can ask ourselves what influences touch our daily tasks and our home, and ask him to cleanse and renew us, trusting that Christ purifies us.
exp.10:33:
It says that if any food or drink comes into contact with a clay vessel into which one of the small creatures mentioned (small animals that move along the ground) has fallen, that food or drink becomes unclean, meaning not fit for the people to use. "Food" refers to what is eaten, and "unclean" means ceremonially impure, not necessarily dirty.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to teach Israel how to live as a people set apart for Him. These rules about what is clean and what is unclean reminded them that God is holy and that death does not belong in His presence. Scholars explain the exact reason for each rule in different ways; some see hygiene, others see symbolic teaching.

For today: let us be careful about what we allow into our lives and into our homes. Let us ask God for sensitivity to set aside whatever defiles the heart, trusting that Christ cleanses us.
exp.10:36:
It says that if the dead body of one of those unclean animals (the ones that crawl or small animals, mentioned earlier) falls on seed that is to be sown, the seed remains clean. The word for "seed" here simply means seed, and "clean" means that it could be used without becoming unclean under the law.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to teach Israel to distinguish between what is clean and what is unclean. These rules protected daily life and reminded the people that they belonged to a holy God. Here we see a practical exception: dry seed does not become contaminated, but if it had been wet, it did (v. 38). Scholars explain the reason in several ways, and the text does not spell it out.

For today: God is just and reasonable; he does not exaggerate or complicate things without reason. We can care for what is holy with seriousness, but also with balance and wisdom, without burdening others with rules that God did not set.
exp.10:38:
This verse speaks of a clean animal, one of those that could be eaten, which dies on its own and not by sacrifice. Anyone who touched its dead body became unclean in the ceremonial sense until evening.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel. These rules taught that God is holy and that his people were to live set apart, with respect for life and death. This uncleanness was not a sin, but a temporary state that was resolved with time and washing. Interpreters explain the exact meaning of these laws in several different ways.

For today: Christ fulfilled these laws, but the call to holiness remains with us. We can take care with what we touch, look at, and consume, and turn to God each day to be cleansed.
exp.10:39:
It says that if someone eats the meat of an animal that died on its own, they must wash their clothes and be unclean until evening. The same applies to whoever carries it or removes it from there. "Unclean" means ceremonially impure, not sinful.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. These laws taught them to distinguish the clean from the unclean and to live as a people set apart for God. Scholars explain the details in various ways: some see reasons related to health, others a spiritual symbolism. The text emphasizes the holiness of God.

For today: God cares about the details of everyday life. Today we can ask him to help us live with care, purity, and gratitude, and to quickly cleanse whatever draws us away from him.
exp.10:43:
God tells the Israelites that he is the LORD their God, and that for this reason they must set themselves apart for him and live as a holy people, because he is holy. That is why they were not to make themselves unclean, that is, become impure, by eating animals that crawl along the ground. "Be holy" means they would dedicate themselves, set themselves apart for God.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, within the laws about clean and unclean animals. These rules set Israel apart from other peoples and taught them to live with attention to God in everyday life. Scholars explain the reason for each prohibition in different ways, but the text emphasizes the call to holiness.

For today: holiness is not only something for Sundays. Ask God to show you one daily habit, such as what you look at, say, or do, that you should give to him in order to live set apart for him.
exp.10:46:
This verse says that the laws before it had a purpose: to teach Israel to make a difference between what is unclean (what, according to the law, was not fit for them) and what is clean, that is, between what they could eat and what they could not. "Unclean" does not always mean dirty; it means set apart or not permitted for the use of God's people.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, and through them to the people just freed from Egypt. He gives these rules because he wants them to be a holy, distinct people, living in a way that acknowledges him in everyday matters, such as eating. Scholars explain the reason for each forbidden animal in various ways, and the Bible does not detail all the reasons.

For today: God is interested in every detail of our lives. Today we can ask ourselves which daily habits or decisions, even small ones, show that we belong to him and that we want to live with discernment.
exp.11:1:
God tells Moses to instruct the people that a woman who gives birth to a boy becomes unclean for seven days, just as she is during her menstruation. A woman who conceives is one who becomes pregnant, and the one who gives birth is the one who brings forth a child. To be unclean does not mean being sinful; it means that for a time she could not take part in worship at the sanctuary.

The LORD speaks to Moses to order the life of the people of Israel under the law of the covenant. These rules treated birth and blood as things that required a time of separation and restoration. Scholars explain the meaning in several ways, and there is no single certain answer.

For today: God is concerned with the most intimate moments of life, such as the birth of a child. We can draw near to Him with thanksgiving, and we can also give newly delivered mothers rest, care, and practical support.
exp.11:4:
The verse says that if a woman gives birth to a daughter, she will be ceremonially unclean for two weeks, just as in her time of menstruation, and after that she will spend sixty-six more days in the blood of her purifying. "Unclean" means ceremonially impure, not sinful. If she had a son, the time was half.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel on how to approach his presence in the tabernacle. Ritual impurity from blood or bodily fluids reminded people that life and death are serious matters before the holy God. Why the time differed according to the sex of the baby is not explained in the text, and scholars interpret it in various ways.

For today: although we no longer live under these rules, we learn that God provides a way to return to his presence after each stage of life. Come to him with confidence, knowing that Christ cleanses us completely.
exp.11:5:
When the days of her purification were complete, whether for a son or a daughter, she was to bring to the priest a year-old lamb as a burnt offering (an offering burned up entirely for God) and a young pigeon or a turtledove as a sin offering. The word "purification" here refers to the cleansing period after childbirth, and the "tent of meeting" is the tent where God dwelt among his people.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel. This law dealt with ritual impurity, not with moral sin: giving birth was not a sin. Some believe these offerings served as a reminder that every life is born into a world marked by sin. Interpreters explain this in several ways.

For today: God invites us to draw near to him with thanksgiving after the great moments of life. Today we give thanks to Christ, whose sacrifice cleanses us and opens the way to God.
exp.11:7:
This verse says that if a woman who had given birth was poor and could not pay for a lamb, she could offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons. One was burnt whole as a burnt offering, and the other was for a sin offering, that is, for forgiveness. In this way the priest made atonement for her, and she was made clean, that is, fit to take part again in worship.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel. After childbirth, the woman went through a time of ritual purification. This did not mean that giving birth was a sin, but rather rules of purity within the covenant. God provided an option for the poor. Luke 2:24 tells that Mary offered this humbler offering.

For today: God does not place barriers because of a lack of money. We can draw near to Him just as we are, and we should make sure that no one is excluded from the community for being poor.
exp.12:9:
He says the priest was to examine the person. If he saw a white swelling in the skin, with the hair in that area turned white, and raw flesh also appeared (an open wound, in healthy red flesh), that was a sign of a serious illness. A swelling is what the verse calls the rising, and it is the rising that the priest was to look at closely.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priests did not act as physicians, but as guardians of the holiness and health of the community. Their careful examination prevented hasty judgments and protected everyone.

For today: before judging someone or drawing conclusions, look carefully and listen. God teaches us to act with patience, truth, and care for others, not with haste or prejudice.
exp.12:20:
This verse says the priest examines the spot on the skin that appeared where there was a swelling or abscess. If there are no white hairs, the spot is not sunken and looks dark or dull, and nothing is declared yet. The priest sets the person apart for seven days to watch whether it changes.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The text speaks of a skin disease, but the Hebrew word covers several conditions of the skin, not only what we today call leprosy. Here the judgment is not rushed: it is waited for and observed. It also protected the community and cared for the person affected.

For today: before we judge someone or a situation, let us give ourselves time. Patience, observation and humility prevent unjust condemnation.
exp.12:22:
This verse says that if the bright spot on the skin stays in the same place and has not spread, it is only the scar of a boil, a swelling full of pus. Then the priest declares him clean. The word "but" is used here to mean that the spot did not spread, and the verse says the spot stayed in its place.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priests were to examine skin conditions patiently, wait a few days, and watch whether anything changed. In this way the health of the community was protected and hasty judgments were avoided. Scholars debate exactly which skin diseases are covered by the term used here for the serious condition.

For today: before judging someone or drawing conclusions, let us take time, observe calmly, and seek the truth. In this way we act with justice and mercy.
exp.12:25:
This verse describes a spot on the skin that appears in a healed burn. If the priest examines it and finds no white hair in the spot, and it is not sunken below the surface of the skin, but looks dull or somewhat dark, he does not give a verdict yet. He orders the person kept apart for seven days to observe them.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priest does not rush to judge: he looks for concrete signs and waits. The texts speak of a serious skin disease, but many scholars think the Hebrew term covered several skin conditions, not only what we today call leprosy.

For today: when there are doubts about a person or a situation, do not judge quickly. Give it time, observe with patience, and seek the truth before drawing conclusions.
exp.12:27:
If, after a burn on the skin, a spot appears and stays in its place, does not spread, and looks dull, then it is only a swelling or scar from the burn. The priest must declare the person clean.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priests had to examine skin diseases carefully and decide whether a person could remain in the camp. Here it is made clear that not every mark on the skin was a serious disease, and that a simple burn that had healed should not condemn anyone. The term used here may cover several skin conditions, not only the disease we call by that name today.

For today: before judging someone, look carefully and seek the truth. Not every flaw or wound from the past defines a person. Be just, patient, and compassionate.
exp.12:31:
This verse describes the priest's second examination, seven days after the first. He looks for three signs: that the scall has not spread, that there is no yellow hair in it, and that it does not appear to go deeper than the skin, meaning that it does not sink beneath the surface of the skin.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. They served to protect the community and to prevent hasty judgments. The priest did not declare anyone unclean at once; he waited and observed with patience. Scholars disagree about exactly which disease is described.

For today: before judging someone or drawing conclusions, let us take time to look calmly and fairly. Patience protects people and reflects the care of God.
exp.12:32:
Then the priest sets the person apart for another seven days to examine it again.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. They served to protect the community and to let the priest examine carefully, without haste or prejudice. Leaving the spot unshaved allowed them to see whether the patch was growing. Scholars are not sure exactly what disease it was.

For today: let us not judge anyone in a hurry. Let us give each situation time, look with patience, and seek the truth before drawing conclusions, both with others and with ourselves.
exp.12:34:
This verse describes a later case. If someone had already been declared clean, but the scall (a skin disease, probably on the head or the beard) starts to spread again, it must be examined once more. The "cleansing" refers to the moment when the priest had declared the person clean.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. The priests were to examine carefully and patiently, without rushing. This protected the community and showed order and justice. It is not known with certainty which exact disease the Hebrew word describes, and scholars interpret it in various ways.

For today: do not consider a matter closed just because it seemed resolved. It is worth humbly examining our hearts and our habits, so that something small does not grow back. We can ask God to examine us and heal us.
exp.12:35:
If, after the person has been declared clean, the scall keeps spreading over the skin, the priest no longer needs to check whether the hair has turned yellow, a sign mentioned earlier. The spreading alone is enough: the person is unclean, that is, ceremonially impure.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. The priest did not act as a doctor but as a guardian of the community's purity. Scholars do not always agree on which exact disease the text describes, so it is best not to claim a modern diagnosis. What is clear is that there was an orderly process, with careful observation and patience.

For today: when something in our lives keeps growing in the wrong way, such as a habit or a wound, we should not ignore it. Let us seek help in time, with humility and from wise people, trusting that God cares for us.
exp.12:37:
This verse speaks of a person, man or woman, who has white spots on the skin. It marks the beginning of a new situation that the law had to examine. The verses that follow clarify that if the spots were somewhat dark, it was not a serious case.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priest would examine the skin to decide whether someone should be temporarily set apart from the community. He was not a doctor in the modern sense, and it is not known exactly which illnesses were meant. The goal was to care for the health and holiness of the people.

Today we can learn to look with calm and fairness before we judge. Not every problem is as serious as it seems, and no one should be labeled in a hurry. Before drawing conclusions about someone, let us seek to understand their situation with patience and compassion.
exp.12:40:
If a man's hair falls out at the front of his head, near the forehead, he becomes bald at the front, but he is not considered unclean. The first word means that the hair had fallen out, and the second word means that, in terms of ceremonial purity, he had no uncleanness at all.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron to guide the priests. They were to examine skin diseases and decide whether someone should be set apart from the community for a time. This rule makes clear that ordinary baldness was not a reason for fear or for excluding anyone. Only if a special sore appeared was the priest to examine it carefully.

For today: let us not judge people by their appearance or by normal changes in the body. God guards against unjust suspicion. Let us seek to be fair, patient, and compassionate.
exp.12:45:
As long as the person had the sore, they would be considered unclean, that is, not fit to be with the people in worship. They had to live alone, outside the camp.

"Camp" is the word the verse uses for the place where Israel lived, so no separate note is needed here.

God gave these instructions to Moses and Aaron, so that the priests would apply them. The people were in the wilderness, and the presence of God dwelt in the midst of the camp. These rules protected the health of the community and taught the holiness of God. Scholars are not sure that this skin disease was the illness we call leprosy today; the Hebrew term seems to cover several skin conditions.

Today we can remember those who live isolated because of illness, shame, or loneliness. Jesus touched people with skin diseases and healed them. We can reach out with a call, a visit, or a prayer to someone who feels set apart.
exp.12:48:
This verse describes a green or red mark that appears on a piece of cloth or on leather, whether in the fabric or weave, or in an article made of leather. In your Bible, the mark is described as mildew contamination, and the item must be brought to the priest to be examined.

God gave these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel as they lived in the wilderness. The priest acted as an inspector, caring for the health and cleanliness of the whole community, and the law shows that God cares even about everyday things like clothing and household goods. Scholars explain the deeper meaning in several ways, and not everything about these laws is clear to us today.

For today: let us not hide the things that are damaging our lives. Bringing them out into the open in time, before God and before someone wise and trustworthy, keeps the damage from spreading.
exp.12:54:
The priest is told to examine the garment again after it has been washed. If the stain still looks the same, even though it has not spread, the garment is unclean and must be burned.

Dios da esta instrucción a Moisés para el pueblo de Israel.

God gives this instruction to Moses for the people of Israel. The priests were to watch over purity in the camp and protect the health and life of the community. Scholars disagree about whether this is mold or some other fungus, and the text also carries a ritual meaning.

For today: scrubbing the surface is not enough. If something harmful in our lives remains after we have tried to fix it, it is wise to be honest and ask for help rather than hide it.
exp.12:57:
It says that if a garment of wool, linen, or leather had a suspicious stain, and after washing it the stain disappeared, it had to be washed a second time. Then it was declared clean.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priest examined the garment and decided whether it was clean or unfit for use. The word for disease used here applies to fabrics, and it probably refers to some kind of mold or fungus, although this is not known for certain. The law sought to care for the health and purity of the people.

For today: when something in your life becomes stained, do not ignore it or give it up for lost. Be patient and cleanse it again with humility. God offers restoration, and often the process of cleansing requires more than one attempt.
exp.13:0:
This verse is an introductory phrase: God speaks to Moses. "The Lord" is the name used for God in this translation. What follows are instructions that Moses was to pass on to the people.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the one who receives and communicates the message. The earlier chapters explained how to recognize skin disease, which probably included several conditions of the skin (not always what is today called leprosy). Now God explains what to do when a person had healed: they were to present themselves to the priest to be declared clean and return to the community. In this way both the health and the dignity of the person were protected.

God is concerned for those who have been set apart or wounded and wants to see them restored. Today we can accompany with kindness someone who has been alone or sick, helping them feel once again part of the family and the community.
exp.13:1:
This verse begins the instructions for when a person who had a skin disease had already recovered. The person was to be brought to the priest. The word for "cleansing" means being healed and declared clean. Note that the Hebrew word does not always refer to the leprosy we know today, but to several skin diseases.

God speaks to Moses to give laws to Israel while they live in the wilderness. The priest did not heal; he only examined and declared whether the person could return to the community. In this way both health was protected and the one who had lived apart was restored.

For today: God is concerned to bring back together those who have been wounded or isolated. We can accompany someone who feels alone, help them return to the community, and welcome them without prejudice.
exp.13:5:
This verse describes one step in the ritual for declaring a person cleansed after healing from leprosy. The priest takes the living bird, along with the cedar wood, the scarlet thread (red yarn or wool), and the hyssop (a plant used for sprinkling). All of these are dipped in the blood of the other bird, which was killed over running water.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. The person was already healed, and this ritual restored them to the community. Scholars explain the symbolism of the elements in several different ways, so it is wise not to be too categorical.

For today: God cares about restoring those who have been set apart. We can help someone who has suffered rejection or shame to feel welcomed again, with patience and kindness.
exp.13:7:
This verse describes the first steps of a person who has already been declared clean of leprosy. He must wash his clothes, shave off all his hair, and bathe in water. Then he is clean to return to the camp. Even so, he must stay seven days outside his tent, that is, without entering his home.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. The person had lived apart because of his illness, and here his return to the community begins. The ritual shows that restoration was gradual and orderly. Scholars do not agree on the exact meaning of each gesture, but all of them see a concern for purity and for life together in community.

For today: restoration is often a process, not a single moment. If someone is recovering from a wound, a mistake, or a difficult season, let us give them time, patience, and a path back, just as God cared for this step by step.
exp.13:10:
This verse says that the priest who carries out the cleansing brings the person who will be declared clean to the entrance of the meeting tent, before God. He does this together with the offerings that were mentioned earlier. The "tent of meeting" was the holy tent where God met with his people. "Present" means setting her before God.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for the cleansing ritual for someone who had been healed of a serious skin disease. The person was already cured, but had to return formally to the life of the community and to God's presence. That is why the priest accompanies her.

For today: when God restores us, he does not leave us alone on the road back. We can come near to him without shame, and also accompany with care those who are returning to the community after a difficult time.
exp.13:16:
It says that the priest takes the oil left over in his hand and puts it on three places of the person being cleansed: the soft part of the right ear, the thumb of the right hand, and the big toe of the right foot. He puts it right on top of the blood of the trespass offering. The soft cartilage of the ear is the flesh of the ear's upper edge, and to atone means to cover over or make right a wrong.

This is part of the instructions God gave to Moses for cleansing someone healed from a skin disease, called leprosy in this translation. The person could then return to the community and to worship. Many see in the ear, the hand, and the foot a sign that the whole person is set apart for God, although the text does not explain it in those words.

For today: God not only forgives, He also restores completely. We can ask Him that what we hear, what we do, and where we walk belong to Him.
exp.13:20:
It says that if the person being cleansed from leprosy is poor and cannot pay all of the above, he may bring a smaller offering. Instead of three lambs, he brings one as a guilt offering, which is lifted up before God. He also brings a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil, and a log of oil (a small measure of liquid). Here, being made right and restored is what it means to be reconciled.

God speaks to Moses, giving him instructions for Israel. A person healed of a skin disease was to return to the community and to worship through this ritual. God allows the poor to take part according to what they can afford, without leaving them excluded.

For today: God does not place financial barriers in the way of our coming near to Him. We can receive His forgiveness with what we are and what we have. We can also make sure that in our church no one feels lesser for being poor.
exp.13:22:
This verse says that the person who was being cleansed of leprosy had to bring the offerings already mentioned to the priest on the eighth day. He was to present them at the entrance of the tabernacle, before the Lord. The "tent of meeting" is the tent where God was present with Israel.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions about the cleansing of the one who had been healed of leprosy. The poor were allowed to offer cheaper animals, such as turtledoves or young pigeons, so that no one was shut out for lack of money. The ritual restored his place within the community and in worship.

For today: God welcomes everyone and does not ask more of us than we can give. We can draw near to Him without shame, knowing that He wants to restore us, and respond with gratitude by offering Him what we have.
exp.13:23:
This verse describes one step in the purification ritual for a person who had been healed of leprosy. The priest takes the lamb offered for guilt and the log of oil (a small measure of liquid). Then he waves them, that is, he lifts them up and moves them back and forth as an offering before God, presenting them to Him.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. The healed person had lived apart from the community, and this ritual, on the eighth day, marked their return to life with their people and their worship. It was an orderly path, full of grace, for being restored.

For today: God not only heals, He also restores. If He has lifted you out of a difficulty, come back before Him with gratitude and do not remain on the sidelines of the community.
exp.13:24:
He tells that the priest kills the lamb of the trespass offering. Then he takes some of its blood and puts it in three places on the man who is being cleansed: the soft part of the right ear, the thumb of the right hand, and the big toe of the right foot.

God speaks to Moses about the rite for the person who has been healed of a skin disease and returns to the community. It is the eighth day of his cleansing. The blood touches ear, hand, and foot, and many understand that this stands for the whole person: what he hears, what he does, and where he walks. But the text does not explain this in detail, so it is an interpretation.

Today we can give God our whole day: what we listen to, what we do, and the paths we walk. Christ cleanses us completely, and with gratitude we say to him: "Lord, guide my ears, my hands, and my steps."
exp.13:25:
This verse describes one step of the ritual. The priest pours some of the oil into the palm of his left hand. He will use that oil right away: with his right finger he will sprinkle it seven times before the LORD, and then he will put it on the ear, the thumb of the hand, and the big toe of the one being cleansed.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the cleansing of a person healed from leprosy (a skin disease). In this way the person could return to the community and to worship. The oil is applied over the blood already placed. Many see it as a symbol of God's Spirit, although the text does not say this in those words.

For today: God cares about the details of our restoration. If He has healed or forgiven you, return to Him with gratitude, and remember that His care reaches everything you are: what you hear, what you do, and where you walk.
exp.13:26:
This verse describes one step in the purification ritual for a person healed of leprosy. The priest pours oil into his left hand, dips his right finger in it, and sprinkles some of the oil seven times before the Lord, that is, in front of the sanctuary. To sprinkle means to scatter drops, and seven usually signals something complete.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. The healed leper did not simply return home: he was brought back into the community and into worship through a rite. First the blood was applied, and then the oil was applied to the same places: ear, hand, and foot. Many understand the oil as a sign of God's Spirit, although the text does not say so in those words.

For today: God cares about fully restoring us, not only about healing us. If someone has lived apart because of pain or shame, you can walk alongside them and welcome them warmly into the community.
exp.13:27:
It says the priest will take oil that is in his hand and put it in three places on the person being cleansed from leprosy: the soft part of the right ear (the cartilage), the thumb of the right hand, and the big toe of the right foot. He will put it exactly where he had earlier put the blood of the guilt offering.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the day when someone healed of a skin disease returned to the community. The rite declared the person clean and restored him before God. Many understand that ear, hand, and foot represent the whole person: hearing, acting, and walking. It is a common interpretation, though the text does not explain it.

For today: offer to God what you hear, what you do, and where you go, trusting that his forgiveness restores you completely.
exp.13:28:
This verse says that the priest would take the oil that remained in his hand and put it on the head of the person who was being purified.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the rite of purification for someone who had been healed of leprosy. Before this, the person had been set apart from the community. The oil was applied after the blood, and many understand it as a sign of consecration and a new beginning. The Bible does not explain every detail of the symbol.

For today: God not only forgives, He also fully restores. If you feel set apart because of your shame or your mistakes, draw near to Him with confidence, because He desires to give you back your peace and a place among His people.
exp.13:30:
It says that the person who was being cleansed had to offer two birds, according to what he was able to pay: one as an offering for sin and the other as a burnt offering, that is, an offering burned up completely. This was done together with the grain offering (the meat offering). In this way the priest made atonement, that is, covered over and reconciled the person before the Lord.

God speaks through Moses in the law given to the Israelites. This passage deals with someone who was recovering from a skin disease and was poor. God allowed a simpler offering, of birds, so that poverty would not close off his way back into the community and into worship.

For today: God does not place economic barriers to drawing near to Him. We can come as we are, with what we have. We can also make sure that in our church no one feels left out for lacking resources.
exp.13:36:
The priest is told to examine the plague on the house carefully. If he sees marks on the walls, small hollows that are greenish or reddish and look lower than the rest of the wall, that is an important sign. A plague here means a visible disease or blight, and the small hollows are little pits or dents in the surface. It probably refers to something like mold or fungus, though this cannot be stated with certainty.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, giving rules for Israel before they enter Canaan. The priest did not act as a doctor, but took care of the purity and health of the community. For that reason the house was first emptied, so that its contents would not be made unclean, and only then was an orderly inspection carried out.

For today: let us not ignore small problems. When something is going wrong in the home or in the heart, it is wise to look at it honestly and ask for help in time, before it grows.
exp.13:42:
If, after the damaged stones have been taken out, the walls scraped, and the walls plastered again with fresh mortar, the mark or mold comes back in the house, the case remains open. The harmful mark is the plague, and to come back and break out again is to appear once more. Scraping the walls is removing the old plaster, and replastering is covering the wall again.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people, who would live in Canaan. The priest acted as an inspector, protecting the health and purity of the community. This verse describes the second step: after the cleaning, the house is checked again. What happens next is explained in the following verse.

For today: when a problem comes back, do not ignore it or lose heart. Honestly check whether the root is still there, ask for help and wise counsel, and act thoroughly, not only on the surface.
exp.13:46:
It says that whoever sleeps in that house, or eats in it, must wash his clothes. That is, prolonged contact with a house under suspicion of a contagious mark left the person unclean, and washing was the step to return to normal. The sentence that explains the old wording of the verse, which concerned the words for sleeping and lying in the house, has been removed, and the verse of the mark is given without quoting the verse's terms: it was a stain or mold that spread across the walls.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel, who would soon live in houses in Canaan. They were rules of ritual purity and also of practical care. The priest would inspect the house, and if the mark grew, it was torn down. Scholars agree that it referred to harmful mold, though not all of them specify the detail.

Today we can learn to take seriously what harms our home, whether mold, disorder, or environments of sin. Cleaning in time protects the family and shows care for the life God gave us.
exp.13:47:
It says the priest comes back to the house to check it again. If the plague (a mark or mold that affected the walls) has not spread after the house was plastered over, and the word "plastered" here refers to a new coat laid over the walls, then he declares the house clean. The reason is simple: the plague has healed.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel, now settled in the promised land. The laws about cleanness protected health and life in the community. Note that the priest did not declare the house clean based on appearance, but only after examining it carefully. The verse that follows begins a ritual of purification.

For today: before we consider something resolved, it is wise to examine it with patience. In a wounded relationship or a bad habit, it is not enough to cover it on the outside; we must verify that it has truly healed, and thank God when it has.
exp.13:48:
It says that when the house has already been declared free of the plague, the priest takes the items to purify it: two small birds, cedar wood, scarlet (thread or wool dyed red), and hyssop (a small plant used for sprinkling).

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, giving laws for Israel. Before entering Canaan, the people receive rules about mold or plagues in houses. This rite is similar to the purification of a person healed from leprosy (Leviticus 14:4-7). Scholars do not agree on the exact meaning of each element.

For today: God cares that what is damaged be restored with order, not with improvisation. You can bring Him whatever in your life or home needs healing, and humbly seek the restoration He offers.
exp.13:49:
It says the priest will kill one of the two small birds in an earthen vessel, and the blood will fall over running water, that is, flowing water such as a spring or a river, not still, stagnant water. To kill the animal means to cut its throat.

God speaks through Moses to Israel. A house had been affected by mold or disease, and now the priest declares it clean. Before the family could go back to using it normally, this rite of purification was performed. Scholars explain the exact symbolism of the rite in different ways; what is certain is that it showed that cleansing comes from God and was carried out with blood and water.

For today: when something in your life or your home has been restored, do not take it for granted. Give thanks to God, for true cleansing and a new beginning come from Him. Christians see in this a shadow of what Christ does for us.
exp.13:50:
This verse describes a rite for cleansing a house where mold or plague had appeared. The priest takes the cedar wood, the hyssop (a small plant used for sprinkling), the scarlet (a red thread or wool), and the living bird. He dips them in the blood of the slaughtered bird mixed with running water, and then he sprinkles the house seven times.

God gives this instruction to Moses for the people of Israel. The laws about purity taught that God wanted a people set apart, and that the priest was to confirm the cleansing. The released bird showed that the house was made free. Some see here a foreshadowing of atonement, although the text does not say this directly.

For today: when something in your life or your home is damaged, do not ignore it. Bring it before God with humility, trusting that he can cleanse and restore.
exp.13:51:
It says that the priest purifies the house that had mold or disease, using several things: the blood of the sacrificed bird, living water (running water, from a spring), the living bird, cedar wood, hyssop (a small plant used for sprinkling), and scarlet (red thread or wool). With all of these he sprinkles the house.

God speaks to Moses to set out rules for Israel. Before this, the priest had already examined the house and, if the problem had cleared up or the house had been repaired, he declared it clean. This rite marked its return to normal use. Scholars do not fully agree on the meaning of each symbol, but the idea of cleansing, life, and atonement is clear.

For today: God is concerned with restoring what is damaged, not only with pointing it out. Think of an area of your life or your home that needs healing, and ask God to cleanse and renew you.
exp.14:3:
This verse says that if a man has a discharge in his body, the bed where he lies becomes ceremonially unclean, that is, impure in the ritual sense. The same is true of anything on which he sits. A discharge is an abnormal bodily fluid, and being unclean does not mean being a sinner. It means being not fit, for a time, to draw near to worship.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to Israel. These laws taught that God is holy and that his people had to live with care in his presence. Scholars also see a practical effect of hygiene and of limiting the spread of illness, although the text focuses on ritual purity.

For today: God cares about the details of our lives and calls us to approach him with reverence. In Christ we do not need these rituals, but we can ask him for a clean heart and care lovingly for others.
exp.14:4:
It says that if someone touches the bed of a man with a discharge (an abnormal bodily fluid), that person must wash his clothes, bathe with water, and be "unclean" until evening. Being "unclean" does not mean sinful; it means ritually impure, set apart from worship for a time.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, for the people of Israel. These laws taught that God is holy and that his presence among the people was to be treated with reverence. They also helped care for the community, although the text stresses above all the spiritual meaning of purity.

For today: God calls us to live with care and reverence before him. We can pause each day to ask him to cleanse our hearts, trusting that Christ purifies us completely (1 John 1:9).
exp.14:5:
It says that if someone sits in a place where a person with a discharge (an abnormal bodily fluid) had sat before, they must wash their clothes, bathe with water, and are considered "unclean" until evening. "Unclean" does not mean sinful, but unfit to take part in worship for a time.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. They were rules for living near the tabernacle, where God dwelt. Many think they also helped prevent the spread of illness, though the text does not say so; its emphasis is holiness and order in the life of the people.

For today: God cares about everyday life and about how we draw near to Him. Today, in Christ, we do not depend on washing rituals, but we can take care of our hearts and ask Him for cleansing with sincerity every day.
exp.14:6:
It says that if someone touches the body of a person with a discharge (an abnormal bodily fluid, probably a sickness), that person must wash their clothes, bathe in water, and remain unclean until evening. Being unclean does not mean being a sinner; it means being ritually unfit to draw near to worship.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to set the order of life for the people of Israel. These rules protected the holiness of the camp, where God dwelt in the midst of them. Some think they also helped prevent the spread of disease, though the text does not say so, and interpreters understand it in various ways.

For today: God cares about what we tend to and how we tend to it. We can take our inner cleanness seriously, coming to God with humility. And we can care for the sick with compassion, without forgetting prudence.
exp.14:7:
This verse says that if a person with a discharge (an abnormal bodily fluid, probably an illness) spits on someone who is clean, that person must wash their clothes and bathe in water. They will be unclean until evening. Here "unclean" does not mean sinful, but impure for worship.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. They were rules to protect the holiness of the place of worship and probably also helped prevent the spread of disease. Some scholars emphasize the ritual side and others the sanitary side; the text does not fully explain this.

For today: our actions affect others, even without meaning to. We can care for the health of others and draw near to God with reverence, remembering that Christ cleanses us completely.
exp.14:10:
It says that if someone touches a person who has a discharge (an abnormal secretion from the body), and that person had not rinsed his hands in water, the one who touched him must wash his clothes and bathe. He became unclean, that is, ceremonially impure, until evening. The saddle or seat on which he sat is also mentioned in the verse of certain words in this part.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. These laws taught that holiness mattered in daily life, since God dwelt in the midst of them. Being unclean was not a sin, but a state that temporarily set a person apart from worship. Some also see an effect of sanitary care, although the text does not explain this.

For today: God is interested in the everyday. We can ask him to help us live with care and purity of heart, and to treat with compassion those who are sick or set apart.
exp.14:12:
This verse says that when a man with a discharge (an abnormal bodily secretion) has been healed, he must wait seven full days. Then he washes his clothes and his body in running water, as from a river or a spring. Then he is clean before the community.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, and they pass these rules on to Israel. They were laws of ritual purity for living near God in the midst of the camp. They were not a moral judgment on the sick person. On the eighth day an offering was presented, and this marked the return to normal life and to worship.

For today: God cares for the processes of restoration. If someone has gone through a time of brokenness, let us give them space and patience, and let us draw near to God with confidence to be renewed.
exp.14:13:
On the eighth day after finishing the seven days of purification, the man who had had a discharge was to take two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the entrance of the tent of meeting. There he gave them to the priest. The "tent of meeting" is the tent where God was present among Israel.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, giving rules of purity for the people. An abnormal bodily discharge left the person ritually unclean, that is, temporarily set apart from worship. According to the following passage, one of the birds was a sin offering and the other a burnt offering. Scholars explain the exact reason for this in different ways, but it shows that God cared both for holiness and for restoration.

Today we can remember that God does not leave us set apart: he invites us back into his presence. Draw near to him with sincerity, trusting that Christ has already made the complete sacrifice.
exp.14:15:
It says that if a man has an emission of semen, he must wash his whole body with water and remain "unclean" until evening. "Unclean" does not mean sinful but ritually impure, that is, not fit to come near the worship. The word translated as "emission" in the verse refers to something coming out or leaving the body.

God spoke to Moses and Aaron to set the order of life for the people of Israel, who had the tabernacle in the midst of them. These rules taught that life and what is holy deserve reverence. Scholars explain the inclusion of these laws in several ways (as a symbol of life, for hygiene, for separation from other peoples), and there is no single certain explanation.

For today: God cares for every aspect of our lives, even what is most private and natural. We can draw near to Him with respect, without shame, and always seek a clean and orderly life before Him.
exp.14:17:
It says that when a man and a woman have sexual relations, both must bathe with water and are "unclean" until evening. Here "unclean" is explained as ceremonially impure, meaning not fit to approach the sanctuary for a time, and not as sinful.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. They were rules for living near the presence of God, who dwelt in the tabernacle. The laws about purity reminded them that life, the body, and what is holy matter. Scholars debate the exact meaning of each rule, but here the marital relationship is not presented as sin.

For today: although we no longer live under these rules, we can learn to treat with reverence everything God has given us, including our bodies and our marriage, and to draw near to Him with a clean heart.
exp.14:18:
It says that when a woman had her period, that is, a normal flow of blood from her body, she was to be set apart for seven days. Whoever touched her was "unclean" (ritually not fit for worship) until evening. This was not about sin, but about a temporary condition.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. These laws taught that life and blood are sacred, and that people had to approach the sanctuary with care. Some think they also helped protect the health or order of the people; the Bible does not explain this clearly.

For today: although Christians no longer live under these ritual rules, we can learn to take God's holiness seriously and to trust that Jesus cleanses us completely. He also treated with tenderness a woman with a flow of blood (Mark 5).
exp.14:19:
This verse says that everything a woman lay on or sat on during her menstrual period became "unclean," that is, ceremonially impure. The days of her set-apart time are the days when she was separated from ordinary activity.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The laws of purity taught that God is holy and that his presence among the people had to be treated with reverence. Scholars debate the exact reason behind each rule; the text stresses above all the holiness of the tabernacle (Lev 15:31).

For today: Christ cleanses us inwardly (Hebrews 10:22), so we do not live under these rules. Even so, we can learn to draw near to God with respect and to value purity of heart above outward things.
exp.14:23:
This verse says that if a man has sexual relations with a woman during her period, and her blood touches him, he becomes ceremonially "unclean" for seven days. In addition, every bed on which he lies during that time also becomes unclean. Here "unclean" does not mean sinful or dirty, but rather not fit, for a time, to take part in worship at the tabernacle.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to set rules for the life of the people of Israel. These laws aimed to make the people take seriously the holiness of God, who dwelt among them. Scholars explain in various ways why these rules were used, and not everything is known with certainty.
