For today: God is interested in every area of life, even the most private ones. We can ask ourselves how to honor him with respect and care in our relationships and in our homes.
exp.14:25:
It says that when a woman has a discharge of blood outside her normal cycle, or one that lasts longer than usual, the bed where she sleeps and the furniture where she sits become unclean, just as they did during her period. The normal cycle is her regular monthly period; the discharge is the bleeding itself; to be unclean means to be ritually impure, not sinful or dirty through fault.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, for the people of Israel, in the book of Leviticus. These rules taught the people to live as a nation set apart for God, close to his presence in the tabernacle. Ritual impurity was a temporary condition, not a punishment. Scholars explain the purpose in several ways: order, respect for life and blood, and limiting contact with what is holy.

For today: Christ fulfilled these ritual laws, but we can learn that God cares for what is holy and also restores the person. Come to him with gratitude, without shame, and treat with compassion those who suffer from illness.
exp.14:26:
Whoever touched the bed, the furniture, or anything on which a woman with a flow of blood during a time other than her normal period had been sitting or lying became unclean, meaning that in ceremonial terms they were not fit to approach worship. They had to wash their clothes, bathe with water, and wait until evening.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to set the order of life for the people of Israel, with the tabernacle at the center. These purity laws do not speak of a sin committed by the woman, but of a ritual state. Scholars explain their purpose in several ways: to teach the holiness of God, the value of life (the blood), and respect for his presence.

For today: God cares for what is holy and at the same time provides the way to return to him. We can draw near to God with reverence and confidence, grateful that Christ cleanses us.
exp.14:28:
This verse speaks of a woman who had a flow of blood outside her normal time, and who has now been healed. On the eighth day, after counting seven days of waiting, she was to bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest, at the door of the tent of meeting, that is, the tent where God dwelt among his people.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. This condition left her ritually unclean before God, that is, impure in a ceremonial sense, not guilty. The birds were a simple offering, one that even the poor could make. One would be a sin offering and the other a burnt offering.

For today: God cares for the weak and offers a path of restoration open to all. We can draw near to him without fear or shame, trusting that Christ, according to the New Testament, cleanses us and restores us completely.
exp.14:30:
God tells the Israelites that they must keep themselves separated from their uncleanness. In this way they will avoid dying because of it, and they will not defile the tabernacle, the sacred tent where God dwelt among them.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, and the instruction is for the whole people. This chapter deals with discharges and bodily conditions that left a person ritually unclean. The sacrifices mentioned in the verses before this one made purification possible. The central point is that God was near his people, and his presence was holy. Scholars explain the meaning of these laws in several ways: holiness, public health, or symbolism of life and death.

Today we can remember that God still wants to be near us. Let us take his holiness seriously, and when we feel dirty or far away, let us come to him with humility, trusting that he himself provides the way to cleanse us.
exp.15:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses after the death of Aaron's two sons, Nadab and Abihu, who died when they drew near before the Lord.

God speaks in response to that tragedy, which is recounted in Leviticus 10, where they offered a fire that God had not commanded them. Then God gives instructions about how Aaron could enter the Most Holy Place without dying, with sacrifices for sin. This prepares for the Day of Atonement.

For today: God is holy, and drawing near to Him is a serious matter, not a matter of routine. But He Himself gives us the way. We can approach Him with reverence and gratitude, trusting in Christ, who opens the door for us.
exp.15:1:
God tells Moses to warn Aaron: he may not enter the holy place whenever he likes, that is, behind the veil, before the lid of the ark (the covering, also called the mercy seat). If he did, he would die, because God makes himself present there in the cloud.

The Lord speaks shortly after the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's sons, who died when they approached God in an improper way. For this reason God sets out clear rules for coming near to him, which are explained right away through sacrifices and special garments for the Day of Atonement.

For today: God is holy and deserves that we come near with reverence and humility. Christians believe that Christ opened the way to God, so we can approach him with confidence, but not carelessly, with gratitude and reverence.
exp.15:2:
Here God tells Aaron how he must come before the holy place, the most sacred part of the sanctuary. He was to bring a young bull, an offering for sin, meant to cover over or cleanse sin, and a ram as a burnt offering, an offering that was burned up completely as a full surrender to God.

God speaks to Moses after the death of Aaron's two sons, who had approached Him in an improper way. This is the beginning of the instructions for the Day of Atonement. God makes it clear that no one comes into His presence in just any way, but only with the sacrifice He Himself appointed.

For today: draw near to God with humility and reverence, never taking that access for granted. Christians believe that Christ made that access possible; for this reason we can pray with confidence, but also with respect and a sincere heart.
exp.15:3:
It says that Aaron, the high priest, had to put on special linen clothing: a holy coat, linen breeches or undergarments, a belt or sash, and a linen headpiece. Before dressing, he had to wash his body with water. These garments are called holy garments.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Aaron about the Day of Atonement. Aaron could not enter the most holy place whenever he wished, because there the presence of God was revealed. The plain linen clothing and the washing show respect, purity, and humility when approaching Him.

For today: draw near to God with reverence and sincerity, without carelessness. Today we do not need special clothing; Christians believe that Christ opens the way for us. Even so, praying with a clean and humble heart is a good way to present ourselves before God.
exp.15:4:
This verse says that the people of Israel were to bring two male goats for the sin offering, that is, to take away sin, and one ram for the burnt offering, an offering that was burned whole as a total surrender to God. A male goat is a billy goat.

God speaks to Moses after the death of Aaron's sons, and He gives him instructions for the Day of Atonement. Aaron already had his own bull calf for his sin, but now the congregation also brings its share. The text shows that sin affected the whole people, and that God provided a way for them to be cleansed and reconciled to Him.

For today: do not downplay sin or try to cover it on your own. God has always provided the way of forgiveness. For Christians, that way is fulfilled in Christ. Come to Him with humility and sincerity.
exp.15:6:
Aarón, the high priest, must take the two male goats that the people brought and stand them before God, at the entrance of the tabernacle, which is called here the tabernacle of the congregation because it held the tablets of the law. Presenting them means placing them before the Lord.

God speaks to Moses, after the death of Aaron's sons, to teach how the Day of Atonement was to be observed. First Aaron made an offering for himself and his family, and then for the people. This moment prepares the casting of lots that follows. The meaning of the name Azazel is explained in several ways, and there is no full agreement.

For today: no one draws near to God lightly. We can come with humility, acknowledging our need for forgiveness, and give thanks that, according to the New Testament, Christ opened the way to God for us.
exp.15:7:
Aaron, the high priest, was to cast lots over two male goats. One lot was for the Lord, and the other was for the scapegoat. Casting lots was something like drawing names, so that the choice did not depend on human preference. The meaning of the word for the scapegoat is uncertain: some think it is the name of a place or of the act of being sent away; others think it refers to a spiritual being of the wilderness.

God speaks to Moses about the Day of Atonement, the most solemn day in Israel. Aaron first offered a young bull for himself and his household, and then the sin of the people was dealt with. One goat was sacrificed, and the other, loaded with the people's sins, was sent alive into the wilderness. Both showed forgiveness and the removal of guilt.

For today: Christians see in Christ the fulfillment of both images, since He paid for sin and took it away from us. Today you can confess your guilt honestly and rest in the fact that God truly forgives.
exp.15:8:
This verse says that Aaron, the high priest, is to bring the goat on which the lot for the Lord had fallen when the lots were cast. That animal would be offered as a sin offering, that is, as a sacrifice to cover sin.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the Day of Atonement. Aaron casts lots over two goats: one is for the Lord and the other is for Azazel. The second is sent alive into the wilderness. The exact meaning of the name Azazel is explained in several ways, and it is not known for certain.

For today: forgiveness has a serious cost, and God himself shows the way to receive it. We can draw near to him with humility, trusting in his provision and not in our own merits.
exp.15:9:
The second goat, the one chosen by lot to be the scapegoat, is not killed. It is presented alive before the Lord, the atonement is made over it (the act of cleansing and removing guilt), and then it is sent away into the wilderness. The name of the goat is a hard word in Hebrew: some believe it means the goat that goes away, others a remote place, and others a being of the wilderness.

God speaks to Moses about the Day of Atonement, when Aaron, the high priest, cleansed the sanctuary and the people from their sins. The two goats showed two sides of the same work: one died for sin, and the other carried the guilt far away.

For today: God does not only forgive, he also removes sin far from us. If you find it hard to believe that God has forgiven you, remember that Christ bore your guilt so that you need not live under it. Rest in that forgiveness and walk in freedom.
exp.15:12:
This verse says that Aaron, the high priest, was to place the incense on the coals before God. The fragrant smoke would cover the mercy seat (the lid of the ark, also called the atonement cover), which was above the testimony, that is, the tablets of the law. In this way, Aaron would not die.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the Day of Atonement. Aaron entered the most holy place once a year. The cloud of incense served as a protection when approaching a holy God. Many understand that it also symbolizes prayer and reverence.

For today: come near to God with respect, but with confidence. According to the New Testament, Jesus opened the way fully (Hebrews 10:19-22). Before praying, pause and give thanks that you can come to God through Christ.
exp.15:13:
It says that the high priest, after killing the bull, would take some of its blood and sprinkle it with his finger on the mercy seat (the lid of the ark of the covenant), on the east side. Then he would sprinkle it seven times in front of it.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Aaron about the Day of Atonement. First the priest offered blood for himself and his household, and then for the people. He would enter behind the veil with incense so that he would not die. The blood showed that sin is serious and needs atonement.

For today: Christians see in this a shadow of Christ, whose blood gives us access to God (Hebrews 9–10). We can draw near with humility and gratitude, without presumption or fleeing in fear, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.15:15:
He says that the high priest was to purify the holy place, or sanctuary, from everything that had defiled it: the uncleanness of the Israelites, their rebellions, and all their sins. He was to do the same for the tabernacle of the congregation, the tent where God's presence was and the tablets of the law.

God speaks to Moses to show how Aaron was to carry out the Day of Atonement. On that day the blood of the bull and of the male goat was used. God lived in the midst of a sinful people, and so he needed a way for that nearness not to end in judgment.

For today: we should not take sin lightly, but neither should we forget that God offers forgiveness. Christians see in Christ the fulfillment of this rite (Hebrews 9). Today we can draw near to God with sincerity and confidence.
exp.15:16:
This verse says that no one could be inside the tabernacle while the high priest went into the most holy place to make the reconciliation, which is the act of cleansing and restoring the relationship with God. He had to make it for himself, for his household, and for all of Israel.

God gives these instructions to Moses for Aaron, in the ritual of the Day of Atonement. Aaron went in alone, with the blood of the sacrifice, because the sin of the people defiled even the place where God dwelled. No one else could help him at that moment.

For today: many Christians see here a foreshadowing of Jesus, who did alone the work that we could not do. You can rest in the knowledge that your forgiveness does not depend on your efforts, and you can draw near to God with gratitude and confidence.
exp.15:17:
He goes out of the Most Holy Place to the altar that is before the Lord. There he will make an atonement, that is, he will cleanse the altar to remove its uncleanness. He will take blood from the bullock and from the goat and put it on the horns of the altar, on all its sides.

God speaks to Moses about the Day of Atonement. On that day, once a year, the whole place of worship was cleansed, because the sin of the people also defiled it. The blood showed that sin is serious and that forgiveness has a cost.

For today: do not minimize sin or come near to God carelessly. Christians believe that Christ offered his blood once for all to forgive us (Hebrews 9:11-14). Therefore you can draw near to God with humility, gratitude, and confidence.
exp.15:18:
It says that the high priest took blood from the sacrificed animals and sprinkled it seven times with his finger on the altar. With this he made it clean and holy, that is, he purified it and set it apart for God. The impurities are the uncleanness and sins of the people, which affected even the place of worship.

God speaks to Moses about the Day of Atonement, and Aaron acts as high priest. It was the day when reconciliation was made for the sanctuary, the priests and all Israel. The number seven is often seen as a number of completeness, although the text does not explain it. Then comes the goat that is sent into the wilderness.

For today: sin is serious, and God provides a way to cleanse us. Christians see in this blood a shadow of Christ (Hebrews 9). We can approach God with confidence and sincerity, without hiding our faults.
exp.15:20:
Aaron, the high priest, lays both his hands on the head of a live male goat. He confesses over it all the wickedness of the people, their rebellions (their open acts of disobedience), and their sins. In this way he symbolically places them on the animal. Then a man appointed for the task leads it away into the wilderness.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the Day of Atonement. First the sanctuary was cleansed with blood. Then, with this second male goat, it was shown that sin was taken away and carried far from the people. It is a symbolic picture, not a punishment for the animal.

Today we can confess our sins sincerely, without hiding or excusing them. Many Christians see in this rite a shadow of Christ, who bore our sin. We can rest in the fact that God truly forgives.
exp.15:23:
Aaron, the high priest, was to bathe with water in a holy place. Then he put on his priestly garments and came out to offer two burnt offerings, one for himself and one for the people. A burnt offering was an offering that was burned whole on the altar. Atonement means cleansing from guilt to restore the relationship with God. Flesh here means his body.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the Day of Atonement. The goat that had been loaded with the people's sins had already been sent out into the wilderness. Aaron had taken off the linen garments to enter the most holy place. Now he prepares again to serve before all the people. He first had to be clean himself in order to intercede for others.

For today: before you serve or help others, recognize your own need for forgiveness. Come before God with humility, knowing that He cleanses and restores.
exp.15:25:
The person who led the goat away into the wilderness, for Azazel, had to wash his clothes and bathe with water. Only after that could he return to the camp.

God speaks to Moses, and the passage explains the Day of Atonement. The goat symbolically carried the sins of the people and was sent far away. The one who led it away became ceremonially unclean from touching something associated with that burden. There are several interpretations of who or what Azazel is: a desolate place, a term for the removal of sin, or a spiritual being. The text does not fully clarify this.

For today: God takes sin seriously and also cleansing. When you serve in difficult situations, do not stop seeking cleansing and rest in God. Christ carried our sins once and for all.
exp.15:26:
This verse says that the young bull (the calf) and the male goat offered for sin were taken outside the camp. Their blood had already been brought into the sanctuary to make atonement, that is, to cover the sin and cleanse. Outside the camp, the skins, the flesh, and the dung were burned up completely.

God speaks to Moses about the Day of Atonement, when the high priest made offerings for his own sins and for the sins of the people. Carrying out and burning what remained showed that sin had to be removed and set apart from the holy community. The Bible does not explain every detail of the ritual, so some points are understood in different ways.

For today: sin is serious and is not dealt with halfway. Hebrews 13:11-12 connects this passage with Jesus, who suffered outside the gate. We can thank Him and come to Him with confidence.
exp.15:29:
This verse says that on the Day of Atonement, God provides a means of making things right with his people. The word "atonement" here means making atonement, that is, covering over or taking away guilt. The phrase about being made clean speaks of becoming pure. The result is that, before the Lord, the people are cleansed from all their sins.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Israel. This day, the tenth day of the seventh month, was a solemn day of rest and of humbling oneself before God. The anointed priest made the sacrifices and entered the holy place on behalf of the people. The cleansing came from what God had established, not from the merits of the people.

For today: if you carry guilt, you do not have to make yourself clean through your own efforts. Christians see in Christ the fulfillment of this day. Come near to God with humility and sincerity, and trust in his forgiveness.
exp.15:31:
This verse says that the priest who has been anointed and set apart to serve in place of his father, that is, the high priest who follows in that office, will be the one who makes atonement. "Atonement" means covering sin to restore the relationship with God. The phrase about having his hand filled means he was formally placed into his office. He would put on sacred clothes made of plain linen.

God speaks to Moses to explain the Day of Atonement. Once a year, a single priest represented all of Israel before God. The plain linen, instead of the ornate vestments, suggests humility when approaching God, though the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: Christians see in Jesus the definitive high priest, who reconciles us with God (Hebrews 9–10). We can approach God with humility and confidence, without trying to earn forgiveness by our own merits.
exp.16:2:
This verse begins a law for the Israelites. It says that any man of Israel who killed an ox, a lamb, or a goat, whether in the camp or outside it, was to do what follows. The full instruction is understood with the verses that come after.

God speaks to Moses and tells him to pass this on to Aaron, to his sons, and to all the people. It was a time when Israel lived in the desert, with the tabernacle at the center. According to the verses that follow, the reason was that the animals were to be brought to the sanctuary as an offering to the LORD and not slaughtered in the open field, a place associated with practices foreign to the people's faith. Scholars discuss how this rule was applied in detail.

For today: God wants to be at the center of the everyday, not only of the religious. We can ask ourselves which ordinary things of our lives, such as our work, our food, or our money, we are living without taking Him into account, and offer them to Him with gratitude.
exp.16:4:
This verse explains the purpose of the law before it. God wanted the Israelites to stop offering sacrifices out in the open country, and to bring them to the entrance of the tent of meeting, where the priest was. There they were to present them as peace offerings, offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving. Offering them to the Lord means offering them to the Lord Himself.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Aaron, his sons, and the whole people. According to the next verse, the reason was that they were not to keep offering sacrifices to demons, as they had done before. Many understand this to refer to idolatrous practices learned from other peoples. The text gives no further detail about what those practices were.

For today: God wants our worship to be directed by Him, not by our own customs or by influences around us. We can ask ourselves whether our way of seeking Him is centered on His will and on gratitude.
exp.16:5:
It says that when someone brought a peace offering, the priest was to sprinkle the blood on the altar of the Lord, at the entrance of the tabernacle. Then he would burn the fat as a pleasing aroma, an expression that speaks of an offering that was pleasing to God.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Aaron, his sons, and all Israel. Before this, some people were killing animals in the field, and the text says they were offering them to demons. God asks that every sacrifice be brought to the priest and to the altar, to protect the people from idolatry and to teach them to approach Him as He had directed.

For today: let us come near to God with sincerity and according to His Word, not according to our own ideas. For Christians, Christ is the open way to God, and we can pray with confidence and gratitude.
exp.16:7:
This verse begins a new instruction from God. Moses must tell the people that the rule applies to any Israelite man and also to the foreigners who lived among them. This verse says they lived as outsiders. The rule concerns whoever offers a burnt offering (an offering completely burned up) or a sacrifice. The sentence is left open and is completed in the following verse.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses must pass it on to Aaron, his sons, and all Israel. Shortly before, it had been forbidden to sacrifice in the open field, and idolatry with false spirits was mentioned. For this reason God asks that every offering be brought to the door of the tent of meeting, where He had indicated. Scholars understand this as protection against false worship.

For today: worshiping God is not a matter of doing it my own way, but of coming to Him with sincerity and according to His Word. Today we do this by trusting in Christ, our complete sacrifice.
exp.16:8:
It says that if anyone, whether an Israelite or a foreigner who lives among them, offers a burnt offering or sacrifice and does not bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting (the tent where God met with his people) to present it to the Lord, he will be "cut off from his people." That phrase means being separated from the community; interpreters debate whether it implied death, banishment, or a punishment from God.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct Israel. Some were offering sacrifices in the open country and had tied them to idolatrous practices. God wants his worship to be orderly, in the place he designated, and for everyone to live it the same way.

For today: worshiping God is not doing it my own way, but drawing near as he has shown, today through Christ, with a sincere and obedient heart.
exp.16:10:
It says that the life of every living creature is in the blood. God himself gave it upon the altar to make atonement for the people, that is, to cover their sin and restore their relationship with him. For this reason the blood of the sacrifice was the means of that atonement.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in the law concerning sacrifices. He forbids them to eat blood and to offer sacrifices outside the tabernacle, because the blood was holy. He wanted them to see sin as something serious, and forgiveness as a gift from him, not something they earned.

For today: Christians understand that this thought reaches its fulfillment in Christ, according to Hebrews 9. Today we can give sincere thanks for that forgiveness, and live with humility, trusting that God has already provided the way to return to him.
exp.16:12:
It says that if an Israelite, or a foreigner who lived among them, hunted an animal or a bird that could be eaten, he had to let its blood pour out and cover it with dust.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in the laws about the altar and the blood. Earlier he said that life is in the blood and that he gave it to make atonement on the altar. For that reason the blood was treated with respect, even in hunting, where there was no sacrifice. Scholars do not fully agree on why it was covered with earth, but the act shows respect for life.

For today: we can learn to treat life as something sacred that comes from God, being thankful for food and avoiding waste or cruelty.
exp.16:14:
It says that if anyone, whether an Israelite or a foreigner, eats the meat of an animal that was already dead or that was torn apart by a wild beast, they must wash their clothes, bathe in water, and be unclean until evening. After that, they are clean. A dead animal that died on its own, without being slaughtered, is what is meant here.

God speaks to Moses for the people. The chapter deals with the value of blood and of life. An animal that died without being properly drained of its blood meant eating blood, which was forbidden. Here the failure is not punished harshly; a clear path to cleansing is offered. Scholars explain the exact meaning of uncleanness in various ways, but all see a call to respect life and to holiness.

For today: when we fail, we should not hide. God always offers a way back to Him. Let us acknowledge the mistake, seek cleansing, and move forward with humility.
exp.16:15:
It says that whoever eats something that died on its own or was torn by a wild animal, and does not wash his clothes and bathe himself, will bear his guilt. The verse you are reading is clear: the person who neglects washing is the one who carries the consequence.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, within the laws about blood and what may be eaten. Those animals had not been drained of blood properly, and that brought ritual impurity. Washing was a simple step to become clean again and not neglect what is holy. Neglecting it was no longer just an accident, but disobedience.

For today: when we recognize a fault, we should not let it pass as if nothing happened. It is good to turn to God soon, confess, and ask for cleansing, trusting that He forgives. As 1 John 1:9 says, if we confess our sins, He is faithful to forgive us and to cleanse us.
exp.17:1:
God asks Moses to speak with the people of Israel and remind them who He is: "I am the Lord your God." The words that are quoted here are in the verse above, so no word needs to be explained or rewritten.

God speaks, and Moses is the messenger. Israel had left Egypt and was heading toward Canaan. Before giving them rules for daily life, God begins with His identity and with the relationship He has with them. The verses that follow explain that they should not imitate the customs of the surrounding peoples, but should follow God's commands.

For today: before we ask what we should do, it is good to remember whose we are. If God is our God, His voice carries more weight than the trends or customs around us. Today you can begin your day by remembering that the Lord is your God, and by asking Him to guide your decisions.
exp.17:8:
This verse forbids sexual relations with one's own sister.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct Israel before they enter Canaan. In this chapter He asks them not to live as the peoples of Egypt and Canaan live. The list of prohibitions protects the family, and the text presents it as part of the holiness of God's people.

For today: let us care for healthy boundaries within the family. The home should be a safe place, where no one is used or harmed. If someone has suffered abuse, seeking help and protection is also an act of obedience and care.
exp.17:23:
The people of Israel were told not to defile themselves with any of the forbidden sexual practices mentioned earlier. "Defile" means to stain or dishonor, and "the nations" are the peoples around them. God explains that those nations had defiled themselves with these behaviors, and that is why he was driving them out of the land.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, before they enter Canaan. He gives them rules to be a people distinct from the neighboring peoples. The text presents the removal of those nations as a consequence of their wickedness, and also as a warning to Israel, which would not be immune if it did the same.

For today: it is not enough to simply go along with the culture around us. We can ask God to help us examine which customs we accept without thinking, and to live with purity and respect, trusting that his ways seek our good.
exp.17:26:
This verse explains that the peoples who lived in Canaan before Israel practiced all the abominations, that is, very wicked conduct in the eyes of God, which are mentioned in this chapter. For this reason the land was defiled, that is, morally stained. The word that appears here was once written differently, and today we would write it simply as the common past tense of the verb.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. Before they enter the promised land, he warns them not to imitate the practices of those peoples. God judged them for their wickedness, and he wants Israel to live differently, as a holy people.

For today: it is not enough for something to be common or accepted around us for it to be right. We can ask ourselves which customs around us we should examine in the light of God's Word, and ask him for help to live with integrity and love.
exp.17:28:
This verse says that whoever practices any of these "abominations" (things God considers detestable, mentioned in this chapter, such as sexual immorality and idolatry) will be "cut off" from their people. The phrase "cut off" means separated or excluded from the community of Israel. Some believe it may include the death penalty; others, expulsion. The text does not make this clear here.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, before they enter Canaan. He warns them not to imitate the customs of the peoples who lived there, because those practices defiled the land. He wants his people to be different and to live in holiness.

For today: ask yourself which customs around you pull you away from God. Decide, with love and firmness, to live differently, trusting that his ways protect your life and your relationships.
exp.18:0:
This verse says that the Lord, that is, God, spoke to Moses. The short phrase serves as an introduction: God is about to give a message, and Moses is to carry it to the people.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the messenger. This phrase is repeated many times in Leviticus to introduce the instructions God gave Israel after bringing them out of Egypt. Here begins a section about how to live as a people set apart for God, and that is why the next verse says: "Be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy."

For today: before giving instructions, God communicates with his people. We can take a short time each day to read the Bible carefully, with the attitude of someone who wants to listen to what God says to them and put it into practice.
exp.18:3:
This verse says that the people must not turn to idols, that is, to images or objects given the place of God. Nor should they make gods of cast metal, meaning figures made from molten metal that has been poured into a mold. Here "turn" means to go to them seeking help. At the end, God introduces himself: "I am the Lord your God."

God speaks to Moses so that he will tell the whole congregation of Israel to be holy, because God is holy. Just before this, the passage mentions honoring parents and keeping the sabbaths. After this verse come rules about sacrifices. Idolatry was a real temptation for Israel, surrounded by peoples with other gods.

Today we can ask ourselves what things occupy God's place in our hearts, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Put God first and trust in him.
exp.18:5:
This verse says that the meat of the peace offering had to be eaten on the same day it was offered or on the following day. If anything was left over until the third day, it had to be burned.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Israel. Just before this, He warns them against idols, and then He explains how to offer this sacrifice willingly. It was a shared meal eaten with joy before the Lord. The verses that follow say that eating it on the third day made it unacceptable. The Bible does not explain the exact reason; some think the aim was to keep it from spoiling or to prevent the holy thing from being treated carelessly, but this is interpretation.

Today we can learn not to put off what we owe to God. If He asks us for gratitude, obedience, or forgiveness, let us do it with a willing heart and at the right time.
exp.18:9:
It says that when harvesting the grapes, the owner must not go back a second time to gather everything that was left, nor pick up the grapes that fell to the ground. Going back over the rows to leave nothing behind is what is forbidden. Those leftovers were to be left for the poor and for the stranger, that is, the foreigner who lived among them without land of his own.

God himself speaks to Israel through Moses. These laws are in a section that teaches how to live in holiness, and they are commanded together with the care of the grain field. The words "I am the Lord your God" remind them that helping the needy is not merely good manners, but obedience to the God who cares for all of them.

Today we can set aside a margin in our finances and our time to help others. For example, setting aside a fixed portion of what we earn to share with a person or family in need, without expecting anything in return.
exp.18:17:
This verse commands not to take revenge or hold a grudge against the people of your own community. Instead, it orders you to love your neighbor as yourself. "Grudge" is that resentment that stays stored up because of an offense. "Neighbor" is the person who lives near you. The phrase "I am the Lord" works like a signature: God himself stands behind the command.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. He gives them laws for living as a holy people set apart for him. Just before this verse, he speaks against gossip and hatred in the heart, and about correcting others frankly. Here love becomes concrete in everyday relationships. Jesus quoted this command as one of the most important (Matthew 22:39).

Today, if someone has wronged you, ask God to help you let go of the grudge. Think of one simple act of kindness toward that person: a prayer, a greeting, or a kind word.
exp.18:18:
God calls Israel to keep his statutes. Within that call, the verse forbids crossbreeding two different kinds of livestock, sowing a field with two kinds of seed, and wearing clothing made of two kinds of material.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, within the law that calls his people to be holy. The text does not explain the exact reason for these rules. Some see them as a sign that Israel was to live set apart and in good order; others see a lesson about not mixing what God has separated. It is interpreted in several ways.

For today: although we do not live under these rules, we can learn to obey God in small things too, and to live with a clear loyalty and without duplicity, as in the love for neighbor that the previous verse mentions.
exp.18:23:
After three years in which the fruit of a newly planted tree could not be eaten, the harvest of the fourth year was to be set apart for the Lord. What is set apart for praise is holy to praise the Lord, an offering of thanks and celebration.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. The fruit of the first three years was not fit to be used. After that, the fourth year belonged to God and the fifth year to the people. Some believe the text teaches us to put God first and trust in his provision.

For today: before enjoying what we receive, we can give thanks and set apart a portion for God, whether time, money, or help for others, recognizing that every good thing comes from him.
exp.18:28:
It says that a father must not defile his daughter by pushing her into prostitution. Here "defile" means to profane or degrade, and "prostitute" is the sense of the word. If this were allowed, the whole land would be corrupted and filled with wickedness.

God (Jehovah) speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, within the laws of holiness. He wanted his people to be different from the neighboring nations. Some scholars think it also refers to prostitution connected with pagan worship, but the text does not make this clear. It is surrounded by commands against idolatrous practices.

For today: parents and those who care for others must protect the dignity of children, never take advantage of them or push them into situations that harm them. Caring for the most vulnerable also protects the whole community.
exp.19:3:
It says that if the people of the land look the other way and do not punish a man who has given one of his children, his offspring, to Molech, and do not have him put to death, they too become guilty. To look the other way means to pretend you did not see.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. Molech was a pagan god to whom children were offered, and scholars debate the exact details of the rite. God treats it as a most serious sin, because it defiles his sanctuary and dishonors his name. Furthermore, the whole community was responsible for not tolerating it.

For today: do not turn a blind eye to injustice and harm to the most defenseless, especially children. With prudence, prayer, and the lawful means available to you, defend those who cannot defend themselves.
exp.19:9:
The verse says that if a man commits adultery with another man's wife, meaning his neighbor's wife, both he and she must be put to death. The words "surely be put to death" mean that the penalty must certainly be carried out.

God speaks to Moses so that he will pass these laws on to Israel, which had just been formed as a people. The passage begins by calling them to keep his statutes because he sets them apart as holy. These laws protected marriage and the holiness of the community under the covenant. It is a law given to Israel in its ancient setting, and Christians read it in the light of Christ, who forgave the woman caught in adultery but also called her to sin no more (John 8).

Today we can take marital faithfulness seriously: guarding the friendships, conversations, and habits that weaken commitment, and asking God for help to honor our spouse.
exp.19:21:
God tells Israel to keep all his laws and put them into practice. His commands and fair rules are what the verse calls his statutes and judgments. To do them means to obey them in real life, not just to know them. The image of the land spewing them out is a strong one: the land would reject a people who live in wickedness. God promises that they will dwell in the land he gives them.

God speaks through Moses, before Israel enters Canaan. He has just given laws about sexual morality and family life. He explains that the peoples of that land did these things, and that is why God will drive them out. Israel was to be different, a people set apart for him.

Today we can remember that obeying God is not an empty burden but a path of life and blessing. Ask yourself: is there some command that I know but am still not putting into practice? Today, take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.19:22:
God tells Israel not to live according to the customs of the peoples whom he is about to drive out of Canaan. To live or behave is what is meant here. The customs of those peoples are what God is speaking about. God rejects these things deeply. He explains that those peoples did the things forbidden in this chapter, and that is why he rejected them.

God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. The whole chapter lists forbidden conduct, above all in matters of morality and worship, together with its consequences. God wants Israel to be a people set apart, different from the neighboring nations, and he warns them that the land itself would suffer because of such conduct.

For today: ask yourself which customs around you you accept without thinking, even though they do not please God. Choose one and, with God's help, decide to live differently, with love and firmness, without despising anyone.
exp.19:23:
God reminds the Israelites of what he had already promised them: that they would inherit the land of the peoples who lived there, a land that flows with milk and honey, meaning fertile and abundant. The word "but" introduces the contrast with what came before, and an inheritance is a possession received as a gift. God tells them that he has set them apart from the other peoples, that is, he has separated them for himself.

God speaks through Moses, at the end of a long list of laws about moral conduct and purity. He warns them not to imitate the practices of the peoples of Canaan, which God considered detestable. The land was a gift, but living well in it depended on obedience. Being set apart meant living differently.

For today: God gives us his grace first and then calls us to live differently. Today you can choose one habit or attitude that does not reflect God's character and, with his help, change it.
exp.20:0:
This verse tells how God spoke to Moses so that he would tell the priests, the descendants of Aaron, that they must not become defiled because of a dead person among their people. Becoming defiled here means becoming ritually unclean, something that happened when a person touched a corpse or took part in mourning rites. It is not a sin, but a condition that kept them from serving in worship for a time.

The Lord is speaking, and the message is for the priests. They served in the holy presence of God, so they were asked to take special care. The next verse makes clear that they could still draw near to their closest relatives. That is why the rule concerns the duty of the priesthood, not a lack of affection.

For today: those who serve others need to care for their lives with attention and reverence. We can also learn that God understands human grief, since he allows mourning for loved ones.
exp.20:3:
This verse says that the priest was not to make himself unclean (become defiled by touching a dead body) for just any person. The verse is hard to translate, and scholars interpret it in several ways. Even so, the central idea is that his position required greater care.

God speaks to Moses to give rules for the priests, the sons of Aaron. Earlier he had allowed one exception: they could become unclean through their closest relatives. Then he calls for holiness, because they presented the offerings to God. Those rules reminded them that serving God was something sacred.

Today, whoever leads others, in the church or in the home, should watch their conduct with even greater attention. Ask God for help to live with integrity, so that your example honors his name.
exp.20:4:
This verse says that the priests, the sons of Aaron, were not to make bald patches on their heads, nor trim the edges of their beards, nor make cuttings in their flesh. Shaving off the corner of the beard and making bald spots are the practices described here, and the cuttings are wounds made on the body.

God speaks to Moses to instruct the priests. These acts were connected with mourning rites, and many scholars think they were customs of neighboring peoples, although the text gives no details. That is why the passage keeps speaking of holiness: the priests offered God's bread and were to represent it with dignity.

For today: God cares how we express our grief and who we say we are. We may weep freely, but without losing hope or forgetting that we belong to God. May our way of living, even in sorrow, reflect trust in Him.
exp.20:8:
It says that if a priest's daughter began to prostitute herself, she would bring dishonor on her father. The punishment was to be burned. It is a very severe law to our ears.

God speaks to Moses about the holiness of the priests, who offered God's bread. Their family was meant to reflect that holiness, because the priest represented God before the people. This was part of the law given to Israel in its time. Scholars debate the details of how it was applied, but it is clear that the sin of a relative of a leader carried special weight.

For today: as Christians we do not live under this law, since Christ fulfilled the law and gave us grace. Even so, the passage reminds us that our conduct affects others and the name of God. We can live with integrity and also treat with compassion those who have fallen.
exp.20:9:
This verse speaks of the high priest, the one who was anointed with oil on his head and set apart to wear the holy garments. The verse asks that he not uncover his head (probably meaning he should not let his hair hang loose, as a sign of mourning) nor tear his clothes, which was another custom of grief.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Aaron and his sons. Since the high priest represented the people before God, his life had to show the holiness of the service. For this reason he is asked to keep stricter rules than the others, even in mourning. Scholars explain the exact meaning of these signs of mourning in various ways.

For today: if God has entrusted us with some responsibility, let us seek to live it with seriousness and by example. We may feel pain, but without neglecting the call to serve with integrity.
exp.20:10:
It says that the high priest was not to go near any dead body, not even that of his father or his mother. The phrase about becoming unclean means that he would be ceremonially impure, not that he had done anything wrong. The word about being disgraced or stained means dishonor or defilement.

God speaks to Moses to give rules to the priests of Israel. The high priest had been anointed and set apart to serve in the sanctuary. For that reason he was asked to take greater care than the other priests. Death stood in contrast to the holiness and the life of God, and his service was not to be interrupted. Some scholars see here a teaching about total devotion to one's calling.

For today: when God entrusts us with a task, it is worth asking ourselves which things, even good ones, distract us from it. Let us ask for wisdom to order our priorities with love and faithfulness.
exp.20:14:
It says that the high priest must not profane his seed, that is, he must not defile or dishonor his children and descendants among his people. The reason is that the Lord is the one who sanctifies them, that is, who sets them apart for Himself.

God speaks through Moses, giving special rules for the high priest of Israel. Because of his service in the tabernacle, his life and his family were to show the set-apart character of God. Scholars explain the exact sense of these rules in several ways, but all agree that they emphasize the holiness of the priesthood.

For today: our decisions affect those who come after us. We can take care of the example we set at home, trusting that God is the one who sanctifies us and helps us live in a way that honors our family.
exp.20:15:
This verse is only an introductory phrase. It says that God spoke to Moses, and that right after this He is going to give him a new instruction.

God Himself is speaking. He is giving Moses rules to pass on to Aaron and the priests, who served in the tabernacle. In this chapter, God asks them to be careful and reverent in their service, because they were drawing near to holy things. What follows deals with who could offer the bread of God. Scholars explain the meaning of these rules in various ways, and it is good to read them in light of God's whole plan.

For today: God speaks clearly and wants to be heard. Before reading the Bible, we can pray with humility and ask Him to speak to us, knowing that He makes Himself known and guides us with care.
exp.20:17:
This verse says that no man with a physical defect could come near to offer the bread of God. It gives examples: the blind man, the lame man, the one with a deformity in his face (the flat nose) or a limb that is too long (the superfluous part). The word "approach" means to come near. Some of the Hebrew words in this list are difficult, and translators do not always agree on them.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses is to tell Aaron. It refers to Aaron's descendants who served as priests. The rule did not say these people were worth less: they still ate of the holy offerings (v. 22). Many understand that the priesthood was meant to reflect the perfection and holiness of God, though not everyone explains this in the same way.

For today: in Christ, all of us can draw near to God with confidence (Hebrews 4:16). May this move us to receive every person in the church with honor, regardless of their limitations.
exp.21:3:
This verse says that a priest descended from Aaron could not eat of the holy offerings if he had leprosy, a discharge or flow from the body, or if he had touched something unclean, such as an animal that had died on its own, or if he had had a seminal emission. He had to wait until he was clean. A dead animal is one that died by itself.

God speaks to Moses and tells him to speak to Aaron and his sons. The priests handled what was dedicated to God, and for that reason they had to take care of their ritual purity. These rules were not about personal sin, but about teaching Israel that God is holy and that approaching Him is done with reverence.

For today: drawing near to God is not something casual. Before we pray or worship, we can stop, confess what gets in our way, and receive the forgiveness that Christ offers, knowing that He cleanses us.
exp.21:5:
It says that any priest who had touched something that made him unclean (such as a dead animal, a reptile, or an unclean person) remained unclean until evening. Before eating the holy things, that is, the offerings that belonged to the priests, he had to wash his body with water. A dead animal, as referred to here, is one that died on its own.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Aaron and his sons, the priests. He teaches them to treat with respect what is set apart for Him. These rules of ceremonial purity reminded them that God is holy and that approaching Him was not a casual matter. It was not about sin, but about order and reverence.

For today: God still deserves respect when we draw near to Him. Before we pray, worship, or take part in the Lord's Supper, we can pause for a moment, acknowledge our failings, and ask Him to cleanse us, trusting that Christ purifies us.
exp.21:7:
This verse says that the priest could not eat meat from an animal that had died on its own, nor from one that wild beasts had torn apart. Eating it would make him unclean. It closes by reminding the reader who gives the command, the Lord.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Aaron and his sons, the priests. They ate part of the holy offerings, so they had to take care of their purity. In the law of Moses, an animal that died without being sacrificed was considered unclean. These rules set the priests apart for the service of God.

For today: if God calls us to a life set apart for him, it is worth taking care of what we let into our minds and hearts. It is not to earn his favor, but to respond with respect to the one who loves us and makes us holy.
exp.21:13:
It says that if someone eats by mistake something that had been set apart for God, which only the priests and their families could eat, that person must make it right. He had to return what he ate and add a fifth part more (twenty percent), and hand the whole amount over to the priest. The words "error" (in the sense of a mistake or oversight) and "fifth" are explained in the verse itself: the added portion is one fifth of the value.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Aaron and the priests about caring for Israel's holy offerings. These offerings belonged to God, and so they were to be handled with respect. Even a careless act done without bad intent required restitution, because what is holy must not be treated as ordinary.

For today: God cares about our mistakes, not only about our bad intentions. When we make a mistake and affect someone or neglect something that belongs to God, the healthy response is to acknowledge it and make things right generously, without excuses.
exp.21:15:
It says that the people should not be allowed to bear the guilt of sin for eating the holy things, that is, the offerings set apart for the priests. The phrase about bearing the guilt means bearing the consequences of the wrong. The phrase about God making them holy means that God sets them apart for himself.

Here the Lord speaks to Moses and gives instructions about the sacred offerings. The verses before explain that if someone ate something holy by mistake, they had to make it right by giving back an additional fifth. The text is somewhat difficult, and there are different ways to understand exactly who "them" refers to, but the general sense is to protect respect for what has been consecrated.

For today: God calls us to treat with reverence what belongs to him. We can take our worship seriously, and if we fail without meaning to, we can make it right with humility, trusting that he is the one who makes us holy.
exp.21:17:
God tells Moses to speak with Aaron, his sons, and all the people. It refers to any Israelite, or to a foreigner living among them, who wanted to bring an offering to the Lord. It might be to fulfill a promise (a vow) or simply out of a desire to give (a freewill offering). The burnt offering is the offering that was burned whole on the altar.

The Lord speaks to Moses right after instructing the priests on how to care for the holy things. Now the instruction reaches all the people. Foreigners could also make offerings, though under the same rules. What follows explains that the animal had to be without defect.

For today: God values the giving that comes from the heart, and he asks us to give him our best, not our leftovers. Think about your time, your money, or your strength: do you offer them to him gladly and sincerely?
exp.21:23:
This verse forbids offering to the Lord animals that are injured, bruised, or crushed, or that are cut or mutilated. It adds that such offerings were not to be made anywhere in the land where the people lived. Some understand it to include the castration of animals; others take it to refer only to animals that were damaged. The text is not entirely clear on that point.

God speaks to Moses to instruct the priests and the people of Israel about the offerings. The animals had to be without defect, as a sign of respect, honor, and sincere devotion to God. To offer what was damaged was to treat God as someone who deserves less.

Today we do not offer animals, but we can still ask ourselves what we give to God: the best of our time, affection, and resources, or only what we have left over? Today you can set aside a quality moment to pray and give thanks.
exp.21:31:
It says that the people must not "profane" God's name, that is, stain it, dishonor it, or treat his holy name lightly. God adds that he will be sanctified, or treated as holy, among Israel. And he reminds them that it is he who makes holy, or sets apart for himself, his people.

God speaks through Moses, addressing Aaron, his sons, and all Israel. This passage deals with offerings and sacrifices, which were to be presented with care and reverence. Obeying the commandments was a way of honoring his name. Then God reminds them that he brought them out of Egypt to be their God.

For today: let us take care how we live and how we speak of God. If we say that we belong to him, let our words, promises, and actions not make him look bad. We can start today by faithfully keeping something we promised.
exp.21:32:
It says that God brought Israel out of Egypt with a purpose: to be their God. The word that brought you out refers to leading them out of the land. The name of the Lord is revealed as the one who sets people free. At the end it repeats the words I am the Lord, like a signature that reminds us who is speaking and with what authority.

God speaks to Moses, so that he may tell it to Aaron, his sons, and all Israel. These laws about the offerings and the holiness of the priests end by recalling the deliverance. Their obedience does not come from fear, but from the fact that God has already rescued them. To profane means to defile or dishonor.

For today: before asking anything of us, God has shown us his love and his rescue. When you obey, remember that you do not do it to earn his affection, but as a response to what he has already done for you. Live today in such a way that his name is honored.
exp.22:2:
It says the people were to work for six days, but the seventh day would be a sabbath, that is, a day of complete rest. It was a holy convocation, meaning a gathering set apart for God. No work was to be done on it, and this applied in all their dwellings, meaning wherever they lived.

God speaks to Moses so that he will repeat it to Israel. Before listing the yearly feasts, such as Passover, he first mentions the sabbath, which came around every week. It was a sign that the people's time belonged to God.

For today: set aside a regular time to rest and remember that God sustains your life, not your effort. Turn off the rush, pray, meet with other believers, and trust that He provides. Christians understand in different ways how to apply the sabbath, but all can learn the value of resting in God.
exp.22:5:
It says that on the fifteenth day of the first month begins the feast of unleavened bread, dedicated to the Lord. For seven days the people were to eat bread made without yeast. Bread made without yeast is bread baked without leavening, and a holy feast means a sacred festival.

God speaks to Moses so that he may tell Israel. This verse is within the list of the Lord's feasts. The Passover was kept on the fourteenth day, and the next day the seven days of unleavened bread began. According to Exodus 12, this reminded them of their hasty departure from Egypt. Some also see in yeast a picture of sin, but that is a later interpretation.

Today we can set apart times to remember with gratitude what God has done for us. We can also ask ourselves what habit we need to put away from our lives so that we may walk with more simplicity and sincerity before Him.
exp.22:9:
God tells Moses to speak to the people. When they enter the promised land and gather their first harvest, they are to bring the priest an omer, a measure of grain, roughly two liters (the exact calculation is debated). The first portion of the crop, the first thing the harvest yields, is what the verse calls the firstfruits. The harvest itself, the time of reaping, and the ripened wheat or barley are all part of what the verse describes.

The LORD speaks and gives instructions for the feasts of the year. This belongs to the Feast of Firstfruits, which comes right after Passover. Israel was not yet in the land, so this was both a promise and a lesson: what comes first belongs to God, who gives the land and its fruit.

For today: before you spend or give away what you receive, such as your wages, your time, or your strength, give God first place with gratitude. You can begin with a simple prayer of thanks and with a generous offering.
exp.22:11:
This verse commands that on the same day the priest presented the omer (a bundle of the first sheaves of the harvest), the people also offer a one-year-old lamb without defect as a burnt offering, meaning an offering that was burned whole for the Lord.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct Israel about the Lord's feasts. Before eating from the new harvest, they were to acknowledge that the land and its fruit came from God. The lamb accompanied the offering of the firstfruits with full devotion and worship.

For today: before we enjoy what we receive, whether a paycheck, the fruit of our work, or a blessing, we can stop to give thanks and put God first. Honoring Him with our best, not with what is left over, is a simple way of saying that everything comes from Him.
exp.22:14:
Here God commands the people to count seven complete weeks. The counting begins on the day after the Sabbath when they brought the sheaf, which was a bundle of the first ears of the harvest. The wave offering was an offering that the priest lifted up and moved before God. When those seven weeks were complete, the next festival came, which later was called Pentecost.

God speaks to Moses so that he may tell Israel. This is part of the Lord's feasts. This counting joined the barley harvest with the wheat harvest, and taught the people to recognize that the land and the bread came from God. Scholars debate which Sabbath the text refers to, but the central idea is the same.

For today: learn to count your days with gratitude. Before you use what you earn or harvest, set apart the first of it for God and give thanks for his provision.
exp.22:15:
This verse says that, after counting seven complete weeks, one must arrive at the day after the seventh Sabbath. That would be the fiftieth day. Then the people were to bring God a new offering of grain. Here the sense of the offering is what is meant, and to count means that they would keep the tally day by day.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct Israel about its feasts. This count begins with the offering of the first ears of barley and ends with the Feast of Weeks, which was later called Pentecost (a word that comes from the number fifty). It was a celebration of thankfulness for the harvest that God gave.

For today: God invites us to pause and thank Him with intention. You might write down three things you have received from Him this week and give thanks for them in concrete ways, without waiting for everything to turn out perfectly.
exp.22:16:
This verse commands that, when the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost) arrives, each household bring from its homes two loaves as a wave offering, that is, lifted up before God. They were to be made from two tenth deals of fine flour and baked with leaven. They were the firstfruits, the first of the wheat harvest, dedicated to the Lord.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about its annual feasts. This feast came fifty days after the offering of the first sheaf of barley. It marked the end of the harvest and was a time of thanksgiving. That the bread contained leaven, something uncommon in offerings, has been explained in several ways; the Bible does not fully clarify it.

For today: before spending what you receive, set aside the first part to give thanks to God, with your time, your money or your service, acknowledging that everything comes from Him.
exp.22:29:
This verse says that if anyone works on the Day of Atonement, God himself will remove that person from among his people. "Any work" means any kind of labor. "I will destroy" is a strong expression that signals a serious judgment from God. Some understand it to mean loss of life, and others, separation from the community; the Bible does not spell out the details here.

God speaks to Moses to give Israel laws about its festivals. This day was special: the people acknowledged their sin, humbled themselves, and received forgiveness. Resting showed that forgiveness is not earned through effort, but is granted by God.

Today we can set aside time to stop, confess our failings, and rest in the forgiveness God offers. We do not need to earn his favor by working harder; we can trust in his grace.
exp.22:33:
God tells Moses to instruct the people: on the fifteenth day of the seventh month the feast of tabernacles begins, which lasts seven days and is for the Lord. The feast of tabernacles was a solemn feast, a time set apart for God. The shelters were temporary booths made of branches.

The Lord speaks to Moses just after the instructions about the Day of Atonement, a day of fasting and repentance. Now the tone shifts to celebration. In the same chapter (v. 43) it is explained that this feast was a reminder that Israel lived in booths when God brought them out of Egypt.

For today: just as Israel moved from repentance to joy, we can set aside times to thank God together with other believers, remembering how he has cared for us during the hard stretches of the journey. A good idea is to write down three things God has done for you this year and share them with your family.
exp.22:39:
God tells Israel that on the first day of the festival they are to gather branches from beautiful trees bearing fruit, palm fronds, thick leafy branches, and willows that grow beside the streams. With these they were to rejoice before God for seven days.

God speaks through Moses within the instructions for the annual feasts. This is the Feast of Booths, which came after the harvest had been gathered in, and the passage that follows connects it with living in booths. The texts do not fully explain how the branches were used; some later Jewish traditions interpret them in different ways.

For today: God wants our gratitude to be joyful and concrete. After a season of work or provision, take a moment to thank him in a simple way: give thanks out loud, share a meal with others, or go out and enjoy his creation.
exp.22:42:
This verse explains the purpose of the festival: that future generations would know that God made the people of Israel live in booths when He brought them out of Egypt. Some older words: "know" is simply the word to know, and "booths" are temporary shelters made of branches.

Here God speaks through Moses. The instruction concerns the Feast of Tabernacles, also called the Feast of Booths, which lasted seven days in the seventh month. It was not just a custom: it was a reminder so that children and grandchildren would know the story of deliverance and of God's care in the wilderness. The text does not describe in detail what those booths were like during that journey.

For today: remember the times when God has sustained you in uncertain seasons, and tell them to your children or to someone younger. Remembering with gratitude strengthens faith.
exp.23:1:
God asks Moses to command the people to bring pure olive oil, the fine oil obtained by crushing the olives, for the light of the tabernacle, so that the lamps would burn continually, without going out.

The Lord speaks, and says this to Moses while Israel is in the wilderness. It is the people who provide the oil, and then Aaron, the priest, tends the lamps every day before God. Many see in this a symbol of God's presence, though the text does not explain it in detail.

For today: God values what we give with care and constancy. We can offer him the best of our time and attention, not the leftovers, and keep a regular life of prayer, so that the light of our faith does not go out.
exp.23:5:
This verse says that the twelve loaves, made of fine flour, were to be placed in two rows, six in each row, on the clean table in the sanctuary, before the Lord. The word "rows" means lines or ranks. "Pure" refers to the table being clean and set apart for sacred use; many translations explain that it was a table overlaid with pure gold.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to Israel about worship in the tabernacle. The twelve loaves are usually understood as representing the twelve tribes, presented continually before God. Every Sabbath the priests renewed them, and the passage calls it a perpetual covenant. Some scholars also see in this a symbol of God's provision, although the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: just as God wanted his people always to be present before him, you can set aside a regular time, weekly or daily, to present your family and your life to him with gratitude and order.
exp.23:8:
This verse says that the bread of the Presence, which was set out before God every Sabbath, would belong to Aaron and his sons, the priests. They were to eat it in the holy place, because it was most holy. A perpetual statute means a rule that stays in force permanently. The offerings made by fire were the ones that were burned in part for the Lord.

God speaks to Moses, giving him instructions for worship in the tabernacle. The twelve loaves represented the constant presence of Israel before God, and the incense was burned as an offering. The bread then sustained the priests who served.

For today: God cares for those who serve him, and what is dedicated to him deserves respect. We can support with generosity those who serve in our church and treat with reverence what belongs to God.
exp.23:9:
This verse introduces a man whose mother was an Israelite and whose father was an Egyptian. He was living among the people of Israel. One day he got into a fight with another Israelite man in the camp.

The people were in the wilderness, near Mount Sinai, receiving God's laws through Moses. The text before this one speaks of holy things, such as the bread of the sanctuary. Here the account turns to a specific case: the quarrel will lead to a serious offense against God's name. The narrator reports what happened, and we are not told what caused the argument.

For today: small conflicts can grow if we do not take care of them. When a disagreement arises, ask God for calm, choose your words carefully, and remember that the way you speak can also honor or dishonor his name.
exp.23:10:
This verse tells of a young man, the son of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian father, who got into a fight with another man in the camp. In the middle of the quarrel he blasphemed the name of the Lord and cursed. Then they brought him before Moses. His mother is named as Shelomith, daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan.

Here the narrator of the Law speaks. Israel was in the wilderness, newly formed as the people of God. The name of the Lord was holy, and the people had just received commands about holiness. That is why they brought the case to Moses, and why he was kept in custody until they knew what the Lord said.

For today: our words reveal what is in the heart, especially when we are angry. Let us ask God for self-control and speak of his name with reverence, even in difficult moments.
exp.23:13:
God commands that a man who blasphemed be brought out of the camp. Those who heard him must lay their hands on his head, and the whole community is to stone him. "Camp" is the word the verse uses for the place outside which he is taken, and "blasphemer" refers to someone who insults or looks down on God.

The LORD speaks to Moses. A man had cursed the Name during a quarrel, and they kept him in custody until they knew what to do. Israel was a nation under the covenant, and God's name was holy. Laying hands on his head is usually understood as passing the guilt onto the one who spoke, or as a sign that the witnesses were declaring what they had heard; scholars explain it in different ways.

Today we do not live under that civil law, but we learn to speak of God with reverence. We can guard our words, avoid using his name lightly, and remember that Christ bore our guilt.
exp.23:16:
It says that if someone kills another person, that person must die.

The phrase about striking someone to death means hitting someone until their life is taken. The phrase about any person means it applies to everyone, no matter who the victim is. The phrase about suffering death means receiving the death penalty.

God speaks to Moses so that he will tell the people of Israel. These laws governed the life of the newly formed nation. Here blasphemy, homicide, and injuries are grouped together, and the same rule is applied to the foreigner and the native. The idea is that human life is sacred and that justice must be even-handed. Many understand that the phrase "as he has done, so shall it be done to him" limited revenge and required a punishment proportional to the offense.

Today we can learn to value every human life as a gift from God. That invites us to guard our words and actions, and to reject violence.
exp.23:21:
It says that in Israel there would be one law for everyone. Both the foreigner who lived among them and the native-born Israelite were to be judged by the same standard. The reason it gives is that the Lord is the God of all of them.

Speaking through Moses in the wilderness, God addresses a case where a man had blasphemed the name of God, and the people needed to know how to judge it. God establishes that justice should not depend on a person's origin. The phrase about an eye for an eye set a limit on punishment: it was to be proportionate to the offense, without excess.

For today: treat everyone with the same justice and respect, regardless of their country, their language, or their position. If you judge, offer an opinion, or help someone, ask yourself whether you would use the same measure with an acquaintance and with a stranger.
exp.24:1:
God tells Moses to speak to the people. When they enter the land that He gives them, the land itself is to keep a sabbath to the Lord, that is, it will rest in honor of the Lord. The land is to keep a sabbath, meaning it will stop being worked for a period of time.

The Lord speaks from Mount Sinai while He gives His law to Israel through Moses. They had not yet entered the promised land. God reminds them that the land is a gift from Him, and that they will care for it as stewards. The verses that follow explain that this rest would come every seventh year.

For today: everything we have comes from God, and He invites us to rest and trust in His provision. We can set apart time to rest without guilt, and care with gratitude for what has been entrusted to us.
exp.24:4:
This verse says that in the seventh year the people were not to harvest what the land produced on its own, nor pick the grapes of the vineyard that had not been tended. Rest means a time of quiet and freedom from labor. To reap means to cut down the crop, and to gather the grapes means to pick them at harvest. The land was to rest for a full year.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, and Moses passes the command on to Israel before they enter the promised land. This rest was a holy year belonging to the LORD. It reminded the people that the land belongs to God, and that they were to trust in his provision. Furthermore, according to the verses that follow, whatever grew by itself would serve as food for everyone, including servants, foreigners, and animals.

For today: Practice rest as a way of trusting God. Set aside time from work and production, and share generously what you have, remembering that everything comes from him.
exp.24:5:
This verse says that whatever the land produces on its own during the year of rest will be food for everyone. It is for you, your servant, your maid, your hired worker, and the stranger who lives with you.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses speaks to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. Every seventh year the land rested like a sabbath to the LORD. Nothing was sown or pruned. Even so, God provides food, and everyone shares in it, regardless of their social position.

For today: God cares for those who depend on us and for the most vulnerable. We can practice rest and trust in his provision, sharing generously what we have, without hoarding everything for ourselves.
exp.24:7:
God tells the people to count seven weeks of years, that is, seven times seven years, which add up to forty-nine years. It is a long count that prepares the way for something special.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, so that he may tell Israel before they enter the promised land. He had already spoken of the sabbatical year, when the land rested every seventh year. Now he extends that rhythm of rest toward the year of jubilee, which would be the fiftieth year, when lands were returned and freedom was proclaimed.

Today we can learn to live with rhythms of rest and generosity. Ask yourself: what burden, debt, or resentment do I need to let go of, and to whom can I give some relief? Trusting God includes stopping and setting free.
exp.24:10:
This verse says that the fiftieth year will be a year of jubilee. In that year the people were not to sow or harvest what the land produced by itself, nor gather the grapes from vines that nobody had pruned.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. The jubilee was announced with a trumpet, returned each family to its property, and proclaimed freedom. Letting the land rest reminded them that it belongs to God and that he cares for his people (vv. 23 and 21).

For today: practice trusting God's provision by taking a real rest. Set aside a time free from the pressure to produce, and give thanks that your worth does not depend on what you accomplish.
exp.24:16:
No one should deceive or take advantage of their neighbor. Instead, each person should have the fear of God, that is, a deep respect for Him. The verse's wording about deceiving means cheating or abusing someone. "The Lord" is God's name, and the phrase "I am the Lord your God" reminds the reader who gives this command.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. Earlier, He explained that land was sold according to the number of years left until the Jubilee, the year when lands returned to their families.
