Since what was really being sold were the harvests, the price had to be fair. It was easy to take advantage of someone in need, and that is why God sets this limit.

For today: when you buy, sell, or negotiate, be honest, even if no one would notice the deception. Remember that God sees, and that treating others justly is a way of honoring Him.
exp.24:17:
God tells the Israelites to carry out his statutes, that is, his laws, and to keep his judgments, that is, his righteous rules. It is not enough to hear them: they must be put into practice and lived out. If they do this, they will dwell in the land in safety, that is, at peace and protected.

The Lord is speaking through Moses. He is explaining the laws of the year of jubilee, when the land returned to its original family. Earlier he had asked them not to cheat one another over prices. Now he promises safety to those who obey, and right after this he speaks of the land yielding its fruit.

For today: obedience to God is not a burden but a path of peace. Think of a truth you already know, such as being honest at work or with money, and practice it this week, trusting that God cares for you.
exp.24:18:
God says through Moses that the land will yield well, that the people will eat until they are full, and that they will live in it peacefully.

Moses speaks for God to the people of Israel. The passage explains the laws of the sabbatical year and the jubilee, when the land rested and was not planted. Before this, God calls for justice between neighbors and for obedience. Then he promises to care for the people, even though stopping planting may seem risky.

For today: trust God by obeying him, even when doing so seems hard or costly. We can be honest at work, give generously, and rest one day, believing that God knows how to care for us. This is not a formula for getting rich, but an invitation to trust.
exp.24:21:
This verse says that in the eighth year the people would sow again, and in the meantime they would eat from the old harvest. The old store means grain kept in storage from before. That stored grain would last them until the ninth year, when the new harvest came in.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. Every seventh year the land was to rest, with no sowing and no harvest. That could cause fear, so God promised to bless the sixth year with a harvest enough for three years. He then makes clear that the land belongs to Him, and that the people are like strangers and pilgrims on it.

For today: trusting God leads us to obey Him even when it seems risky. We can set aside time to rest, or give from what we have, believing that He cares for us and that everything we possess comes from Him.
exp.24:23:
This verse says that, throughout the land that each family received as an inheritance, the land must be allowed to be bought back or returned. The verse tells the people that they must grant the right of recovering land that had been sold. This reading is rendered with the idea of giving back what had been let go.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. He reminds them that the land belongs to Him and that they are like strangers and temporary residents, stewards rather than absolute owners. For this reason the land could not be sold forever. If someone became poor and sold his property, a close relative, the one who could buy it back, could recover it for the family.

For today: everything we have is a loan from God, not absolute ownership. We can use what we have to help a relative or friend in trouble get back on their feet, without taking advantage of their need.
exp.24:24:
It says that if an Israelite becomes poor and has to sell part of his land, his closest relative, called the redeemer (in Hebrew, goel), must buy it back. To become poor means to fall into poverty, and to redeem means to get something back by paying its price.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. He explains that the land belongs to Him and that they are only strangers and temporary residents, that is, stewards and not absolute owners. That is why the land could not be sold forever, and the family had to help make sure no one lost their inheritance.

For today: when a relative or a brother in the faith goes through financial need, we should not ignore him. We can help him with concrete support, advice, or money, without humiliating him, remembering that everything we have comes from God.
exp.24:26:
If a poor Israelite sold part of his land and later manages to gather money, he may buy it back. He must count the years from the sale until that moment, pay the buyer only what corresponds to the time left until the jubilee, and return to his property.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. In this law the land belonged to God, and families were not to lose it forever. That is why there was the redeemer (a close relative), the right of repurchase, and the jubilee, which returned the lands every fifty years.

For today: God cares for the dignity of whoever falls into need and opens paths of restoration. We can imitate that by helping someone who is in debt or in crisis, not taking advantage of their trouble, but seeking to help them stand up again.
exp.24:27:
This verse says that if a person sold his land because of need and does not manage to gather enough money to get it back, the land stays in the hands of the buyer only until the year of jubilee. In that year, the buyer gives it back, and the original owner returns to his possession. The phrase about having the means can be understood as being able to pay enough, and getting the land back is buying it back from the buyer.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. In this law, the land belonged to God, and the families received it as an inheritance. The jubilee, every fifty years, kept anyone from losing his inheritance forever and protected the poorest.

For today: God cares for those who fall into debt or loss, and invites us to be generous and to give second chances. We can help someone get back on his feet, without taking advantage of his need.
exp.24:30:
It says that houses in small villages, those without a wall around them, were treated the same as a field for growing crops. They could be bought back by paying the redemption price at any time, and they returned to their original owner in the year of the jubilee.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. The land belonged to God and was to remain within the families. Village houses were tied to the land that provided their living, which is why they were protected in the same way. By contrast, houses inside walled cities did not return in the jubilee after a year. It is commonly understood that this reflected a way of life less tied to the land, though the text does not fully explain it.

God cares for the most vulnerable and does not want a bad stretch of luck to leave anyone without hope. Today we can give second chances, generously helping someone who has lost something, without taking advantage of their need.
exp.24:31:
This verse says the Levites had a special right: they could buy back their houses in the cities that fell to them, at any time, with no time limit. "Redeem" means to buy back something that had been sold. Other houses in walled cities could only be recovered during the first year.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses to Israel, about the laws of the Year of Jubilee. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes; God was their inheritance. For that reason, their houses in the Levitical cities were their only property, and God protected them from being lost forever.

For today: God cares for those who serve him and depend on him. We can support with generosity those who dedicate themselves to serving in the church, and trust that God also provides for us.
exp.24:35:
If an Israelite falls into poverty, you must not take advantage of his need by charging him interest or any extra gain on what you lend. Instead, you must act with reverence toward God, showing respect and awe for Him, so that your brother can keep living beside you without losing his dignity.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in the laws of the Year of Jubilee. These rules protected families who fell into poverty, so that they would not be trapped in debt. God reminds them that He brought them out of Egypt, where they had been slaves, and for that reason they must treat the needy with mercy.

Today, when someone close to us goes through financial hardship, we can help him without taking advantage of his situation: lending to him without pressure, or giving generous support, remembering that God has treated us with grace.
exp.24:39:
It says that if an Israelite becomes poor and sells himself to another, he must not be treated as a slave, but as a hired servant or a sojourner, that is, as a paid worker who lives temporarily in the household. He will work until the year of jubilee, the fiftieth year, when everyone was set free.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. He had just brought them out of Egypt, where they had been slaves, and he regarded them as his own. For this reason no fellow Israelite could be ruled over like a slave. This law protected their dignity and assured them that they would return to their family and their land.

For today: if you have authority over someone, such as an employee, treat with respect and justice the person who depends on you, especially if they are going through hardship. Never take advantage of their poverty. Remember that God has treated us with mercy.
exp.24:42:
An Israelite is told not to rule over a fellow Israelite who has fallen into poverty and has been forced to serve him with harshness. This verse says that to rule over someone means to dominate them like a master. Treating someone with harshness means treating them roughly and without compassion. The reason given is the fear of God: respecting Him and taking Him seriously, knowing that He sees how we treat other people.

God speaks to the Israelites through Moses. This part of the law regulated how impoverished brothers were to be treated. God reminds them that they belong to Him, since He brought them out of Egypt, where they themselves had suffered oppression. For that reason they could not be treated as ordinary slaves. Later the law does allow owning servants from other nations, a reality of that time that is hard for us to accept today.

For today: if you have authority over others, whether at work, at home, or in the church, exercise it with respect and compassion, remembering that you answer to God.
exp.24:46:
If a foreigner living among you prospers, but a fellow Israelite who lives near him becomes destitute and sells himself to that foreigner or to a member of the foreigner's clan, it can happen in the community God was building. The verse describes a real hardship: a poor brother becomes dependent on someone outside the covenant family.

God speaks to Moses for the people, within the laws of the year of jubilee. He had already said that an Israelite must not be treated harshly as a slave. Here the case is anticipated of a brother falling under a foreign master, and the verses that follow command that he be redeemed by his relatives.

For today: God wants the family of faith not to abandon those who fall into need. We can ask ourselves who around us is called to help them get back on their feet, with real support, without humiliating them or taking advantage of their situation.
exp.24:49:
This verse says that the Israelite who sold himself as a servant because of poverty must settle accounts with the one who bought him. The years are counted from his sale until the year of jubile, and the price is divided according to those years. So his time of service is valued like that of a hired worker, not like that of a slave without rights.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. In this chapter He gives laws about the year of jubile, when every fifty years debts were forgiven and people returned to their family and their land. This rule prevented abuses and kept the redemption of a impoverished brother fair. The details of how it applies are understood in different ways, but the purpose of justice is clear.

Today we can treat with justice and dignity those who depend on us, such as employees or debtors, without taking advantage of their need.
exp.24:51:
It says that if an Israelite sold himself as a servant to a foreigner living in the land, and only a few years remain before the Jubilee, the years still left are to be counted. This is how one works out how much he must pay to be set free.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. These laws protected the poor who, because of debts, had to sell themselves. The Jubilee, every fifty years, gave back freedom and land to families. No one was meant to be a slave forever, because God had redeemed them from Egypt.

For today: deal fairly and with compassion toward anyone who depends on you, whether at work or through a loan. May your accounts always be honest and merciful, because God sees how we treat others.
exp.24:52:
It says that an Israelite who sold himself as a servant to a foreigner living among them must be treated like a hired worker, employed year by year. His master must not rule over him with harshness or cruelty, and the others must watch to see that this is so.

God speaks through Moses, giving laws for Israel. An impoverished Israelite could sell himself, but his relatives could buy him back, and in the year of jubilee he was set free. God reminds them that Israel belongs to him, since he brought them out of Egypt, where they had known oppression.

For today: if you have authority over others, as a boss, teacher, or parent, use it with respect and kindness. Remember that every person is precious to God, and treat others as you would want to be treated.
exp.24:53:
If an Israelite who had sold himself as a servant to a foreigner is not redeemed, neither by his relatives nor by his own means, he will still go free in the year of jubilee. He will leave, and his children with him.

God speaks to Moses and to Israel, giving them laws for life in the promised land. The jubilee came every fifty years. The verses that follow give the reason: the Israelites are servants of God, whom he brought out of Egypt, so no one should treat them harshly as slaves without rights.

For today: God cares for the dignity of every person. We can treat with justice and respect those who work for us or depend on us, remembering that we all belong to God and that he always offers freedom and new beginnings.
exp.24:54:
God says that the Israelites are his servants, meaning they belong to him, because he himself brought them out of Egypt. For that reason, no Israelite could remain the slave of another person forever. The word "servants" here speaks of belonging to God and serving him.

God speaks through Moses, giving laws to the people at Sinai. Earlier, the text explains that an Israelite who sold himself because of debts was to be treated as a hired worker, not harshly. If he was not redeemed, he went free in the year of jubilee. The final reason is that God had already set them free, and they were his.

For today: if we believe that every person belongs to God and is valuable to him, we should treat with respect and justice those who depend on us, such as employees or family members, without abusing our position.
exp.25:1:
It says the people must take care of the days of rest that God set apart, the sabbaths, and treat with deep respect the place where God met with them. "Keep" means to carefully observe, and "reverence" means to honor with respect. "I am the Lord" is God's signature: He is the one who commands.

God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel in the wilderness. He has just forbidden them idols, and now He shows them how to worship Him rightly: by resting and respecting the sanctuary. Then comes the promise of blessing if they obey Him.

For today: let us set aside regular time to rest and seek God, without letting work and hurry push Him out of the way. And when we gather to worship, let us do so with an attentive and respectful heart.
exp.25:4:
It says the harvest will be so abundant that the threshing of the grain will last until grape-gathering time, and the grape-gathering will extend until the next sowing. Threshing means separating the grain from the straw; grape-gathering means picking the grapes; the time of sowing is the season for planting. Fullness means abundance, being satisfied. It also promises that they will live safely in the land.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, at Sinai. These words are part of the blessings of the covenant: if the people obeyed, God promised rain, fruit, peace and protection. It was a promise addressed to Israel in its particular situation, as the covenant people.

For today: although not every material promise applies in the same way to us, we learn that God is the one who sustains our daily life. We can obey him with confidence, give thanks for what we have, and share it generously, without living dominated by fear of scarcity.
exp.25:5:
This verse promises that God will give peace in the land. People will be able to lie down to sleep without fear, because no one will frighten them. It also says that God will rid the land of evil beasts, that is, the wild and dangerous animals, and that the sword, or war, will not pass through their country.

Here God himself speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel, while they were near Mount Sinai. After giving them his laws, he sets before them blessings if they obey him: rain in its season, abundant harvests, and safety. It is part of his covenant with Israel. Warnings follow if they turn away from him.

For today: true peace comes from trusting God and living in his way. Before going to sleep, hand your fears over to him in prayer and remember that your security rests in him, not only in your circumstances.
exp.25:6:
This verse says that if the people obey God, they will be able to pursue their enemies, and their enemies will fall before them by the sword.

God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel in the wilderness, near Mount Sinai. He offers blessings if they keep his covenant: abundant harvests, peace, and security in the land. Victory over enemies is part of that promise, and the text presents it as a gift from God, not as something the people earned. It is a promise given to Israel under that covenant.

For today: we do not use this text to justify violence. Rather, we can remember that true security comes from God, not only from our own strength. Today we can seek his help and obey him in our daily struggles, trusting that he cares for us.
exp.25:9:
It says that God promises so much harvest to his people that they will still be eating the grain stored from earlier years when the new harvest arrives. They will have so much that they will have to bring out the old to make room for the new.

God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel at Sinai. This is part of the blessings that accompany faithfulness to the covenant (Leviticus 26:3-13). The abundance is a sign that God keeps his promise, and the following verse shows the greatest gift: his presence among them.

For today: God cares for us generously, though not always in the form of wealth. We can trust that He provides, and share gladly what we have instead of hoarding it out of fear. The best thing we receive is to be close to Him.
exp.25:11:
It says that God himself will walk among his people, and that the relationship between them will be close: he will be their God and they will be his people. "I will walk among you" means that God will be present and near, not distant.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel. This is part of the promises of blessing they would receive if they kept the covenant. Earlier he had already promised to make his dwelling among them. Then he reminds them that he brought them out of Egypt and freed them from slavery. Next he warns what would happen if they did not obey him.

For today: God desires a close relationship with his people, not just rules. You can begin the day by recognizing that he walks with you, and ask him for help to live in a way that honors that companionship.
exp.25:13:
It says a warning is coming. After the promises of blessing, he now begins to explain what would happen if the people turn their backs on him.

God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel. Earlier he reminded them that he brought them out of Egypt, freed them from slavery, and gave them dignity. For that reason, obedience was the response to a God who had already cared for them. The verses that follow describe the consequences of rejecting his covenant.

For today: God speaks to us with clarity and love, and listening to him is a serious matter. Today you can choose a teaching from the Bible that you already know and put it into practice this week, remembering that God first showed you his kindness.
exp.25:24:
God says that if his people remain rebellious, he will bring a sword upon them, meaning a war that carries out the consequences of the broken covenant. The people will take refuge in their cities, but there a deadly plague will arrive. In the end they will be delivered into the hands of their enemies.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, at the close of the law given at Sinai. He sets before them blessings for obedience and warnings for rejecting the covenant. This punishment comes in stages, after repeated chances to turn back. Its purpose is to call the people to return.

Today we can take God's gentle corrections seriously before the harsh ones arrive. If something in your life troubles you in light of God's Word, do not put it off: surrender it today, trusting that God is patient and wants to restore you.
exp.25:28:
It says that, if the people keep rebelling, a famine will come so terrible that parents will eat the flesh of their own sons and daughters. It is a very harsh image. The verb is future: a warning, not a command.

God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel. At the end of the covenant in Leviticus 26, He first promises blessing for obedience and then warns about the consequences of rejecting it. This is one stage of the punishment, which grows more severe, becoming complete. Later, in besieged cities, the Bible mentions similar events (2 Kings 6:28-29; Lamentations 4:10), which shows that the warning was fulfilled in a tragic way.

For today: let us take God's warnings seriously. He does not treat sin lightly, but His cautions aim to bring us back to Him before the harm grows. Let us respond today with humility and repentance.
exp.25:31:
God says that He Himself will leave the land of Israel in ruins, empty and desolate. So much so that the enemies who come to live there will be left astonished and horrified at how it turned out.

Here God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel. At the end of the law, He sets before them blessings if they obey and consequences if they rebel and follow idols. This is a warning within that covenant. The text then explains that the land would finally receive the rest of its Sabbaths, something Israel had not respected.

For today: God is serious, but His warnings are an expression of care, not of whim. We can ask ourselves what things we have put in God's place and return to Him sincerely, trusting that His mercy remains open to anyone who repents.
exp.25:35:
He says that God will make the survivors of Israel, already exiled in enemy land, feel a fear so deep that even the sound of a leaf stirred by the wind will make them run. They will flee as one escapes from a sword, and they will fall even when no one is chasing them. The word for "faintness" here means a fear that takes away strength, and "sword" refers to a blade.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. This is part of the warnings of the covenant: if the people turned away from God and did not obey, consequences would come, among them exile. These words are meant not only to frighten but to call the people to repentance, for later in the same chapter it promises that God will remember his covenant with those who turn back to him.

For today: when we live far from God, fear and insecurity can take hold of us without a clear reason. Let us return to him with sincerity, because his peace sustains the heart.
exp.25:36:
It says that, in the future, the people of Israel will be so overcome with fear that they will stumble over one another, as though fleeing from a sword, even though no one is chasing them. The word "sword" here is used for the weapon that the verse names. And in the end, they will have no strength to face their enemies.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. Before they enter the promised land, He sets before them blessings if they obey and consequences if they reject His covenant. This verse describes one of those consequences: if they persist in disobedience, they will live as exiles, dominated by fear. It is not an expression of a desire for revenge; the warning aims to bring them back to God.

For today: when we live far from God, fear can dominate us even without a real threat. We can bring our anxieties to God in prayer, trust in His care, and return to Him sincerely, knowing that His mercy is always near.
exp.25:41:
This verse says that God does not forget the promises he made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. "Remember" here does not mean that God had forgotten something, but that he acts in line with what he promised. It is striking that the order is Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham, the reverse of the usual one. "I will remember the land" means that God also keeps in mind the land he promised to that people.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel. Earlier he has warned that, if they disobey, discipline and exile will come. But if they acknowledge their sin and humble themselves, God responds with faithfulness to his covenant. Even in the punishment, he does not abandon them completely.

For today: when you have failed, do not run from God. Confess honestly and return to him, trusting that his faithfulness depends not on your perfection, but on his character.
exp.25:42:
It says that while the people are in exile, the land will be left empty and will finally rest, as if it were keeping the Sabbaths that were never given to it. The people will bear the consequences of their sin, because they rejected God's judgments and their souls loathed his statutes.

God speaks, through Moses, at the close of the blessings and warnings of the covenant. If Israel was unfaithful to him, exile would come. But this verse sits between two promises: God will remember his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and will not reject them completely. The discipline is real, but it is not the end.

For today: when you face the consequences of your mistakes, do not run from the truth or sink into despair. Acknowledge your failure with humility, and trust that God disciplines to restore, not to destroy.
exp.25:44:
He says that God will remember his people even after punishing them. He did this in order to be their God. The phrase "I am the Lord" is like signing his promise with his name.

God himself speaks here, through Moses, at the end of the warnings in Leviticus 26. Earlier he announced punishments if Israel disobeyed, even exile. But here he promises that he will not cancel his covenant. His discipline aims to correct, not to destroy.

For today: when you fail or feel that God is far away, remember that his faithfulness does not depend on your perfection. Return to him sincerely, trusting that he remains faithful to his promises.
exp.26:6:
This verse says that if a person sixty years old or above had been dedicated to God through a special vow, the amount to pay in order to buy back that person and be free of the vow was fifteen shekels for a male and ten shekels for a female. The shekel was a unit of weight in silver. The amount set for that payment was called the value set on the person.

God gives these instructions to Moses so that he can pass them on to Israel. Someone could make a voluntary vow to dedicate a person to the service of the sanctuary, and then pay a sum to buy that person back. The rates varied according to age and sex. Scholars explain in several ways why the amounts differ; many think they reflected the working capacity of the time, although the text does not make this clear.

For today: when you promise something to God, do it with seriousness and sincerity, knowing that your words matter. Think before you commit yourself, and fulfill what you promised with gratitude.
exp.26:7:
If someone made a special vow to God but does not have the money to pay the set value, they must present themselves before the priest. The priest will decide how much they can pay, according to that person's means.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about vows, when someone promised to dedicate a person (or their own service) to the Lord. That person could be redeemed by paying an amount in silver shekels. This law makes an exception for the poor, so that no one would be excluded for lack of money.

For today: God values sincerity more than the amount. Keep what you promise to God with seriousness, but according to your real ability, and help those who have less with compassion.
exp.26:8:
This verse speaks of the animals that a person promised to God. If it was an animal of the kind that could be offered in sacrifice, what was given to the Lord became holy, that is, set apart for God. It was no longer for common use or for the owner's use. The word "offering" refers to what was presented at the altar.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to the people of Israel about vows, that is, the promises made to God. Earlier, it was explained how persons dedicated to the service of the Lord were valued. Now the subject is animals. The following verses make clear that a good animal could not be exchanged for a bad one, nor swapped for another as if it were an ordinary deal.

For today: what we promise to God should be taken seriously. If we make a promise, let us keep it sincerely, without haggling or looking for excuses to give less than what was promised.
exp.26:12:
If a person had dedicated an unclean animal to God and then wanted to take it back, the verse says he had to pay the value the priest had set on it and add one fifth more. To buy it back means to purchase it again, and the estimated price is the worth the priest assigned. The fifth is twenty percent.

God speaks to Moses so that he may pass the words on to Israel. This chapter deals with vows, that is, promises to give something to the Lord. An unclean animal could not be offered in sacrifice, so its value was assessed in money. The added amount made sure that no one took lightly what was promised to God or backed out of it without cost.

For today: think carefully before you promise something to God or to others. Words carry weight. If you commit yourself, be faithful; and if you get it wrong, act with humility and honesty, knowing that God values a sincere heart.
exp.26:13:
This verse speaks of someone who decides to dedicate his house to God. The priest was to set a price on it, whether the house was good or in poor condition, and that value stood firm.

God speaks to Moses to give laws to the people of Israel. People could make voluntary offerings, and the priest set a fair value to avoid confusion or abuse. If the owner wanted to get his house back, he had to pay that value plus a fifth part, according to the verses that follow.

For today: when we give something to God, let us do it with sincerity and commitment, not lightly. Keeping what we have promised shows that we value our relationship with Him and that our words carry weight.
exp.26:14:
It says that if a person dedicated his house to God and later wants to take it back, he must pay the value the priest set and add one fifth more, that is, an extra twenty percent. Then the house becomes his again. The person who dedicates something to God is the one who sets it apart for Him, and the amount calculated as its price is the worth assigned to it.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses to Israel, about vows and freewill offerings. What was dedicated to the Lord belonged to the sanctuary, so the priest assessed it fairly. If someone changed his mind and wanted to get it back, he had to pay a surcharge. In this way the promises made to God were taken seriously.

For today: think carefully before promising God something, and when you do, keep your word with sincerity. Your words carry weight before Him, and offering Him something should come from a settled heart, not from a passing impulse.
exp.26:15:
It says that if someone dedicates to God a portion of the land he inherited, the priest must calculate its value according to the amount of seed needed to sow it. An omer of barley (a measure of grain, about 220 liters according to some estimates, though the exact measure is debated) is equivalent to fifty shekels of silver. Setting something apart for God is what is meant here.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. This chapter explains how to fulfill promises made to the Lord with goods, houses, or fields. Land was a family inheritance and could not be lost forever, so a fair price was set so that it could be redeemed. The details of the calculation tied to the jubilee are explained in the following verses.

For today: when you promise something to God, do it with seriousness and without carelessness. Think carefully about what you can give joyfully, and keep what you have promised, because God values a sincere and orderly heart.
exp.26:18:
It says that if someone dedicated his field to God and then wants to take it back, he must pay the value the priest calculated and add a fifth more (20 percent). In this way the land becomes his again. The value set is the price fixed, and to buy back means to repurchase.

God speaks to Moses and gives Israel rules about vows and offerings. In Israel land was not sold forever, since it belonged to God and returned to its family in the year of jubilee. The added payment made dedicating something to God a serious matter, not something done lightly.

For today: let us think carefully before promising something to God, and keep faithfully what we have said. A promise made sincerely deserves reflection, not impulse, because God values a faithful and honest heart.
exp.26:19:
It says that if the man who dedicated his field to God does not buy it back by paying the set amount, or if the field is sold to another person, he will no longer be able to recover it. "Redeem" here means to buy back or rescue. Some scholars debate who makes the sale, but the general sense is that the chance to buy it back is lost.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. In this chapter He regulates the promises and offerings dedicated to Him. The field was a family inheritance, so dedicating it was a serious matter. The law gave an opportunity to buy it back, but not an everlasting way out. Later, at the Jubilee, the field passed to the priest.

For today: think carefully before promising something to God. If you make a commitment, keep it responsibly and on time, because God takes our word seriously.
exp.26:21:
This verse speaks of a person who dedicates to God a field that he bought, not one he received as a family inheritance. The law distinguishes between inherited land, which had belonged to the family since the division of Canaan, and purchased land, which was a temporary possession.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. The land belonged to God, and the year of jubilee returned every property to its original family. For this reason, a purchased field dedicated to the Lord did not remain forever in the hands of the sanctuary, but returned to its original owner in the jubilee.

For today: we can give to God generously, but with order and honesty, giving what is truly ours and respecting what belongs to others. Everything we have is a loan from God.
exp.26:22:
It says that if someone dedicates to God a piece of land that they bought (not one from their family inheritance), the priest will work out its worth according to the years remaining until the jubilee. On that same day the person must pay that amount, which is set apart as a holy thing, that is, consecrated to the Lord. The worth calculated is the value, and the amount fixed is the price agreed upon.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. These laws governed the vows made to God. Land belonged to families by inheritance, so a piece of land that had been bought was held only until the jubilee, when it returned to its original owner. That is why only that remaining time was valued.

For today: God values sincerity and order in what we promise to him. Before promising something, calmly think about what you can truly give, and keep what you said with honesty and joy.
exp.26:26:
This verse speaks of an "unclean" animal, that is, one that could not be offered in sacrifice, such as a horse or a camel. If someone had promised it to God, they could get it back by paying the value set by the priest, plus an extra fifth. If they did not buy it back, the animal was sold for that same value.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. They are rules about vows, or promises made to God. Since some animals were not fit for the altar, the law provided a fair way out: the value of the promise went to the sanctuary, so that no one was cheated.

For today: when you promise something to God or to others, think it over carefully and keep your word with honesty. God values a sincere heart that does not take lightly what it says.
exp.26:29:
It says that the tenth part of everything the land produces, both the seed and harvest and the fruit of the trees, belongs to God. The tithe means the tenth part, that is, ten percent. Something set apart for God means set aside for him, as something holy.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct the people of Israel, shortly before they arrive in the promised land. This chapter closes the book of Leviticus and deals with what was dedicated to God. The tithe supported worship and the Levites, who did not receive an inheritance of land. The verses that follow allow part of the tithe to be redeemed by paying an extra fifth.

For today: we can remember that everything we have comes from God. Giving with order and gratitude, according to our conscience and our church, is a way of honoring him and not leaving it for last.
exp.26:31:
Of all the livestock, whether cattle or sheep, the verse says that every tenth animal belongs to God. The phrase about what passes under the rod refers to counting the animals one by one as they walked past the shepherd, who probably touched them with a staff. Each tenth animal was set apart as holy, meaning dedicated to the Lord.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, giving laws to Israel. This is the close of the book of Leviticus. The tithes acknowledged that the land and its produce came from God, and they also supported worship and the Levites. The verse that follows indicates that one was not to choose between good and bad animals.

For today: let us give to God with order and gratitude, not with what we have left over. Let us think of an offering that is planned, simple, and generous, given with a thankful heart for everything he has given us.
exp.13:32:
This verse is an introductory phrase. It says that the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron to give them new instructions. Here there is not yet a full teaching, but a notice that a new law is coming.

God speaks, and addresses the two leaders: Moses, who passed the law on to the people, and Aaron, the priest. Earlier, the text spoke of the disease of skin conditions in people and of their cleansing. Now a different subject begins: the plagues that appeared in houses, which God would give once the people were living in Canaan. The term for this disease here covers several skin conditions and also mold or fungi on walls and fabrics. Scholars do not agree on exactly which ones they were.

For today: God is concerned even with the details of our home. We can listen to him attentively and also bring to him in prayer the everyday matters of our household.
exp.20:11:
This verse says that the high priest was not to leave the sanctuary or desecrate it, because the consecration of the anointing oil of his God was on him. Here "consecration" speaks of what sets him apart as holy to the LORD, and "desecrate" means treating as common what is holy. When a family member died, he was not to leave his service to take part in the rites of mourning.

God speaks to Moses, so that he may pass it on to Aaron and the priests of Israel. The high priest had been anointed and set apart to represent the people before God. For that reason a stricter holiness was required of him. Scholars explain in various ways whether "must not leave" means he could never leave, or only that he was not to abandon his service because of mourning.

For today: God values complete dedication. If you belong to him, ask him for help to guard your witness and your priorities, and to live in a way that honors his name.
exp.24:50:
This verse says that if many years still remain before the year of jubilee, the price the Israelite must pay to be freed will be higher. It is worked out in proportion to the years that are left. A "redemption" is the payment that wins back one's freedom, and the "purchase price" is the original amount for which the man was sold.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. A poor Israelite had sold himself as a servant to a foreigner living among them. The law protected that man: his family could buy him back, and the arrangement had to be fair, like that of a hired worker and not that of a slave. In the year of jubilee he would be free in any case.

For today: when someone owes you something or depends on you, treat them with justice and compassion, without taking advantage of their need. God cares for the vulnerable, and we too should do the same.
exp.9:10:
This verse continues the previous sentence and says that the priests had to stay clear-minded for one more task: to teach the people all the laws that the LORD gave them through Moses. "Laws" here means the rules and instructions God gave his people. "The LORD" is the name of God.

God speaks to Aaron after the death of his sons Nadab and Abihu, who offered unauthorized fire before the LORD. Many think they may have been drinking, although the text does not say so. For this reason God asks the priests for a clear mind: their service and their teaching required sound judgment.

Whoever teaches others about God needs an alert mind and an attentive heart. Today we can ask God for self-control and take care with whatever clouds our judgment, so that our example and our words help others know him better.
exp.10:21:
Here God permits four kinds of insects to be eaten: the locust, the katydid, the cricket, and the grasshopper. These are Hebrew names that are hard to identify with certainty. Scholars believe they refer to different kinds of grasshoppers, locusts, or related jumping insects, but there is no certainty about which is which. The verse names these creatures by their kinds, so each one is allowed according to its own type.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel about clean and unclean foods. These rules helped Israel live as a people set apart for God, and their purpose was to remind them that he is holy. The criterion given here is that the insect had long legs for jumping.

For today: God is interested in the details of everyday life, even what we eat. We can ask ourselves whether we are also giving him the small, ordinary things, and living with gratitude and obedience.
exp.9:0:
This verse tells us that Nadab and Abihu, sons of Aaron, each took his censer (a vessel for burning incense), put fire and incense in it, and came before the Lord. But the Bible says they offered "unauthorized fire," fire that God had not commanded them to use.

This happens right after the priesthood was set up and God accepted the sacrifices with fire (Leviticus 9). The narrator of the book relates the event. It does not explain in detail exactly what they did wrong; some think the fire was not from the altar, others that the timing or the manner was not the right one. What is clear is that they acted contrary to God's command.

Today we learn that worshiping God is not only sincerity or emotion, but also reverence and obedience to what He has revealed. We can ask ourselves: am I seeking to please Him, or only doing what seems good to me?
exp.7:34:
It says that Aaron and his sons were to stay at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, day and night, for seven days. There they were to carry out what God required and keep the Lord's charge, so that they would not die. The phrase "the testimony" refers to the place where the ark with the commandments was kept. Moses makes clear that this was not his own idea, but a command he had received.

Moses speaks to Aaron and his sons at the end of their ceremony of consecration as priests. For seven days the rites that atoned for sin, that is, that covered it, were repeated. The warning "so that you will not die" shows how serious it is to draw near to a holy God. In the end, they obey everything.

For today: God values constant obedience, not just a good moment. We can set aside time each day to be with Him, to pray and to listen to His Word, recognizing with reverence that He is holy and also welcomes us.
exp.3:28:
The person who sinned unintentionally was to lay his hand on the head of the sin offering. Then he would slaughter the animal at the place of the burnt offering, that is, beside the altar. "To slaughter" here means to cut the throat. The sin offering was the offering that made atonement for the sin.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel. This passage deals with a sin committed unintentionally by someone from the common people. Laying the hand on the animal is usually understood as a way of identifying oneself with it, although scholars explain it in somewhat different ways. Afterward the priest would present the blood, and forgiveness was granted.

For today: we no longer need sacrifices, but this text reminds us that sin is serious, even when we do not commit it on purpose. Christians see in Christ the final sacrifice. We can draw near to God with humility, acknowledge our faults, and receive his forgiveness.
exp.4:5:
This verse says that the person who has sinned must bring to the LORD a female lamb or goat from the flock as a sin offering. "Atonement" means covering or cleansing a wrong so that the relationship with God is restored. The phrase "bring it to the LORD" means that the person brings the offering before God, and the priest makes atonement on his behalf. The result is forgiveness.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel. In context, someone has sinned without realizing it, such as by a careless oath, and then recognizes it. God does not ignore sin, even when it is unintentional, but he also offers a clear way to be forgiven. First comes the confession, then the offering.

For today: when you recognize a wrong, even if you notice it late, do not hide it. Confess it to God honestly. Christians believe that Christ is the final sacrifice who gives us forgiveness.
exp.15:27:
The person who burned the remains of the bull and the goat of the sin offering had to wash his clothes and bathe himself with water. Only after that could he reenter the camp of Israel.

God speaks to Moses about the Day of Atonement. The animals of the sacrifice were burned outside the camp. Whoever handled these remains became ceremonially unclean, so he had to wash before returning to the community. The point was not physical dirt, but protecting the holiness of the people. Some see here a picture that is later connected with Christ suffering "outside the gate" (Hebrews 13:11-12).

For today: when we deal with sin, whether our own or someone else's, we need to return to God to be cleansed. We can pray with humility and ask him to renew our heart before we move forward.
exp.0:9:
This verse says that if someone wanted to present a burnt offering from the flock, they could bring a sheep or a goat. It had to be a male with no defects, meaning no visible physical flaw. The burnt offering was an offering that was burned whole on the altar.

God speaks to Moses from the tent of meeting and gives instructions for the people of Israel. Earlier, the bull was mentioned; now an option is given for those who had fewer resources. Scholars understand the burnt offering as an expression of total surrender to God and of seeking forgiveness, although it is explained in several ways.

For today: God deserves our best, not what is left over. We can ask ourselves what part of our time, money, and affection we give him sincerely. And God accepts what each person can give with a devoted heart.
exp.17:5:
None of you are to approach any close relative to have sexual relations. The command means coming near with the purpose of sexual intimacy, and it is addressed to everyone. The closing words, "I am the LORD," present God himself as the one who gives this command, which gives it full authority.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel. They had just left Egypt and were about to enter Canaan. God calls them to live differently from the surrounding nations and to obey his laws. This verse opens a list of forbidden relationships within the family, meant to protect people and to keep the home holy.

For today: take care to keep healthy boundaries in your family. Respect and protect your relatives, and reject any abuse or disrespect toward them. A home should be a safe place.
exp.11:0:
This is a simple introduction. It says that the LORD spoke to Moses. The words "Then the LORD said to Moses" mark the beginning of a new instruction from God.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the messenger who must pass his words on to the people. We are in the book of Leviticus, where God gives laws to Israel about how to live as his people, close to his presence. This chapter deals with the birth of a child and the purification of the mother. Interpreters explain the sense of ritual uncleanness in various ways, but it was not a sin.

For today: Before teaching or deciding anything, it is good to first listen to God in his Word. He cares even about the everyday moments of life, such as the birth of a child, and wants to be with us in them.
exp.26:5:
This verse sets a price for a person between one month and five years of age: five shekels of silver if the person is a male, and three shekels if a female. "Valuation" means the assessed value, so the verse is fixing what that value is. A shekel was a unit of weight, used for measuring out silver in payment.

God speaks to Moses so that he can tell Israel. A person could make a vow, that is, a solemn promise to dedicate someone to the Lord. This table made it possible to fulfill that vow by paying an amount instead of handing over the person. The difference in price was probably related to the working capacity of the time, and not to the person's worth before God. Scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: when you promise something to God, do it with seriousness and keep it. It is better to promise little with sincerity than much without thinking.
exp.6:11:
It says that if someone wanted to give thanks to God with a sacrifice, they were also to bring bread without yeast. These were cakes mixed with olive oil, thin breads coated with oil, and well-kneaded cakes of fine flour mixed with oil.

The phrase "sacrifice of thanksgiving" appears in the verse itself. The "peace offerings" were the fellowship or peace sacrifices, the sacrifices shared in a meal.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes these instructions on to Israel. This peace offering was given voluntarily, and the person ate part of the meat along with the bread, as a meal before God. The verses that follow add bread with yeast, and one portion was for the priest. Scholars explain the meaning of the yeast in different ways, but here the central point is gratitude.

Giving thanks to God deserves something concrete. You can thank him today with a sincere prayer, an offering, or a shared meal with someone who needs company.
exp.13:34:
This verse says that the owner of the house must go to the priest and tell him that something like mildew has appeared in his house. Note that it says "something like mildew": it does not claim with certainty that it is mildew, only that it appears to be.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, before Israel enters Canaan. He gives them instructions to care for the health and purity of the people. The owner does not decide alone; the priest examines the case. Scholars believe this may refer to some kind of mold or fungus on the walls, though the text uses the same word for it that it uses for leprosy.

For today: when you notice a problem in your life or in your home, do not hide it or ignore it. Speak soon with someone wise and trustworthy, and seek help in time.
exp.19:6:
God commands his people: "Consecrate yourselves," that is, set yourselves apart for God and cleanse yourselves of whatever dishonors him. Then he adds: "and be holy," or in other words, live in a way that reflects his character. The reason is simple: "because I am the LORD your God." They belong to him.

God speaks, through Moses, to Israel. Just before this, he warned against worshiping Molech and against consulting mediums and spiritists. Afterward he asks them to keep his statutes and makes clear that it is he who makes them holy. So holiness is the people's obedience and also God's work.

For today: if God is our God, our lives must be distinguished from whatever takes his place. Today you can identify a habit or influence that competes with God in your heart, surrender it to him in prayer, and ask for his help to obey him.
exp.12:0:
This verse is only the introduction to a new topic. It says that the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron.

The LORD, the God of Israel, speaks and addresses two leaders: Moses, who led the people, and Aaron, the priest. God gives them these rules so that the priest could examine carefully anyone who had a mark on the skin, and so protect the health and purity of the whole community. Scholars debate whether the "leprosy" here is exactly what we today call leprosy, since the term seems to include several conditions.

For today: God does not leave important matters to improvisation. Before judging a person or a situation, it is good to listen to God and examine the facts with patience, care, and compassion.
exp.14:22:
If someone touches the bed or the furniture where a woman with a flow of blood has sat, he is ritually unclean until evening. "Unclean" here means ritually unclean, not sinful or dirty through personal fault. The words "until evening" show that the uncleanness was temporary.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel. These laws were part of the purity rules of the covenant. They taught that God is holy and that his presence among the people had to be treated with reverence, especially in connection with the tabernacle. Scholars offer several explanations for the exact reasons behind these rules, but the text emphasizes holiness.

For today: God wants us to live with reverence toward him. Today we do not draw near through purity rituals, but through Christ, who cleanses us. We can ask ourselves each day: how can I approach God with gratitude and a clean heart?
exp.14:31:
This passage sums up part of the law about bodily impurities. A "discharge" is an abnormal flow from the body, and "an emission of semen" is a release of semen. The verse says these laws apply to the man who is "unclean" because of these causes.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. These rules were not about moral wickedness, but about what kept a person from approaching the tabernacle, where God dwelt. They taught that God is holy and that his presence among them was to be taken seriously. Scholars explain the exact meaning of these rules in several different ways.

For today: God cares for every area of our lives, even the most private ones. We can draw near to him with reverence and gratitude, knowing that he cleanses us and lets us stand in his presence.
exp.23:11:
They placed him in custody, meaning they held him in a temporary place of confinement until God made clear what they should do with him. The word for the place points to a temporary holding area, not a long sentence. The phrase about the will of the Lord being made clear means it was made known to them.

This is part of the account of the man who fought in the camp and cursed the Name of God. The narrator tells us that the people did not decide on their own. Because this was a new and serious case, they waited for God's answer, and then the Lord spoke to Moses (v. 13).

For today: when we face a hard conflict, we should not act in anger or haste. It is wise to stop, pray, seek God's guidance in His Word, and ask for counsel before we decide.
exp.15:5:
It says that Aaron, the high priest, had to bring a bull as a sin offering. That animal was for his own sin, not the people's. The verse uses the word "offer," meaning to bring or present the bull. "Atonement" here refers to making things right between Aaron and God, dealing with sin so that the relationship is restored. That offering was for him and his household.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions about the Day of Atonement. Before helping the people, Aaron had to deal with his own condition before God. The priests were also sinners and needed forgiveness. After that would come the two goats, one of them for Azazel, a term that is understood in several different ways.

For today: whoever leads others, in the family, the church, or the workplace, should begin by acknowledging their own faults. Coming close to God with humility, without pretending to be perfect, prepares us to serve with sincerity.
exp.12:52:
It says that if, after seven days, the priest examines the garment again and sees that the mildew has not spread, the final verdict is still not given. "Mildew" here refers to a stain or growth that affected the cloth, and the verse names the kinds of material involved: fabric, weave, knit, or leather. Here it speaks of clothing or leather items that had a suspicious mark.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel, and the priest is the one who examines the case. The garment had been set apart for seven days so that it could be watched calmly. In this way hasty decisions were avoided and the purity of the camp was protected. Scholars are not sure exactly what this mildew was; some think it was a kind of mold or fungus, but this is not known with certainty.

For today: do not judge quickly. Before deciding about a situation or a person, take time, observe with patience, and seek God's wisdom.
exp.1:12:
Every grain offering the people brought to God had to include salt. Salt could never be left out, because it was "the salt of the covenant of your God." A gift is what the offering is, and to season it means you add salt to it.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to Israel, in the instructions about sacrifices. Shortly before this, yeast and honey were forbidden in burnt offerings. Salt, on the other hand, was required. Many understand that salt pointed to something lasting that does not spoil, and for that reason it was linked with a firm agreement. The Bible does not explain this in detail, so it is an interpretation.

For today: if our relationship with God is a covenant, then what we give to him, such as time, work, or money, should come from steady faithfulness and not only from passing impulses. Let us ask him for help to be people who are steadfast and keep our word.
exp.13:17:
The priest takes the oil left in his palm and puts it on the head of the person who is being made clean. In this way the priest makes atonement for that person before the LORD.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the ritual of cleansing someone who has been healed of a skin disease. Before this step, the priest had already put oil on the ear, the thumb, and the big toe, along with the blood. Many understand the oil as a sign of God's presence, although the text does not explain this directly.

For today: God does not leave anyone half-restored. When someone returns to the community, they deserve to be received fully. We can welcome with kindness those who have suffered or made mistakes, and remember that God wants to restore our whole life.
exp.21:22:
This verse speaks of an ox or a sheep that has a deformed or stunted limb. It says that such an animal could be presented as a freewill offering, but that it is not acceptable to fulfill a vow. "Acceptable" means received with approval, and a "vow" is a promise made to God.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Aaron, the priests, and all Israel. The surrounding passage requires animals without defect to be offered to the Lord. This exception shows that a spontaneous offering had more flexibility than a formal promise. Interpreters explain in various ways why this difference existed, and the text does not fully clarify it.

For today: when we make a promise to God, we should keep it with integrity and with the best we have, not giving what we have left over. Giving generously and sincerely pleases Him.
exp.18:36:
It says the people must keep all the laws God gave them, and not only know them but put them into practice. The word "statutes" refers to God's commands; "ordinances" refers to his fair decisions, that is, his rules for living justly. The phrase "follow them" means to carry them out in action. At the end, "I am the LORD" reminds us who gives the orders: the Lord himself.

God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel, who have already been freed from Egypt. This chapter gathers instructions for living as a holy people: loving one's neighbor, being honest, and not oppressing others. Just before this, it speaks of honest scales and weights, that is, of being upright in business. This verse closes the chapter and sums up everything: obeying in daily life.

Today we can ask ourselves: is there something I already know God asks of me that I still do not do? You can choose one concrete thing, such as being honest at work, and put it into practice this week.
exp.24:25:
This verse speaks of an Israelite who became poor and sold part of his land, but who has no close relative to buy it back for him. It says that if he later prospers and gathers enough to redeem his land, he may buy it back himself. The "redeemer" is the close relative who pays to recover what was lost.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. The land belonged to God, and each family received it as an inheritance. These laws protected the poor so that they would not lose their inheritance forever. Even if no one helped, there was still hope, because in the year of jubilee the land returned to its owner.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we can help to get back on their feet. Perhaps a family member or a neighbor needs support to get out of debt. God invites us to be generous and supportive, and not to forget that He cares for those in need.
exp.15:32:
This verse says that the high priest will make atonement for the most holy place, the tent of meeting, the altar, the priests, and all the people of the assembly. To "make atonement" means to cleanse and cover sin so that the relationship with God is restored. "Assembly" refers to the whole community of Israel.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the Day of Atonement, a day of rest and self-denial. The anointed priest, dressed in holy linen, represented the people. Nothing and no one was left out: not the place, not the leaders, not the ordinary people. It was to be done once a year, as a lasting statute.

For today: each person needs to acknowledge their sin honestly, without excuses, including leaders. Christians see in Christ, our high priest, the complete atonement (Hebrews 9). Today we can approach God with humility and confidence, grateful for his forgiveness.
exp.6:19:
If a person is ritually unclean and still eats the meat of the peace offering, which belongs to the LORD, that person must be cut off from their people. The "peace offering" refers to the fellowship or thanksgiving offering. As for being "cut off," scholars do not agree: some think of expulsion from the community, others of a punishment from God, and others of death; the text does not give the details.

God speaks through Moses to Israel, within the instructions about the sacrifices. This offering was eaten in a meal before God, and for that reason care was taken that no one took part while ritually unclean. In this way God taught that his presence is holy and that coming near to him calls for respect.

For today: before we draw near to God in prayer, at the Lord's Supper, or in worship, it is good to pause, confess our failings, and come with humility. Christ cleanses us, but approaching with reverence remains important.
exp.23:3:
This verse says that the priest was to tend the pure gold lampstand and keep its lamps trimmed, arranged, and burning in the presence of the LORD. "Pure gold lampstand" refers to the lampstand made of solid gold, and "tend" means to look after the lamps with care, keeping them ready and lit. "LORD" is the name of God.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness, while Israel prepares to worship him in the tabernacle. He gives instructions about the oil and the lamps, which Aaron was to tend each evening until morning. Then he mentions the bread on the table. Some see in the light a symbol of God's presence, although the text does not explain this directly.

For today: cultivate with steady faithfulness your life of prayer and worship, even in small and repeated things. God values daily faithfulness, not only special moments.
exp.23:19:
This verse says that the punishment must match the harm done. "Fracture" means a broken bone. "Injury" is a wound or harm to the body. If someone injured another person, the penalty was to be equal to what he did, no more and no less.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, within the laws that organized their life as a nation. This rule was applied in the courts and gave equal justice to the foreigner and to the native. Its purpose was to limit revenge: no one was to take back more than had been done to him. Scholars debate whether it was always applied to the letter or whether a payment of compensation was often made instead.

For today: when someone wrongs you, do not respond with more harm than you received. Seek justice with fairness, and remember that Jesus invites us to go further and respond with grace (Matthew 5:38-39).
exp.10:42:
This verse tells the people of Israel not to defile themselves by eating animals that crawl along the ground. The "crawling creatures" here include small animals that creep or move close to the earth. To be "unclean" means to be impure, not fit to draw near to God in worship.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel, shortly after bringing them out of Egypt. These food laws set Israel apart from the peoples around them. The verses that follow explain the background: "I am the Lord your God: consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy." Scholars differ about the reason for each prohibition, but the text keeps returning to holiness.

For today: holiness begins in everyday life. We do not follow those food rules now, but we can ask which small habits draw us away from God, and choose to live in a way that honors him.
exp.4:2:
If a person touches human uncleanness, meaning something that makes a person ceremonially unclean, and does not know it, the verse says that person is guilty once they realize what happened. "Unclean" here refers to the state the law defines, not necessarily to wickedness. The word "realizes" means becoming aware of it, and "guilty" means the person must answer for it.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about sin offerings. These laws taught that God's holiness is serious, even when the wrong is done without intention. The passage goes on to call for confessing the sin and bringing an offering (Leviticus 5:5-6). Interpreters explain the exact meaning of this guilt in different ways, but all of them see here the need for cleansing and forgiveness.

For today: it is not enough to say "I did not know." Ask God to show you your hidden faults, and when you discover them, confess them with humility. He is faithful to forgive (1 John 1:9).
exp.23:17:
If someone kills an animal that belongs to another person, they must make restitution. Restitution means giving back or replacing what was lost. Here the verse speaks of killing the animal, and the wording "life for life" shows that the loss is to be paid back in kind.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses to Israel, in the wilderness. This law appears alongside others about justice: blasphemy, homicide, and injuries. Its purpose was that punishment be fair and proportionate, the same for the foreigner and for the native. Some understand the principle behind it as a limit on revenge.

For today: if you damage something that is not yours, take responsibility for it and make it right honestly, without excuses and without waiting to be asked.
exp.19:24:
God tells Israel that they must tell the difference between clean and unclean animals, and between clean and unclean birds. They were not to make themselves unclean by eating what He had declared impure, including anything that crawls on the ground. Making oneself unclean means becoming contaminated, and "set apart" means marked off as different.

The Lord speaks through Moses to the people before they enter the land of Canaan. He reminds them that He had set them apart from the other nations. These food rules were a visible sign that Israel belonged to God and was to live differently from the neighboring peoples.

For today: God still calls His people to a set-apart life. We do not follow the food rules today, but we can ask ourselves which customs around us pull us away from God, and decide, with kindness and firmness, to live differently for Him.
exp.25:10:
God promises to make his dwelling place among his people. He says that his soul will not despise them, that is, that he will not reject them or look down on them with contempt.

God himself speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel. This promise is part of the blessings that would come if they kept the covenant. It is a promise of nearness: the God who brought them out of Egypt wanted to live among them as their God.

For today: many Christians understand that, through Christ, God receives us and lives in us through his Spirit. If you sometimes feel that God is far away or angry, remember his desire to be close. Speak to him today with confidence, without fear of being rejected.
exp.7:5:
Moses presented Aaron and his sons and washed them with water. The first comment about the word the verse doesn't use has been removed, and the phrase is simply "washed them with water," which matches the verse. Washing them was the first step before they were dressed in the sacred garments.

Moses is the one who acts, following what God commanded him, and he does it before the whole assembled people at the entrance of the tabernacle. This was the ceremony in which Aaron and his sons were set apart as priests. Before they were clothed, they had to be cleansed. Many see here a symbol of purity for drawing near to God, though the text gives no further explanation.

For today: before serving God or drawing near to Him, it is good to do so with humility, recognizing that we need to be cleansed. We can pray asking Him for forgiveness and a clean heart, trusting that He receives us and prepares us to serve Him.
exp.4:4:
This verse says that when someone realizes they have done wrong in any of the cases mentioned, they must openly confess the sin they committed. The phrase "the sin he has committed" points to the specific wrong, and "must confess" means they are to acknowledge it openly, without hiding it or making excuses.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes these instructions on to the people of Israel. These are sins committed without realizing it at the time, such as touching something unclean or making an oath carelessly. Once the person discovered it, they were already responsible. Before bringing their offering, they had to confess their wrong. The offering showed that sin is serious and that God offers forgiveness.

For today: when God shows you a fault, do not hide it or justify it. Tell him honestly what you did. The Bible promises that God forgives those who confess (1 John 1:9).
exp.4:9:
In this verse, after the first bird was offered for the sin, the priest was to prepare the second bird as a burnt offering, following the ordinance that had been set. In this way the priest made atonement for the person for the sin he had committed, and he was forgiven.

God speaks to Moses and gives Israel instructions about the offerings. Here the case is someone poor who could not bring a lamb, so God allowed them to bring turtledoves or young pigeons. What mattered was the forgiveness, not the cost of the offering. One bird was offered for the sin, and the other was burned whole as a giving over to God.

For today: God does not place forgiveness beyond anyone's reach. If you have failed, do not stay hidden or think you have nothing to bring. Come near with sincerity, and remember that Christians see in Christ the complete sacrifice that reconciles us to God.
exp.24:2:
This verse says that the Israelites could work their land for six years. They could sow their fields, prune their vineyards, and gather in the crops. "Prune" means cutting away extra branches so that the plant produces better fruit. "Gather in" means collecting the harvest.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives instructions for the people who would enter the promised land. These six years of work prepare for the next command: in the seventh year the land would rest, like a sabbath to the LORD. First there is steady work, and then rest that trusts in God.

For today: God values both responsible work and rest. Work with dedication, but set aside time to rest and trust that God cares for you.
exp.12:42:
The priest is to examine the person closely. If a swelling from an infection appears on his bald head or forehead, and it is reddish-white and looks like a skin disease on the body, then it must be taken seriously. The phrase "like a skin disease" means that the sore looks like the disease when it appears on the skin.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The word "leprosy" here probably covered several skin diseases, not only what we today call leprosy. Being bald was not a problem; the priest had to tell the difference between something normal and a disease. These rules cared for the health and purity of the community.

For today: before judging someone or something, we should look with patience and not rush. God invites us to discern with wisdom and to treat those who suffer with compassion.
exp.12:8:
This verse says that when a person develops a skin disease, he must be brought to the priest. A "plague" here refers to a wound or mark on the skin. The Hebrew word often translated "leprosy" was used for several skin diseases, so we cannot be certain it was what we today call leprosy.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives them instructions for the people of Israel. The priest did not act as a physician; rather, he examined the person and declared whether he was clean or unclean. This protected the community and showed that the life of Israel belonged to God.

For today: when something in our life is sick or broken, let us not hide it. Let us seek help in time, whether from a pastor, a counselor, or a doctor, and bring everything before God with sincerity.
exp.20:21:
This verse says that a priest with a physical defect could not present the offerings before God, but he could still eat the sacred food of the priests. "The most holy food of his God" refers to the portions of the offerings that God gave to the priests. "Most holy" and "holy food" were different levels of offerings set apart for God.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to Aaron, his sons, and all Israel. The rules about service in the sanctuary were strict, and physical defects limited certain tasks. Even so, this verse shows that the priest with a defect was not excluded from God's provision or from his priestly family. Scholars explain the reasons for these rules in various ways; the text links them to the holiness of the sanctuary.

For today: even though we may have limitations or wounds, God does not remove us from his table. We can receive his care, and we can also welcome with dignity those who have limitations.
exp.9:17:
Moses tells Eleazar and Ithamar that the blood of that sin offering was not brought inside the sanctuary. Because of this, they should have eaten the meat in the sanctuary area, just as God had commanded.

Moses speaks with anger, shortly after the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron. The priests were to eat the meat of this offering as part of their service. But the male goat was burned completely. Aaron explains that, because of his mourning, eating that day would not have been appropriate, and Moses is satisfied. Scholars discuss the exact details of the case.

For today: God values obedience, but He also looks at the heart and understands our pain. Let us obey with seriousness and explain with humility.
exp.22:7:
For seven days you were to present a food offering to the LORD, an offering given to God and burned on the altar. The seventh day would also be a sacred assembly, a gathering set apart for worship, and on that day the people were not to do their regular work.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel. In Leviticus 23 the LORD lays out the appointed feasts of the year. This feast came after the Passover and remembered the departure from Egypt. God wanted the people to pause, remember, and worship at the beginning and at the end of the week.

For today: God invites us to set apart time for Him, setting aside work and hurry. You can keep a fixed time each week to pray, give thanks, and remember what God has done for you.
exp.23:6:
The verse says that pure frankincense was to be placed near each row of bread. That frankincense served as a memorial portion for the bread, a food offering to the LORD, meaning a part that was burned on the altar and represented the whole loaves before God. "Pure" means clean, without any mixture. Scholars often call the bread the "bread of the presence."

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness, giving instructions for the tabernacle. The twelve loaves are commonly linked with the twelve tribes of Israel, although the text does not say this directly. Each Sabbath they were replaced, and the priests ate the loaves in the holy place. It was a constant reminder of God's relationship with his people.

For today: God values what we offer him with purity and consistency. We can set aside a fixed moment each week to thank him, pray, and remember that we depend on him, coming with a sincere heart and without pretense.
exp.15:21:
The verse says that the goat would carry on itself all the guilt of the people and be sent away into a solitary place, out in the wilderness.
