"Iniquities" means the sins and wrongs of the people; "a solitary place" means a place where no one lives. The animal carried the guilt far away, to a place from which it would never return.

God speaks to Moses about the Day of Atonement, the most solemn day in Israel. Before this, Aaron had cleansed the sanctuary with the blood of the sacrifice. Then he laid his hands on this male goat and confessed the sins of the people. It was a visible picture that God removes the guilt of his people. Christian interpreters often see here a shadow of Christ, although the text itself does not say so.

For today: when you confess a sin to God, do not keep carrying it as though it still rested on you. God promises forgiveness and to remove guilt far from you. Pray with sincerity, receive his forgiveness, and walk in freedom.
exp.21:0:
This verse is an introductory phrase. It says that the LORD spoke to Moses and gave him a message to pass on. The Hebrew word behind "the LORD" is the divine name, and the Berean Standard Bible renders it in small capitals. The verse does not yet bring the content; it only marks that what follows comes from God and not from Moses.

God speaks, and does so through Moses, who hands the instructions to Aaron and his sons, the priests. In what follows, God asks them to handle with respect the holy offerings of the people and not to approach them in a state of ritual impurity. The purpose is that his holy name not be treated as something common.

For today: before reading the Bible, praying, or serving in church, we can pause for a moment and listen carefully. If God speaks, it is worth responding with reverence, with a sincere heart, and without taking lightly what he considers holy.
exp.4:16:
This verse says that if someone violates one of God's commandments even though they were unaware of it, they are still guilty and must bear the consequences. The phrase "even though he was unaware" shows that guilt does not depend only on knowing what you did. The phrase "shall bear his punishment" means the person will have to answer for the wrong they have done.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about the offerings. In this part of the law, sin committed through ignorance or carelessness was also taken seriously, but God provided a way of forgiveness: a ram without blemish, brought to the priest, and so the person was forgiven.

For today: it is not enough to say "I didn't know." We can ask God to show us our hidden faults through his Word, and come to him with humility, trusting that he offers forgiveness to those who approach him sincerely.
exp.14:14:
This verse says the priest will sacrifice the two birds the healed person brought: one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering, which was burned whole on the altar. "The priest is to sacrifice them" means the priest would carry out the offering. In this way the priest made atonement for the man before the LORD, cleansing him from the uncleanness caused by his discharge and standing before God on his behalf.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, giving Israel laws about ritual uncleanness caused by bodily discharges. After being healed and waiting seven days, the person returned to the community and to worship through this offering. The text does not say that having a discharge was a personal sin; it was a matter of ritual uncleanness, and scholars explain the meaning of the two offerings in various ways.

For today: God cares that we return to his presence and to the community. When you feel far away or unfit, remember that God provides the way back; for Christians, that way is Christ.
exp.0:7:
It says that Aaron's sons, the priests, are to arrange on the burning wood on the altar the pieces of the animal that has already been cut up, including the head and the fat. The fat referred to here is the fat that covers the intestines. To arrange means to set the pieces in place with care.

God speaks to Moses from the tabernacle and gives him instructions for the offerings. The burnt offering was burned whole, and the person who brought the animal offered it willingly. The priests carried out the part of the service at the altar. Many understand that this offering expressed total devotion to God.

For today: God values order and care in worship. We can offer Him what we do each day, not in a hurry or carelessly, but with attention and from the heart, as one who hands over something that matters.
exp.26:2:
If someone had promised to dedicate a person to God, including themselves, they could fulfill that vow by paying a set amount. For a man from twenty to sixty years old, the amount was fifty shekels of silver. The word "valuation" in the verse means the assessed price. The sanctuary shekel was the official unit of weight used in worship.

God speaks to Moses so that he may teach Israel. Vows were serious promises made to the LORD. This law gave an orderly way to fulfill them with an offering. Scholars explain in different ways why the amounts vary according to age and sex. It is not a judgment about the worth of the person before God.

For today: think before you promise something to God. If you make a commitment, keep it with seriousness and sincerity. God takes our word seriously.
exp.7:35:
This verse says that Aaron and his sons obeyed everything the LORD commanded them through Moses. They did not add anything or leave anything out; they did what they were asked.

Here the account of the consecration of the priests comes to its close. For seven days, Aaron and his sons remained at the entrance of the tabernacle, the tent where God met with his people. Moses had passed on God's instructions, with sacrifices and rituals to set them apart for service. The text stresses their complete obedience, and shows that taking the command seriously was a matter of life and death.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we obey God only in what seems easy or convenient. Choose one clear instruction from the Bible that you have left undone, such as forgiving or being honest, and decide to carry it out this week with steady commitment, trusting that God will help you.
exp.6:31:
This verse says that when someone presented a peace offering, they had to give the priest the right thigh of the animal as their contribution. The thigh is the upper part of the hind leg, and the offering was set apart as a gift to the priest from the sacrifice.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Israel. These rules explained how to divide the meat of these offerings: part was for God, part for the priests, and part for the one who offered it. In this way, the priests, who had no land of their own, received their provision.

Today we can learn to generously support those who serve in the church and to give thanks to God with the best we have, recognizing that everything comes from Him.
exp.18:6:
This verse says that if any of the meat of the peace offering was eaten on the third day, it was tainted, meaning spoiled and unfit, and it would not be accepted, that is, God would not receive it with pleasure.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel on how to live as a holy people. The peace offering was offered voluntarily and eaten together in community, with thankfulness. It was to be eaten that day or the next; whatever was left over was burned. The exact reason is not explained here; some think it taught not to treat what is holy with carelessness, and others see a practical concern with the meat. This is not certain.

For today: let us give God our best and our hearts on time, without leaving gratitude for later. When God blesses us, let us thank Him promptly and sincerely, not out of routine.
exp.14:32:
This verse closes the chapter's list of cases of ritual impurity. "A woman in her menstrual period" refers to a woman during her monthly flow. "Discharge" is a secretion from the body, whether from a man or a woman. And "a man who lies with an unclean woman" is the one who had relations with a woman in that state. All of them were ceremonially impure for a time.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. These rules taught that God is holy and that He dwells in the midst of His people, in the tabernacle. This concerned ritual purity, not moral sin. Scholars explain the background of these laws in various ways, but the text itself emphasizes God's holiness and the care due to His presence.

Today we can take seriously that God is holy and that drawing near to Him is a privilege. For the Christian, Christ cleanses us and gives us access. Let us respond with gratitude and with a sincere life.
exp.6:20:
This verse repeats a warning: if anyone had become unclean, whether by touching something defiled, by human impurity, by an unclean animal, or by anything unclean and detestable, they could not eat any of the meat of the peace offering that belongs to the LORD. If they did, they would have to be cut off from their people. That phrase may mean they were separated from the community, or perhaps a more serious punishment; scholars understand it in several ways. The peace offering is the sacrifice of fellowship or thanksgiving.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. That sacrifice was a meal before the LORD, and God wanted it to be eaten with reverence. Ritual purity taught them that God is holy and that approaching Him is not a light matter.

Today, we do not follow those ritual laws, but we can learn to approach God with respect and sincerity. Before praying or taking part in the Lord's Supper, we can pause, confess our failings, and trust that Christ cleanses us.
exp.23:20:
Leviticus 24:21 says that whoever kills an animal must make restitution, but whoever kills a man must be put to death. The verse uses "make restitution" for a killed animal, which means paying back or replacing what was lost. And it uses "must be put to death" for a killed person, which is the penalty for taking a human life.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes the law on to Israel. These laws set up justice among the people and limited revenge: the punishment had to match the harm, no more and no less. The same law applied to the foreigner and to the native-born. Some scholars think that the principle of "an eye for an eye" set a limit on justice, and was not permission to take revenge.

For today, human life is worth far more than goods or animals. We can learn to repair the harm we cause and to treat everyone with the same justice, without favoritism or revenge.
exp.17:15:
It tells you not to have sexual relations with your brother's wife. The verse gives the reason: doing this would shame your brother.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, just before they enter Canaan. This chapter sets limits on family relationships so that Israel would be different from the neighboring peoples. Some scholars think it refers to a woman married to the brother; in Deuteronomy 25:5 there is an exception when a brother died without children, and scholars debate how the two passages relate.

Today we can care for the marriages in our family and among our friends. Respect your relatives' spouses, avoid flirting, and protect the trust between brothers.
exp.25:21:
God says that if the people keep rebelling, he will send wild animals against them. These animals will take away their children and destroy their livestock, and their numbers will be reduced until the roads lie empty, because almost no one will dare to travel them.

The Lord speaks through Moses at the end of the book of Leviticus. He gives Israel a warning within the covenant: obedience would bring blessing, and persistent rebellion would bring discipline. These consequences increase in stages, growing seven times over. Their purpose was to lead the people back to God, not merely to punish them.

For today: God corrects us so that we return to him, and that correction is a sign of his care. If you feel that God is calling your attention to some path you have taken, do not harden your heart. Listen to him promptly, confess, and change direction.
exp.25:8:
It says God promises to turn toward his people with favor. The phrase "I will turn toward you" means looking on them with kindness and attending to them. He promises that they will grow, that they will be many, and that he will keep his covenant firm, that is, the solemn agreement or promise he made with them.

God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel. These words are in the part of blessings that God promises if the people walk in his commandments. Warnings follow if they disobey. God wants Israel to understand that his care and his faithfulness are the foundation of their life as a nation.

For today: we can trust that God is faithful to his promises, even when we feel small or weak. If we have wandered far, we can turn back to him with simplicity, knowing that he receives us. Today, take a moment to thank him for his faithfulness and to place a specific need in his hands.
exp.20:7:
It says the priest must be treated as someone set apart for God. "You are to regard him as holy" means you are to honor him and treat him as holy, that is, set apart for a sacred purpose. "The food of your God" refers to the offerings the priest presented on the altar. God gives the reason: "I the LORD am holy—I who set you apart," and he also makes his people holy.

God speaks to Moses, so that he may instruct the priests, the sons of Aaron. They served up close at the offerings, so they were expected to live in a way and keep a home that honored that calling. The rules about marriage and family showed that their whole life represented God before the people.

For today: when you serve God in any way, take care with your example and your integrity. And respect with gratitude those who serve others in the faith, without demanding perfection, but encouraging them to live with sincerity before God.
exp.14:9:
If anyone touches anything that the person with a discharge sat or lay on, that person becomes unclean until evening. Whoever carries such an object must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he too remains unclean until evening. "Unclean" means ceremonially unclean, not sinful. A "discharge" refers to an abnormal secretion from the body.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel. These rules of purity protected the health and the living together of the people, and they reminded them that God is holy and dwells among them. Scholars agree that they taught reverence toward God; about their hygienic or symbolic reasons there are different opinions.

For today: take care what you touch and what you carry with you, because what surrounds us influences us. Seek inner cleanness, asking God to purify your heart, for Christ cleanses us completely.
exp.6:33:
God says that he took two portions from the peace offerings the people brought: the breast, which was waved from side to side before him, and the thigh, which was lifted up as a gift. He gave these parts to Aaron and his sons, the priests. The thigh here is the upper part of the animal's hind leg, and "a permanent portion" means a share that is meant to last.

God himself speaks within the instructions about the sacrifices. The priests served at the tabernacle and did not receive land as the other tribes did. So God arranged that they would live from what the people brought to him. It was a way of caring for them while they served.

For today: let us give value to the work of those who serve and teach in the church, and support them with generosity and gratitude as a way of honoring God.
exp.13:14:
This verse describes one step in the purification ritual for a person healed of leprosy. The priest takes oil from the "log," which was a small measure of liquid (less than half a liter, though its exact size is debated), and pours it into his left palm to use right away.

God gives these instructions to Moses so that the people will know how to welcome back into the community someone who is already healthy. Before this, blood was put on the ear, the hand, and the foot; now the oil will be placed on those same places. Many understand the oil as a sign of consecration and of God's Spirit, although the text here does not explain it.

God does not only heal; he also restores and returns the person to the community. Today we can welcome with kindness someone who has been restored, without reminding them of their past.
exp.13:56:
This verse closes the section on skin diseases. It says these instructions are "to determine when something is clean or unclean." The verse also states that this is the law regarding skin diseases and mildew, so the reader can see that the law covers both people and fabric or buildings.

God gives this law to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priests were to examine people and things and declare whether they were clean or not. This protected the community and reminded the people that God is holy. Many scholars also see a symbolic meaning, although the law itself deals with health and ritual purity.

For today: God cares about the real life of his people, and also about their care for one another. We can ask ourselves whether we help others to heal and return to the community, instead of setting them aside with contempt.
exp.10:34:
It says that if the dead body of certain unclean animals falls onto an object, that object becomes "unclean," meaning it is not fit for the people's ordinary use. An oven or a cooking pot had to be smashed. The verse says these items are unclean and will remain unclean for you, so they were to be treated as impure and not used.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel. These laws taught the people to distinguish between clean and unclean, and to live as a people set apart for God (Leviticus 11:44-45). Scholars explain the reason behind each rule in various ways, and the Bible does not detail every reason.

For today: God is concerned with everyday life, even with the kitchen and the home. Today we can ask ourselves which small things in our daily routine draw us closer to God or defile us, and take care to make our common decisions with reverence.
exp.1:9:
This verse says that after a small portion of the grain offering was burned on the altar, the remainder belonged to Aaron and his sons, that is, to the priests. It is called "a most holy part" because it was something very special, set apart for God. An "offering" is a gift presented to God, and the "food offerings to the LORD" were the gifts brought to him at the altar.

God speaks to Moses and gives instructions about the offerings in the tabernacle. This offering was made of flour, oil, and incense. In this way God provided for the priests, who served on his behalf and had no land of their own as an inheritance.

Today we can learn to support with gratitude those who serve God and his people. Giving generously reminds us that everything we have comes from God, and that he cares for those who dedicate themselves to his service.
exp.21:20:
It says that when someone brings a peace offering to the LORD, whether to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering, the animal must be without any blemish or defect to be acceptable. The "peace offering" here refers to the fellowship or peace offering, and "blemish" means a flaw or stain. Only an animal without defect will be "acceptable," that is, well received by God.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Aaron, his sons, and all Israel. These laws teach the priests and the people to approach a holy God with reverence. Animals with defects could not be offered, although the text that follows allows some minor exceptions for freewill offerings, but not for vows.

For today: when we give something to God, whether time, money, or service, it is good to give our best and not what is left over. Christians do not offer animals, but we can offer a sincere, grateful life given wholeheartedly.
exp.3:32:
Leviticus 4:33 describes what the person bringing a sin offering had to do. They were to lay their hand on the head of the animal, then slaughter it as a sin offering at the place where the burnt offering was slaughtered. The sacrifice was meant to cover over and take away the guilt of sin.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes these instructions on to Israel. They are rules for sins committed without intention. Laying the hand on the animal shows that the animal was taking the place of the person. Everything was done in a set place, with the priest guiding the process.

For today: sin is serious and has a cost. Christians see in these sacrifices a sign that points to Christ, who bore our guilt. We can come to God with sincerity, admit our failings, and trust in his forgiveness.
exp.10:23:
It says that whoever touches the dead body of certain animals, which God has just declared unclean, will be unclean until evening. Unclean does not mean dirty from lack of cleanliness, but unfit, for a time, to take part in worship.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron so that they may teach Israel. These laws taught the people to live as a nation set apart for God, who said, "Be holy, for I am holy." Scholars do not agree on the exact reason for each rule: some see hygiene, others symbolism or separation from neighboring customs. Here the impurity was temporary, lasting until evening.

Today we are not under these rules, but we can learn to take care of what we touch and take in. Ask God to help you live with a clean heart, set apart for Him.
exp.19:2:
God says he will oppose anyone who gives their children to Molech. To be "cut off from his people" means to be removed from the community. "Offspring" means the children, and to "defile" means to make something unclean or dishonor it. This practice pollutes God's holy place and dishonors his holy name.

The Lord speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. Molech was a false god worshiped by the neighboring nations, and his worship included offering children. God forbids this because Israel was a people set apart for him and because children's lives are precious. Scholars debate the exact details of the ritual.

For today: do not give what is most valuable to any modern idol, such as money, success, or comfort. Care for and protect children, and teach them to know and honor God.
exp.12:1:
This verse describes what to do when someone noticed a swelling, a rash, or a bright spot on their skin that might be an infectious skin disease. The person was not to decide alone or keep it hidden: they had to be brought to Aaron the priest or to one of his sons who served as a priest.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to give instructions to the people of Israel. The Hebrew word that the verse uses for these skin conditions covered several kinds of skin disease, and we cannot be certain that it matches what we call leprosy today. The priest examined the case to protect the health and purity of the whole community.

For today: when something worries us, whether in the body, in the heart, or in our conduct, it is not wise to hide it or judge it alone. Let us seek wise help, such as a doctor, a pastor, or a trusted friend, and let them guide us with honesty and care.
exp.22:20:
On the day of the Feast of Weeks, also called Pentecost, the people were to proclaim a sacred assembly and gather together. On that day they were not to do any regular work, meaning the everyday labor of their jobs and trades. This rule was a permanent statute, a lasting command, to be kept wherever they lived and for the generations to come.

God speaks here, giving these instructions to Moses for Israel. The feasts marked the people's calendar and reminded them that the harvest and life came from the LORD. Then the text mentions leaving part of the harvest for the poor and the stranger, joining worship with generosity.

For today: set aside regular time to stop, gather with others to worship, and give thanks to God. And let that gratitude become sharing with those who have less.
exp.12:13:
If raw flesh appears on a person (an open wound, showing red and healthy flesh), then from that day the priest declares him unclean. Unclean means ceremonially impure, not fit to enter worship with the people. The "leprosy" of the Bible was a broad name for several skin diseases, not only the one we know today.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives rules for the priest to examine cases of diseased skin among Israel. It is striking that if the whole body turned white, the person was declared clean, but raw flesh marked impurity again. Scholars explain this in several ways, and it is not entirely clear.

For today: let us not hide our wounds or pretend to be well. Let us allow God and trusted people to see them honestly, because healing begins when we stop pretending.
exp.22:18:
This verse commands that two other offerings be presented at the Feast of Firstfruits: a male goat as a sin offering, that is, a sacrifice to cover sin, and two male lambs a year old as a peace offering, an offering of fellowship and thanksgiving with God.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Israel about its feasts. This is the Feast of Weeks, which came after the wheat harvest. Although it was celebrated with joy, the people were to acknowledge that they needed forgiveness before offering their thanksgiving. Many Christians see here a sign pointing to Christ, although the text itself does not say so.

For today: before thanking God for his blessings, take a moment to acknowledge your failings and receive his forgiveness. In this way your gratitude springs from a sincere heart and is at peace with him.
exp.12:46:
This verse begins a new section of the law. It speaks of a mildew or mold that may appear in clothing or cloth, whether wool or linen. The word translated "contaminated" describes something harmful that spoils or stains, and the mildew described here is the kind that can spread through fabric.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. Earlier, the sick person was discussed; now the subject is the garment. The priests were to examine the case, and in this way the health and purity of the whole community were cared for. Scholars are not sure exactly what mold or stain is being described.

For today: God is concerned with the small details of everyday life. We can honestly look at what is slowly being damaged in our lives, and ask Him for help in time.
exp.20:13:
This verse says that the high priest could not marry a widow, a divorced woman, or a woman defiled by prostitution. He had to marry a virgin from his own people. A "divorced woman" is a woman who has been sent away from her husband, and "defiled by prostitution" refers to a woman who has sold herself sexually.

God speaks to Moses about the high priest, who had been anointed with oil and set apart for service in the sanctuary. His rules were stricter than those for the common people, to show the holiness of his office. Some understand this as a symbol of purity and total dedication; the Bible does not explain every reason in detail.

For today: those of us who serve God must take care of our lives and our decisions, because our example matters. In addition, in Christ every person, whatever their past, is received and forgiven.
exp.24:47:
This verse says that if a poor Israelite had to sell himself as a servant to a foreigner, he is not lost forever. He keeps the right to be bought back, that is, freed by paying the price. And the first one who should do it is someone from his own family, one of his brothers.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses speaks to the people, in the laws of the year of jubilee. These laws protected the poor and kept debt from enslaving a family forever. The verses that follow mention the uncle, the cousin, or a close relative as possible redeemers, the one who buys back what was lost. Here the key idea is to buy back a person who has been sold.

For today: if a relative or a brother in the faith falls into need, do not look on from a distance. Ask how you can help him get back on his feet, with money, time, or support, as a good brother would.
exp.25:15:
God says that if his people disobey him, he will bring upon them sudden terror, wasting disease, and fever that will destroy their sight and drain their life. Sudden terror means fear that comes on without warning, wasting disease means a sickness that slowly leaves the body weak and worn out, and fever is a burning sickness that can destroy sight and drain strength. The people will also sow their seed in vain, because their enemies will eat what they harvest.

God himself speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel in the covenant made at Sinai. Before this passage (Leviticus 26:3-13) he promises blessings for obedience. Here he warns of the consequences of rejecting his covenant. These warnings were meant to lead the people to repentance, not to destroy them, and the verses that follow show a progressive punishment.

For today: do not take every illness or loss as punishment, since the Bible does not teach that. But this text invites us to examine whether we are listening to God with sincerity. Today, set aside a few minutes to read his Word and ask him to show you something you should correct.
exp.24:19:
This verse records a question the people would ask with worry: "What will we eat in the seventh year if we do not sow or gather our produce?" In that year they would not plant, and they would not bring in a harvest. The idea of gathering in the crop is simply the idea of harvesting what the land produces.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. He had commanded them to let the land rest every seventh year. God knows that obeying would seem risky, so he names their doubt ahead of time and then promises to bless the sixth year with enough harvest to last three years.

Today, obeying God sometimes seems like an economic or personal risk. We can bring that worry to him honestly, as the people would have, and take a concrete step of obedience, such as setting aside time to rest or being generous, trusting that God cares for those who obey him.
exp.18:15:
It says we should not go about from one person to another spreading gossip among the people of our community. "Spreading slander" here refers to spreading rumors or lies that harm others. The second part, "You must not endanger the life of your neighbor," can be understood in two ways: do nothing that puts another person's life in danger, for example through false accusations, or do not stand idly by when their life is at risk. It ends with "I am the LORD," which reminds us who gives this command.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. In this chapter he teaches them how to live as a holy people. The verses around it deal with justice in judgment, the care of the weak, and love for one's neighbor instead of hatred and revenge.

For today: before repeating something about someone, ask yourself whether it is true, whether it is necessary, and whether it helps. If not, it is better to keep silent, or to go and speak directly with the person.
exp.6:18:
This verse says that if meat from the peace offering touched anything unclean, it could no longer be eaten and had to be burned up. By contrast, any other meat could be eaten by anyone who was ceremonially clean. The word "unclean" here means ceremonially impure, not necessarily dirty.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Israel about the offerings. The peace offering was shared in fellowship, and because it belonged to the LORD it had to be treated with respect. These rules taught that drawing near to God requires purity and reverence, although the details of that system applied within the context of the old covenant.

For today: when you come to worship or to pray, do not take it lightly. Examine your heart, confess whatever defiles you, and remember that Christ cleanses us so that we may approach God with confidence and gratitude.
exp.17:10:
This verse forbids having sexual relations with the daughter of your father's wife, born to your father. The phrase "uncover the nakedness" is an old expression for having sexual relations. The text says she is your sister, even though she has a different mother.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Israel before they enter Canaan. These laws were meant to protect families and to keep the people distinct from the customs of Egypt and Canaan (18:3). Some scholars see here a case of half-sisters already mentioned in verse 9; others see a clarification about adopted daughters in the family. There is no complete certainty.

For today: take care to maintain healthy boundaries in your family. Treat your relatives with respect and purity, and seek help if someone crosses those boundaries.
exp.13:43:
This verse says that the priest will come back to inspect the house. If the mildew has spread again, even after the stones were removed and the walls were scraped and re-plastered, it is a destructive mildew, meaning a growth that keeps eating away at the structure, and the house is declared unclean. The verse's description of the decay as destructive points to this kind of steady damage, and the plaster here refers to the coat of mud applied to the walls.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people who were going to enter Canaan. They were rules of ritual purity and also of care for the community. The priest examined the case calmly, and only after several attempts was the house ordered to be torn down.

For today: when a problem keeps coming back again and again, it is not enough to cover it up. It is wise to examine it honestly, to seek wise counsel, and to have the courage to remove at the root whatever is causing harm, even when it costs us.
exp.0:8:
The verse says that the entrails and legs must be washed with water before the priest burns the whole animal on the altar. A burnt offering is one that is burned completely. The BSB calls the offering "a food offering" and "a pleasing aroma to the LORD," which means God received the offering with pleasure.

God speaks to Moses from the tent of meeting and gives him instructions so that Israel may draw near to Him. The burnt offering expressed total surrender and acknowledgment of sin. Scholars understand the washing as a way of presenting the offering clean, though the text does not explain all its details.

For today: God deserves the best of us, not leftovers. We can sincerely offer Him our time, our decisions, and our hearts, trusting that Christ, according to the New Testament, makes us acceptable before Him.
exp.10:13:
This verse continues the list of birds the Israelites were not to eat. It names the kite and falcons, "any kind of falcon," meaning the whole group of birds of that kind. Today it is not easy to know exactly which bird each one was, since the Hebrew names are understood in different ways. They are birds of prey or scavengers. "Abomination" here means something they were to refuse as food.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel, his newly freed people. These laws about clean and unclean animals taught them to live set apart for God. Scholars offer several reasons: hygiene, separation from other peoples, or spiritual teaching. The text emphasizes that God calls his people to be holy.

For today: although Christians understand that Christ changed those dietary rules (Mark 7:19; Acts 10), the call to holiness remains. Ask yourself: what habits or influences should I reject in order to live closer to God?
exp.7:22:
It says that Moses slaughtered the ram of the ordination and put some of its blood on three parts of Aaron's body: the earlobe of his right ear, the thumb of his right hand, and the big toe of his right foot. The word "slaughtered" means "killed," as the animal was put to death for the ceremony.

This is part of the ceremony in which Aaron and his sons were set apart as priests. Moses acts following what God commanded him. The blood signified purification and dedication to God. Scholars often see in the ear, the hand, and the foot a symbol of hearing, working, and walking for God, though the text does not explain it in those words.

We can ask God that what we hear, what we do, and where we walk belong to Him. Today, before starting the day, offer Him your ears, your hands, and your steps in a simple prayer.
exp.25:2:
This verse begins a condition. The words "if you follow" can be understood as "if you live" or "if you walk the path." The laws God gave are his statutes, carefully keeping his commandments means guarding them closely, and putting them into practice means actually doing them, not only hearing them.

God himself speaks to Israel through Moses, shortly after giving them the law at Sinai. Earlier he had asked them not to worship idols and to honor the Sabbath. Now he sets out the covenant: if they obey him, blessings will come, such as rain in its season, good harvests, and a secure life in their land. This was a promise to Israel as a nation, within their covenant with God.

For today: obedience to God is not only knowing what the Bible says but living it. Choose one teaching you already know, such as forgiving or being honest, and put it into practice today, trusting in God.
exp.21:28:
When someone offers a thank offering to the LORD, it should be given so that it will be acceptable to God on their behalf, not out of obligation or pressure. It also notes that the offering's acceptance is the point of the instruction, and that this reflects the purpose behind the sacrifice.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Aaron, his sons, and all Israel on how to care for what is holy. In this chapter he calls for offerings without defect and made with reverence. The thank offering was to be eaten that same day, as the following verse points out, and everything ends with a call to obedience in the name of the LORD.

For today: when you give thanks to God, whether with your time, your service, or your resources, do it with a sincere and joyful heart. Before you give or serve, pause and remember why you are thankful.
exp.6:0:
This verse opens the instructions about the guilt offering. The sacrifice was offered to make things right after a wrong, especially when harm had been done to God or to one's neighbor. It is described as "most holy," meaning that it was set apart for God and had to be treated with respect.

God gave these laws to Moses so that he would pass them on to Israel. The book of Leviticus teaches how the people could live near a holy God and what to do when they failed. The guilt offering showed that sin is serious and needs to be dealt with, not ignored.

For today: we should not take our wrongs lightly. When we have offended God or someone else, it is good to acknowledge it honestly, ask forgiveness, and repair the harm. Christians believe that Christ offered the final sacrifice, and that encourages us to draw near with humility and confidence.
exp.10:35:
A spring (a natural fountain of water) or a cistern (a pit where water gathers) remains clean, even if dead animals are nearby. But a person who touches a carcass inside that water becomes unclean. The word translated "unclean" means ceremonially impure, not fit for worship, and does not necessarily mean "dirty" or "sinful."

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel. The laws about dead animals and vessels taught that God is holy and that his people were to live differently. Many scholars also see a practical concern for health, although the text stresses above all holiness. The reason for the special treatment of plentiful water is not explained; some think that running or abundant water does not become contaminated easily.

For today: God cares about the details of everyday life. Let us ask him for wisdom to take care of what we touch, see, and say, and to live with purity of heart in our daily lives.
exp.22:10:
This verse tells the priest to wave the sheaf before the LORD. Waving meant lifting and moving the offering back and forth, as a way of presenting it to the Lord. The sheaf is a bundle of the first stalks of the barley harvest. By bringing it, the people would be accepted by God on their behalf. The verse gives the timing as "the day after the Sabbath." Scholars disagree about which Sabbath is meant: some think it is the weekly day of rest during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and others think it is the first day of that feast.

God speaks to Moses to teach Israel about the feasts. When the people entered the promised land and brought in their harvest, they were to acknowledge that the harvest came from the Lord, so they gave him the first portion first.

For today: before you spend or share what you receive, whether wages, time, or talents, give God the best first with gratitude, remembering that everything comes from his hand.
exp.13:18:
In the ceremony for declaring cleansed a person who had had leprosy, the priest first sacrifices the sin offering. With it he makes atonement, that is, he covers or repairs what kept the person from drawing near to God. After that, he slaughters the burnt offering, an offering that was burned whole on the altar. The verse does not say how the animal was killed, so we should not assume more than the text tells us. The "uncleanness" refers to ceremonial impurity.

God speaks to Moses and gives instructions for the priest. The person was already healed of the illness, but still needed to be restored before God and before the community. The rites follow an order: first the guilt and sin are dealt with, and then comes total surrender to God.

For today: God does not only want to heal us; he also wants to restore our relationship with him. We can draw near with humility and confidence, remembering that Christ, according to the New Testament, fulfilled what these sacrifices foreshadowed.
exp.21:14:
The passage says that the priests must not treat as common the sacred offerings that the Israelites present to the LORD. To profane something means to treat as ordinary what God has set apart for himself. Here, "set apart" means that the Israelites separate or dedicate those offerings to the LORD.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Aaron and the priests. Earlier, the rules explained who could eat of the sacred offerings: the priest's family, but not an outsider. With this, God protects the holiness of what is given to him and keeps the priests from bearing guilt. The following verse reminds us that it is God who makes holy.

For today: what belongs to God deserves respect and sincerity. We can care for our worship, our service, and our offerings with reverence, without taking them lightly or using them for our own gain.
exp.21:1:
God tells Moses to warn Aaron and his sons, the priests, that they must treat with respect the sacred offerings the Israelites dedicate to him. If they handle these offerings carelessly, they dishonor his holy name, treating it as something ordinary. The verse closes with "I am the LORD," as if reminding them who is speaking.

The Lord speaks to Moses, and Moses is to pass the message on to the priests. Israel's offerings were dedicated to God, and the priests handled them. The verses that follow explain that they were not to approach them while in a state of uncleanness.

For today: when we pray, serve, or teach something about God, it is good to do so with reverence and a sincere heart. What belongs to God should not be treated with carelessness or out of mere habit.
exp.17:3:
You are to practice God's judgments and keep His statutes by walking in them. The verse below sets out what that means.

It says God asks his people to put into practice his fair rules and decisions, and to keep his laws. Living by them means following them in your everyday life. The verse closes with the reason behind it all: "I am the LORD your God."

God speaks, through Moses, to the Israelites. They were about to enter Canaan after having lived in Egypt. God tells them not to copy the customs of those peoples, and shows them another way. Right after this come laws about purity in family and sexual relationships.

For today: before following what "everyone does," ask yourself what God wants. His Word can guide your daily decisions, even when that means going against the crowd.
exp.12:21:
If the mark on the skin spreads further, the priest must declare the person unclean; it is an infection. "Unclean" here means ceremonially impure, not necessarily wicked. The condition is a skin problem that spreads or gets worse. In that time, the Hebrew word translated as "leprosy" covered several skin conditions, not only what we today call leprosy.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, giving instructions to the people of Israel. The priest did not act as a doctor, but as one who watched over the purity and orderly life of the community. Before deciding, he observed, waited, and examined again. The spreading of the spot was a clear sign.

For today: let us not downplay what is growing in us, such as anger, bitterness, or a bad habit. Rather, let us seek help and wise counsel soon, and ask God to heal us.
exp.26:16:
If a person dedicates his field to God during the Year of Jubilee, the price stands as it was set: the full amount is paid, calculated according to what is sown in the field (fifty shekels of silver for each homer of barley). To consecrate something means to set it apart for God. The valuation is the amount the priest assesses.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. The land belonged to God, and each family received it as an inheritance. The Jubilee, which came every fifty years, returned the land to its family. Therefore, the value of a dedicated field depended on how many years remained until the next Jubilee. At the beginning of the Year of Jubilee, the value is at its highest.

For today: what we give to God should be offered with sincerity and with clear accounts, without haggling. And let us remember that everything we have is lent to us by Him; offering it with gratitude and honesty is a form of worship.
exp.18:27:
This verse forbids two things: cutting or gashing the body because of someone who has died, and putting any mark on the skin. The reader's version says "tattoo marks," so the verse should use that same wording. The verse ends with "I am the LORD," which gives the command the weight of an order from God himself.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, within the laws of holiness. The neighboring peoples had mourning rites and religious practices that included cutting or marking the body. God wanted a distinct people, one that would not mix their faith with those customs. Scholars disagree about exactly what kind of tattooing was meant, but the context points to pagan practices connected with the dead.

For today: when you suffer a loss, bring your pain to God with prayer and sincere weeping, and lean on your community. He cares for you, and your body belongs to him.
exp.23:18:
The verse says that if someone injures another person, the same must be done to him. An "injures" is a physical wound or harm, and "neighbor" is the person next to us, a fellow, in this case another Israelite. The phrase means that the punishment should match the harm done.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes the law on to the people of Israel after a case of cursing and violence in the camp. This rule, often called the "law of retaliation," set a limit on revenge: one could not take back more than had been done. It also placed the matter with judges and the community, not with personal vengeance. Some believers see here a principle of equal justice for all; others stress that Jesus later taught to go further (Matthew 5:38-39).

Today we can learn to be fair and not to answer evil with more evil. Before reacting in anger, let us ask God for wisdom to act with equity and mercy.
exp.13:45:
Anyone who entered the house during any of the days that it was closed up was unclean until evening. "Unclean" means ceremonially impure, not necessarily guilty of anything. The phrase "until evening" marks the limit of that condition.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel, who are already looking forward to living in Canaan. The matter concerns a house with a persistent mold or growth. The closing up served to observe whether the problem spread. The word translated as "leprosy" is very broad and does not refer only to the skin disease we know today. The temporary impurity protected the community and cared for the order of worship.

For today: when something harmful appears at home, in a relationship, or in a habit, it is wise not to ignore it. It is better to pause, seek wise counsel, and act with care, also thinking about protecting others.
exp.25:33:
It says that when the people are taken far away and their land is left destroyed and empty, the land will finally rest. In the Berean Standard wording, the land "enjoys its Sabbaths" during all the days it lies desolate, while the people are in the land of their enemies. The rest the land receives is the rest it did not get while the people lived on it. Here "Sabbaths" means the years of rest for the land that were not kept while the people lived there.

God speaks through Moses to Israel. Before they enter the promised land, he warns them what would happen if they turned away from their covenant. He had commanded that the field be left to rest every seventh year (Leviticus 25), and this warning shows that God takes that command seriously. Later, the book of Chronicles connects the exile with this passage.

For today: God designed rest as a gift, not as a burden. It is worth examining whether we are living without pauses, and setting aside regular time to rest and to trust that God sustains our lives.
exp.24:12:
This verse says that when the year of jubilee arrived, every family would return to the property it had received as its share of the land. The word "property" refers to the land each family inherited. The phrase "shall return" means they would get it back, even if they had sold it or lost it through debt.

God speaks to Israel through Moses at Sinai, before entering the promised land. The jubilee came every fifty years and was a holy time of rest for the land. Its purpose was to keep some families from being left with nothing forever, and to remind people that the land ultimately belongs to God (v. 23).

For today: we can live with generosity and justice, remembering that what we have is a gift from God. That invites us not to take advantage of someone in trouble and, when possible, to help others get back on their feet and recover their dignity.
exp.5:23:
This verse is an introductory phrase. It says that the LORD spoke to Moses. It is the formula repeated throughout Leviticus to signal that a new instruction is coming.

God is the one speaking, and Moses is the one who receives his words to pass them on to the people and the priests. With this verse a new section begins about the offerings, in this case the law of the sin offering. Other offerings were mentioned earlier; now God explains how the priests were to make this offering and how to handle what was most holy. This shows that the rules of worship did not come from human ideas but from God.

For today: before reading the Bible, ask God to speak to you. When each instruction begins with "the LORD said," we can read with respect and a readiness to obey, not only to learn facts.
exp.22:40:
God commands the Israelites to celebrate a feast to the LORD for seven days each year, in the seventh month. It is to be a permanent statute for the generations to come. The phrase "permanent statute" means a law that does not end, and "generations to come" refers to the people of each age.

God speaks to Moses so that he may pass this on to the people. The feast, called the Feast of Tabernacles or of Booths, came after the harvest. It was a time of joy and thankfulness. The verses that follow explain that living in booths would remind them of how God cared for them when they left Egypt and wandered through the wilderness.

Today we too can set aside regular times to give thanks to God and remember his faithfulness. Perhaps it could be writing a list of the times God helped you and sharing it with your family, so that the younger ones also know what he has done.
exp.22:30:
It says that on the Day of Atonement no one was to do any work. It was a law for all time, which the people were to keep through every generation and wherever they lived. "A permanent statute" means a lasting rule. "Generations" are the successive generations of people. "Wherever you live" refers to the places where they made their homes.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for Israel about the Lord's appointed feasts. On that day, the tenth of the seventh month, the people humbled themselves and acknowledged their sins. Setting aside all work showed that forgiveness is not earned by one's own effort, but comes from God. Christians understand this in different ways as to how it applies today.

For today: set aside a time without hurry or tasks to be with God, confess your failings to him, and rest in his forgiveness, trusting that you do not have to earn it.
exp.16:13:
The verse says that the life of every living creature is in its blood, and for that reason God forbade eating it. The phrase "must be cut off" means that the person would be separated from his people; some understand that he would be expelled, and others that he would be punished with death.

God speaks to Moses so that he will tell the Israelites and the foreigners who lived among them. He teaches them that blood is sacred, and that for this reason it was used in the sacrifices to cover sin (Leviticus 17:11). By pouring out the blood of the hunted animal and covering it with earth, the people acknowledged that life belongs to God.

Today we can learn to respect life as a gift from God, caring for people and for creation. We can also give thanks because, according to the New Testament, Christ gave his life for us.
exp.22:6:
On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the people were to gather for a sacred assembly, a meeting set apart for God. The phrase "regular work" refers to the ordinary, demanding daily labor of each person, such as their trade or work in the fields. On that day they were to set it aside.

God speaks to Moses to give the people of Israel their yearly feasts. The Passover was celebrated on the fourteenth day of the first month, and the next day seven days of unleavened bread began. This feast reminded them of their deliverance from Egypt. The first and seventh days were days of holy gathering and rest from work.

Today we can set aside time to remember what God has done for us. Even when we are busy, it is good to pause to pray, give thanks, and meet with other believers. Resting is also a way of trusting God.
exp.3:26:
This verse begins a new instruction about sin committed unintentionally. "The common people" refers to an ordinary person, not a priest, a leader, or a king. The verse describes someone who sins unintentionally and does what the LORD's commandments prohibit, and so becomes guilty.

God speaks to Moses, and the instructions are for Israel. Earlier it was explained what to do when the priest or a leader sinned; now it speaks of any person among the people. This shows that no one was outside God's care or his standard. The sacrifices showed that sin is serious and that God offers a way of forgiveness.

For today: do not minimize your mistakes, even when they were made without bad intent. Ask God to show you what you should correct, confess simply, and receive his forgiveness in Christ, who fulfilled what those sacrifices pointed to.
exp.10:20:
This verse makes an exception. It says that certain flying insects that walk on all fours could be eaten, provided they also had jointed legs above their feet for hopping on the ground. The phrase "flying insects" names the creatures this verse is about, and the word "however" signals a contrast with the rules before it. The next verse names some of them, such as the locust.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel about what is clean and what is unclean. These rules helped the people live set apart for God and remember that they belonged to Him. Scholars explain the exact reason for each rule in various ways, and not everything is known with certainty.

For today: God is interested in the details of our daily lives, even in what we eat. We can ask ourselves whether our customs, decisions and habits reflect that we belong to Him, and ask Him for wisdom to live with gratitude and obedience.
exp.24:14:
This verse says that the price of a piece of land must be calculated according to the number of years left until the next Jubilee. The buyer does not acquire the land permanently, but the right to its harvests until that time. Here "neighbor" means a fellow Israelite.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. Every fifty years, at the Jubilee, the land returned to the family that had inherited it. For that reason, selling a field was really like leasing its harvests. This rule guarded against abuse and deception among brothers, and it reminded them that the land belongs to God.

For today: when you buy, sell, or negotiate, be honest and fair. Do not take advantage of another person's need or ignorance. Ask yourself whether your dealings respect the person and honor God, who sees every transaction.
exp.13:3:
This verse says that the priest would order that, for the person who was going to be declared clean, two live, clean birds be brought, along with a piece of cedar wood, a red yarn or thread, and a sprig of hyssop, a small plant that was used for sprinkling.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. Here the person had already recovered from a skin disease, which the Bible calls "leprosy," although we do not know exactly what disease it was. This ritual did not heal them; it declared that they could again live with the community. Scholars explain the meaning of each object in various ways, but the text does not make it clear.

For today: God is concerned not only with healing people, but also with restoring them to the community. We can welcome with kindness those who have been hurt, sick, or set apart, and help them feel part of things again.
exp.12:58:
This verse closes the instructions about mildew in clothing. It states the rule for deciding whether a garment made of wool or linen, woven or knit, or any leather article, should be pronounced clean or unclean. The contamination is a mildew, not the skin disease we know today, and it probably refers to some kind of mold or fungus.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to guide the people of Israel. The priest was to examine carefully and declare whether something was clean or not. In this way the health of the community was protected and its orderly life was cared for. Scholars understand this in several ways, but all of them see a practical and spiritual concern.

Today we can learn that God cares about the details of our lives. It is wise to examine honestly what is becoming stained in our hearts and to cleanse it in time.
exp.10:0:
The LORD spoke again to Moses and Aaron, telling them to pass His message on to the people. This verse is only an introduction. Here the name of God is "the LORD," and the verse says He spoke to both men at once.

Here God Himself is speaking. He addresses Moses, the leader of the people, and Aaron, the priest. This time He speaks to both of them together, because both were to teach the people what God required. What follows is instruction about which animals Israel could eat and which it could not. These rules were part of God's covenant with Israel, and scholars explain their purpose in several ways, since the text does not fully spell it out.

For today: God speaks with clarity and expects His word to be passed on faithfully. We can set aside time to listen carefully to His Word and share it with others with humility and without changing it.
exp.20:19:
It says that a descendant of Aaron with certain physical conditions could not approach to offer the offerings. A hunchback is someone with a hump on the back; the verse names the hunchback, and that is who is meant here. The verse's words "an eye defect" cover the eye problems this part describes, and "a festering rash" and "scabs" cover the skin conditions, while "a crushed testicle" refers to a damaged testicle.

God speaks to Moses so that he tells Aaron and his sons. It was a rule for the priesthood of Israel, which was meant to reflect the holiness and wholeness of worship. Scholars explain it in several ways. Even so, these men remained priestly family and could still eat the holy bread.

For today: Jesus is our perfect High Priest, and through Him all of us can draw near to God with confidence. Our worth does not depend on our body, but on His grace.
exp.19:16:
It says that if a man marries or has sexual relations with his sister, whether she is his father's daughter or his mother's daughter, it is a disgrace. The penalty was to be cut off publicly, in the sight of the people. "He has uncovered the nakedness of his sister" refers to having sexual relations with her. "He shall bear his iniquity" means he will carry the weight of his wrongdoing.

God speaks to Moses to give laws of holiness to Israel, newly set apart from the customs of Egypt and Canaan. These rules protected the family and showed that the people belonged to God. Scholars debate exactly how these punishments were carried out, but the seriousness of the sin is clear.

For today: take care to maintain healthy boundaries in your family. Protect the most vulnerable, reject all abuse, and seek help if anyone is suffering it. God cares for the dignity of every person.
exp.25:29:
God says that he will tear down the "high places," meaning the raised sites where the people worshiped idols. He will also cut down their incense altars and heap the people's lifeless bodies on the lifeless remains of their idols. "My soul will despise you" means that God will feel deep disgust toward them.

God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel. This is part of the warnings at the end of Leviticus: if Israel abandons the covenant and persists in rebellion, increasingly severe consequences will come. Before this, God had promised blessings for obedience. Idolatry was a serious break in their relationship with Him.

For today: examine what things occupy in your heart the place that belongs to God, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Bring them honestly before God. He corrects because He wants us to return to Him, and His forgiveness is always available.
exp.19:11:
This verse forbids a man from having sexual relations with his daughter-in-law, the wife of his son. The law says that both of them must be put to death. The verse says that such an act is perverse, a corruption that breaks what God established in the family. The phrase "their blood is upon them" means that they themselves carried the guilt for their punishment.

God speaks to Moses to give Israel laws of holiness. He wanted his people to be different from the nations around them, such as Egypt and Canaan. These laws protected the family, and the punishment was very severe because it was a grave offense within Israel's covenant.

For today: guard the boundaries that protect your family. Be faithful and respectful in your relationships, and flee from anything that could harm trust and purity in the home.
exp.1:2:
This verse says that what remained of the grain offering, after a handful was burned on the altar, was not wasted. It belonged to Aaron and his sons, the priests. The phrase "what remains" refers to the rest of the grain offering, and the offering itself is the grain offering. It was called "a most holy part" because it was set apart in a very special way for God, and only the priests ate it.

God speaks to Moses and gives Israel instructions on how to worship Him. One part was burned for God, and the other part sustained the priests, who served in the sanctuary and did not have a share of land like the other tribes.

For today: what we give to God is not lost, and He cares for those who serve. We can generously support our church and those who serve it, and receive what we have as something that comes from God.
exp.17:18:
This verse forbids having sexual relations with a woman during her menstrual period. The phrase "during her menstrual period" refers to the days of her menstruation, and the wording describes the act of sexual intimacy itself.

God speaks to Moses to give laws to the people of Israel. Before entering Canaan, they were to live differently from the neighboring peoples. "Uncleanness" here means ritual impurity, not sin or something shameful in itself. Interpreters explain the reason in various ways: ritual purity, respect for the body, or the holiness of life. The text does not spell it out.

For today: although Christians do not live under these ritual laws, the principle of care and mutual respect in marriage still applies. We can speak honestly with our spouse, consider their needs and well-being, and seek to make intimacy reflect love rather than selfishness.
exp.7:3:
Moses did exactly what the Lord had commanded him. He gathered all the people, called "the assembly", at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. The "Tent of Meeting" is the sacred tent where God was present among Israel. The word "gathered" in the verse means "came together".

Here the narrator describes what Moses did after receiving instructions from God. The time was approaching to set apart Aaron and his sons as priests. God wanted the whole people to be present, so that they would see that this service was not a human decision but a calling from God.

For today: to obey God simply and openly. When we know what He asks, we can act without delay or excuses, and serve in such a way that others also draw near to Him.
exp.24:0:
It says that God, whose personal name is LORD, spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai. The phrase "said to Moses" introduces a message that Moses is to pass on to the people.

The one speaking is God, and he speaks to Moses, his messenger. This happens at Sinai, the place where Israel received the law after leaving Egypt. What follows concerns the year of rest for the land. The verse makes clear that these instructions are not Moses' own ideas but the word of God. Scholars discuss how this law was applied in practice, but the text presents its origin plainly.

For today: before following any advice or custom, ask yourself what God says. Set aside time to listen to his Word, because he also knows what rest we need.
exp.8:17:
Aaron killed the ox and the ram as the people's peace offering. His sons brought him the blood, and he splattered it on all sides of the altar.

The phrase "peace offering" means an offering that expresses peace and fellowship. Splattering means throwing the blood against the altar on every side.

This took place on the eighth day of the priests' consecration. Moses had given the instructions, and Aaron offers sacrifices for the first time, both for himself and for the people. The peace offering expressed gratitude and fellowship with God. The blood reminded them that drawing near to God has a serious cost.

For today: God wants us to draw near to Him with gratitude and reverence. Christians believe that Jesus, with his blood, opened the way to peace with God. Today you can give thanks for that, and live in fellowship with Him and with others.
exp.26:11:
It says that when someone had promised an animal to God that was not clean and so could not be offered on the altar, the priest was to set a price on it. The word "value" here means to work out what something is worth, and the "valuation" is that figure. Whether the animal was high or low in quality, the priest's assessment was the one that counted.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel, at the end of Leviticus, about vows. Whoever had promised something to God had to fulfill it, or else redeem it by paying its worth. Leaving the valuation in the priest's hands prevented disputes and haggling, and showed that things dedicated to God were treated with seriousness.

For today: What we promise to God is not something to take lightly. Before making a promise, let us think carefully, and once we make it, let us keep it honestly, without looking for excuses or tricks.
exp.26:17:
If someone consecrates his field to God after the Jubilee has passed, the priest will calculate its price in proportion to the years left until the next Year of Jubilee. The fewer years remaining, the lower the value. "Consecrates" means setting something apart and dedicating it to God, the "price" is the amount the field is assessed at, and "reduced" means the valuation goes down.

God speaks to Moses on behalf of the people of Israel. The land was a family inheritance, and in the Year of Jubilee it returned to its original owner. For that reason, what a person could dedicate was in reality the use of the land until that year. This calculation prevented abuses and kept the arrangement fair.

For today: when you want to give something to God, do it with sincerity and with order, without exaggerating or giving with deceit. God values a generous heart and also honesty in what we promise.
exp.5:24:
God tells Moses to instruct Aaron and his sons, the priests, about the law of the sin offering. "Slaughtered" here means the animal is killed by cutting its throat. This offering was to be slaughtered in the same place as the burnt offering, before the LORD. The phrase "most holy" means set apart completely for God.

The LORD speaks to Moses in the middle of the instructions about the sacrifices. The priests had to know these rules well. Using the same place for both offerings may have kept those who sinned from being singled out, although the text does not give that reason and some understand it in another way.

Today we can learn that God takes sin seriously, but also offers forgiveness. Christians see in Christ the fulfillment of these sacrifices. Therefore we can approach God with sincerity and gratitude, without hiding our faults.
exp.17:25:
It says that the people of Israel must keep God's statutes and ordinances and must not commit any of the detestable practices listed in this chapter. This applies to everyone: both the native-born Israelite and the foreigner who lives among them. The words "statutes" and "ordinances" refer to God's commands and rules.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, before they enter Canaan. In chapter 18 he forbids harmful sexual practices and other pagan customs. He says that the nations who came before had defiled the land and suffered the consequences. God warns Israel not to repeat that path.

For today: God's rules protect us, not only limit us. Today you can ask yourself: which custom around me am I accepting without examining it in the light of the Bible? Ask God for wisdom to live with integrity, even when others do not.
exp.8:10:
This verse says that Aaron took the flesh and the hide of the sin offering animal and burned them up, but not on the altar. He burned them outside the camp.

"Camp" here means the place where the people of Israel lived. The hide is the skin of the animal.

We are on the day when Aaron and his sons began their service as priests. The account tells it as something done just as the LORD had commanded Moses. The fatty parts were burned on the altar, and the rest was taken outside the camp. Some see here a picture that Hebrews 13:11-12 later connects with Jesus, who suffered outside the gate.

For today: obeying God in the details, even in what seems small or uncomfortable, is a way of taking sin seriously and of thanking Him for the forgiveness He gives.
exp.22:26:
This verse says that the tenth day of the seventh month is the Day of Atonement. On that day the people were to gather for a sacred assembly, humble themselves, and present a food offering to the LORD. The offering here is a sacrifice that was burned on the altar.

God speaks to Moses to set out the feasts Israel was to keep. This day was unique: it served to reconcile the people with God and to cleanse sin. The verses that follow call for complete rest and warn that whoever does not humble themselves will be cut off from their people.

For today: I know that God invites us to be sincere with Him. You can set aside time to pray, acknowledge your faults without excuses, and give thanks that, for Christians, Jesus offered the sacrifice that reconciles us with God.
exp.15:33:
This verse says that the Day of Atonement would be a permanent rule for Israel. Once a year, atonement would be made for the sins of the people. A permanent statute is a law meant to last indefinitely, and atonement means covering sin and cleansing it so that the relationship with God is restored. The verse closes by saying that Moses carried out everything the Lord had commanded.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes the instructions on to Israel. The chapter describes the yearly ritual in which the high priest made purification for the sanctuary, the altar, the priests, and all the people. It shows that sin is serious and that only God provides the way to be forgiven.

For today, Christians see in this ritual a shadow of Christ, whose sacrifice offers complete forgiveness (Hebrews 9–10). You can draw near to God with a sincere heart, acknowledging your faults and trusting in his forgiveness, and respond with obedience, as Moses did.
exp.8:6:
Moses tells Aaron to come near to the altar and present several offerings. First, the sin offering and the burnt offering, which was burned whole, to make atonement for his own sins and for the people's. Then he must present the people's offering and make atonement for them, that is, restore their relationship with God. Everything is done "as the LORD has commanded."

Moses speaks right after the seven days in which Aaron and his sons were set apart as priests. Now their public service begins. The whole congregation is present, and Moses has promised them that the glory of the LORD would appear to them if they obeyed. Aaron, before helping others, must offer for himself, since he too was a sinner.

For today: God draws near to us with humility and obedience. Before serving others, let us recognize our own need for forgiveness. Christians believe that Jesus is the perfect priest who offered once for all the sacrifice that Aaron only foreshadowed.
exp.4:1:
This verse says that if someone touches anything unclean, such as the carcass of an unclean wild animal, livestock, or crawling creature, that person becomes unclean and is guilty, even if they were unaware of it. The word "unclean" means ritually impure, not fit to draw near to what is holy. The word "guilty" means that a wrong was committed and needs to be made right.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel on how to live as a holy people. Earlier, the text spoke of keeping silent in the face of injustice; afterward, it turns to other impurities and oaths. All of this teaches that sin can also happen without intention, and that God provided a way of forgiveness through confession and the offering.

For today: it is not enough to say "I did not realize it." Ask God to show you your hidden faults, confess them simply, and receive with gratitude the forgiveness that Christ offers.
exp.18:4:
When you bring a peace sacrifice to the LORD, it is to be offered for your acceptance, meaning freely, by your own choice, so that it is received by God. The phrase "you shall offer it" means to bring it up to God. A peace sacrifice is also called a fellowship or thanksgiving offering.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. This chapter teaches how to live as a holy people, set apart for God. Before this, it speaks of honoring one's parents, keeping the Sabbath, and not following idols. Afterward, it gives rules about when this offering may be eaten. God takes care that worship is sincere and orderly.

For today: God does not seek forced obligations or mere habit. Before you pray, give, or serve, examine your heart and offer it with gratitude and freedom, not out of duty or appearance.
exp.22:25:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that the LORD spoke again to Moses. With these words a new instruction begins within the list of the LORD's feasts. The word "said" introduces what follows as a message that Moses was to pass on to the people.

The context is the book of Leviticus, where God teaches Israel how to live as his people. Just before, he spoke about the feast of trumpets, on the first day of the seventh month. Now he presents the Day of Atonement, ten days later. The one speaking is the LORD himself, and Moses is the messenger.

For today: God speaks to us clearly and with purpose. We can set aside a simple time each day to listen to his Word, without rushing, and ask him what he wants to teach us today.
exp.13:2:
The priest goes outside the camp to meet the person and examine him. If the skin disease has already healed, he can move on with the process to declare that person clean.

The disease the verse describes is called a skin disease, and scholars are not certain it was the same condition we call leprosy today.

God speaks to Moses and gives instructions for the people of Israel. The person with this disease had been living outside the camp, which is why the priest goes out to see him. These laws protected the health and purity of the community, and they also showed the way for the healed person to be welcomed back in.

For today: God cares about restoring those who have been set apart. We can reflect that same heart by approaching anyone who feels excluded with patience and compassion, and by helping them return to the community.
exp.6:35:
This verse says that God commanded the Israelites to give the priests a portion of the peace offerings. That command was given on the day God anointed them, that is, the day he set them apart with oil for their service. The verse calls this a permanent portion for the generations to come, meaning the arrangement was to continue from one generation to the next.

Here the narrator is speaking, repeating what the Lord commanded Moses at Sinai. God had just explained the sacrifices, and now he clarifies that the breast and the thigh belonged to Aaron and his sons. In this way the priests, who had no land of their own, could live from their service in the sanctuary.

For today: God cares for those who serve others in his name. We can support, with gratitude and generosity, those who dedicate their lives to teaching, praying, and caring for the community of faith.
exp.24:44:
This verse allows the Israelites to buy servants from among the foreigners who lived among them, and also from the children born to those families in the land. Those servants became the "property" of their owner, that is, under his authority.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, within the laws about the year of jubilee. The context is the ancient world, where servitude existed in all nations. The law distinguishes between the Israelite brother, who was not to be treated harshly or as a permanent slave, and the foreigner. This shows a regulation of a custom of the time, and Christians understand in different ways how to read it today.

For today: what God requires is fear and respect in how we treat others. Today we rarely have servants, but we do have employees or people under our care; treat them with justice and dignity, remembering that you too will give account to God.
exp.1:15:
This verse says that the priest would burn on the altar a portion of the crushed grain, together with the oil and all the frankincense. That portion was called the memorial, because it served as a reminder before God of the whole offering. The offering was a food offering made to the LORD.
