God gives these instructions to Israel through Moses, in the time of the tabernacle. The verses before this one speak of the firstfruits, that is, the first fruits of the harvest. With them the people acknowledged that everything they received came from God. The priests burned only a part; the rest was for their sustenance.

For today: let us give God the first and the best, not the leftovers. It can be time, money, or attention. Doing so with simple gratitude reminds us that everything we have is a gift from him.
exp.6:16:
What it says: If any meat from the sacrifice of peace was still left over until the third day, it could not be eaten. It had to be burned up. The word "remaining" in the verse above refers to what is left over. The "sacrifices of peace" are the fellowship or peace offerings, which were shared in a meal.

Context: God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes the instructions for the sacrifices on to Israel. This sacrifice was a meal of thanksgiving and fellowship before God. The time limit protected the holiness of the offering. Some think it also kept the meat from spoiling, but the text does not state this clearly.

For today: What belongs to God deserves respect and should not be handled carelessly. We can learn to give thanks in its proper time, without putting gratitude off until it grows cold. Living thankful day by day keeps our hearts simple and attentive to God.
exp.25:20:
If you keep walking in hostility toward God and refuse to obey him, he will multiply your troubles, adding more and more discipline as your rebellion continues. Living in hostility toward him means setting yourself against him in a stubborn way. "Seven times" points to a discipline that keeps growing stronger, and "plagues" refers to blows or calamities. He does this "according to your sins," meaning in proportion to how serious their rebellion is.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel in the covenant at Sinai. He promises blessing if they obey and warns of consequences if they despise him. The earlier punishments were meant to correct them and wake them up. Many understand "seven times" as a way of saying "much more," not necessarily an exact number.

For today: when God corrects us through the Bible, through wise counsel, or through our circumstances, let us not harden our hearts. Listening in time and repenting prevents greater harm and brings us back to his care.
exp.13:15:
This verse says that the priest would dip his right forefinger into the oil he held in his left palm, and with that finger sprinkle some of the oil seven times before the LORD, that is, toward the sanctuary. "Sprinkle" here means to scatter or splash lightly. The measure of liquid mentioned was a small unit.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the ritual of cleansing someone who had been healed of a skin disease (translated as "leprosy"). First came the blood and then the oil, and this allowed the person to return to the community and to worship. The number seven often indicates something complete. Many see in the oil a picture of God's Spirit, although the text does not say this directly.

For today: God cares about every detail of restoring a person. If someone returns to the community after a difficult time, welcome them with kindness and without reproach.
exp.6:3:
These are the parts of the animal that were offered on the altar: both kidneys, the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver, which was removed along with the kidneys. Everything was carefully separated out.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel, within the law of the guilt offering. Its purpose was to restore the relationship with God after a wrong. The fat was considered the best part and was given entirely to the LORD. Scholars do not fully agree on the exact symbolism, but it is commonly seen as an offering of what is best.

For today: God deserves our best, not our leftovers. We can give him the best of our time, attention and affection, and remember that Christ offered everything for our guilt (Hebrews 10:10).
exp.12:47:
This verse continues to describe where the mark can appear on fabrics and leather. It mentions any weave or knit of linen or wool, and any article of leather. The fabric may be woven or knitted, so the mark could be in the threads running lengthwise or crosswise, or in the fabric itself.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, giving Israel rules about purity. Here the "mark" on clothing was probably mold or fungus, though this cannot be known with certainty. Everything had to be shown to the priest so that he could examine it with order and care, and so protect the community.

Today we can learn not to hide what is harming us in our lives, even when it seems small. Bringing it to God in prayer and seeking wise counsel from someone we trust helps us clean up what could otherwise spread.
exp.12:6:
If the rash spreads further on the skin after the priest has already declared the person clean, the person must present himself again to the priest.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives them instructions for the people of Israel in the wilderness. These laws protected the health of the community and placed the priest as the one who examined each case. Scholars debate exactly which disease this passage's "leprosy" refers to, since the Hebrew term covered several skin conditions.

For today: let us not stop examining our hearts and asking for help when something seems to return or grow. An honest check, done in time and with someone we trust, cares for us from greater harm.
exp.19:18:
This verse forbids having sexual relations with an aunt, whether a sister of one's mother or of one's father. The BSB phrase "exposing one's own kin" describes such a relationship as a betrayal of close family ties. The words "both shall bear their iniquity" mean that both people would be held responsible for the wrong they had done.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel, his people newly freed from Egypt. These laws aimed to protect families and to keep the people set apart from the practices of the surrounding nations. The nearby verses show that these offenses were taken very seriously within the covenant.

Today we can learn that God cares for dignity and purity within the family. We can set clear boundaries in our relationships, protect the most vulnerable, and seek God's help when we face temptation.
exp.8:0:
On the eighth day Moses summoned Aaron, his sons, and the elders of Israel. "On the eighth day" simply means that this gathering took place on that day. The elders were the leaders who represented the people.

Moses speaks and gathers everyone after the seven days in which Aaron and his sons were set apart as priests (Leviticus 8). Now their public service was beginning. The verses that follow show Moses passing on God's instructions about the sin offerings and the burnt offerings. Many understand that the "eighth day" marks a new beginning, though the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: God acts with order and invites us to draw near to Him with reverence and preparation. Before serving, it is good to pause to pray, acknowledge our faults, and listen to His Word.
exp.25:26:
It says that if the people, after the earlier punishments, still refuse to listen to God and set themselves against him, harsher consequences will follow. The phrase "But if in spite of all this you do not obey Me" means "if you still will not obey me." The phrase "continue to walk in hostility toward Me" means that they keep acting against God, with stubborn resistance toward him.

Here God speaks to Israel through Moses, at the close of the law in Leviticus. He sets out blessings for obedience and warnings for disobedience. These warnings come in stages: each time the people refuse to be corrected, the warning becomes more serious. The purpose was to call them back to the covenant, not simply to destroy them.

For today: when you sense that God is correcting you through Scripture, through other people, or through your circumstances, do not harden your heart. Listen promptly, acknowledge your error, and return to him, for he is patient and wants to restore you.
exp.24:33:
The verse says that the open pastureland around the Levites' cities could not be sold. This was common land on the edge of a town, used to graze livestock. The phrase "permanent possession" means it belonged to them for good.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. The Levites did not receive a portion of land like the other tribes, but cities in which to live. Their houses could be redeemed, and they returned to them in the Jubilee. With this law, God protected the livelihood of those who served in worship, so that they would not be left with nothing.

For today: God cares for those who serve and for the most vulnerable. We can support our pastor, our teachers, or our missionaries with generosity and fairness, and not take advantage of anyone's need.
exp.13:33:
This verse says that when the people of Israel had entered the land of Canaan, which God was giving them as their own property, God Himself might allow a contamination of mildew to appear in a house in that land. The word for this affliction can mean a stain or sickness, and the same word is used for skin disease in people and for mildew in cloth and walls.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, right after the laws about skin disease in people. The people were still in the wilderness, and God was preparing them for their future life in the land. These rules aimed to protect health and keep the people clean. The priests examined the case.

For today: when a problem appears in your home or in your life, do not hide it. Report it early, seek help, and trust that God cares for you even in everyday matters.
exp.17:21:
The verse says: "You must not lie with a man as with a woman; that is an abomination." The phrase "lie with" means to have sexual relations. "Abomination" refers to something God considers detestable, contrary to what He wants for His people.

God speaks to Moses so that he may tell Israel, before they enter the land of Canaan. The chapter calls the people to live differently from the neighboring nations and to guard holiness in family life and sexuality. Christians debate how to apply the laws of Leviticus today, but this verse shows the ideal God gave to Israel.

For today: seek to live with integrity and faithfulness in your intimate life, according to what you understand of the Word. And at the same time, treat every person with respect, kindness, and dignity, because each one was created by God and is loved by Him.
exp.17:9:
This verse forbids sexual relations with a granddaughter, whether she is your son's daughter or your daughter's daughter. The Berean Standard Bible states the prohibition directly and gives the reason: such relations would shame your family. Because the granddaughter is of your own blood, she belongs to your closest family, and the verse treats any sexual relationship with her as a breach of that closeness.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. Before entering Canaan, the people receive rules for living differently from Egypt and from Canaan. This chapter protects the family and sets clear limits against abuse within the home.

Today it reminds us that the home should be a safe place. Let us care for the young members of the family, and if anyone suffers abuse, let us seek help and protection without keeping silent.
exp.24:8:
On the tenth day of the seventh month, the day of atonement, the horn was to be sounded far and wide. It was to sound throughout the whole land. That day was the Day of Atonement. The horn that announced the year of jubilee was a ram's horn.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. After counting seven times seven years, the fiftieth year would be special: liberty was proclaimed, each person returned to their property and their family, and the land rested. The sound of the horn marked the beginning of that new start, on the very day when atonement was made for sin.

For today: God joins forgiveness with freedom and restoration. We can ask God for forgiveness, and also seek peace with someone, forgive a debt, or help someone in need.
exp.17:6:
This verse forbids having sexual relations with your father or with your mother. The phrase "expose the nakedness" is an old expression for sexual relations. The verse repeats that she is your mother, to make it very clear that there is no exception.

God himself speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, just before they enter Canaan. He gives them rules so that they would live differently from Egypt and Canaan, and that is why he repeats the words "I am the LORD." The laws protected the family and showed that Israel belonged to God.

For today: take care of healthy boundaries in your family. Respect the dignity of every person, protect those who are most vulnerable, and if there is abuse, seek help and speak with someone you trust.
exp.22:0:
This verse is simple: it says that the LORD spoke to Moses. The word "said" introduces a message that Moses was to pass on to the people.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the one who receives his words and communicates them to the people. In this chapter, God explains to the Israelites their feasts and appointed times, which are called holy gatherings, that is, special assemblies to worship him. First he mentions the day of rest, the Sabbath, as the foundation of all those sacred times.

For today: before making plans, it is wise to listen to God. You can set aside a moment each day, and also a time each week, to read the Bible, pray, and rest. In this way your life is ordered by what God says and not only by your hurry.
exp.8:20:
It says that Aaron took the breasts of the animals from the peace offering and the right thigh, and he lifted them up and moved them before God. This was a ritual gesture: raising them and moving them toward the altar as an offering. The word "waved" means the same as "lifted up," and everything was done just as God had commanded Moses.

This is the account of the ordination of Aaron and his sons, on the eighth day of their ministry. Here the narrator tells how Aaron offered sacrifices for the first time, both for himself and for the people. It highlights exact obedience to the instructions received. Afterward come the blessing and the glory of God being revealed.

For today: God values sincere obedience, even in small and repetitive things. Doing what He asks faithfully, without shortcuts, prepares the heart to see His work in our lives.
exp.24:43:
This verse says that the Israelites could have male and female servants, but that they were to get them from the nations around them. "Servants" here refers to a slave or a worker under the authority of another. "The nations around you" means the neighboring peoples.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. He has just commanded that poor Israelites not be treated as slaves, because God brought them out of Egypt. This law regulates a common practice of that time, and it does not mean that God approves of every abuse. Even so, some nearby passages allow lifelong servitude for foreigners, and that troubles many readers. Interpreters understand this in different ways.

For today: learn that human dignity matters to God. Treat with justice and respect those who work for you or depend on you, and never use them for your own advantage.
exp.13:13:
The verse says that the priest takes some of the blood of the guilt offering and puts it in three places on the body of the person being cleansed: the right earlobe, the thumb of the right hand, and the big toe of the right foot.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the ritual of cleansing someone who had been healed of a skin disease (translated as "leprosy"). That person had been set apart from the community and was now returning to it. The blood is placed on the ear, hand and foot. Many understand that it represents the whole person: what they hear, what they do, and where they go. This is an interpretation, since the text does not explain it.

Today we can ask God to cleanse and guide what we hear, what we do, and the paths we take, trusting in his forgiveness and in his complete restoration of us.
exp.12:50:
The priest is told to look at the suspicious garment again on the seventh day. If the mildew has spread in the fabric, the weave, the knit, or the leather, then however the item is used, it is a harmful mildew, and the article is unclean.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. They wanted to protect the community and to teach the difference between what is clean and what is unclean. Scholars think this mildew on clothing was probably some kind of mold or fungus, though this cannot be known for certain.

For today: do not ignore small harms. Examine them with patience and honesty. If something keeps growing and doing damage, deal with it in time, asking for the help of God and of wise people.
exp.18:16:
It says we should not keep hatred in our heart against our brother. Instead of staying silent and resenting him, we should speak to him directly, correcting him honestly. The phrase "directly rebuke" means to speak to him face to face, with honesty. The last sentence can be understood in two ways: not bearing guilt for keeping silent about his sin, or not leaving his wrongdoing unaddressed among you.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, within the laws about the holiness of the people. Before this, he speaks of justice and of not spreading gossip; afterward, of not taking revenge and of loving your neighbor as yourself. Correcting someone directly is presented as a form of love, not of attack.

If someone has offended you, do not talk about it with others or hold on to resentment. Speak to him calmly and respectfully, seeking reconciliation and not winning an argument.
exp.26:10:
This verse speaks of someone who made a vow and promised God an animal that the law counted as unclean, meaning one that could not be brought as an offering to the LORD, such as a horse or a donkey. That animal had to be brought before the priest so that he could assess it. The phrase "must be presented before the priest" means that the animal was taken and placed in front of him.

God speaks to Moses so that he may tell Israel. This chapter deals with vows, or promises made to God. Since an unclean animal could not be sacrificed, the priest estimated its value, and the person could keep the animal by paying that price plus a fifth of it. In this way the vow was fulfilled in an orderly manner.

For today: what we promise to God is serious. Let us think carefully before we commit ourselves, and if we make a promise, let us keep it with sincerity and order.
exp.6:34:
This verse says that the portion of the food offerings made to the LORD belongs to Aaron and to his sons. These offerings were the ones presented on the altar to the LORD, and this share was set aside for the priests. The verse links that portion to the day they were presented to serve the LORD as priests, and from that day on the share belonged to them.

God speaks through Moses to Israel, giving instructions about the peace offering. The priests had no inheritance of land like the other tribes, so God assigned them this portion for their support. The text calls it a permanent rule for that period.

Today we can learn to support generously those who serve in teaching and in the spiritual care of the church. Giving with gratitude acknowledges that God cares for those who dedicate their lives to serving him.
exp.24:37:
God presents himself: "I am the LORD your God." He reminds them that he brought them out of Egypt, where they had been slaves, with a twofold purpose: to give them the land of Canaan and to be their God. Charging interest on a loan is what the verse forbids, and the food or provisions a people need to survive are what is at stake here.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in the laws given at Sinai. Just before this, he commands them not to take advantage of a brother who has fallen into poverty by lending to him at interest. God grounds that command in what he himself did for them: he freed them when they were poor and oppressed. For that reason they must treat the needy with mercy.

For today: if God has helped and forgiven you, let that shape how you treat someone in difficulty. When someone close to you needs help, offer it generously, without seeking to profit from their need.
exp.12:51:
It says that if a fabric, woven or knitted, made of wool or linen, or an item made of leather, was contaminated by a mildew that kept spreading, it had to be burned completely. The verse describes the item as a fabric, weave, or knit, and the mildew as harmful, which is why the whole article is destroyed. The mildew described is most likely a mold or fungus that gradually damages the material; it is not the same disease as leprosy in human skin.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priest would examine the item, set it aside for seven days, and look at it again. If the mildew had spread, the item was regarded as unclean and was destroyed. In this way the health and purity of the camp were protected.

For today: there are small things that, if we let them grow, damage everything, such as a grudge or a bad habit. Examine your life honestly and, with God's help, remove in time whatever is harming you.
exp.21:10:
What it says: A priest could buy a slave with his own money, and that slave could eat his food. The same applied to a slave born in the priest's household. The verse uses the word "slave" for the person bought, and "food" for what the priest's household shared, especially the portion God gave to the priests.

Context: God speaks to Moses to instruct Aaron and his sons. He wanted them to guard what was holy and not treat it as ordinary. People from outside, such as guests or hired workers, did not eat of the holy things, but those who belonged to the priest's household did. At that time slavery was part of society, and this law regulated that reality without our needing to see it as an ideal of God.

For today: Belonging to God's family is a gift, not something earned. If Christ has received us into his house, let us live with gratitude, treating with respect what he gives us.
exp.4:8:
This verse describes what the priest did with the blood of the bird offered for sin. He would sprinkle some of it on the side of the altar, and the rest would be drained out at the base of the altar.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. They are laws for anyone who had sinned and wanted to be forgiven. God allowed cheaper offerings, such as birds, so that the poor could also draw near to Him. The blood showed that sin is serious and has a cost.

For today: God does not want anyone to stay far from Him because they lack resources. Christians believe that Jesus gave his life for everyone, so we can come to God with confidence, acknowledge our faults, and receive his forgiveness.
exp.22:13:
It says that the people of Israel could not eat bread, roasted grain, or new grain until they had brought the firstfruits as an offering to God. "Roasted grain" refers to barley or wheat kernels toasted over the fire, and "new grain" refers to tender grain not yet fully ripe.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel, just before they enter the promised land. This rule belongs to the Feast of Firstfruits. Before enjoying the harvest, they were to acknowledge that everything came from God and give Him the best first.

For today: before using what you receive, such as your wages, your time, or your strength, put God first. You can begin the day by thanking Him, or set aside your offering first, with a grateful heart and not out of obligation.
exp.13:4:
Here the priest orders that one of the two small birds be slaughtered over fresh water, in a clay pot, so that its blood falls into the water. The phrase "fresh water" means water that is not stagnant, such as that of a spring or a river. A small bird is a little bird. A clay pot is a simple pottery container.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. This is the rite for declaring clean a person who had already recovered from a skin disease. Its purpose was to restore that person to the community.

Scholars explain the exact symbolism in several ways, but all of them see here the idea of a life given up and a person restored.

For today: God is concerned not only with healing, but with restoring the person and returning them to their place among others. We can help someone who feels excluded to feel welcome again.
exp.14:8:
Any saddle on which the man with the discharge rides will be unclean. Here "discharge" refers to an abnormal discharge from the body, and "unclean" does not mean sinful; it means ritually unfit to come near the sanctuary until purified.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to give laws to Israel. These laws protected the holiness of the tabernacle, where God dwelt, and also helped prevent the spread of infection. Scholars agree on the first point; on how much the second played a role, there are different opinions.

For today: God takes purity and care for others seriously. We do not follow these rituals today, since Christ cleanses us, but we can care lovingly for what we touch and share, and draw near to God with a clean heart.
exp.13:41:
This verse describes the steps for repairing a house that had mold in its walls. The contaminated stones were removed and replaced with different stones. Then new mortar was made and the house was replastered, meaning a fresh layer of plaster was put on the walls.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives rules for Israel when they would enter the land of Canaan. The priest would inspect the house and decide whether it was clean or not. Scholars are not sure exactly what this mold was; many think of mildew or fungus, although the text uses the Hebrew word for the "skin disease." These rules protected the health and purity of the people.

For today: when something in our life is damaged, it is not enough to cover it over on the surface. What is rotten must be removed and rebuilt properly, with humility and with help.
exp.3:6:
The passage describes what the priest did with the blood of the bull. First he put some of it on the horns of the altar of fragrant incense, which stood inside the Tent of Meeting before the LORD. Then he poured out the rest of the blood at the base of the altar of burnt offering, which was at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. The "altar of fragrant incense" was the altar where incense was burned, and the "Tent of Meeting" was the place where the people met with God.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people. This case concerns the sin offering for an anointed priest, whose wrongdoing affected everyone. The blood represented a life given over, and it showed that sin is serious and needs to be covered.

For today: do not take sin lightly, neither the sin of others nor your own. And give thanks, because according to the New Testament, Jesus offered his own blood once for all, and today we can approach God with confidence and ask for forgiveness with sincerity.
exp.6:37:
This verse closes the section of laws about the sacrifices. It says that the LORD gave all these instructions to Moses on Mount Sinai, on the day He commanded the Israelites to present their offerings to the LORD in the Wilderness of Sinai.

The word "commanded" in this verse means to give an order with authority, making something known as a command. The phrase "present their offerings" means bring their gifts to the LORD.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who sums up what came before: the burnt offerings, the grain offerings, the sin offerings and the guilt offerings, the ordinations, and the peace offerings. Israel had just come out of Egypt and was learning to live near a holy God. These laws taught them how to approach Him with reverence, and also how to receive forgiveness and live in fellowship with Him.

For today: God is not approached in just any way, but with care and gratitude. Today we too can draw near to Him with respect and sincerity, giving Him our best in our time, our affection, and our obedience.
exp.18:30:
God tells his people not to turn to mediums or spiritists, and not to go looking for those who claim to know hidden things or the future. "Defiled by them" means becoming unclean and impure before God. He closes by saying, "I am the LORD your God," reminding them who their true Lord is.

God speaks through Moses to Israel, a people who lived surrounded by nations with occult practices. This chapter teaches how to live as a holy people, set apart for God. The verse appears among commands about worship, respect for the elderly, and fair treatment of the foreigner, because faithfulness to God touches every part of life.

For today: when you feel fear about the future, do not look for answers in horoscopes, mediums, or superstitions. Bring your worry to God in prayer, read his Word, and ask for counsel from mature brothers and sisters in the faith. He is worthy of your trust.
exp.23:7:
Every Sabbath day, the priest is to set out the bread before the LORD. It is a permanent covenant on behalf of the Israelites. The word "permanent" means that it lasts without end, and the regular weekly setting out means it happens without interruption.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness, giving instructions about the holy place. The twelve loaves, one for each tribe, were renewed every week on the clean table, with incense placed on top. Afterward, Aaron and his sons would eat them. It was a constant reminder of the covenant between God and his people, and that he sustained them.

For today: God values steadiness in our relationship with him. We can set aside a fixed moment each week to give thanks and to remember that he sustains us, and not wait until everything is perfect before doing so.
exp.10:27:
Whoever picks up the dead body of one of those animals must wash his clothes. He will be unclean until evening, meaning ceremonially impure. The word for "carry" in this verse refers to lifting and bearing, and the "clothes" are the garments a person wears. God requires that such an animal be regarded as unclean.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to give laws to the people of Israel. These rules helped them live as a people set apart for God (Leviticus 11:44-45). Scholars explain the reason behind each rule in several ways, and not everything is known for certain. Here the uncleanness was temporary and was resolved by washing and waiting.

For today: Christ cleanses us inwardly (1 John 1:9). Even so, we can learn to take care with what we touch and carry with us, and when we fail, to return quickly to God to be cleansed.
exp.22:28:
On the Day of Atonement, every Israelite was required to humble himself and repent, usually by fasting. Anyone who did not do so would be cut off from his people, a phrase that can mean being separated from the community or facing God's judgment. Scholars understand it in several ways.

God speaks to Moses so that he may tell the people. This day, the tenth of the seventh month, was the most solemn day of the year. Atonement was made for sin, and the people were reconciled with God. The command was serious because forgiveness was not to be taken lightly.

Today, as Christians, we believe that Christ has already made atonement for us. Even so, we can set aside time to acknowledge our failings with humility and sincerity before God, and to receive his forgiveness with gratitude.
exp.25:39:
This verse says that, while in exile, the people will confess their sin and also the sin of their ancestors. The word "unfaithfulness" in this verse means a betrayal of a commitment. The phrase "walked in hostility toward Me" means that they lived in opposition to God, unwilling to obey him.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. At the end of Leviticus, he warns what would happen if the people broke the covenant: they would be taken into enemy lands. But even there he leaves a door open. If they confess their sin and humble themselves, God will remember his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

For today: sincere confession is the way back to God. It is not about making excuses or blaming others, but about telling the truth with humility. God responds to a repentant heart with mercy.
exp.3:23:
This verse describes what a ruler who had sinned unintentionally was to do. He would lay his hand on the head of the goat and slaughter it at the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered, before the LORD. To slaughter here means to kill the animal by cutting its throat. Atonement means that the sacrifice covered or paid for the sin.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. Here the text speaks of the leader, the one in authority, who sinned by mistake. Even those who held authority needed to acknowledge their fault. Laying the hand on the animal is usually understood as a way of identifying oneself with it, although scholars explain it in several ways.

For today: if you hold a position of responsibility, do not hide your mistakes. Acknowledge them humbly before God, and remember that Christians see in Jesus the complete sacrifice that gives us forgiveness.
exp.10:10:
The passage says that the water animals without fins or scales, such as shellfish or certain aquatic reptiles, were not to be eaten. "Abomination" here means something the people were to reject and keep far away, not something evil in itself. They were also to detest their dead bodies and not touch them.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives them these instructions for Israel. These laws about clean and unclean animals helped the people live set apart and dedicated to God, since He tells them: "You shall be holy, for I am holy." Scholars explain the exact reason behind each rule in several different ways.

For today: although Christians are not under these food rules, the passage invites us to ask which everyday habits draw us closer to God or pull us away from Him, and to live with purpose, as people who belong to Him.
exp.22:23:
God tells Moses to speak to the people: on the first day of the seventh month there is to be a day of rest, a sacred assembly announced by trumpet blasts. The day is set apart as a time of stopping, and it is marked by the sound of trumpets, calling the people together before the Lord.

The Lord speaks within the set of feasts that Israel was to keep each year. Shortly before this, God had asked them to leave the edges of the field for the poor and the foreigner. In this way his people learned both to worship and to be generous. This day later came to be known as the feast of trumpets. The text does not explain in detail what was being remembered, and interpreters understand it in several ways.

For today: set aside a regular time to pause, rest from your work, and remember that God is the one who sustains your life. Do it with gratitude and, if you can, with your community of faith.
exp.24:11:
This verse says that the year of Jubilee is a time set apart for God ("it shall be holy to you"). During that year, the people did not plant or harvest. They ate only what the land produced on its own, the crops taken directly from the field.

God speaks to Moses so that he will tell Israel, as the people were preparing to live in the promised land. The Jubilee, every fifty years, brought freedom and returned each family to its property. It was a reminder that the land belongs to God and that He cares for His people.

For today: trusting that God provides helps us rest without anxiety. We can set apart time to rest, give thanks, and be generous to others, without living as though everything depends only on our own effort.
exp.12:41:
It says that if someone has a bald head, whether at the back of the head or at the front, and a reddish-white sore breaks out there, it is an infectious disease. The bald forehead is the bald part at the front of the head.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priest was to examine the person. Being bald did not make anyone unclean; only that specific sore did. In this way the health and order of the community were protected.

For today: let us not draw hasty conclusions about others based on their appearance. Let us distinguish what is ordinary from what truly needs attention, and let us wisely care for our own health and the health of others.
exp.26:9:
If someone promised an animal to the LORD, they were not allowed to substitute another for it. The verse forbids replacing a good animal with a bad one, or a bad one with a good one. "Replace" and "exchange" both mean to swap one thing for another. If a person did substitute, then both animals, the one promised and the one put in its place, became holy, that is, set apart for God.

God speaks to Moses for the Israelites, in the chapter about vows and promises. Once something was dedicated to the LORD, it already belonged to him. The rule prevented deception and bargaining, and it taught that what is given to God should be offered with seriousness and without tricks.

For today: when you promise something to God, such as your time, your help, or an offering, keep your word sincerely. Do not look for ways to replace your commitment with something cheaper, or keep the best for yourself. God values a faithful and honest heart.
exp.23:15:
Leviticus 24:16 says that whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD, meaning whoever insults it or treats it with contempt, must surely be put to death. The whole assembly was to stone him. The law applied the same way to a foreign resident and to a native-born Israelite.

God speaks to Moses just after a man cursed the Name during a quarrel in the camp of Israel (vv. 10-14). Israel was a nation under the covenant, and God had made himself known among them. This law shows how holy his name is and that justice was the same for everyone. Christians understand in different ways how these civil laws of Israel apply today.

For today: learn to speak of God with respect and reverence. Watch your words, and avoid using his name lightly or in mockery.
exp.21:26:
It says that when an ox, a sheep, or a goat is born, it must remain with its mother for seven days. From the eighth day on, it will be acceptable as a food offering presented to the LORD. The phrase "food offering" refers to an offering that is burned on the altar. "Acceptable" means worthy of being received, with favor.

God speaks to Moses to instruct the priests and the people about the offerings. Earlier it was required that the animals have no defects. This rule continues that idea: the animal had to be ready and worthy. Scholars do not fully agree on the exact reason for the seven days, but it is commonly seen as a concern for the newborn animal and for the offering.

For today: God values that we give him our best, without haste or carelessness. We can ask ourselves whether we offer him our time, service, and resources with patience, with care, and with a sincere heart.
exp.17:19:
It says that a man must not have sexual relations with his neighbor's wife, that is, the wife of the man next door or of a fellow countryman. Doing so "defiles" him, which means it makes him unclean before God.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct the people of Israel, just before they enter Canaan. In this chapter God describes a holy sexual conduct, different from that of Egypt and Canaan. This command protects marriage and trust between neighbors. The verses that follow connect it with other serious prohibitions, such as sacrifice to Molech.

Today it reminds us that another person's marriage deserves respect. We can guard our eyes, conversations and friendships so as not to harm any home, and support the couples around us.
exp.25:3:
God promises that he will send rain at exactly the time it is needed. Then the land will produce its crops, and the trees of the field will bear their fruit. "Rains in their season" means rain that falls at the right time of year. "Produce" refers to the plantings and harvests.

The Lord spoke through Moses to the people of Israel before they entered the land he had promised them. This promise is part of the covenant: if the people obeyed and honored God, blessing would come. Since Israel lived by farming, rain was vital. Here the blessing is tied to obedience within that covenant with Israel.

For today: we can remember that everything we receive comes from God's hand. Today, instead of seeking only results, you can trust God and obey him in everyday life, without thinking that every difficulty is punishment.
exp.5:5:
This verse says that the person who sinned must bring to the Lord a ram without defect, from the flock, and give it to the priest as a guilt offering. "Guilt offering" here means the sacrifice that deals with the sin and repairs the wrong. "Unblemished" means without defect. The phrase "of proper value" indicates that the ram had to be worth what the situation required, although the verse does not explain in detail who decided that value.

God speaks to Moses about laws for the people of Israel. Before this, the person had to return what was stolen or gained by deceit, plus an added fifth. After repairing the harm done to a neighbor, he had to be reconciled with God through the sacrifice. Thus, sin against another person was also seen as sin against the Lord.

For today: if you have harmed someone, it is not enough to ask God for forgiveness alone. Seek to repair what you can with honesty and generosity, and then draw near to God, trusting in Christ, who offered the perfect sacrifice for us.
exp.26:4:
The verse describes a special vow made to the Lord in which a person, either oneself or a family member, was dedicated. When the person was between five and twenty years of age, a fixed amount was paid: twenty shekels for a male and ten shekels for a female. The word "valuation" refers to the price that was set. A shekel was a unit of weight in silver.

God speaks to Moses so that he will tell the people of Israel. These were vows of dedication to the Lord. If someone wanted to buy back what had been promised, they paid that amount to the sanctuary. The figures varied by age and sex; the full reason is not known for certain, and it is often connected with the working capacity of the time. They did not measure a person's worth before God.

For today: our promises to God matter. Before promising something, think about it with sincerity, and gladly keep what you said.
exp.16:1:
God instructs Moses to speak to three groups: Aaron, his sons (the priests), and all the Israelites. What follows is not Moses' own opinion, but what "the LORD has commanded." The phrase "speak to" and the words "tell them" in the verse you read show the same instruction being given to each group.

Here the LORD speaks, and Moses is the messenger. Leviticus 17 begins a section about blood and sacrifices. The command is for everyone, not only for the priests, because worship involved the whole people. Scholars explain the exact purpose of these rules in various ways, but the text stresses that life and worship belong to God.

For today: before we obey or teach something, let us remember who is speaking. Let us listen to God in his Word with attention and humility, and not simply do what seems right to us.
exp.22:19:
This verse says that the priest presented the two lambs together with the bread of the firstfruits by waving them before the LORD, as a gesture of offering. "Waving" means moving them back and forth, and a "wave offering" was an offering shown in this way before the LORD. Afterward, the bread and the two lambs were set apart as holy to the LORD and belonged to the priest.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Israel about the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after the firstfruits of the barley harvest. It was a celebration of thankfulness for the wheat harvest. The loaves showed that everything received comes from God, and the text that follows adds care for the poor and the stranger.

For today: before you spend or save what you earn, set aside a portion with gratitude to God. You can give it in your church or by helping someone in need, remembering that everything you have is provision from him.
exp.19:20:
This verse forbids a man from marrying his brother's wife. The phrase "an act of impurity" means something impure, something that defiles. "He has uncovered the nakedness of his brother" is an old way of speaking about intimate relations. "They shall be childless" is usually understood as a consequence: they would have no descendants, or their children would not be recognized. Scholars explain this in several ways.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel, a people newly freed from Egypt and close to entering Canaan. These laws aimed to protect families and keep the people set apart from the practices of the neighboring nations. Later, the law makes an exception: if a brother died without children, the surviving brother was to marry the widow (Deuteronomy 25:5).

For today: take care of loyalty and respect within your family. Commit to protecting marriages and family relationships, avoiding anything that could harm them, and seek God's guidance to live with purity and honor.
exp.24:32:
According to this verse, if someone buys a house from a Levite, that house must be returned to its owner in the year of jubilee. The houses in the Levite cities were their property among the people of Israel. The verse says the house would be released and go back to the Levite, so the Levite would keep that home.

God gave these laws to Moses to organize the life of Israel. The Levites did not receive a territory like the other tribes, but cities in which to live and serve. For that reason their houses had special protection, so that they would not be left without a home.

Today we can learn that God cares for those who serve and for those who are vulnerable. When we buy, sell, or lend, let us seek to be just and not take advantage of others' need. We can ask ourselves whom we should protect with our generosity.
exp.12:43:
The verse says that if a person has an infection on the head, the priest must declare them unclean. The reference to a bald patch at the back or front of the head describes where the hair has fallen out in that area, and this is part of what the priest looks for. "Unclean" means impure according to the law, not necessarily dirty. The condition described here may have covered several skin diseases, not only the one we call leprosy today.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priest examined the case and made the decision, to protect the health and purity of the community. He was not a doctor who healed, but the one who declared the condition of the person.

For today: when someone is sick or suffering, let us not judge them or leave them alone. Let us approach them with compassion, as Jesus did, who touched and healed lepers.
exp.5:20:
This verse says that the grain offering of the priests was to be prepared on a griddle with oil. It was brought well-kneaded and then broken into pieces, and presented to the Lord as a pleasing aroma, that is, an offering that pleases him.

The Lord speaks to Moses about the offering that Aaron and his sons were to present on the day of their anointing. It was a continual offering, morning and evening. The verses that follow say that all of it was burned, with none of it eaten. The passage does not explain every detail of the rite, but it shows that the priests also had to present themselves before God with complete devotion.

For today: God values a life given to him steadily, not only in special moments. You can begin and end the day by offering God your work, your thoughts, and your decisions, simply and with gratitude.
exp.25:37:
This verse says that the people of Israel, if they turn away from God, will die far from their land, among the nations. The phrase "will perish" means they will die or come to an end. The phrase "will consume you" means that the land of their enemies will wear them away, little by little.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. At the end of Leviticus 26, He explains the blessings of obedience and the consequences of disobeying His covenant. This warning is part of those consequences. The verses that follow show that the purpose was to lead them to recognize their sin and return to God.

For today: God's warnings come from His desire for us to return to Him. If you notice that you have drifted away, do not harden your heart. Confess your failure sincerely and come back, because He still receives the one who repents.
exp.10:15:
This verse continues the list of birds that God declared unclean, meaning that the Israelites were not to eat them. It mentions the ostrich, the screech owl, the gull (probably a sea bird or another kind of seabird; scholars are not sure), and any kind of hawk, each one along with birds of its own type.

Here God speaks, giving instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. These food laws helped Israel live as a people set apart for God. The exact names of some of the birds are uncertain, because the ancient Hebrew is difficult to translate precisely.

For today: although Christians are not under these food rules, we can learn that God calls his people to live differently and in obedience. Ask yourself today: in what part of my everyday life can I show that I belong to God, with decisions that please him?
exp.6:4:
It says that the priest will burn the separated fat portions of the animal on the altar, and that this is a food offering to the LORD. The phrase about a guilt offering refers to the offering made to repair a wrong.

God speaks to Moses, giving instructions to Israel about the offerings. Here the subject is the guilt offering, which was made when someone had failed against God or against their neighbor. The fat was regarded as the best part and was given to God. The rest was eaten by the priests in the holy place.

Today, Christians believe that Christ offered himself once for all. Even so, this text reminds us that guilt is serious and that God provides forgiveness. If you have failed, do not hide it: acknowledge it before God, make amends for the harm if you can, and receive his forgiveness with gratitude.
exp.12:36:
If the priest sees that the scaly outbreak is unchanged and black hair has grown in it, then it has healed. The priest must then pronounce him clean, meaning fit to live normally among the people. The phrase "in his sight... unchanged" means the outbreak has stopped spreading.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel, and the priests carried them out. They were not only medical matters but also matters of ritual purity and life in the community. Scholars debate exactly what disease these ancient words describe, so it is best not to claim a certain diagnosis. What is clear is that the priest examined carefully and also confirmed the healing.

For today: God takes no pleasure in shutting people out but in restoring them. We can imitate him by joyfully recognizing real change in others, without holding on to their past.
exp.14:21:
This verse says that if anyone touches any piece of furniture where a woman sat during her period, they must wash their clothes and bathe with water. They will be "unclean" until evening. "Unclean" does not mean dirty or sinful, but ceremonially impure, that is, not fit to come near worship. The word for her period is the time she is set apart.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel while they lived in the wilderness. These laws taught respect for the holiness of God, who was present in the tabernacle. Scholars explain the purpose in several ways: symbolic, community order, or hygiene. The Bible does not detail everything.

For today: let us learn to take God's holiness seriously and to care, with humility, how we present ourselves before Him. In Christ, the deeper cleansing has already been provided.
exp.15:19:
This verse says that when the high priest finishes purifying the Most Holy Place, the Tent of Meeting, and the altar, he is to bring forward the goat that is still alive. "Purifying" here means making these holy places clean through a sacrifice, so that sin's effects are dealt with. The "Tent of Meeting" is the sacred tent where God's presence was.

God gives these instructions to Moses for Aaron, on the Day of Atonement. First the place of worship was cleansed with blood. Then came the second goat, which symbolically carried the sins of the people and was sent away into the wilderness. Interpreters see it as a picture of sin being taken away.

For today: Christians see in Jesus the fulfillment of this, since his sacrifice cleanses us and removes our guilt. We can draw near to God with sincerity, confess what we have done wrong, and trust that He truly forgives.
exp.13:12:
He says the priest will kill the lamb in the sanctuary area, the same place where the sin offering and burnt offering are killed. "Slaughter" means to kill an animal for an offering. A "guilt offering" is the offering made to make up for a wrong. The text explains that this offering, like the sin offering, belongs to the priest, and that it is "most holy," meaning it is set apart for God.

God speaks through Moses. This is the ritual by which a person healed of a serious skin disease could return to the community. Being physically healed was not enough; the person needed to be declared clean and restored. The place and the care given to every detail show that everything had to be done in the presence of God.

For today: when God restores us, let us not take it lightly. We can respond with gratitude and reverence, remembering that our restoration has great value.
exp.12:56:
If the spot reappears in the clothing, whether in the fabric, the weave, or the knit, or on any leather article, there is no doubt left: it is a plague that keeps breaking out again. The word "spreading" here means that it reappears and keeps coming back. Then the contaminated article must be burned completely.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priest examined the garments patiently, and if the spot returned, there was no choice but to destroy them. This protected the health and purity of the community. Scholars do not agree on exactly what this "plague" in clothing was; it could have been mold or fungus.

For today: some things cannot be fixed with a simple washing. If a bad habit keeps coming back, it is wise to ask God and trustworthy people for help, and to make firm decisions to cut it off at the root.
exp.18:32:
The verse says that when a foreigner lives with you in your land, you must not oppress him. The word "resides" means to live there, and "oppress" means to treat someone who has less power harshly or unjustly.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in laws about how to live as a holy people. Around this verse are commands to honor the elderly and to be fair in business. The next verse gives the reason: they themselves were foreigners in Egypt, and they knew what it was to suffer abuse.

For today: treat immigrants and those who come from outside with respect and justice, at work, in your neighborhood, or in your church. You can greet them, not take advantage of their need, and help them when you can.
exp.26:30:
If a person wants to keep back something that was set aside as a tithe, they may buy it back, but they must pay its value plus an extra fifth. A tithe is the tenth part of the harvest that belongs to God. Adding a fifth means paying twenty percent more.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, at the end of the book of Leviticus. The laws about offerings and vows taught that the tithe of grain and fruit belonged to the LORD. The extra payment worked as a small penalty for keeping something already set apart for God. Animals, by contrast, could not be exchanged or bought back.

For today: when you decide to give to God, do it with seriousness and from the heart. Think over your commitment calmly, and do not change it lightly when it suits you.
exp.5:4:
It says that if someone lied under oath to keep something that belonged to another, he must give back the whole thing and add a fifth of its value on top, that is, twenty percent extra. He pays it to the owner on the day he acknowledges his guilt. The "atonement" here refers to the moment he makes right his wrong before God.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to the people of Israel. These laws show that sin against one's neighbor is also sin against the LORD. That is why they were required to repair the harm and also present a ram to the priest.

Today we can learn that asking God for forgiveness is not enough if we harm someone. If we have deceived or kept something that is not ours, we must acknowledge it, return it, and repair the harm honestly, trusting in God's mercy.
exp.13:11:
The verse says the priest is to take one of the male lambs and present it as a guilt offering, along with the log of olive oil. He then waves them as a wave offering before the LORD. The log is a small measure of liquid. To wave the offering means to lift it up and move it before the LORD as a gesture of dedication.

God speaks through Moses, giving instructions for the person who has been healed of leprosy (or of a serious skin disease; the Hebrew term can cover several conditions). Once healed, the person returns to the community, and on the eighth day is restored through sacrifices. The guilt offering shows that the restoration needed reconciliation with God.

God wants not only to heal, but also to restore the relationship with Him and with His people. If you have been through a wound or a time of distance, come to God with humility and gratitude, and let Him restore you completely.
exp.24:36:
This verse commands that the needy not be taken advantage of. Lending money at interest is forbidden, and so is selling food to a poor brother in order to profit from his hardship. God says, in plain terms, that you must not lend him your silver at interest or sell him your food for profit.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, before they enter Canaan. If an Israelite became poor, his family was to help him and take him into their home. The reason is that God had redeemed them from Egypt, so they were to treat the vulnerable with compassion. Scholars debate how this law applied to other kinds of loans, but its purpose of helping the poor is clear.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we generously help someone going through a hard time. If you lend to a relative or friend in need, do so without taking advantage of their situation.
exp.2:11:
This verse says that if someone wants to present a goat as an offering, they must bring it before the LORD, that is, to the place where God had commanded the sacrifices to be offered. The instruction to present it is the same as the one stated in the verse above. Here begins the third option within the peace offering: first a bull was mentioned, then a lamb, and now a goat.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses must teach it to the people. Peace offerings were a way of giving thanks and of having fellowship with God. This instruction allowed both a person with more resources and a person with fewer to draw near to Him with what they had.

For today: God receives each person according to their reality, not according to what others are able to give. You can come to Him with sincerity and gratitude, with what you have: your time, your prayer, and your service.
exp.18:24:
It says that when the tree had completed its fourth year and its fruit had been set apart for God, in the fifth year the people could eat from it. The promise is that in this way the harvest would grow. "Your harvest will be increased" means that the yield would be more abundant. "I am the LORD your God" is God's seal: he stands behind what he commands.

God speaks to Moses for all Israel, before they enter the land of Canaan. He teaches them to live as a holy people. For the first three years, the fruit was considered unclean, that is, not fit to eat. The fourth year was for giving praise to God. Scholars understand this as a way of acknowledging that the land and its fruit come from him.

For today: honor God first with the best of what you receive, your time, your work, or your income, and trust that he knows how to care for you. Patience and gratitude open the way to his provision.
exp.12:10:
When the skin disease has already become chronic and settled into the body, the priest is to declare the person unclean. He does not need to isolate the person for observation, because the case is already clear. The word "unclean" here means ceremonially unclean, not necessarily guilty of anything.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, giving instructions to the priests of Israel. These rules protected the community and showed the importance of living in purity before God. Scholars explain that the Hebrew word translated "leprosy" covered several skin conditions, not only the disease we today call leprosy.

For today: when something is damaged in our lives, it is better to acknowledge it honestly than to hide it or let it pass. Bringing it before God and before trusted people opens the door to healing and restoration.
exp.18:1:
God tells Moses to speak to the whole community of Israel. The message is: "Be holy, because I, the LORD your God, am holy." The verse's wording "speak" and "tell them" are the plain forms of "speak" and "tell." "Holy" means set apart for God, different, and also pure in conduct. "LORD" is the name of God as revealed to Israel.

It is God himself who speaks, and he addresses the whole community, not only the priests. This opens a section of laws for daily life: respect for parents, rest on the Sabbath, rejection of idols, and fair treatment of one's neighbor. Holiness is explained with very concrete examples, and its foundation is the character of God.

For today: holiness is not only a matter for the church or for special people. Today you can ask yourself how to reflect God in everyday life: in your work, your family, and your words, with honesty and respect.
exp.12:23:
This verse describes a person who has been burned on the skin. As the burn begins to heal, a spot appears in the raw area that is reddish-white or white. It does not yet say what to do; that comes in the verses that follow.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priest was to examine the skin and decide whether it was only a scar or a contagious disease. The word "leprosy" here covered several skin conditions, and we do not know exactly which ones. These rules protected the health and life of the people.

For today: before drawing conclusions about something that worries us, it is wise to examine it calmly and seek a wise opinion. God values patience, care for our health, and the help of others.
exp.3:7:
This verse commands that the priest set aside from the bull offered for sin all the fat: both the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is on them. "Fat" refers to the animal's fat, and "atonement" means covering or cleansing sin through a sacrifice.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about the sin offering of the anointed priest, whose wrong affected the whole people. The fat was considered the best part of the animal and was burned on the altar. For this reason, many understand it as a way of giving God what was most valuable. The exact details of its symbolism are interpreted in various ways.

For today: when you recognize a fault, do not give God leftovers or excuses. Bring him a sincere and devoted heart, trusting that Christ has already offered the perfect sacrifice for your sin.
exp.22:1:
God tells Moses to speak to the people of Israel and tell them that these are His appointed feasts, the feasts of the LORD. They were to announce them as sacred assemblies, meaning holy gatherings for the whole people. God says these feasts belong to Him.

God speaks, and He does so through Moses. In Leviticus 23 God sets out a calendar of feasts for Israel, and it begins with the Sabbath. His purpose was that the people would stop their work, gather together, and remember who God is and what He has done for them. The time was not theirs, but the LORD's.

For today: set aside a fixed time each week, without excuses, to rest, pray, and meet with other believers. Treat it as an appointment with God, not as leftover time.
exp.20:20:
This passage says that no descendant of Aaron the priest who had a defect could come near to present the food offerings to the LORD. A "defect" is any physical flaw or impairment, and "approach" means to come near. The offerings are the sacrifices made by fire on the altar, which the verse calls the food of his God.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to Aaron and his sons. The priests represented holiness and wholeness before God. This man was not rejected: the next passage says he could still eat of the holy things. Scholars explain the rule as a symbol of perfection, not as a judgment on his worth.

Today, Christ is our perfect priest, and through Him all of us can draw near to God with confidence. Remember that no one is excluded because of their limitations.
exp.26:27:
This verse says that anything a person sets apart completely for the LORD, whether a person, an animal, or inherited land, cannot be sold or bought back. "Set apart" means dedicated to God. "Buy back" means to purchase it again. "Most holy" describes something that belongs entirely to God.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel at the end of the book of Leviticus, in a chapter about vows and offerings. This kind of giving, called "a devoted thing" or "total dedication," was different from other offerings, because there was no going back. The verse that follows, about people, is difficult. Many understand it as a judgment on condemned enemies rather than a voluntary offering, although it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: think carefully before promising something to God, and when you do, keep your word sincerely. He values a heart that is given over and faithful, not words spoken lightly.
exp.5:18:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that the LORD spoke to Moses, and with it a new instruction begins. The word "said" introduces the message God is about to give for Moses to pass on to the people.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the messenger. Earlier, God explained how the priests were to eat the grain offering, and now he moves to another subject: the offering that Aaron and his sons would present on the day they were anointed. In this way the book shows that the rules do not come from human ideas, but from the word of God.

For today: before we act, it is worth stopping to listen to God. We can read the Bible carefully and ask him for direction, remembering that his word deserves our respect and obedience.
exp.22:32:
This verse is an introductory phrase. It says that the LORD spoke to Moses to give him a new message. After speaking about the Day of Atonement, the LORD is going to teach about another festival: the Feast of Tabernacles. The word "said" shows that Moses was to pass on what he heard.

The one speaking is the LORD, and Moses is the messenger who carries his words to the people. Earlier, the LORD had given instructions about the Sabbath rest and the fast, when the people humbled themselves. Now another section begins, about a time of celebration. It moves from repentance to thankful joy, and in this way it shows that the LORD has a calendar for Israel to remember.

For today: God still speaks through his Word. Today we can set aside a fixed time to listen to him in the Bible, not only when we have problems, but also to learn to give him thanks.
exp.6:29:
The person who offers a peace offering is to bring to the LORD with his own hands the portion that is burned: the fat along with the breast of the animal. The breast was waved, that is, moved back and forth before God as a gesture of presenting it to Him.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct the people of Israel. The peace offering was a shared meal: one part for God, another for the priest, and another for the one who offered. According to the following verse, the breast went to Aaron and his sons. Scholars explain the exact meaning of the waving gesture in different ways.

For today: "With his own hands he is to bring" reminds us that gratitude to God is personal. It is not enough to leave it to others. Today you can set aside a specific moment to give thanks and offer Him something of your time, your service, or your possessions.
exp.20:22:
This verse says that a priest descended from Aaron who had a physical defect could not go past the veil into the most holy place, and could not come near the altar to present the offerings. The word "veil" refers to the curtain that separated the holy place from the most holy place. Even so, he could eat of the holy bread, as the previous verse says. God adds that this keeps his sanctuary from being desecrated, because he is the one who makes them holy.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to Aaron, his sons, and all Israel. These rules were part of the law of the priesthood, which taught the holiness and perfection that God deserves. Interpreters explain the meaning of these rules in various ways, but they are not presented as a judgment on the worth of the person.

For today: we can draw near to God with reverence, remembering that he is the one who makes us holy. And in Christ, our high priest, all of us have access to his presence, with our weaknesses.
exp.22:37:
These offerings were in addition to the offerings for the Lord's Sabbaths, to your gifts, to all your vow offerings, and to all the freewill offerings you give to the Lord. The offerings for these celebrations did not replace anything else. They were given alongside the weekly Sabbath offerings, the gifts the people brought, the vow offerings, and the freewill offerings. A "gift" is a present or contribution, and "in addition to" means "apart from" or "on top of."

God speaks to Moses so that he can tell Israel. After listing the yearly feasts, this verse works as a clarifying note: the feasts had their required offerings, but personal generosity and the keeping of vows continued separately. Right after this, the Feast of Tabernacles is explained.

For today: worship is not reduced to doing what is required. We can ask ourselves whether, beyond what we do out of habit, we give something from the heart: our time, help to someone, or a freewill offering, given with joy and without pressure.
exp.21:11:
What it says: If a priest's daughter married a man who was not a priest (someone outside the priestly family), she could no longer eat of the sacred contributions, that is, the holy portions that the people brought to God and that were set apart for the priests and their household.

Context: God speaks to Moses to instruct Aaron and his sons. He wanted what was holy to be treated with respect. Eating from that portion depended on belonging to the priestly household. By marrying someone from outside, the daughter passed into another household. Afterward, if she was widowed or divorced without children and returned to her father's house, she could eat again.

For today: God takes care that what is holy is not treated lightly. Learn to draw near to God with reverence, and remember that today, in Christ, all his children are invited to his table.
exp.10:37:
It says that if the seed was already wet and a dead body of one of those unclean animals falls on it, that seed must be considered unclean. "Seed" refers to grain or sowing seed; "it is unclean for you" means it must be considered unclean and not used.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to teach Israel to live as a set-apart people. Before this, dry seed remained clean if something dead fell on it. With water, by contrast, it was thought that uncleanness clung more easily. Scholars explain this distinction in several ways, and the text does not give all the reasons.

For today: what is "wet," that is, open and receptive, more readily absorbs whatever falls on it. Let us be careful about what we allow into our hearts and minds, especially when we are sensitive or tired.
exp.6:28:
The passage says that Moses must speak to the people of Israel about the rules for the peace offering, also called the fellowship or thanksgiving offering. Whoever presented it to the Lord had to bring it himself as his own sacrifice to the Lord. The term "peace offering" is an older name for that sacrifice. The wording about presenting and bringing it shows that the offering was voluntary and personal.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for the people. Just before this, he commanded that no blood be eaten. Then he explains which part was burned on the altar and which part the priests received. This sacrifice was shared in a meal before God, and it expressed gratitude and fellowship with him. Some details of its meaning are interpreted in different ways.

Today we can learn that giving thanks to God should be personal and sincere. No one can give thanks on our behalf. You might set aside a moment this week to thank God in your own words and share your joy with others.
exp.22:34:
On the first day there is to be a sacred assembly, a call to come together before the Lord. "Sacred assembly" means a gathering set apart for worship. The verse also says that you must not do any regular work. That means the daily work by which a person earned a living was set aside, and on that day the people were to rest from it.

God speaks to Moses so that he may pass these instructions on to Israel. The feast began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month and lasted seven days, with a special gathering at the beginning and another on the eighth day. It was a time of offerings and thanksgiving, and the people remembered that God had cared for them.

For today: set aside a time in your week to pause and worship God, without the rush of work. Resting and meeting with other believers reminds you that your life depends on God and not only on your own effort.
exp.7:16:
This verse tells us that Moses took the bull of the sin offering, with its hide, its flesh, and its dung, and burned it outside the camp. The phrase "outside the camp" matches the wording of your verse. Moses did this just as the LORD had commanded him.

It is the day when Aaron and his sons are set apart as priests. Moses leads the ceremony. First the altar was purified with the blood, and only the fat was burned on it. The rest of the animal was burned outside. Some see in this the seriousness of sin and its distance from the presence of God, though the text does not explain it.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he also provides forgiveness. Today we can obey with humility, without downplaying what God has said, and trust in his mercy.
exp.3:20:
This verse says that the priest must take the bull outside the camp and burn it, just as he burned the first bull. The word "atonement" here means covering or cleansing sin through a sacrifice. This is a sin offering for the whole assembly, that is, for the entire people of Israel.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes the instructions on to Israel. This passage deals with sin committed without realizing it, when the whole people fails. Burning the bull away from the camp showed that sin is something unclean that must be removed from the midst of the people. Afterward, the text continues with the sin of a ruler.

For today: we should not minimize sin, even when it is unintentional. It must be acknowledged with humility, and we must turn to God. Christians see in Christ the final sacrifice, who suffered outside the gate (Hebrews 13:12), so that we may have forgiveness.
exp.19:8:
He says that anyone who curses his father or mother must be put to death. "Cursing" here means speaking with contempt, treating parents with disrespect, or wishing harm on them. The phrase "his blood shall be upon him" means that he himself is responsible for his punishment; no one else is to blame for his death.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. He has just called the people to be holy, set apart from the nations around them. These laws were part of the covenant with Israel as a nation, and they show how seriously God took respect for the family, the foundation of society. What follows deals with other serious sins within the household.

For today: Christians do not live under those civil penalties of Israel, but we do learn that God values honor toward parents. We can be careful with our words toward them, even when there are differences, and look for ways to respect and help them.
exp.13:8:
On the seventh day of his time waiting outside the camp, the person being purified was to shave off all his hair: his head, his beard, his eyebrows, and the rest of his hair. The word "shave" means removing hair completely with a razor. Then he washed his clothes and bathed his body in water. With this, he was declared clean.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. They are rules for how someone who had a skin disease (the word "leprosy" covered several conditions) could return to the community. It was a process in stages, guided by the priest. Scholars explain the meaning of the shaving in various ways, but almost all agree that it symbolized a new beginning.

For today: God cares for the return of the one who was set apart. We can help others come back into the community, without haste and without blame, giving them room to start again.
exp.12:2:
This verse describes how the priest was to examine an infection on the skin. If the hair in the affected area had turned white and the sore appeared deeper than the skin around it, the priest was to declare it a skin disease and pronounce the person unclean. The word "skin" in the verse refers to the surface of the body, and "unclean" means not fit to take part in worship and community life. The Hebrew word behind "skin disease" covered several conditions, not necessarily what is called leprosy today.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, giving the people of Israel rules for caring for the health and purity of the community. The examination was done by the priest, not a folk healer, and it followed clear signs, not opinions.

For today: when we evaluate others or a difficult situation, let us do it with patience and with facts, not with prejudice. And when something worries us about our health, let us seek help in time.
exp.20:5:
This verse says that the priests, the sons of Aaron, were to live set apart for God and not dishonor his name. The reason is that they present the food offerings to the LORD, which is here called "the food of their God." To profane means to treat as common what is holy.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct the priests. Before and after this verse there are rules about mourning, appearance, and marriage. Their closeness to the altar required a conduct that reflected the holy character of God before the people.

For today: whoever serves God, or simply says they follow him, represents his name through daily life. We can ask ourselves whether our words, decisions, and dealings with others honor God, rather than making him look bad before others.
exp.26:32:
When someone set aside the tithe of their livestock, they could not inspect whether the animal was good or bad, and they could not substitute another animal for it.
