If they did make a substitution, both the original animal and the substitute would become holy, set apart for God. Neither could be redeemed by paying money in its place.

This section closes the book of Leviticus. God speaks to Moses, giving Israel instructions about offerings and vows. The tenth animal was counted as it passed under the shepherd's rod, so it was selected by chance, without favoritism or trickery. Commentators often see here a safeguard against deception.

For today: when we give something to God or to others, let us do it with honesty and generosity, not picking only what we have left over or looking for advantage. Giving with a sincere heart honors God more than calculating what suits us best.
exp.19:10:
It says that if a man has sexual relations with his father's wife, he has uncovered his father's nakedness, and the law ordered that both of them be put to death. The phrase "lies with" means to have sexual relations. "Uncovered his father's nakedness" is a Hebrew expression for intimate relations that are forbidden. The words that their blood is upon them mean that they would be responsible for their own deaths. This refers to the father's wife, probably a stepmother.

God spoke to Moses to give laws to the people of Israel, who had just come out of Egypt and would live in Canaan. These rules protected the family and set the people apart from the neighboring nations. They were laws for Israel in that time and place.

For today: God values faithfulness and respect within the family. We can keep healthy boundaries in our homes, honor our parents, and avoid what damages trust among family members.
exp.1:8:
The priest is to take the memorial portion from the grain offering and burn it on the altar. That portion is called the memorial, and the verse describes it as a food offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. Burning it on the altar means the priest makes it go up in smoke there as part of the offering.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes these instructions on to Israel. This offering was an expression of gratitude and devotion to God. One part was burned, and the rest was for the priests, as the following verses explain. Some think the memorial was a reminder of the covenant between God and his people, although the text does not fully explain this.

For today: God values what we give him with a grateful heart, even when it is simple. Today you can offer God your work, your time, or your resources, recognizing that everything comes from him.
exp.24:22:
This verse says that the land of Israel must not be sold permanently. "Permanently" means completely and with no possibility of getting it back. God gives the reason: the land is his, and the people are foreigners and residents with him, meaning guests who live in it by God's permission, not its absolute owners.

God speaks through Moses in the laws of the year of jubilee. First he promises blessing in the sixth year, so that the people can let the land rest. Then he commands that the land can be redeemed, and that a close relative can buy back what a poor brother had to sell. In this way families were protected from losing their inheritance permanently.

For today: everything we have, whether a home, money or work, we manage as God's stewards. This invites us to use our possessions generously and to help those in need, rather than clinging to them.
exp.20:2:
This verse makes an exception: the priest could become defiled, that is, ceremonially unclean from touching a dead body, if his unmarried sister who lived near him died. "Unmarried" here describes a sister who has no husband, and "near to him" means she depended on his family, because she had no husband to care for her.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to the priests, the sons of Aaron. They served in the holy place and had to guard their ritual purity. Even so, God allowed them to mourn and bury their closest relatives. The following verse is difficult to translate and is understood in several ways.

For today: God cares about holiness, but He does not ask us to be cold toward our family. We can serve Him with seriousness and, at the same time, be present with love in our loved ones' moments of grief.
exp.2:15:
What it says: The priest burns the fatty parts of the animal on the altar. The verse calls the burnt portion "food" for the offering made by fire, and describes it as a pleasing aroma to the Lord. It states plainly that all the fat belongs to the LORD.

Context: God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about the peace offering, a fellowship offering in which part was burned and part was eaten. The fat was considered the best part of the animal. By reserving it for God, the people acknowledged that He deserves the first and the choicest. The following verse forbids eating fat and blood; scholars explain the exact meaning of that rule in various ways.

For today: We can ask ourselves whether we give God the best of our time, affection, and resources, and not just what we have left over. Today you might set aside a quiet moment to pray with gratitude.
exp.13:39:
This verse says that if the mark kept spreading on the walls of the house, the priest would order the contaminated stones to be pulled out. Those stones were carried outside the city and thrown into a contaminated place, meaning a set-apart spot considered unfit for what is clean. Here the word "contaminated" refers to a stain or infection on the wall, probably some kind of mold or fungus, though this is not known for certain.

God speaks through Moses to Israel, before they enter the promised land. These laws protected health and kept the people set apart for God. First the house was waited on and examined, and only afterward was action taken.

For today: there are things in our lives that spread quietly, like a grudge or a bad habit. It is wise to examine them calmly, ask for help, and remove what is damaged before it contaminates everything.
exp.17:29:
God tells the Israelites to be careful to keep what He has commanded. "Keep my charge" means to obey His instructions. He asks them not to practice any of the detestable customs that the people before them practiced, so that they would not make themselves unclean through them. He closes with his own name, "I am the LORD your God," reminding them who gives the commands and to whom they belong.

God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel. Before this verse He listed prohibitions concerning sexuality and other practices, and warned that the land of Canaan would vomit out those who polluted it, as it had already done with its former inhabitants. He wants His people to be different.

For today: before following along with what "everyone does," ask yourself what pleases God. His identity as your God gives you reason and strength to live differently, with integrity and trust in Him.
exp.16:3:
If an Israelite killed an ox, a lamb, or a goat and did not bring it to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting to present as an offering to the LORD, that act would be counted as bloodguilt. To be "counted" means to be charged to his account. It is as if he had poured out blood without permission. To be "cut off from among his people" means he would be separated from the community. Scholars debate whether this implied death or only expulsion.

God speaks to Moses so that he would tell Aaron, his sons, and all Israel. God wanted the lives of the animals never to be taken lightly. He also aimed to keep the people from offering sacrifices out in the open field, as other peoples of the time did, and to bring them near to Him alone.

For today: value life as a gift from God and come to Him with gratitude and reverence, rather than doing things your own way. Christ, through His blood, opens for us a better way.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that the grain offering, prepared in a pan, had to be crumbled into pieces, and that oil was poured over it. A grain offering is an offering brought to God. Fine flour is flour of the highest quality.

God speaks to Moses to teach the people of Israel how to bring grain offerings. They were a way of giving thanks to God and acknowledging that everything comes from Him. Crumbling the bread into pieces allowed the oil to cover all of it. Many believe the oil represents the Spirit of God or His blessing, although the text here does not explain this directly.

Today we can give God the best of our work and our time, with gratitude and in small details. What we do in everyday life can also be an offering to Him.
exp.9:5:
Moses tells Aaron and his sons Eleazar and Ithamar not to let their hair become disheveled, and not to tear their garments, as was done in mourning. If they did, they could die, and the LORD's anger would fall on the whole congregation. The rest of the Israelites, however, could mourn over the fire that the LORD had sent. The fire is the one referred to in the verse.

Moses speaks here after the death of Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, who offered strange fire before the LORD. The priests had been anointed and set apart for service. For that reason, at that moment, they were to continue their service and not take part in the public mourning that everyone else was doing.

Today we see that serving God is a serious matter, and that He deserves reverence. We also learn that grief is real, but we can carry it with humility, and ask God and the community of faith to sustain us.
exp.12:19:
This verse says that the priest must examine carefully the area of skin where a swelling had been before. If the mark appears to be beneath the skin and the hair in it has turned white, the priest would declare it unclean, that is, ceremonially impure. The word "plague" here refers to several skin diseases, not necessarily what we today call leprosy.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for Israel. The priests did not act as physicians but cared for the purity of the people and of the community living near the tabernacle. Scholars explain the exact purpose of these laws in different ways.

For today: before judging a situation, look calmly and seek clear signs. God taught people to examine with patience, not to condemn based on appearances.
exp.12:30:
If the priest examines a scaly infection on the head or the beard and finds that it does not appear to be deeper than the skin and that there is no black hair in it, he does not yet declare the person unclean. Instead, he isolates the infected person for seven days so that the condition can be watched. The word "scaly infection" describes a skin condition marked by crusting, and "deeper than the skin" means the sore has not gone beneath the outer layer of the skin.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priests were to examine carefully and not decide in haste. These rules protected the health and order of the community. Scholars debate exactly which diseases this chapter describes.

For today: before judging someone, let us take time to observe, listen, and understand. Patience prevents unfair judgments and makes room for compassion and truth.
exp.18:14:
It says that a judge, or anyone who decides a matter, must not pervert justice. They must not show partiality to someone because they are poor, out of pity, nor favoritism to someone because they are rich, to win their favor. Unfairness is a wrong or a harm, and giving special treatment because of someone's position is partiality.

God himself speaks to Israel through Moses. The whole chapter repeats the words "I am the LORD," and teaches how to live as a holy people. Before and after this verse there are commands about paying the day laborer, caring for the weak, not slandering, and not holding a grudge. Justice appears as part of loving one's neighbor.

For today: when you have to give an opinion, evaluate, or settle a conflict, whether in the family, at work, or in the church, check whether pity or fear of someone important is pulling you to one side. Look for the facts, and treat everyone with the same truth and respect.
exp.14:2:
This passage says that when a man has an abnormal discharge from his body, he is "unclean," meaning ritually impure. The verse says this applies whether the discharge flows out or whether his body blocks it. In this context, "unclean" does not mean sinful, but not fit to come near the sanctuary.

God speaks to Moses and to Aaron, the priest, so that they may instruct the people. These laws of purity taught Israel that God is holy and that they must guard His presence in the midst of the camp. Some also see in them a concern for the health of the community, although the text does not explain this.

For today: God takes holiness seriously, but today He cleanses us through Christ, not through rituals. We can draw near to Him with confidence, and treat with compassion those who suffer from illness.
exp.21:16:
This verse is an introductory phrase. It says that the LORD spoke to Moses. The words "Then the LORD said to Moses" are a formula repeated often in Leviticus, and they signal that a command from God is coming. The name "LORD" is God's personal name in the Old Testament.

God is the one who speaks, and Moses is the one who receives the message to pass on to Aaron, the priests, and all the people. Earlier, God had spoken about the care of holy things. Now a new instruction begins: the offerings that are brought must be without defect. This shows that approaching God is done with respect.

For today: before you pray, serve, or give, remember that God speaks to us first and deserves the best of us. We can listen to his Word with attention and answer him with sincerity, not with what we have left over.
exp.22:17:
Along with the bread, the people were to present seven unblemished male lambs a year old, one young bull, and two rams. All of it was to be a burnt offering to the LORD, completely burned on the altar. The grain offering was the offering of flour, the drink offerings were the wine poured out, and "a pleasing aroma" is a way of saying that God received it with delight.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about the Feast of Weeks, also called Pentecost, held fifty days after the offering of the firstfruits. It was a celebration of thanks for the wheat harvest. Animals without defect showed that God deserves the best.

For today: let us give God our best, not the leftovers. Before you spend your time, money or energy, thank Him sincerely and offer Him the first and best of your day.
exp.2:12:
He says that whoever brings a goat must lay his hand on the animal's head, and then slaughter it in front of the Tent of Meeting. The sons of Aaron, that is, the priests, splatter its blood on all sides of the altar.

God speaks to Moses and gives instructions about the peace offerings. This passage explains the case of someone who offers a goat instead of a bull or a lamb. Laying the hand on the animal shows that it is his personal offering. The blood, which represents life, is handled with respect, and only the priests handle it. Scholars understand the gesture of the hand in several ways, but all agree that it unites the worshiper with his offering.

Today we do not offer animals, but we can draw near to God with sincerity and with our whole heart, not simply going through the motions out of habit. Christians remember that Christ offered his life for us.
exp.8:4:
They brought to the front of the Tent of Meeting everything that Moses had commanded. Then the whole community came near and stood before the LORD. The Tent of Meeting is the sacred tent where God met with his people. "Community" means the assembly of Israel.

This takes place on the eighth day, when Aaron and his sons begin their service as priests. Moses reports what God commanded, because the Lord had promised to appear that day. The people obey and come forward with reverence, expecting God's presence.

For today: before seeking God, it is worth preparing ourselves with an obedient and humble heart. When we gather to pray or worship, we can approach with attention and respect, trusting that God desires to meet with us.
exp.19:25:
God tells Israel that they must be holy, meaning set apart for him, because he himself is holy. In the Berean Standard Bible, the words "You are to be" carry the sense of "you must be." God has set Israel apart from the nations so that they belong to him. The idea of "holy" speaks of being different and dedicated to God.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, just before they enter the promised land. He has just warned them not to imitate the customs of the neighboring nations. He asks them to distinguish between clean and unclean animals as a daily reminder that they are a distinct people. The verses that follow deal with divination, practices that God forbade Israel.

Today we can remember that we belong to God, not only to our culture. This is not pride but identity. We might ask ourselves this week: in what concrete decision can I show that I live for God, with honesty, purity, or generosity?
exp.18:10:
This verse forbids three things: stealing, deceiving, and lying to another person. "Stealing" means taking what belongs to someone else; "deceiving" means trying to gain an advantage through tricks or dishonesty. Here "neighbor" means the person who lives near you, your fellow countryman or neighbor.

God speaks, giving these laws to Israel through Moses. Shortly before, he commands that part of the harvest be left for the poor and the foreigner, and afterward he speaks of not swearing falsely and not holding back a day laborer's wages. All of this is part of the call to be a holy people, one that reflects the character of God in daily dealings.

Today we can examine our words and our business: not exaggerating to sell, not hiding defects, not keeping a little extra change. Being honest in small things honors God and cares for others.
exp.13:6:
This is what the verse says: the priest sprinkles the person who is being cleansed from the skin disease seven times. Then he pronounces them clean and releases the live bird into the open field. The phrase "the open field" here means the open country. The skin disease described in this verse is not always what we today call leprosy.

Context: God speaks through Moses to Israel. This ritual was performed when someone had already been healed and needed to return to the community. One bird is killed and the other, dipped in its blood, is set free. Many see it as a picture of death and new life, although the text does not explain it.

For today: God not only heals, he also restores. If someone has lived apart out of shame or because of mistakes, we can receive them with kindness and help them begin again, like someone releasing a bird into freedom.
exp.19:0:
This verse is only an introduction. It says that the LORD spoke to Moses, and what follows are the words God wanted him to pass on. The phrase "Then the LORD said" appears many times in Leviticus and marks that what comes next is not human ideas but instructions given by God to the people.

Here God is speaking, and Moses is the messenger. Israel was about to live among peoples with very different customs, and God wanted to keep it away from practices that harmed people and dishonored his name. The chapter opens with a serious warning about the worship of Molech, which involved giving children. Scholars discuss the exact details of that rite.

For today: before hearing a command from God, it is worth remembering that he is the one who speaks. We can read the Bible with respect and attention, willing to obey, even when something is hard to understand.
exp.24:15:
This verse says that the price of a piece of land should depend on how many years remain until the Jubilee. If many years remain, the land is worth more, because the buyer will be able to harvest from it for a long time. If few years remain, it is worth less. In reality, the land was not being sold forever, but rather a set number of harvests. The crops or yields are the produce of the land, and to lower the price is to reduce it.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. In the Jubilee year, which came every fifty years, the land returned to its original family. That is why God gives this rule: so that no one would take advantage of the one who was in need, and so that everyone would deal justly with their neighbor.

For today: when you buy, sell, or negotiate, be honest and charge a fair price. Do not take advantage of another person's need or ignorance. Act with integrity, because God sees every transaction.
exp.19:26:
Leviticus 20:27 says that any man or woman who is a medium or spiritist must surely be put to death. They were to be stoned, and their blood would be upon them, meaning they bore the responsibility for their own death.

God was speaking to Israel through Moses. He had just called the people to be holy and set apart from the neighboring nations, who practiced sorcery and consulted the dead. This was a civil law for the nation of Israel under the covenant given through Moses. Christians do not apply it as a penalty today, and there are different ways of understanding how it should be read.

For today: when we look for direction or comfort in life, instead of turning to horoscopes, spiritists, or cards, let us turn to God in prayer and to his Word, trusting that he guides his own.
exp.25:0:
This verse forbids making idols, carved images, sacred pillars, or stones with figures to worship them. The words "carved image" and "sculpted stone" in the verse above refer to a carved figure and a stone set up for worship. The phrase "to bow down to it" means to give it worship.

God himself speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel. This chapter opens the blessings and warnings of the covenant before they enter the land. God joins the prohibition of idols with keeping the sabbath and reverencing the sanctuary, asking them for exclusive and faithful worship. The reason is clear: "For I am the LORD your God."

For today: an idol can be anything that takes God's place in the heart, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Today you can ask yourself what receives your trust first, and give it back to God in prayer.
exp.3:21:
This verse speaks of a leader, that is, the head of a tribe, who sins unintentionally. That means without meaning to, by mistake or oversight, and not in deliberate defiance. Even so, he did what the LORD his God had prohibited, and that makes him guilty.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes the words on to Israel. Here the law explains how sin was to be dealt with according to each kind of person: the priest, the whole congregation, the leader, and the common people. Leaders also needed forgiveness, and sin committed without intention still mattered before God.

Today we can learn that no one is above the need to acknowledge their failures. If you hold any position or influence, ask God to show you your mistakes, even the ones you commit without realizing it, and come to Him with humility to receive forgiveness.
exp.10:45:
This verse sums up what God has just taught: the law regarding animals, birds, all living creatures that move in the water, and all creatures that crawl along the ground. It is like the closing of a long list of animals that were permitted and forbidden for eating.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel. He reminds them that he brought them out of Egypt to be their God, and that they must be holy, that is, set apart for him. These food rules marked a visible difference between Israel and other peoples. Scholars explain the reasons for each animal in different ways, but the text emphasizes holiness.

For today: God is interested in everyday details, such as what we do and decide each day. You might ask yourself, "Does today's decision show that I belong to God?" And ask him for help to live faithfully in small things.
exp.3:19:
He says that the priest will do with this second bull the same thing he did with the first, the one offered for his own sin. The word "atonement" means covering or cleansing guilt through a sacrifice. The phrase "they will be forgiven" means that God pardons them. Here "them" refers to the whole congregation of Israel.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people. The chapter deals with sins committed unintentionally, that is, without meaning to or through carelessness. If the whole community failed, it needed a sacrifice. The elders laid their hands on the bull, and the priest offered it. Many Christians see here a shadow of Christ's sacrifice, though the text does not say so directly.

For today: do not downplay the mistakes you make without realizing it. Ask God for forgiveness simply, and trust that he offers real pardon to anyone who comes to him with humility.
exp.13:21:
It says that the poor person, once healed of leprosy, was also to bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons, whichever he could afford. One of the two was offered as a sin offering, and the other as a burnt offering, which was burned whole.

The phrase "whichever he can afford" means "whatever he was able to pay for." Atonement means covering over guilt so that a person may be forgiven.

God speaks to Moses, giving rules for the cleansing of someone who had recovered from a serious skin disease, called leprosy in this version. The poor person was allowed to offer something less costly, so that he could return to the community and to worship without money being an obstacle.

For today: God receives us as we are and knows what we are able to give. We can draw near to Him without shame over how little we have, and we can also help make sure that no one is left out for lack of resources.
exp.25:18:
God says he will break down the stubborn pride of his people, the confidence they place in their own strength. Their stubborn pride is the arrogance of feeling strong and secure without him. The sky will be like iron and the land like bronze: the sky will hold back rain, and the hard ground will produce no harvest. It is a picture of severe drought.

Here God speaks to Israel through Moses. This passage is part of the warnings of the covenant: if the people kept disobeying, the consequences would grow in stages. That punishment was meant to bring them back to him, not merely to make them suffer. The words about punishment coming "seven times" over express more intense discipline; many understand this as a way of saying "much more."

For today: examine the things you trust in more than God, such as your work, your money, or your abilities. Give them to him with humility and listen to his voice before life forces you to do so.
exp.17:12:
This verse forbids sexual relations with your mother's sister, that is, your aunt on your mother's side. The reason given is that she is your mother's close relative.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Israel, just before they enter the land of Canaan. These laws were meant to protect families and to set apart a way of life different from that of the neighboring peoples. The text gives the same kind of rule for your father's sister in the verse before.

For today: take care with the boundaries in your family relationships. Treat your relatives with respect and purity, and do not use trust or closeness to take advantage of anyone. The family should be a safe place.
exp.15:24:
This verse says that Aaron, the high priest, was to burn the fat of the sin offering on the altar. "Fat" refers to the animal's fat, which was considered the best part. "Atonement" means covering or taking away guilt through a sacrifice.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions about the Day of Atonement, the most solemn day in Israel. Aaron had already presented the blood in the sanctuary and offered sacrifices for himself and for the people. Burning the fat on the altar was part of the order of the ritual. It was done with care, because God taught that sin is serious and that forgiveness has a cost.

For today: when you ask God for forgiveness, do not do it lightly. Give thanks because Christ offered the complete sacrifice, and bring him your best with gratitude.
exp.3:12:
This verse describes the case where the whole nation of Israel strays into sin without intending to. Straying "unintentionally" means they did wrong without meaning to. "The matter escapes the notice of the assembly" means nobody noticed it at the time. Even so, by violating one of the LORD's commandments, they were "guilty," meaning they had a real responsibility before Him.

God speaks to Moses so that he can instruct Israel. These laws about sin offerings taught that sin, even unintentional sin, affects our relationship with God, and that God Himself provided a way to cleanse it. Earlier the text spoke of the priest, and here it speaks of the whole community.

For today: it is not enough to say, "I didn't know." We can ask God to show us our hidden faults, and remember that Christ offers us complete forgiveness.
exp.25:25:
He says that God will cut off your supply of bread, that is, the thing that holds up your food supply. Bread was the basic daily food, the thing a person leans on to stay strong. So little grain will be left that ten women will bake in one oven, something each household would normally do on its own. The bread will be handed out by weight, in measured portions. People will eat, but they will still be hungry.

God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel. These words are part of the warnings of the covenant: if Israel turned away from God, the consequences would grow more severe. God does not say this to destroy them, but to call them back to Him.

For today: we can have food or money and still feel empty if we live far from God. Today, ask Him to be your true sustenance, and return to Him sincerely.
exp.5:0:
The verse says that the LORD, the name of God, spoke to Moses. The wording in the source uses the word "a" for "to," which is the same in modern English usage. It is only an introduction: God is about to give Moses a new instruction for him to pass on to the people.

We are in Leviticus, where God teaches Israel how to live in holiness and how to be forgiven. This message opens a new topic: what must be done when someone wrongs their neighbor through deceit, theft, or lying. The verses that follow explain that this too is sinning against God.

For today: God cares about how we treat others. If we have deceived someone, kept what was not ours, or failed to be truthful, it is good to acknowledge it before God, ask for forgiveness, and make right the harm with honesty.
exp.7:11:
Moses takes the special anointing oil and pours it on Aaron's head. "Anoint" means putting oil on someone or something to set them apart for God. The phrase "to consecrate him" means setting him apart, making him dedicated to the service of God.

Here the narrator describes the ceremony in which Aaron is consecrated as high priest, following what God commanded Moses. Earlier, Moses had anointed the tabernacle, the altar, and its utensils. Afterward come Aaron's sons and the sin offering. It shows that neither the place nor the people could serve God without first being set apart.

For today: God still calls his people to live set apart for him. You can begin each day by asking him to use you and to direct your work, your family, and your words to honor him.
exp.25:12:
God says that he is the one who brought Israel out of Egypt so that they would no longer be slaves. The "bars" are the wooden pieces that hold a yoke in place on a pack animal. Breaking them means removing the burden completely. "Enabled you to walk in uprightness" means being able to walk with dignity, without shame or submission.

God himself speaks, through Moses, in the covenant with Israel at Sinai. Before this, he promises to live among his people. Here he reminds them of what he has already done for them, as the basis for their trust. After this come the warnings in case they disobey.

For today: before asking us for anything, God reminds us of what he has already done for us. We can obey him not out of fear but with gratitude, and live with our heads held high, knowing that he sets us free and is near.
exp.25:17:
God says that if the people, after suffering the earlier punishments, still refuse to obey him, he will discipline them again with even greater force, seven times more. The words "I will proceed to punish you" mean that God will keep going with the discipline. The phrase "sevenfold" probably expresses full intensity, not necessarily an exact count.

God himself speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel in the covenant at Sinai. After the blessings promised for obedience, he warns of the consequences of rejecting the covenant. The punishments come in stages and aim to make the people recognize their error and return to him, not merely to make them suffer.

For today: when we feel that God is getting our attention through our circumstances or through other people, let us not harden our hearts. It is better to stop early, acknowledge our wrong, and return to him than to wait until the difficulties grow.
exp.5:2:
This verse describes someone who finds property that another person has lost, then lies about having it, and to avoid responsibility swears falsely. "Lost property" refers to something that belongs to another person and has gone missing. "Swears falsely" means stating something untrue while calling on God as a witness.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to the people of Israel. This list of wrongs against one's neighbor is also counted as a wrong against the LORD, because lying and deceit damage the trust between people and dishonor God's name. The law then calls for admitting the guilt, returning everything, and adding a fifth more.

For today: if you have something that is not yours, or you have lied to keep it, return it honestly and repair the harm. God values a sincere heart that makes right what has been done wrong.
exp.23:22:
Moses spoke to the Israelites, and they took the blasphemer outside the camp and stoned him. In this way they did what the LORD had commanded. "Blasphemer" here means the one who speaks with contempt about the name of God.

God was forming Israel as a nation under his covenant. Shortly before, a man had blasphemed the name of God during a quarrel, and he was held under guard while waiting for God's decision. The same law applied to the foreigner and to the native-born. This penalty was part of the law given to Israel at that time, and Christians understand it in different ways today.

Today we learn to treat the name of God with respect and to speak of him with reverence. We also see that justice must be the same for everyone, without favoritism.
exp.16:9:
This verse forbids eating blood. The rule applied to the Israelites and also to the foreigners who lived among them. God says that he will "set his face against" anyone who does it, meaning he will oppose that person seriously. To "cut him off from among his people" means that he would be separated from the community; scholars debate whether this implied death, exile, or some other consequence.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct Israel. In context, the sacrifices were to be brought to the tabernacle and not to other places. God explains that life is in the blood and that he gave it to make atonement upon the altar. Blood was a sacred sign of life and of forgiveness.

For today: this text invites us to respect life as a gift from God. Christians remember that Christ shed his blood for us, and that leads us to live with gratitude and reverence.
exp.12:39:
It says that if a man loses his hair and becomes bald, this does not make him unclean. The word used here means being left without hair, and the word for "clean" means that, according to the law, he could live and worship normally among the people.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives them instructions for priests to examine skin diseases. These rules protected the health and order of the community. The word for "leprosy" here may have covered several skin conditions, not only the disease we call that today. This verse makes clear that ordinary baldness was not a reason to set anyone apart.

Today we can learn not to judge people by their appearance or by normal changes in the body. God cares for every person, and we too should discern with wisdom and treat everyone with respect and compassion.
exp.23:14:
This verse says that if anyone curses their God, they will have to bear the consequences of their sin. The word "curses" means speaking with contempt or irreverence against God. The phrase "consequences of his sin" means that the person will be held responsible for their guilt and will receive the punishment.

God speaks to Moses so that he can explain to the people what to do with a man who had blasphemed the name of God in the middle of the camp. Israel lived under a law given to that people at that time, and the name of God was considered holy. The law applied equally to the foreigner and to the Israelite.

For today: God deserves respect in our words. We can take care how we speak of Him, avoiding irreverent jokes or mockery, and remember that Jesus teaches us to treat His name with love and reverence.
exp.18:35:
God commands the use of honest scales, weights, and measures. The "ephah" was a measure for dry goods, such as grain, and the "hin" was a measure for liquids. Notice that the verse says "you shall maintain," which means these honest measures are to be kept up as a regular practice. At the end, God reminds them who he is: the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.

Here God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel. This chapter teaches how to live as a people set apart for Him. Just before this, God asks them to love the foreigner and not to cheat in judgments or in measures. The reference to Egypt reminds them that God rescued them from oppression, so they were not to oppress others.

For today: be honest in every financial dealing, whether selling, charging, paying, or working. Do not cheat on price, hours, or quality. If God has shown you mercy, treat others with justice.
exp.21:21:
This verse lists animals that could not be presented to God: any that were blind, injured, or maimed, and any with a running sore, a festering rash, or a scab. The animal had to be whole and healthy. The part of the animal burned on the altar as a food offering was also not to be made from any of these.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Aaron, his sons, and all of Israel. The animals had to be without defect. This taught that coming near to God is a serious matter and that He deserves the best, not what is left over. Many also see here a sign of the holiness of God.

Today we might ask ourselves what we give to God: our best time, attention, and resources, or only what we have to spare? We can give Him the first and the best, with gratitude and sincerity, trusting that Christ brings us near to Him.
exp.19:4:
God himself says he will set his face against the man who gave his children to Molech, and against his family as well. The words "cut him off from among his people" mean removing him from the community; scholars debate whether this includes death, expulsion, or judgment by God. The phrase "all who follow him in prostituting themselves" speaks of being unfaithful to God, not only of sexual sin.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, as the people were preparing to live in Canaan. Molech was a pagan god to whom children were offered. God warns that if the community looked the other way, they too would be held responsible. He wanted a holy and faithful people.

Today we can ask ourselves what things have come to take the place of God in our lives. He also calls us not to stay silent in the face of injustice against the weak, but to defend them with love, prayer, and concrete actions.
exp.13:44:
If the mark appears again in the house after it has been repaired, the house must be torn down completely. Its stones, its timbers, and all its plaster are pulled apart. (The "plaster" here is the mud or plaster coating the walls.) Everything is carried outside the city to an unclean place, that is, a set-apart spot where what was impure was thrown away.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for when Israel lives in Canaan. The "gnawing leprosy" in a house seems to be harmful mold or fungus, although scholars do not fully agree on exactly what it was. The priest examined it carefully, and repair was tried first. The measure protected the health and purity of the people.

For today: there are things that should first be corrected, but if the damage keeps growing, we must be brave and cut it off at the root. This applies to habits or relationships that destroy.
exp.18:13:
This verse forbids two kinds of mistreatment of people with disabilities. To curse the deaf is to speak evil of them or wish them harm, knowing they cannot hear it or defend themselves. To place a stumbling block before the blind is to put an obstacle in their path so that they fall. "But you shall fear your God" means that one must live with respect and reverence toward God. "I am the LORD" is God's signature on the command.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. In this chapter he gives laws for living as a holy people: not stealing, not lying, paying the hired worker, and judging with justice. All of them seek to protect the vulnerable. God sees what people do even when the victim does not notice it.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I treat well those who cannot defend themselves? That includes not mocking anyone, not speaking ill of them behind their backs, and removing barriers that make life harder for others. Obeying God shows in how we care for the weak.
exp.12:55:
If the priest examines the garment after it has been washed and finds that the mildew has faded, he must cut the contaminated section out of the fabric, leather, weave, or knit.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives rules for the people of Israel. These instructions about mildew or decay in cloth and leather helped protect the health and ritual purity of the community. Here the mildew has faded, so the whole garment was not burned, only the affected section. Scholars debate the exact kind of mildew.

For today: God attends to details and does not exaggerate. If something in our life has been damaged, let us ask him for help to remove what harms it with wisdom and gentleness, without destroying everything that is still worth keeping.
exp.24:28:
If a man sold a house inside a walled city, he had the right to buy it back, but only within one full year after the sale. If the house was not bought back during that year, the sale became permanent.

God spoke to Moses on behalf of the people of Israel, who would soon live in the promised land. Land in the countryside belonged to God and was to return to the families in the Jubilee year. Houses inside walled cities followed a different rule: if they were not bought back within a year, they stayed with the buyer. Scholars often see here a distinction between the family inheritance of land and urban dwellings.

For today: God is concerned with how we handle our possessions and our debts. Before selling or committing something important, think calmly, because some decisions have deadlines that cannot be undone.
exp.26:25:
This verse says that the firstborn male of a cow, a sheep, or a goat already belongs to the LORD by right of birth. For that reason, no one can consecrate it, that is, set it apart as a voluntary offering, because it was already the LORD's. The word "But" at the start of the verse marks the contrast with the previous rule, and "ox" here refers to the cattle.

God speaks to Moses to give Israel laws about vows and offerings to the LORD. Earlier, God had commanded that the firstborn be given to him as a reminder that he delivered them from Egypt (Exodus 13). No one could offer as a gift something that already belonged to God.

For today: God deserves the first and not what is left over. We can ask ourselves whether we give him priority in our time, money, and attention, instead of thinking we are doing him a favor.
exp.8:15:
He presented the burnt offering, that is, an animal that was burned whole on the altar as a complete surrender to God. The phrase "according to the ordinance" means that he carried it out in the way God had set down, following the instructions God had given. Here "presented" and "offered" describe the same act of carrying it out.

This takes place on the eighth day of the consecration of the priests. The text is a narrative, and Moses had passed on what God commanded. Aaron had already offered for his own sin and now offers for the people. All of this prepares for the glory of the Lord to be revealed to Israel.

For today: God values that we seek him with sincerity and obedience, not with improvisations. Today we can ask ourselves whether we are listening to his Word and living according to it, trusting that Christ, our high priest, brings us near to God.
exp.2:10:
This verse says the priest will burn on the altar the fatty parts of the animal offered as a peace offering. The word "food" in the verse means nourishment, and "a food offering to the LORD" is an offering burned on the altar. So that portion was presented to God as food, a way of speaking that expresses that it belonged to Him.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel. These instructions explain how to offer the peace offering, which was connected with thankfulness and fellowship with God. The best part, the fat, was set apart for Him. Scholars explain the exact symbolism of each part in several ways, so it is wise to be careful.

Today we can learn to give God our best, not the leftovers. One practical way is to begin the day by thanking Him and dedicating the first moment to Him, before our other tasks.
exp.23:2:
This verse says that Aaron was to tend the lamps of the lampstand in the tent of meeting. "Tend" means to prepare, arrange, and keep in good condition. He was to do this outside the veil that hung before the Testimony, from evening until morning, continually before the LORD. A permanent statute is a law meant to last for the generations to come.

Here God speaks, giving Moses instructions for the people of Israel. First he asks for pure olive oil so that the light would never go out. It was part of the order of worship: the priest served continually in the place where God dwelt among his people. Scholars see in the light a symbol of God's presence, although the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: God values faithfulness in what is simple and constant. Even when no one sees it, caring for your prayer life and your service each day is important to him.
exp.10:12:
God told Israel that certain birds were not to be eaten. They are called "detestable," a word that here means something the people were to reject and avoid as food. The verse names the eagle, the bearded vulture, and the black vulture, birds of prey or ones that feed on flesh and carrion. The exact identities of some Hebrew bird names are uncertain, and modern translations differ in how they render them.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel, newly established as the people of the covenant. These laws about clean and unclean animals taught them to live set apart for God, according to 11:44-45: "be holy, for I am holy." Scholars offer different reasons for the list: symbolism, health, or identity. The text emphasizes holiness.

For today: Christ declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), so this is not a matter of diet rules. But the call to holiness remains: ask yourself which everyday habits help you live as someone who belongs to God.
exp.24:34:
If a fellow Israelite falls into hardship and cannot support himself, do not turn him away. You are to help him, just as you would help a foreigner or a stranger, so that he can keep living among you. "Falls into hardship" means he has become destitute; "cannot support himself" means he can no longer provide for his own needs; "help him" means you take care of him and keep him going. He is to remain among you as a welcomed guest, not pushed out.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. The verses before this one protected the land of the Levites. Now the law protects the poor, so that financial misfortune does not leave a person without a home or dignity. The verses that follow forbid charging him interest. Many understand the phrase "as a stranger" here to mean showing him hospitality, without humiliating him as if he were a slave.

For today: if someone close to you is going through difficulties, help them with generosity and respect, without taking advantage of their need or making them feel lesser.
exp.2:9:
This verse continues the instructions for the peace offering. It calls for setting apart both kidneys, the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver, which is to be removed along with the kidneys. The loins are the lower sides of the animal's body. The lobe of the liver is the part to be taken away together with the kidneys.

God speaks to Moses and gives the people of Israel rules on how to offer this sacrifice. It was an offering of fellowship and thanksgiving. The fat, considered the best part, was burned on the altar and belonged to the LORD. Scholars agree that it showed surrender and honor toward God, though not all explain every detail in the same way.

For today: let us give God our best, not our leftovers. We can do this with our time, attention, and gratitude, thanking Him sincerely for the peace we have with Him in Christ.
exp.8:13:
Here it is told that Aaron washed the entrails and the legs of the burnt offering with water. Then he burned them on the altar, atop the burnt offering that he had already placed there. The phrase "burned them" simply means that he burned them.

Moses had already explained these instructions on God's behalf. Now, on the eighth day, Aaron begins his service as priest. First he offers for his own sin and then for the people. The burnt offering was burned whole, and it expressed complete surrender to God. Washing the parts showed that the offering was to be presented with care and cleanness.

God attends to the details when we worship him. Today we do not offer animals, but we can give God our whole heart, including what is hidden, and not only what others see. Ask him to cleanse you inwardly and live with sincerity.
exp.5:7:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that the LORD spoke again to Moses. The phrase "then the LORD said to Moses" signals that God is continuing his speech and about to begin a new section of instructions.

The one speaking is the LORD, and Moses is the one who receives the message to pass on to the people. In the verses before this, God explained how atonement was made for certain wrongs. Now he moves on to instructions for the priests, beginning with the law of the burnt offering, the offering that was burned whole on the altar. What follows is directed to Aaron and his sons.

God does not leave his people guessing how to draw near to him. He speaks with clarity and gives specific directions. Today we can set aside time to listen to his voice in the Bible, with the attitude of someone who wants to obey and not merely to be informed.
exp.12:49:
This verse says that the priest is to examine the mildew on a cloth or a leather object closely. Then he must isolate the contaminated fabric and keep it set apart for seven days. Here the mildew is a stain or suspicious sign, and the word for leprosy refers to a condition that made something unclean, not necessarily the disease we know today.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives them instructions for the people of Israel. The priest did not act in a hurry: he observed, waited, and looked again. These laws cared for the health and purity of the people. Scholars explain in various ways exactly what this mildew was, perhaps some kind of mold or fungus.

For today: when faced with a problem that seems harmful, do not react in haste. Pray, observe with patience, and seek wisdom before deciding.
exp.10:41:
Do not eat any creature that moves along the ground, whether it crawls on its belly or walks on four or more feet; these creatures are detestable. This verse forbids eating any small creature that moves close to the ground, including those that crawl on their bellies, such as snakes or worms, and those that walk on four or more feet, such as certain insects or crawling creatures. "Detestable" means something that is loathsome, which God asks the people to keep far away. The phrase "creatures that move along the ground" includes many small animals that crawl.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel, which had just come out of Egypt. These rules about food and purity helped the people live differently and remember that they belonged to God. Scholars explain the exact reason for each rule in various ways; the text especially emphasizes holiness.

For today: God cares about the details of everyday life. We can ask ourselves which habits, however small they may seem, draw us away from living for Him, and give them to Him with simplicity.
exp.10:29:
This verse follows a list of small animals that crawl along the ground, which God declares "unclean," meaning not fit for the people to use. "Unclean" here does not mean sinful, but ceremonially impure. The exact identities of these animals are uncertain in Hebrew, and the names given in English differ from one translation to another. Your verse names the gecko, the monitor lizard, the common lizard, the skink, and the chameleon, which are all kinds of lizards.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, and through them to Israel. These laws taught the people to live set apart for God, reminding them in everyday life that He is holy.

Today, Christians do not follow these food rules, because Jesus cleanses us from within. But we can learn that God cares about everything in our daily lives. Today you might ask yourself: does the way I speak, work, and rest show that I belong to God?
exp.12:33:
After seven more days, the priest examines the scaly outbreak again. It was a skin condition, possibly affecting the beard or the scalp. If it has not spread and does not appear to be deeper than the skin, the priest pronounces the person clean. The phrase "has not spread on the skin" means the outbreak has not grown wider, and "does not appear to be deeper than the skin" means it does not seem to sink beneath the surface. The priest declares the person ceremonially clean. Then the person washes his clothes and is clean.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, giving laws for Israel. These rules protected the health of the community and cared for its ceremonial purity. The priest did not heal; he examined patiently and declared the person's condition. It is not known with certainty exactly what disease this was.

For today: God values patient and fair examination, not hasty judgment. We can give time and grace to others, and encourage someone who is recovering to return to the community.
exp.25:14:
This verse describes a people who turn away from God completely. The phrase "reject My statutes" means treating God's laws and rules as worthless, and "despise My ordinances" means looking down on His decisions and the instructions He has set. To "neglect to carry out all My commandments" is to let His commands go undone, and "break My covenant" means treating the agreement with God as if it meant nothing. It is not just a stumble, but a rejection that comes from the heart.

God Himself speaks, through Moses, to Israel in the wilderness. He had just promised blessings if they obeyed, and the rescue from Egypt was the reason to trust Him. Now He solemnly warns what would happen if they broke the covenant. The consequences that follow are warnings, given clearly so that they would return to Him.

For today: examine whether obeying God feels to you like a burden or like a response of gratitude for what He has already done. Ask Him for a heart that loves His word, not just one that keeps it out of obligation.
exp.12:38:
This verse says that the priest must examine the person carefully. If the spots on the skin are dull white, it is not a serious illness. It is a harmless rash that has broken out on the skin, and the person is declared clean.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. In that time, the priest had to tell apart the skin conditions that required separating someone from the camp from those that did not. Here it is made clear that not every mark is grounds for exclusion. Scholars are not sure which exact diseases the text describes, although it is often translated as "leprosy."

For today: before judging someone by an appearance or a mistake, look calmly and seek the truth. Mercy begins with a fair examination, without condemning in a hurry.
exp.16:6:
This verse says that the Israelites were no longer to offer sacrifices to the goat demons, the beings they had given themselves to as someone who is unfaithful to a spouse. "Prostituted themselves" here is an image of spiritual unfaithfulness. The Hebrew word translated "goat demons" refers to beings with the form of goats, a kind of idol of the field; scholars debate its exact meaning. This rule was to be a permanent statute: a regulation meant to last for all generations to come.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Aaron, his sons, and all Israel. The Israelites were sacrificing animals in the open field, and probably some were doing so for false gods. God commands that every sacrifice be brought to the entrance of the tabernacle, where the priest presented it to the LORD alone.

For today: our hearts can give themselves to other "gods," such as money, fame, or pleasure. Let us make God our first and only loyalty, and seek him sincerely and openly, not in secret.
exp.7:2:
God tells Moses to call the whole people of Israel to come together at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, the place where God met with them. The verse points out that the word for "assemble" is spelled differently in older manuscripts, and that "whole congregation" means the entire community. The sacred tent that held the tablets of the law, the sign of God's covenant with his people, is also described.

The Lord speaks and gives Moses instructions. He is going to set apart Aaron and his sons as priests, with garments, oil, and sacrifices. God wants the entire people to witness this. In this way, the priestly service would not be a private matter, but something known and recognized by everyone.

For today: what God does in the midst of his people has value when it is lived out with openness and in community. We can seek to live our faith alongside other believers, to be accountable with humility, and to support with prayer those who serve in our church.
exp.19:15:
If a woman comes near an animal in order to have sexual relations with it, the verse says both she and the animal must be put to death. The phrase about their blood being upon them means that they are held responsible for their own deaths.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, who were about to enter Canaan. These laws were part of the holiness code, which aimed to set Israel apart from the practices of the neighboring peoples. Here the death penalty was a civil rule for Israel as a nation at that time. The animal is included in the sentence, and scholars explain that detail in different ways.

For today: God cares for the dignity of sexual life and calls his people to live differently. Ask him to help you honor your body and to keep your thoughts and habits pure, trusting in his forgiveness in Christ.
exp.6:10:
This verse opens a new section with instructions for the peace offering, also called the fellowship offering. It was an offering that the people presented to the LORD, and its meaning is tied to the idea of peace and well-being. The phrase "that one may present to the LORD" shows that the whole offering was directed to God.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses must pass these rules on to Israel. The book had already explained other offerings, and now it details this one, in which part of what was offered was shared in a meal before God. The verses that follow speak of cakes and loaves, and of thanksgiving.

Today we can learn that God desires a close relationship with us, not only duties. One practical way is to thank God aloud each day for something specific, and to share a meal with someone, remembering his goodness.
exp.25:30:
God says that if his people turn away from him, he will reduce their cities to rubble and lay waste their sanctuaries. Sanctuaries are places of worship. The phrase "refuse to smell the pleasing aroma of your sacrifices" means that God will not accept the offerings they bring, even though those offerings were meant to be a pleasing aroma to him.

The Lord speaks through Moses at the end of Leviticus. Before Israel enters the promised land, it receives blessings for obedience and warnings against rebellion. These words are part of the warnings. The sanctuaries mentioned here seem to be the places of worship the people had built for idols, and even their religion becomes empty when the heart is far from God.

Today we can remember that God is not looking only for ceremonies, but for an obedient heart. Before going to church, or before praying, it is good to ask ourselves: is there something I need to correct or confess before God?
exp.11:3:
After the first seven days of uncleanness following the birth of a son, the woman was to remain in purification for thirty-three more days while her bleeding continued. During that time she could not touch anything sacred or go into the sanctuary. The word "purification" means cleansing or making clean, and the sanctuary was the place of worship.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct Israel. This law belongs to the ritual system of the covenant with Israel. The uncleanness here was not sin, but a ceremonial condition connected with blood and birth. Scholars explain it in different ways, and there is no single certain answer about its exact reason.

For today: God cares for seasons of recovery and teaches us to draw near to Him with reverence. We can support new mothers by giving them rest, food, and companionship, without haste or demands.
exp.18:25:
This verse says that the people were not to eat meat that still had blood in it, nor to practice divination or sorcery. Those who practice divination are people who believe they can read the future in signs, such as the flight of birds or certain strange events. To seek knowledge of what is hidden by means that do not come from God is what this verse forbids.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, in the law of holiness. He wants his people to live differently from the neighboring nations, whose religious practices included divination. Blood was treated with respect, for it represented life (Leviticus 17:11). Some scholars also see here a rejection of certain pagan rites involving blood, although the text does not make this clear.

For today: when you are afraid of the future, instead of looking for horoscopes or superstitions, bring your doubts to God in prayer and trust that He watches over your path.
exp.13:54:
This verse is part of a list that sums up the laws about "leprosy." Here it refers to mildew in clothing or in a house, that is, the mold or fungus that could damage fabric and walls. The original word is broader than what we today call leprosy, and it can cover various conditions affecting the skin and also objects.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, and they teach the people. These rules helped the priest decide what was clean and what was unclean. In this way Israel cared for health, order, and the life of a community set apart for God. A long section on this subject closes here.

For today: God is concerned with everything that forms part of our lives, even the home and the everyday. We can ask ourselves whether there is anything hidden at home or in the heart that is slowly decaying, and bring it honestly to God, trusting in his forgiveness and his cleansing.
exp.17:7:
This verse forbids sexual relations with one's father's wife. The phrase "uncover the nakedness" is an old expression for intimate relations, but your verse states the prohibition directly. It refers to a stepmother, or another of the father's wives, not to one's own mother, whom the previous verse addresses. It says that such a relationship would dishonor your father, because this woman belongs to his marriage and is bound to him.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, before they enter Canaan. He gives them clear limits on family relationships, so that they would live differently from the peoples around them. The words "I am the LORD" are repeated to remind them who stands behind these commands.

For today: guard the holiness of your family. Respect the bonds and the boundaries, and avoid anything that could harm trust and honor between parents and children.
exp.13:40:
This verse says the priest will have the entire inside wall of the affected house scraped completely. The verse's word for this is "scraped," which means removing the layer of plaster that covers the walls. The scraped plaster is not left in the house. It is dumped outside the city, into an unclean place, that is, a set-apart spot marked for what is impure.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, and these laws were for Israel when they would enter the land of Canaan. The matter concerned a plague in the houses, which was probably mold or fungus, though the text gives no further details. The priest would inspect, and the measures came in steps to protect the community and keep the order and holiness of the people.

For today: let us not allow harm to grow hidden. If something damaging gets into your home or your heart, such as resentment or a bad habit, remove it at the root and with seriousness, and ask God for help.
exp.9:7:
This verse is very short: it says that God spoke directly to Aaron. It is the introduction to a command that comes right after. The name "LORD" is God's name.

It comes just after the death of Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's sons, who offered a fire that God had not commanded them to offer. Aaron and his other sons were to continue their service without public mourning. It is notable that here God speaks to Aaron himself, not through Moses, which is unusual. Interpreters do not agree on the exact reason, but it shows that God did not abandon Aaron in his grief.

For today: God speaks to us even in moments of pain and confusion. We can open the Bible and pray with confidence that he wants to guide and sustain us, not only correct us.
exp.24:41:
This verse says that the Israelites could not be sold as slaves, because they belong to God. "Servants" here refers to those whom God brought out of Egypt. The phrase "they are not to be sold as slaves" means they may not be sold the way a common slave is sold.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. If a brother became poor and went to work for another, he was to be treated as a hired worker, not as a slave, and he was set free in the year of jubilee. The memory of the deliverance from Egypt is the reason: God is their owner, not another man. The rules about servants from other nations, which follow later, reflect the customs of that time.

For today: treat the people who depend on you, such as employees or needy family members, with dignity and respect, remembering that God loves them and gives them worth.
exp.25:32:
This verse says that God would scatter his people among the nations if they were unfaithful to him. The phrase "draw out a sword" means pulling the sword from its sheath to attack, and it signifies that war would pursue them. Words like "desolate" and "laid waste" mean torn apart and destroyed, and empty and abandoned. The land and the cities would be left without people.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, at the end of the blessings and warnings of the covenant at Sinai. He had promised blessing if they obeyed him, and this is one of the consequences if they abandoned him. The context that follows explains that the land would rest during the sabbaths the people had not kept.

For today: God is serious, but his warnings aim to bring us back to him. Ask yourself today what area of your life you have neglected before God, and take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.14:24:
If a woman has a discharge of blood for many days at a time other than her regular period, or if the bleeding continues beyond her period, she is unclean for as long as the unclean discharge lasts, just as she is during the days of her period. Bleeding is what the discharge is, and her regular period is what "other than" refers to. Unclean does not mean sinful; it means ritually unfit to come near the sanctuary.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for Israel. They were rules of ritual purity that taught that God is holy and that his presence among the people had to be treated with reverence. Scholars explain the symbolism of these laws in several ways, and there is no single certain answer.

For today: God cares about everything we go through, even the most personal things, and he invites us to draw near to him with reverence. In Christ, he also cleanses us and receives us with compassion (Mark 5:25-34).
exp.13:53:
This verse closes the first part of the instructions about skin diseases. It says: "This is the law for any infectious skin disease, for a scaly outbreak." The word "leprosy" in the Bible refers to several skin diseases, and it can also describe mold in clothing and houses. It is not always the leprosy we know today. A "scaly outbreak" seems to be a condition of the skin or scalp, and an "infectious skin disease" is a sickness that could spread and affect the body.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to guide Israel. These rules helped the priest examine, separate, and declare a person or thing clean. The material just before this verse describes the rite of cleansing the house with the bird, which showed cleanness and forgiveness. Scholars explain the exact meaning of these symbols in various ways.

For today: when something harms you, inside or out, do not ignore it or hide it. Seek wise help and pray, trusting that God cares for you and restores.
exp.13:29:
This verse says that the person being purified must offer one of the turtledoves or one of the young pigeons, whichever he can afford. "Young pigeons" are the young of the dove, and "whichever he can afford" means the one he is able to pay for.

God speaks through Moses to Israel. This passage deals with the purification of someone healed of a skin disease, which the Bible calls "leprosy" (it is not known with certainty whether it was the same disease that carries that name today). The poorest could present birds in place of lambs. In this way no one was shut out from returning to the community and to the presence of God for lack of money.

For today: God receives us as we are and does not ask more than we can give. Draw near to Him with simplicity, and do not let shame or scarcity hold you back.
exp.0:1:
God tells Moses to speak to the Israelites. When any of them wants to bring an offering to the Lord, they may bring an animal from the herd or the flock: a cow or ox from the cattle, or a sheep or goat from the flock. The word translated "bring" here means to bring something near to God.

God speaks from the tabernacle, the tent where his presence dwelt among Israel. It had only recently been built, and now God teaches the people how to draw near to him. This offering was voluntary, as the next verse shows, and it was a means of being accepted and forgiven.

God does not want us to seek him in just any way, but with sincerity and devotion. Today we do not bring animals, because Christians believe that Christ is the complete sacrifice. But we can still offer him something precious: our time, our affection, and our obedience, given with a willing heart.
exp.10:8:
This verse says that the people of Israel could eat the water animals that had fins and scales, whether they lived in the seas or in the streams. The phrase "you may eat" gives them permission, and "anything with fins and scales" describes the creatures that were allowed.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to give laws to the people he had brought out of Egypt. These rules separated the clean from the unclean and marked Israel as a people set apart for God. Scholars do not fully agree on the reasons behind each rule: some see a symbol of holiness, others a teaching about order and obedience.

Today, Christians do not live under these food rules, but we can still learn to obey God with attention, even in everyday life. We can ask ourselves: do I live each day, even in small things, as someone who belongs to God?
exp.17:16:
This verse forbids having sexual relations with a woman and also with her daughter, or with her granddaughter, whether through her son or through her daughter. The Berean Standard Bible states this plainly: sexual relations with both a woman and her daughter are not allowed, and neither is marrying a granddaughter and having relations with her. The text calls them close relatives and describes such conduct as depraved.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Israel. Before entering Canaan, the people were to live differently from Egypt and from the Canaanites. These laws protected families from abuse and confusion in their relationships. Some scholars see here a general principle: close kinship, even through marriage, sets sacred limits.

For today: care for your family as a safe place. Respect the boundaries in your relationships and do not use your position or closeness to take advantage of anyone. Ask God for purity and respect toward everyone.
exp.12:18:
If a white swelling or a reddish-white spot appears in the place where a boil once was, the person must present themselves to the priest. The verse describes a skin change that comes up where an earlier boil (an inflammation or abscess of the skin) had been, and the priest is the one who must examine it.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. At that time there was no medical profession as there is today, and the priest had the task of examining the skin and deciding whether someone could live among the others or had to stay apart for a time. The texts speak of a skin disease that is traditionally called "leprosy," but scholars are not sure it is exactly the disease we call that today; it may have included several skin conditions.

For today: when something in your life seems to be wrong, do not hide it or ignore it. Seek help in time, whether medical, spiritual, or from someone you trust.
exp.19:14:
This verse says that if someone had sexual relations with an animal, that person was to be put to death, and the animal was also to be killed. The phrase "lies carnally with an animal" means to have sexual relations with an animal. The word "animal" in this verse is the same one used for any living creature, and the command "you are also to kill the animal" is addressed to the whole people.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, shortly before they enter the land of Canaan. These laws belong to what is often called the Holiness Code. They aimed to set Israel apart from the practices of the neighboring nations and to protect the dignity of life and of the family. For that nation at that time, they were civil laws. Scholars explain in several ways why the animal was killed; one idea is that it was considered defiled by the act.

For today: Christians do not live under those civil penalties, but we do learn that God cares for what is healthy and pure. We can ask him for help to live with respect and self-control.
exp.10:5:
This verse says the rabbit was not to be eaten. It has one trait that seems to qualify it, because it chews the cud, that is, it brings its food back up to chew again. But it lacks the other, since it does not have a divided hoof. Because it meets only one of the two signs, it was considered unclean, meaning not fit to eat or for the use of God's people. The verse's wording "it is unclean for you" means "you shall count it as unclean."

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel, the people He had just freed from Egypt. These laws helped distinguish the clean from the unclean and to live as a people set apart for Him. Scholars do not fully agree on the reasons for each prohibition, and about the rabbit there is debate over how to understand chewing the cud.

For today: God cares about the details of everyday life. We can ask ourselves which daily habits, such as what we look at, say, or choose, reflect that we belong to Him, and ask Him for help to live in grateful obedience in Christ.
exp.15:30:
This verse says that the Day of Atonement is a Sabbath of complete rest, a day of solemn stillness set apart for the Lord. The phrase "that you may humble yourselves" points to humbling oneself and setting aside self-indulgence, and many understand that it included fasting. And "a permanent statute" means a rule that was to be observed every year.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct Israel. On this day, the tenth of the seventh month, the priest offered sacrifices to cleanse the people and the sanctuary. The people did not work, because the cleansing came from God and not from their efforts.

For today: set aside time to stop, honestly acknowledge your failures, and rest in God's forgiveness. Christians see in Jesus the fulfillment of this day (Hebrews 9:11-14), so we can come to Him with humility and confidence.
exp.17:11:
This verse forbids having sexual relations with your father's sister, that is, your aunt on your father's side. The phrase "uncover the nakedness" is an old expression for intimate relations, but your verse states the prohibition directly. The verse gives the reason: she is your father's close relative.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct the people of Israel. Before they enter Canaan, God gives them rules for living differently from Egypt and the Canaanite nations. This list protects the family, orders family bonds, and cares for the most vulnerable within the household.

For today: treat family relationships with respect and purity. Let your home be a safe place where no one is used or abused. If you know someone who is suffering family abuse, listen to them, believe them, and help them seek protection.
exp.17:20:
This verse says that the people of Israel were not to give their children to be sacrificed to Molech, a god worshiped by the neighboring peoples. To "sacrifice" here means to offer something to a god, and the verse makes clear that this is forbidden. To "profane" means to dishonor or defile. Doing this would dishonor the name of God, and the verse ends with God declaring: "I am the LORD."

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, who were about to enter Canaan. He gives them laws so that they would live differently from the nations around them. Scholars debate exactly what this sacrifice involved, but it is clear that God rejects it completely. The verses nearby speak of purity and faithfulness.

Today, although Molech is no longer worshiped, we can ask ourselves what things we place above God, such as success or money, and whether we are sacrificing the well-being of our children for them. Caring for children honors God.
exp.12:16:
The priest is to examine him again. If the infection has turned white, the priest pronounces the infected person clean, and then he is clean. The word "infection" in this verse refers to a sore or lesion on the skin. "Unclean" means not fit to take part in worship, and "pronounced clean" means declared healthy.
