God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priest did not heal anyone. He examined and declared. These rules protected the health and purity of the community, and they also cared for the sick person, since they opened the way for him to return to his family and to worship.

For today: God delights in restoring, not only in pointing out what is wrong. We can reflect that heart by receiving with joy and without reproach someone who has risen from a fall, and by trusting that God also declares us clean when we come to him.
exp.19:12:
This verse forbids a man from lying with another man as with a woman, and it calls this an "abomination," a strong word meaning something detestable to God. The penalty was death for both, and "their blood is upon them" means that they themselves bore the responsibility.

God speaks to Moses to give laws to the people of Israel, newly freed from Egypt. Chapter 20 gathers punishments for sexual sins and for idolatry, so that Israel would be a people set apart, distinct from the neighboring nations. These were civil laws for that nation in particular. Christians interpret them in different ways as to how they apply today.

For today: this passage reminds us that God takes holiness in intimate life seriously. At the same time, Jesus calls us to treat every person with truth and with love, without mockery or contempt.
exp.16:0:
This verse is only an introduction. It says that the LORD spoke to Moses. The phrase "Then the LORD said to Moses" is repeated many times in Leviticus and announces that what follows is not Moses' own idea but the word of God.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the messenger who must pass his instructions on to Aaron, to his sons, and to the whole people. What comes next deals with where and how the animals were to be brought for sacrifice. Many scholars see here a call for the people to worship the LORD alone and in the way He indicated, although the details are interpreted in several ways.

For today: before deciding how to live and worship, we can pause to listen to what God says in his Word. Reading the Bible with attention and humility helps us follow his voice and not only our own customs.
exp.0:4:
It says that the person bringing the offering slaughtered the young bull before the LORD. Then Aaron's sons, the priests, presented the blood and splattered it on all sides of the altar, which stood at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. To "slaughter" here means to cut the throat, and the Tent of Meeting is the tent where God met with his people.

God speaks to Moses from the tent and gives him instructions for the burnt offering, a voluntary offering that was burned whole. The person laid his hand on the animal, and the animal represented him before God. The blood, a symbol of life, showed that drawing near to God has a serious cost. The priests served as mediators.

For today: this passage invites us to take sin seriously and to value that God allows us to draw near to him. Christians see in Jesus the complete sacrifice that reconciles us to God. We can respond with gratitude, giving him our lives sincerely and willingly.
exp.20:12:
The verse says that the high priest had to marry a woman who was a virgin. In the Berean Standard Bible, the wording is "The woman he marries must be a virgin." This means she had not had sexual relations before the marriage. It is a very specific rule for one office in Israel.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions about the priests. The verse before this one speaks of the priest anointed with oil, that is, set apart for God. For this reason he had stricter rules than the rest of the people, and the verses that follow exclude widows, divorced women, and other women. Scholars understand the purpose in several ways: ritual purity, a clear lineage, or a symbol of total devotion to God. The text does not fully explain it.

Today we are not under this law, but we can learn that serving God calls for taking our most important decisions, such as marriage, seriously, seeking that they honor God.
exp.24:38:
It says that if a fellow Israelite becomes destitute and, out of necessity, sells himself to another Israelite, the other must not force him into slave labor. "Becoming destitute" means falling into deep poverty, and "selling himself" means offering his labor in exchange for help to survive.

God speaks to Moses to give laws to the people of Israel. He has just said not to take advantage of the poor through interest-bearing loans. He reminds them that he brought them out of Egypt, where they had been slaves. Therefore, among countrymen, poverty was not to become a source of humiliation or of control over another person.

For today: if someone close to you goes through hardship, help them with respect and without taking advantage of their situation. Treat them as a brother, not as someone beneath you, and seek to help them recover their dignity and stability.
exp.20:6:
This verse says that priests were not to marry a woman defiled by prostitution, meaning a woman who lived in sexual immorality, nor a woman who had been divorced or put away by her husband. The reason is that the priest is holy, that is, set apart for his God.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to the priests, the sons of Aaron. They presented the offerings and the bread of their God, so their daily lives were to show that they belonged to God. These rules were stricter for them than for the rest of the people. Some scholars see here a protection of the sacred service and of the priesthood's reputation; the Bible does not explain every detail of the reason.

For today: if we serve God in any way, our most important decisions, such as whom we form relationships with and how we live, should seek to honor him. Ask him for wisdom before deciding.
exp.3:18:
It says the priest will take all the fat from the sacrificed animal and burn it on the altar. "Fat" here refers to the fat that covers the inner organs. The phrase "burn it" means he will burn it up.

God speaks to Moses about what to do when the whole congregation of Israel sins without realizing it. The elders lay their hands on a young bull, and the priest performs the ritual with the blood. The fat was considered the best part, and it was given to God. Scholars understand this as a way of offering him the best, although the text gives no further explanation.

When we fail, God does not want a half-hearted apology. He wants a sincere heart that gives him everything. Today we can come to Him with confidence, because Christ offered his life for us, and we can ask for forgiveness without hiding anything.
exp.19:17:
This verse forbids a man from having sexual relations with a woman during her menstrual period. A woman who is menstruating is the one meant here. The phrase "lies with a menstruating woman and has sexual relations with her" describes the act, and "exposed the source of her flow" refers to the bleeding. If both did this, they would both "be cut off from among their people," that is, set apart from the community. Scholars debate whether this meant expulsion, divine punishment, or something else.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct Israel. These laws aimed to form a holy people, distinct from the neighboring nations, and they showed that life, blood, and intimacy belong to God. This rule appears in a list of laws about sexual morality.

Today, what remains in force is the principle: marital intimacy is to be lived out with respect, care, and obedience to God. Ask yourself how you honor your spouse in everyday life.
exp.7:27:
Moses receives the offerings from the hands of Aaron and his sons, the portions they had lifted up before the LORD. Then he burns them on the altar, on top of the burnt offering. The phrase "ordination offering" refers to the offerings used in the ceremony of setting these men apart as priests. The words "a pleasing aroma" express that the offering was pleasing to the LORD. A "food offering" is one that was burned in the fire of the altar.

The book of Leviticus tells how God commanded that Aaron and his sons be set apart as priests. Moses acts as the one who directs the ceremony, following what the LORD had ordered. Here the priests place everything into Moses' hands, and he presents it to the LORD in the fire. Scholars explain the symbolism of each detail in various ways, but all of them see a service given fully to God.

For today: serving God begins by giving Him everything we are. Today you could present to Him in prayer your work, your time, and your decisions, so that what you do may be pleasing to Him.
exp.12:15:
This verse says that if the raw flesh, which before was reddened and sick, changes and turns white, the person must go back to the priest. The words "changes and turns white" match the verse's own wording, and "raw flesh" refers to skin with an open sore or red, exposed flesh.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The laws about the skin disease (a term that probably included several skin conditions, not only what is today called leprosy) protected the health and order of the community. The priest examined the person and declared whether they were clean or not, and the next verse shows that the person could be declared clean.

Today we can learn that God does not leave us permanently in a condition of sickness or shame. When something changes in us, it is good to return with humility, seek guidance, and trust that God offers restoration.
exp.18:29:
This verse says that the people must set apart the days of rest, which are the sabbaths, for God, and treat his sanctuary with deep respect. "You must keep My Sabbaths and have reverence for My sanctuary" means honoring and looking upon these things with respect. At the end, God identifies himself: "I am the LORD," that is, the LORD himself commands it.

God speaks, through Moses, to Israel in the wilderness. This chapter gathers commands for living as a holy people, set apart from the customs of other nations. Before and after it there are orders against pagan practices, such as rites for the dead and consulting fortune-tellers. Keeping the sabbath and having reverence for the sanctuary kept the life of the people centered on God.

For today: set aside a regular time to rest and worship God, without rush or distractions. When you gather with other believers, come with an attentive and respectful heart, remembering that God deserves first place.
exp.0:16:
This verse says that the priest was to tear the bird open by its wings, but without dividing it completely. Then he would burn the whole bird on the altar, on top of the burning wood. The offering is called a burnt offering, a food offering, and a pleasing aroma to the LORD, which means God received it with delight.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. This passage deals with the offering of birds, meant for those who had fewer means than the one who offered a bull or a lamb. That the bird was kept whole and burned entirely shows total devotion. Some see in this an image of giving oneself completely to God; the text itself does not explain this further.

For today: God values sincere devotion, not the size of what we give. We can offer Him our time, work and obedience with our whole heart, holding nothing back, trusting that Christ makes us acceptable before Him.
exp.25:43:
This verse says that even when the people of Israel are in exile, living in the land of their enemies, God will not reject them completely. In the Berean Standard Bible the wording is "reject or despise," and the verse's sense is that God will not turn away from them, and he will not destroy them or break his covenant, because he is their God.

God himself speaks, through Moses, at the end of the warnings in chapter 26. Earlier he had announced punishments if the people despised his laws, including exile. But here he adds hope: the punishment corrects, it is not a final abandonment. His faithfulness rests on the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

For today: when you feel that you have failed and that God is far away, do not run from him. His discipline seeks to restore you, and his love does not depend on your perfection, but on his faithfulness. Return to him with sincerity.
exp.13:35:
This verse says that when someone reported a suspicious mark in their house, the priest first ordered the house to be cleared. Only after that did he go in to examine the mildew on the walls. The word "plague" here refers to a mark or affliction, and the "leprosy" in this passage is not exactly the disease we know today; it was probably mold or fungus on the walls, though scholars explain it in various ways. "Unclean" means being declared ritually impure.

God speaks to Moses and to Israel, before they enter Canaan. These rules cared for the purity of the people and protected families. With this order, the owner did not lose his belongings through a hasty decision, since what was taken out was not declared impure until there was a verdict.

For today: before judging a problem, take care of what is valuable and act with order. Facing a conflict or a failure, protect others and what is important, and then examine things calmly.
exp.18:26:
It says that the people of Israel were not to cut off the hair at the sides of their head, nor to clip off the edges of their beard. The "sides" and "edges" here refer to the outer parts of the head and beard.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, within the laws of holiness. These commands appear alongside prohibitions against seeking omens and cutting marks into the body for the dead. For that reason many believe these were customs tied to pagan rites of neighboring peoples, although the Bible does not explain this in detail and there is no complete certainty. The purpose was that Israel would be set apart and belong to God alone.

For today: this is not about rules on hairstyles, but about asking whether our customs show that we belong to God. Examine which habits you copy without thinking, and choose to live with a clear and faithful identity.
exp.25:45:
This verse sums up what has just been said: these are the rules God gave to Israel. "Statutes," "ordinances," and "laws" all refer to what God commanded and established for his people. The phrase "through Moses" means that God gave them by way of Moses. This took place on Mount Sinai.

The speaker is the narrator, and he closes the chapter where God set out blessings for obedience and consequences for disobedience. Even so, God had earlier promised that he would not completely abandon his people, because he would remember his covenant. This verse reminds us that all of this flows from a relationship, not only from rules.

Today we can read God's Word not as a cold burden, but as the guidance of a faithful God. Obeying him means responding with trust to the one who keeps his promises, even when we fail and return to him.
exp.21:2:
God tells Moses to give this warning to the descendants of Aaron, who are the priests: if anyone approaches the holy things, meaning the sacred offerings that the Israelites set apart for the LORD, while in a state of uncleanness, that person must be cut off from God's presence. The word "descendants" is the verse's way of speaking about the family line that follows after them. The phrase about being cut off is best understood as being separated from God's presence, although scholars explain it in several ways.

The LORD speaks through Moses. The priests ate part of the offerings, and God teaches them to handle these holy things with respect. The verses that follow give examples of what made a person unclean, such as certain skin diseases or contact with a dead body.

For today: drawing near to God in prayer and worship is not something to take lightly. Before we pray or serve, we can pause, confess our failings, and ask for his cleansing, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.20:1:
This verse is an exception to the rule just before it. Priests were not to make themselves unclean by touching a dead person, but they could do so for their closest relatives: their mother, their father, their son, their daughter, and their brother. The word "immediate family" in this verse means their own closest family, and to be made unclean means to become ritually impure by touching a dead body or coming near one.

God speaks to Moses to instruct the priests, the descendants of Aaron. They were to keep themselves set apart for service in worship, and contact with death left them impure for a time. Even so, God allows this exception so that they can care for and bury their nearest loved ones. It shows that the holiness God asks for is not at odds with family love.

For today: God values our caring for and standing with our family in their hardest moments. Serving God does not excuse us from loving and being present with our own.
exp.20:18:
This explanation of Leviticus 21:19 says that no man descended from Aaron who had a broken foot or a broken hand could approach the altar to offer the bread of God. A broken foot or hand means an injury or deformity in one of those parts of the body. It is one of several physical conditions listed in this passage.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Aaron and his descendants, the priests. These rules applied to service in the sanctuary of Israel. Interpreters explain their meaning in different ways: some see an image of the perfection and holiness God required, and others see a ritual order suited to that time. It should be noted that these men still ate of the sacred food (Leviticus 21:22), so they were not rejected as family.

For today: Jesus, our perfect high priest, allows us to draw near to God with confidence, regardless of our weaknesses or wounds.
exp.10:22:
This verse says that flying insects with four legs, which do not have long legs for jumping, are detestable to you and are not to be eaten. The phrase "all other flying insects" refers to winged insects. The verses before it allow only certain locusts, such as the locust.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel. These laws about clean and unclean animals helped the people live set apart for God. Scholars explain the exact reason for each rule in several ways, and the Bible does not always detail it.

For today: God is concerned with every aspect of daily life, including what we do and choose. Today we can ask God in prayer which everyday habits honor him, and obey him with gratitude, not out of fear.
exp.13:9:
On the eighth day, the person was to bring two unblemished male lambs, one unblemished ewe lamb a year old, a grain offering of three-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with olive oil, and one log of olive oil, a small measure of liquid.

God speaks to Moses, giving instructions for the person who had been healed of a skin disease, which this version calls "leprosy." After seven days of washing and waiting, the person returned to the community through offerings made before the LORD. Scholars often see here a path of restoration, not only physical cleansing.

For today: God cares for the complete restoration of a person, not only their relief. We can accompany with patience and kindness those who return to the community after a difficult time, helping them feel welcome again.
exp.15:28:
God sets a rule that lasts forever: every year, on the tenth day of the seventh month, the people were to humble themselves, and this was commonly understood to mean fasting. No one was to do any work, whether a native Israelite or a foreigner who lived among them.

God speaks to Moses so that he may pass it on to Israel. This is the Day of Atonement, when the high priest offered sacrifices for the sins of the people. Before this verse, the text describes how the remains of the animals were carried outside the camp. Afterward, it explains that on that day God cleansed them from their sins.

For today: forgiveness is a gift from God, not an achievement of ours. We can set aside time to stop, honestly acknowledge our wrongs, and give thanks that Christ reconciles us to God.
exp.18:22:
This verse says that when the people enter the promised land and plant trees for food, they must regard the fruit of the first three years as forbidden, meaning it is not to be used, and they must not eat it. The idea of the fruit being "uncircumcised" is figurative: it means that this first fruit is set aside and left unused.

God speaks through Moses to Israel, within the laws of holiness that shaped a people set apart from the nations around them. The immediate context mentions the forgiveness of sin through a sacrifice. Afterward, in the fourth year, the fruit was dedicated to God with praise, and from the fifth year they could eat it. Scholars explain the reason for the three years in various ways, and the text does not detail it.

For today: learn to wait and to put God first. Before you enjoy your achievements, give thanks to him and trust that his timing is good.
exp.19:7:
And you shall keep My statutes and practice them. I am the LORD who sanctifies you.

The verse says the people must carry out what God commanded, not only know it. "Statutes" are the laws or rules God gave. "Practice them" means to act on them and live them out. And God adds: "I am the LORD who sanctifies you," that is, "I am the one who sets you apart for Myself and makes you holy."

God speaks to Israel through Moses. He had just warned them not to turn to mediums or those who practice magic, and he called them to be holy. Then come laws about family and morality. The idea is that being God's people shows in the way they live. Holiness begins with God's work, but it also calls for obedience.

For today: do not be content just to admire what the Bible teaches. Choose one concrete teaching today, such as forgiving or speaking the truth, and practice it, trusting that God gives you strength to live it.
exp.23:0:
This verse is a simple introduction: God speaks to Moses. "Lord" is the name of God in this translation, and "to" is the word used here for Moses. What follows are instructions that Moses is to pass on to the people.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the one who receives the message to pass on to Israel. In this part of Leviticus, the people are in the wilderness, and God is giving them instructions about worship and life together as a community. Here it begins with the care of the lamps of the tabernacle, which were to be kept burning.

For today: God still speaks, and we can turn to listen to His Word with attention. Before acting, it is worth beginning the day by reading the Bible and praying, ready to obey what He shows us, even in small and everyday matters.
exp.4:17:
A person who sinned without realizing it must bring to the priest an unblemished ram of proper value from the flock as a guilt offering. The priest makes atonement on their behalf for the wrong they committed in ignorance, and they are forgiven. Here "atonement" means making things right with God through the sacrifice, and the ram's value is set by what is proper rather than by the person's own estimate.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes these instructions on to Israel. In this part of Leviticus it is taught that sin still counts even when it is committed in ignorance, because God's law is holy. That is why God provides a way of forgiveness through the sacrifice and the priest.

For today: it is not enough to say "I didn't know." We can ask God to show us our hidden faults and come to Him with humility. Christians believe that Christ is the perfect sacrifice who gives complete forgiveness.
exp.21:24:
It says that the Israelites were not to present defective animals as food offerings to God, and that this rule applied even when the animal came from a foreigner's hand. "Deformed" and "flawed" describe physical damage or a defect. God states plainly that such animals would not be accepted.

The Lord speaks to Moses, within the laws for the priests and the offerings. The animals had to be healthy, since they represented the best the people gave to God. Foreigners could bring offerings, but they were asked for the same quality. Scholars explain the mention of the foreigner in several ways: perhaps it refers to animals bought from them or brought by them.

For today: when we give something to God, whether time, money, or service, let us try to give him our best and not what is left over or what we no longer want.
exp.17:17:
This verse forbids a man from taking his wife's sister as a rival wife and having sexual relations with her while his wife is still alive. The old expression "uncover her nakedness" is not in the Berean wording, so the verse speaks plainly of sexual relations, and the key idea is marrying a second woman while the first is still living.

God speaks to Moses so that he may tell the people of Israel. This chapter sets clear limits in family relationships, to protect people and to set Israel apart from the customs of Egypt and Canaan. This case prevents rivalry and pain within the home. The story of Rachel and Leah is recalled, although the text does not mention it.

Today, let us care for our family relationships so that there is no jealousy or competition that hurts others. Let us strive to treat each person with respect, honor our commitments, and seek peace in the home.
exp.10:40:
It says that the small animals that crawl along the ground, such as certain reptiles and creeping creatures, were not to be eaten. The word "detestable" here refers to something God regarded as loathsome or unacceptable for his people. "Reptile" refers to creatures that move close to the earth.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel. These laws about clean and unclean animals helped the people live set apart, as God's people. Scholars explain the meaning of these rules in various ways: some see a reason of holiness and distinction, others see reasons of health. The text itself emphasizes holiness.

God cares for the details of the daily life of his people. Today we can ask ourselves which habits, though they may seem small, draw us closer to or further from living for God, and ask him for help to choose what does us good.
exp.25:34:
This verse says that while the land of Israel lies empty and in ruin, it will receive the rest that it could not have when the people lived in it. The phrase "lies desolate" means lying empty and ruined. The "Sabbaths" mentioned here are the years of rest for the land.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel. In the law He had commanded them to let the land rest every seventh year (Leviticus 25). Here He warns that if they disobey, they will be scattered, and the land will receive the rest that they denied it. Later, in 2 Chronicles 36:21, this rest is mentioned in connection with the exile.

For today: God made us with limits, and rest is not laziness but obedience and trust that He provides. Today you can set aside time each week to rest without guilt, thanking God for His care.
exp.10:17:
This verse continues a list of birds that the Israelites were not to eat. It names the white owl, the desert owl, and the osprey. The identities of these birds are hard to pin down with certainty, and translators have differed on them.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel about which animals were clean or unclean. These rules helped the people live set apart for God, for he says: "Be holy, for I am holy" (Leviticus 11:44).

Today Christians do not follow these food rules, since in Christ they were fulfilled (Mark 7:19; Acts 10). But we learn that God cares about everyday life. Ask yourself today: do my ordinary decisions, such as what I look at, say, and do, show that I belong to God?
exp.10:30:
These animals were regarded as unclean, meaning not fit for ritual use. These are the small creatures that crawl, mentioned earlier in the chapter, such as the weasel, the mouse, the frog, and the lizard. If someone touched one of them after it had died, that person stayed unclean until evening.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct the people of Israel. These rules helped the people learn to tell the clean from the unclean and to live with reverence before a holy God. Scholars explain the reason for each animal in different ways, and not everything is known for certain. What is clear is that this uncleanness was temporary and could be dealt with.

For today: let us be careful about what we touch and what we allow into our lives, because it matters. And let us remember that God always offers a way to be made clean again.
exp.18:33:
This verse commands that the foreigner who lives among the people be treated as one of the country's own. The word "native" refers to someone born there. The phrase "foreigners" describes people who come from outside the nation. God adds, "love him as yourself," and gives the reason: the Israelites themselves were foreigners in Egypt.

God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel, within the laws of holiness. Shortly before, he commands them to honor the elderly and not to oppress the stranger. Then he asks for justice in judgments and in the measures used in trade. Love for the foreigner appears joined to everyday justice. God reminds them of their own history: he brought them out of Egypt.

For today: think of an immigrant, a new neighbor, or a coworker who came from another place. Greet him by name, listen to him, and help him with something concrete. Remember when you felt lonely or new.
exp.23:4:
God tells Moses to take fine flour, the best quality, and bake twelve loaves. Each loaf was to use two-tenths of an ephah, a unit of measure for dry goods. Its exact equivalent in liters is calculated in different ways. "Fine flour" is very finely refined flour.

God speaks to Moses while giving instructions for worship in the tabernacle. These loaves were placed each week on the table before the LORD. Many understand that the twelve loaves represented the twelve tribes of Israel, although the text of this verse does not say so directly.

For today: God deserves our best and asks for it consistently, not only when we have something to spare. We can faithfully set apart time, attention, and affection for Him, remembering that He also cares for all His people.
exp.12:12:
This verse says that the priest will examine the person. If the disease has covered the entire body and all of it has turned white, he pronounces the person clean. The word "leprosy" was the name for several skin diseases, not only the one we call that today. The phrase "covered his entire body" refers to a skin condition spread over the whole body. The phrase "he is to pronounce the infected person clean" means declaring someone ritually pure.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. They were rules about ritual purity and life in community, and the priest acted as the examiner. Why skin that was entirely white was considered clean, while raw flesh was not, is not explained here; scholars interpret this in different ways.

For today: let us not hide our failings halfway. When we honestly acknowledge everything we are before God, without concealing anything, He can heal and restore us.
exp.24:29:
It says that if someone sold a house inside a walled city, they had a full year to buy it back by paying its value. If that year passed without the house being bought back, it was permanently transferred to the buyer and his descendants. It was not released even in the Jubilee. "Redeem" means to buy back. The phrase about the house being held by its owner is what the wording means by the old phrase about the house being held by its owner.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, giving laws for life in the promised land. The fields belonged to families and returned to them in the Jubilee, because the land belonged to God. Houses in walled cities were different. Many understand that they were not tied to the tribe's inheritance of farmland, although the text does not give all the reasons.

Today we can learn to act wisely and on time. There are opportunities with a deadline, such as mending a relationship, asking for forgiveness, or keeping a commitment. It is wise not to let them pass, because later it may be too late.
exp.21:4:
This verse continues a list of things that made a priest unclean. It says that if he touched a crawling creature, or a person who made him unclean, whatever the uncleanness may be, he became unclean. A "crawling creature" refers to an animal that moves along the ground, and "or" simply joins the items in the list.

While he remained unclean, he could not eat the holy things.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct Aaron and his sons, the priests. The offerings of the people were holy, and whoever handled them had to take care to stay pure. Each case was resolved with time, washing with water, and waiting until evening. These rules belonged to the covenant with Israel, and they taught that God is holy.

For today: draw near to God with reverence and without carelessness. We do not follow these ritual rules today, but we can ask him to cleanse our hearts before we pray or serve.
exp.21:30:
It says the people must carefully carry out what God commanded them. "Keep" means to hold fast to and obey; "practice them" means to put them into action, not just hear them. And it ends with "I am the LORD," which is like saying: "I am the LORD, and my word has authority."

God speaks to Moses so that he will tell the priests and all Israel. This chapter deals with offerings and with approaching what is holy with reverence. Earlier, the LORD asked for offerings given from the heart and in good order. Afterward, he asks that they not dishonor his name, and he reminds them that he brought them out of Egypt.

For today: obeying God is not only knowing what he says but doing it, even in small things. Choose one teaching from the Bible that you already know and practice it simply today, remembering that the one who commands is the same one who rescued you and loves you.
exp.17:24:
Even the land has become defiled, so I am punishing it for its sin, and the land will vomit out its inhabitants. This verse says that the land was made unclean by the sins of its people. God punishes the wickedness of those who live there, holding them accountable for what they have done. The image of the land vomiting out its inhabitants is a strong one: the land pushes them out, the way the body rejects something that harms it. "Defiled" means stained or dishonored.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, before they enter Canaan. He warns them about sexual and moral practices that corrupted the peoples of that land. He reminds them that those nations were driven out because of these actions, and that Israel would be no different if it did the same. Scholars understand this image in different ways, but all agree that it shows how serious sin is.

For today: God cares about how we live, and our choices affect others and the world around us. Let us ask Him to help us live with integrity and to take care of what He has entrusted to us.
exp.25:22:
This verse says: "And if in spite of these things you do not accept My discipline, but continue to walk in hostility toward Me..." The phrase "do not accept My discipline" means that the people refuse to let themselves be corrected, and "continue to walk in hostility" means that they keep acting in opposition and rebellion against God. It is a condition: God speaks of what would happen if the people keep refusing to change.

Context: God speaks to Israel through Moses, at the end of the covenant laws in Leviticus. He warns them that disobedience would bring consequences, but that this discipline was meant to bring them back to him. The punishment increases in stages, not because God is impatient, but because the people kept resisting.

For today: When God corrects us, through his Word, wise counsel, or the consequences of our actions, let us not harden our hearts. Let us ask him for humility to listen, to recognize our error, and to change in time.
exp.3:22:
When the leader of the people, the "ruler," becomes aware that he has sinned without meaning to, he must bring as an offering an unblemished male goat. "Sinned without meaning to" means that he fell short or did wrong, and "unblemished" means an animal that is healthy and unmarked, the best that he had.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions about sin offerings. Leviticus 4 explains what to do depending on who sins: the priest, the whole congregation, a leader, or an ordinary person. Here the sin is one committed unintentionally, that is, not on purpose. Many understand that this shows God takes seriously even the faults we do not see right away, and that leaders also need forgiveness.

For today: no matter what position we hold, we all need to acknowledge our faults with humility. When God makes us see an error, we should not hide it; we should go to Him with sincerity. Christians believe that Christ is the perfect sacrifice who gives us forgiveness.
exp.19:13:
If a man marries both a woman and her mother, the Bible calls it depraved, a serious and shameful wrong. The punishment was that he and both women were to be burned, so that such wrongdoing would not exist among the people.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, who had recently come out of Egypt and were near the land of Canaan. These laws protected the holiness of families and set Israel apart from the customs of the neighboring nations. They were civil laws for Israel at that time. How they were applied in practice is debated by scholars.

For today: guard the boundaries that protect your family. Work to keep your relationships pure and respectful, and never cause harm or confusion to others.
exp.21:18:
This verse says that when someone wants to bring an offering to God, they must offer a male animal without any defect. It may come from the cattle, the sheep, or the goats. The BSB wording "in order for it to be accepted on your behalf" points to the same idea: an offering given freely still had to meet God's standard to be accepted. "Without blemish" means without injury or sickness.

God speaks to Moses and tells him to speak to Aaron, his sons, and all the people, including the foreigners who lived among them. These rules in the book of Leviticus taught that drawing near to God required reverence. What was given to Him had to be the best, not what was left over.

For today: when we give God our time, money, or service, let us do it generously and from the heart, not with what we have left over or out of obligation.
exp.12:4:
After a week of isolation, the verse says, the priest was to examine the person with the skin infection again. If the infection was seen to be unchanged and had not spread on the skin, the priest would isolate the person for another seven days to observe it once more. An "infection" here refers to a sore or mark on the skin, and to "isolate" means to keep the person apart from others for a time.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. They sought to protect the community and to avoid hasty decisions. Waiting and watching were expected before anyone was declared clean or unclean. Keep in mind that the condition described can cover several skin diseases, not only the one we know today by the name leprosy.

Today we can learn to be patient before we judge others. Before drawing conclusions about a person or a situation, let us give it time, look carefully, and act with justice and compassion.
exp.15:11:
What it says: Aaron, the high priest, takes a censer (a vessel for burning incense) with burning coals from the altar that stands before the Lord. He also takes two handfuls of finely ground fragrant incense. With all of this he goes inside the veil, into the most holy place.

Context: God speaks to Moses about the Day of Atonement, when the high priest entered once a year into the presence of God. First he offers a bull for himself and for his household. The smoke of the incense covered the cover of the ark, and so Aaron did not die, since he drew near with reverence and as God had commanded.

For today: God is holy, yet He allows us to draw near to Him. Today we can pray with humility and gratitude, trusting that Christ opened the way, as Hebrews teaches.
exp.25:19:
Verse 20 says that the people's effort will come to nothing. They will work with all their strength, but the land will not produce its crops, and the trees will not bear their fruit.

Here God speaks to Israel through Moses, near the end of Leviticus. Before the wilderness and the Promised Land, God explains the blessings of obedience and the consequences of rejecting his covenant. This is a stage of warning: if they keep ignoring him, the discipline will increase. The heavens like iron and the earth like bronze describe a drought that leaves the ground hard and lifeless.

For today: we can work hard and still end up empty if we live far from God. It is worth pausing to ask him whether there is something we need to correct, knowing that his discipline seeks to bring us back to him.
exp.21:8:
God tells the priests to carefully keep what he has commanded about holy things. "My charge" means the duty or responsibility God has given them, so the verse follows the verse's own wording here: "My charge" refers to what God has entrusted to them. To profane something is to treat as common what is holy. If they do this, they will bear guilt and could die. And God reminds them who he is: the LORD who sanctifies them, that is, the one who sets them apart for himself.

God speaks to Moses so that he will tell Aaron and his sons. In this chapter he explains when a priest may eat the holy offerings and when he may not, for example, if he is unclean. These rules taught that approaching God is a serious matter.

For today: God still deserves our respect. Before we pray, serve, or take part in the church, we can pause, acknowledge that he is holy, and ask him for a sincere and obedient heart.
exp.22:12:
Along with the burnt offering lamb, a grain offering of two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil was to be brought. The grain offering is the offering of flour and oil, and the part burned on the altar was a food offering to the LORD, a pleasing aroma. The phrase about a pleasing aroma means the offering was acceptable to God. The drink offering was poured-out wine, a quarter hin, which was a measure of liquid, about four liters, though the exact calculation is uncertain.

God speaks to Moses to give Israel instructions about the Feast of Firstfruits. Before eating from the new harvest, the people were to bring the first sheaf to the priest and offer sacrifices. In this way they acknowledged that the harvest came from God.

For today: before we use what we have received, we can give God the first and best of it, with gratitude. This can be time, money, or help for others, recognizing that everything comes from Him.
exp.10:9:
These are the water creatures that God declared detestable to the Israelites: every creature in the seas or streams that does not have fins and scales. The word "detestable" does not mean morally wicked, but something the people were to reject and not eat. The phrase "teeming life" refers to creatures that move or abound in the water. "Detestable to you" means they were to regard such creatures as unclean and avoid them.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to teach Israel how to live as a people set apart for Him. These laws distinguished what was clean from what was unclean. The Bible does not explain the reason for each of these rules, and scholars propose several ideas, but the context emphasizes holiness (Leviticus 11:44).

For today: although many Christians understand that these dietary rules do not bind us now (Mark 7:19; Acts 10), the principle remains: asking God to guide my everyday habits, even the simplest ones, so that I live with gratitude and devotion to Him.
exp.19:19:
If a man has sexual relations with his uncle's wife, the uncle's wife being his father's brother's wife, he dishonors his uncle. The phrase "he has uncovered the nakedness of his uncle" is an old way of describing sexual relations. "They will bear their sin" means they will carry the consequences of what they have done. "They shall die childless" is commonly understood to mean they will have no descendants, though some read it as a punishment from God.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. Before they enter the promised land, He gives them laws so that they will live differently from the peoples around them, protecting the family and the purity of the community. This verse is part of a list of prohibitions on sexual conduct within the family.

For today: let us guard the boundaries of respect within the family. Honoring our relatives means keeping faithfulness and avoiding what breaks trust and harms households.
exp.3:30:
The verse says the priest had to remove all the fat, the suet, from the animal offered for sin, in the same way that fat was removed from the peace offering. He then burned it on the altar as a pleasing aroma to the LORD. Atonement means covering over or cleansing the guilt, and the verse says that in this way the priest will make atonement for the person, and he will be forgiven.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about sin offerings for sins committed unintentionally. Here the case is an individual from the people who brings a goat. The sacrifice showed that sin is serious and that forgiveness has a cost. Christians often see in this a shadow of Christ, as the letter to the Hebrews teaches.

For today, when you fail, do not hide your guilt or make light of it. Come before God with sincerity, trusting that the sacrifice of Jesus is enough to forgive you.
exp.24:45:
God says that the Israelites could keep servants bought from other nations as property, and leave them to their children as an inheritance, to be slaves for life. But they were not to treat a fellow Israelite harshly, ruling over him with cruelty.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, in the laws of the Jubilee, which protected poor Israelites from losing their freedom forever. The enslavement of foreigners here is hard to read. Many Christians understand that the law regulated an ancient custom without approving it as an ideal. Later the New Testament teaches that in Christ all people have equal dignity (Galatians 3:28).

Today, if you have authority over others, such as a boss, a parent, or a leader, use it with respect. Never treat anyone harshly or as a thing to be used. Every person has worth before God.
exp.9:16:
Moses asks Eleazar and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron, why they did not eat the sin offering in the holy place. He reminds them that the offering is most holy and that God gave it to the priests so that they would take away the guilt of the people and make atonement for them before the LORD. Here "atonement" refers to the sin offering, and "guilt" refers to the wrong the people have done.

Moses speaks shortly after the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, the other sons of Aaron. He finds that the male goat had been burned instead of eaten, as God had commanded. His anger comes from care to obey holy instructions. Aaron will answer later, explaining his grief. The text does not detail everything each of them was thinking.

God takes obedience seriously, but he also knows the heart. Today we can obey him with reverence, and remember that Jesus, our high priest, took away our guilt to reconcile us with God.
exp.10:19:
This verse says that flying insects that walk on four legs were considered detestable for the people of Israel, meaning something they were to reject and not eat.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to give the people of Israel instructions about which animals were clean and which were not. These laws helped Israel live as a people set apart for God. The following verses make an exception: they could eat certain jumping insects, such as the locust. Some animal names are difficult to identify with certainty.

Today, we are not under these food rules, but we can learn that God cares about the details of our daily lives. We can ask ourselves: are there habits I should leave behind in order to live more closely to God?
exp.7:30:
Moses tells Aaron and his sons to boil the meat and eat it at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, along with the bread from the basket of ordination offerings. They are to do this at the tent where God met with his people, just as God had commanded.

Moses speaks while setting the priests apart for service, following what God commanded him. Eating that meal at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting showed that God received them and gave them his provision for their service. Scholars explain the exact meaning of this meal in different ways, but all agree that it marked a solemn commitment.

Today we can learn to obey God carefully and to eat, so to speak, in his presence: giving thanks for what he gives us and dedicating our service to him with reverence, not out of habit.
exp.10:11:
It says that every animal of the water that does not have fins and scales must be seen as detestable, that is, as something the people were to reject and not eat.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel. These food rules set Israel apart as a people dedicated to God. Scholars explain the exact reason for each rule in several ways: holiness, the order of creation, or separation from other nations. The text itself stresses the call to be holy (Leviticus 11:44).

Today Christians understand that these food rules do not bind in the same way (Acts 10; Mark 7:19). Even so, the principle remains: ask yourself which habits or daily decisions show that you belong to God, and take care to live with intention and reverence.
exp.24:40:
When the year of jubilee comes, the Israelite who sold himself because of poverty will be set free. He and his children will be released, and he will return to his clan and to the property of his fathers. The phrase "return to his clan" describes his going back to his own family group, and the land of his ancestors is handed back to him.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. In the jubilee, every fifty years, debts were forgiven and the lands returned to their original owners. God gives the reason in the following verse: the Israelites are his servants, whom he brought out of Egypt, and for that reason no one should treat them harshly.

For today: God cares that no one remains trapped forever in poverty or debt. We can treat with dignity those who work for us or owe us something, and offer them real opportunities to rise again.
exp.14:1:
God tells Moses and Aaron to speak to the people. If a man has a bodily discharge, the discharge makes him "unclean," that is, ritually impure. The word here does not refer to something ordinary, but to a discharge from the body, probably a sign of illness.

God is the one speaking, and he speaks through Moses and Aaron, the leader and the priest. He gave these rules to Israel to teach them how to live near his presence, which was holy. Impurity was not sin, but a temporary condition that set the person apart from worship until they were made clean. Some scholars believe it also protected the health of the people, although the text does not say so.

God cares for his people even in the details of the body and daily life. Today we can remember that nothing about us is outside his concern, and that drawing near to him with a clean heart is always important.
exp.5:6:
This verse says that the priest would present the sacrifice before the LORD on behalf of the person who had done wrong, and so that person would be forgiven. The phrase "will make atonement" means that the guilt was covered and set right through the sacrifice. The phrase "anything he may have done to incur guilt" refers to the wrongs this person had committed, such as those mentioned just before: deceiving, stealing, or swearing falsely.

God speaks to Moses and gives instructions for Israel. Before the sacrifice was required, the law required that what had been stolen be returned with an added fifth. Forgiveness was linked to repairing the harm done to a neighbor. Afterward, the text moves on to the rules about the burnt offering, another offering of worship.

For today: if we have hurt or harmed someone, it is not enough to simply feel bad. We can ask God for forgiveness sincerely and, where possible, make right the harm with concrete actions. Christians see in Christ the sacrifice that brings complete forgiveness.
exp.11:2:
It says that when a boy is born, on the eighth day his foreskin must be circumcised. The foreskin is the skin that covers the tip of the male organ, and "the flesh of the boy's foreskin" refers to that skin, which is cut away. "Is to be circumcised" means that someone will make that cut.

God speaks to Moses so that he will tell it to Israel. Circumcision had already been the sign of the covenant since Abraham (Genesis 17). Here it is joined to the rules about birth. The text does not explain why the eighth day was chosen, so it is not wise to claim reasons that the Bible does not give.

For today: God cares for the signs of his covenant and wants families to obey him from the beginning of life. We can ask ourselves how to teach our children the faith with consistency, prayer, and example, without leaving it for later.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that the person who brings the offering must skin the animal and cut it into pieces, into its parts. To "skin" means to strip off the hide. A "burnt offering" was an offering burned whole on the altar. Here the text speaks of a calf, which is a young bull.

God speaks to Moses from the tabernacle and gives instructions to the people of Israel on how to draw near to Him. In the text, the one who offers the animal seems to be the same one who prepares it, and the priests take charge of the blood and the fire. Scholars explain the meaning of each detail in various ways, but everything shows that the offering was made with care and reverence.

For today: to approach God with seriousness and total devotion, not lightly. Today we do not offer animals, since Christians see in Christ the complete offering, but we can give God an entire life, holding nothing back.
exp.4:13:
The verse says that the Lord spoke again to Moses. The phrase "Then the LORD said to Moses" is a short sentence that signals the start of a new message from God and the move to a new topic.

Here God speaks, and Moses receives the message for the people. Up to this point, the laws dealt with sins committed through carelessness or neglect. Now a new set of instructions begins: what to do when someone unintentionally fails regarding the things set apart for God. A ram without blemish was to be brought, along with making restitution for the harm and adding a fifth part.

For today: God takes both forgiveness and restitution seriously. When we fail, it is not enough to feel sorry; it is wise to ask for forgiveness and, where possible, to make right the harm we have caused.
exp.7:15:
Moses took all the fat from the bull: the fat that covered the entrails, the lobe of the liver, and both kidneys with their fat. He burned all of it on the altar.

This takes place at the consecration of Aaron and his sons as priests. The narrator tells what Moses did following God's command. First the altar was purified with the blood of the sin offering. Then the best part, the fat, was offered to God. The rest of the animal was burned outside the camp. Scholars often see the fat as the choicest part, though the text does not give a detailed explanation.

For today: God deserves the best of us, not the leftovers. Today you can give him the best of your time, your attention, and your affection, trusting that forgiveness comes through his grace.
exp.22:8:
God spoke to Moses again to give him a new instruction. "The LORD" is the name of the God of Israel. The phrase "said to Moses" introduces a new command, a pattern repeated throughout Leviticus. Here a different instruction begins, about the firstfruits of the harvest.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the messenger who must pass it on to the people. Before this, God had spoken about the Passover and the unleavened bread, with days of rest and worship. Now he changes the subject: he will explain how to give thanks for the first harvest once they are living in the promised land.

For today: God deserves the first, not what is left over. We can begin the day, the week, or our income by giving thanks to him, recognizing that everything good comes from his hand.
exp.18:34:
It says we must not act unfairly in three areas: in judgments, in measuring land, and in the weight or measure of what is bought and sold. The core idea is harm or unfair treatment. Measuring land refers to how property is measured. The point is simple: we must be honest and fair in everything.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, within the laws about how to live as a holy people. Just before this, he commands that the foreigner be treated well, reminding them that they too were strangers in Egypt. Then he commands the use of honest scales and weights. In this way, justice is not only for the courts, but also for everyday trade.

For today: be honest in daily life, such as giving a fair price, keeping what you promise, paying what is owed, and not taking advantage of someone who knows less than you do. That integrity reflects the character of God.
exp.21:12:
If a priest's daughter is widowed or divorced, has no children, and returns to her father's house as she was in her youth, she may share her father's food, which is the holy food belonging to the priest's family. No outsider may share it.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Aaron and the priests about the care of the holy offerings. The previous rule said that a daughter who married a man from outside the family stopped eating of those offerings. Here she is given a protective way back: if she was left alone and without children to support her, she returned to her family and to its provision.

For today: the law shows care for those who are left alone and vulnerable. We can ask ourselves whom, in our family or church, we can open the door to and offer support.
exp.19:5:
If someone turns to mediums or spiritists, those who claimed to speak with the dead or to reveal the future, God sets himself against that person. Turning to prostitution here is a picture: abandoning God to give oneself to other powers, like an unfaithful spouse. Being cut off from his people means being separated from the community of Israel. Scholars debate whether this meant death or expulsion.

God speaks through Moses to Israel. He had just told them not to follow the practices of the surrounding nations, such as the worship of Molech. He wanted a faithful people set apart for Himself, who would trust Him alone.

For today: when you feel fear or uncertainty about the future, do not rush to horoscopes or the occult. Pray, open the Bible, and seek advice from mature believers. God is faithful and wants you to trust in Him.
exp.22:3:
These are the Lord's appointed feasts, the sacred assemblies that the people were to announce at their appointed times. The verse calls these gatherings holy because they were set apart for God, and it tells the people to proclaim them when the right time came.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct the Israelites. Before mentioning the yearly feasts, such as the Passover, God recalls the Sabbath, a weekly day of rest and worship. These appointed times helped the people remember what God had done for them and live as his people.

For today: set aside fixed times for God, such as a day of rest or meeting with other believers. If you do not plan them, other responsibilities easily push them aside.
exp.7:10:
Moses takes some of the anointing oil and sprinkles it seven times on the altar. Then he anoints the altar, all its utensils, the basin with its stand, and the basin (the large bowl of water used for washing) along with its stand (the base it rested on). He does this to consecrate them, that is, to set them apart for the service of God.

Here the narrator of the book tells how Moses obeys what the LORD commanded him. Israel was beginning worship in the tabernacle, and Aaron and his sons were about to be consecrated as priests. First the places and objects are set apart, and then the people. The number seven is often associated with completeness, although the text does not explain this.

For today: what belongs to God is set apart with intention. We can deliberately give to him our time, our home and our work, asking him to use them for his service.
exp.15:10:
Aaron must bring the bull that is his own sin offering. The word "atonement" refers to a sacrifice that covers sin, and "reconciliation" is the act of restoring peace with God. He does this first for himself and for his household. "Slaughter" means he will put the animal to death by cutting its throat.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the Day of Atonement, and Aaron is the high priest. The chapter begins by recalling the death of Aaron's sons, who approached God in an improper way. For this reason, before serving the people, the priest had to acknowledge his own need for forgiveness.

For today: before correcting or guiding others, it is wise to present ourselves humbly before God and acknowledge our faults. Christians see in Jesus the high priest who did not need to offer for himself (Hebrews 7:27).
exp.22:22:
This verse is an introductory phrase. It says that the LORD spoke to Moses. With these words a new instruction begins, just as elsewhere in Leviticus. "Said" is a simple word: God speaks, and Moses is to pass the message on.

The context is the chapter about the LORD's appointed feasts. Just before this, God spoke about leaving the edges of the field for the poor and the stranger. Now, with this phrase, he moves on to the feast of trumpets, in the seventh month. The one speaking is God, and Moses is the messenger who carries his words to the people of Israel.

For today: God does not speak at random, and his word deserves attention. A practical way to apply this is to set aside a few minutes each day to read the Bible calmly, asking yourself: "Lord, what do you want to say to me today?" Then do what you understand.
exp.22:27:
This verse commands that on the Day of Atonement no one should do any work. The phrase "the Day of Atonement" points to a day set apart for making atonement, which means wiping away guilt so that peace with God can be restored.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about their festivals. This day fell on the tenth day of the seventh month. It was a holy assembly in which the people humbled themselves and presented offerings. God required complete rest so that everyone could focus on forgiveness, not on their own efforts. The verses that follow show how serious this day was.

Today we can set aside a quiet time to ask God for forgiveness, without rush or distraction. Christians believe that Christ made the final atonement, so we can rest in his forgiveness with gratitude.
exp.22:35:
This verse says that for seven days the people were to present to God a food offering, meaning an offering burned on the altar. On the eighth day there was a sacred assembly, a special gathering for worship. On that day another food offering was also presented. The phrase "you must not do any regular work" refers to ordinary daily labor, which was set aside on those days.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct the Israelites about the Feast of Booths (or of Tabernacles), which began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month. It was a time of worship, rest, and thanksgiving to the LORD. The verses that follow place it among the fixed feasts of Israel's calendar.

For today: God invites us to set aside time to pause, rest from work, and give thanks. You can choose a fixed moment, such as a day or a few hours, to pray, gather with others, and thank him for his blessings.
exp.12:44:
This verse says that a person with a skin disease, a sore on the body, had to wear torn clothes and leave the head bare, with the hair loose and unkempt. He also had to cover his mouth and cry out, "Unclean, unclean!" Covering the mouth here means hiding the lower part of the face, and crying out means announcing it loudly so that others would know to keep their distance.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron about how the priests were to examine skin diseases. The condition is called "leprosy" in many English versions, but scholars believe it covered several skin conditions, not only what is today known as leprosy. These rules protected the community and showed the holiness of God among his people. The gestures were signs of mourning and warning.

Today we can approach those who suffer isolation or shame with compassion. Jesus touched people with skin diseases and healed them. We can offer companionship, listening, and respect.
exp.18:12:
It says we should not take advantage of our neighbor or take from him what is his. It also says that a hired hand's wages must not be held back until morning. In other words, someone who is paid for daily work should receive that pay the same day.

The word "defraud" means to treat someone unfairly or to take advantage of them.

God speaks here, giving Israel laws to live as a holy people. Before and after this verse He speaks of honesty, of respect for the deaf and the blind, and of justice toward both the poor and the powerful. A day laborer depended on his daily pay to eat, so holding it back left him in need.

For today: if you have someone who works for you, whether in your home or your business, pay them in full and on time. Treating fairly those who depend on their wages is a way of honoring God.
exp.5:26:
Verse 27 says that anything that touches the flesh of the sin offering will become holy, that is, set apart as belonging to God. If some of its blood is spattered onto a garment, that garment must be washed in a holy place, the courtyard of the tabernacle. Here "holy place" refers to that sacred space.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Aaron and his sons, the priests. This is the law of the sin offering, which is a most holy thing. Israel needed to learn that sin is serious and that God is holy. Some scholars understand the phrase "will become holy" to mean that whatever is touched takes on holiness; others, that it comes under special rules. The text allows both readings.

For today: let us treat with reverence what belongs to God and not take forgiveness lightly. Christ, our offering for sin, invites us to live with gratitude and purity.
exp.18:11:
This verse forbids using God's name to back up a lie. "Swear" means making a promise while calling God as your witness. "Profane" means treating his name as something ordinary, without respect. God says that swearing falsely by his name dishonors who he is. It ends with "I am the LORD," which works like a signature: he is the holy God who is speaking.

Here God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel. He gives them instructions for living as a holy people. Before and after this verse there are commands about honesty and justice: do not steal, do not cheat, do not oppress the poor or the hired worker. So honesty toward people and reverence toward God are joined together.

For today: keep what you promise and do not use God to persuade others. If you say "I swear to God" or "God knows," make sure it is true.
exp.26:28:
This verse says that a person set apart for destruction, one given entirely to God and devoted to be put to death, could not be bought back with money. Such a person had to be put to death.

Moses passes on these words from God at the end of Leviticus, in laws about vows and offerings. Many understand that it refers to cases like enemies condemned by God in war, not to human sacrifices, which the Law forbids. Some scholars interpret it in other ways, so it is wise to read it with humility.

Today, this text reminds us that God is holy and that we should not make promises lightly. Think carefully about what you promise the Lord, and keep your word sincerely, trusting in the grace of Christ.
exp.3:1:
God tells Moses to speak to the Israelites about what to do when someone sins unintentionally, that is, without meaning to or by mistake, by doing what the Lord has forbidden. The verse says the person "sins unintentionally against any of the LORD's commandments and does what is forbidden by them," so the focus is on the act itself and the person's lack of intent.

The Lord speaks from the tabernacle to Moses, who passes his words on to Israel. Here the law of the sin offering begins. God teaches that even unintentional wrongs matter, and so he provides a way of forgiveness and cleansing. Some scholars see here a sign of how serious sin is and of God's grace.

Today we too can take our faults seriously, even those we commit without realizing it. Let us ask God to show us where we fall short, confess with humility, and trust in his forgiveness.
exp.22:43:
This verse closes chapter 23. It says that Moses announced to the Israelites the appointed feasts of the LORD. "Appointed feasts" means sacred days set apart for gathering and honoring God.

God gave these instructions to Moses, and Moses taught them to the people. The chapter mentions the Sabbath, the Passover, the firstfruits, the trumpets, the day of atonement, and the feast of tabernacles. These were times to remember what God had done, such as bringing Israel out of Egypt and caring for them in the wilderness. Moses did not invent anything; he passed on what God commanded.

For today: set aside regular times to remember God's faithfulness, whether in church, at home with family, or alone. You can write down how He has cared for you and share it with your children or friends, so that gratitude passes from one generation to the next.
exp.20:23:
This verse closes the instructions about the priests. It says that Moses told all of the above to Aaron, to his sons, and to all the Israelites. The message was not meant only for one group, but was spoken to the priests and to the whole nation.

God gave these rules to Moses, and Moses passed them on. They were regulations for the priests, who had to guard their purity and their service in the sanctuary. The verses before it speak of a priest with some physical defect, who could eat of the holy food but could not approach the veil or the altar. There are different ways to understand the meaning of these rules, and the text stresses that God makes his people holy.

For today: God wants his Word to be known and shared with everyone, not only with the leaders. We can read it together in community and pass it on faithfully, without adding or taking away anything.
exp.17:27:
This verse says that the land of Canaan will not "vomit" out the people of Israel if what they do defiles it, just as it earlier vomited out the peoples who lived there. The verse's wording is "vomit," so the picture is that the land rejects those who foul it with wickedness. The word "vomit" is the strong image here: the land pushes away those who defile it.

God speaks to Moses so that he may tell Israel. Before they enter the promised land, he warns them not to imitate the immoral practices of the Canaanites, which the chapter describes in detail. This applies equally to the Israelite and to the foreigner who lives among them. Holiness was a responsibility of the whole people.

For today: what the people around me consider normal is not always good before God. Today I can ask myself which custom in my surroundings I should leave behind, and ask God for help to live with integrity, knowing that his commands seek to protect us.
exp.10:14:
This verse is part of the list of birds that God declared unclean. It says that any kind of raven was to be avoided as food. The word "abomination" here means something the people were to reject and not eat. The raven is a scavenger bird, although the text does not give its exact reason.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel. These food laws distinguished between the clean and the unclean, and they helped the people live as a nation set apart for God (Leviticus 11:44-45). Scholars explain the reason for each prohibition in various ways, and not everything is known with certainty.

For today: God is interested in every detail of our lives, even in ordinary things, such as what we eat. We can ask ourselves what daily habits show that we belong to Him, and ask Him for help to live in obedience and gratitude.
exp.7:18:
Moses slaughtered the ram and splattered its blood on all sides of the altar. The blood was used in the consecration of the priests.

This is a narrative, not a speech. God had commanded Moses to consecrate Aaron and his sons as priests. Before this, they had placed their hands on the animal, a gesture that many understand as identifying themselves with it. Moses acted as God had commanded him. The blood points to the fact that drawing near to God requires atonement. Christians see here a shadow of Christ, although the text does not say this directly.

For today: we do not rely on our merits to draw near to God. We can come with gratitude for the sacrifice of Jesus and respond with sincere obedience.
exp.24:3:
It says that every seventh year the land of Israel was to have a complete rest. The word "Sabbath" here means a time of quiet set apart for God, and the verse says the field was not to be sown and the vineyard was not to be pruned.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and tells him to speak to the people before they enter the promised land. Through this year of rest, Israel was reminded that the land belonged to God and that He was the one who sustained them. The verses that follow show that whatever the land produced on its own would serve as food for everyone, including servants and foreigners.

Today we can learn to rest by trusting that God provides. This week, set aside a time without working or worrying, and place it in God's hands.
exp.0:14:
This verse describes how a bird was offered on the altar. The priest brought it to the altar, twisted off its head, and burned it there. Its blood was drained out on the side of the altar. The reader's wording says the blood "should be drained out," so the verse sticks to that description and does not comment on how the blood was made to flow.

God speaks to Moses from the tent of meeting and gives instructions for the burnt offering, a gift that was burned completely. Birds were the option for someone with few resources, so no one was left unable to come near to God. The blood was a reminder that sin costs a life. Many Christians see here a shadow of Christ, although the text does not say this directly.

Today we do not offer animals, but we can learn that God welcomes gladly anyone who comes to him sincerely, whether they have much or little. Give God today what you have, with your whole heart.
exp.1:0:
It says that when someone wanted to bring God an offering of grain, they were to bring fine flour, that is, flour that was fine and of good quality. Olive oil was to be poured over it, and frankincense was to be put on it. The phrase "meat offering" refers to an offering given as a gift or tribute, and "will offer" here means bring before.

God speaks to Moses from the tent of meeting, shortly after Israel left Egypt. He is teaching how his people were to approach worship. This offering was different from the animal sacrifices. It was a gift that expressed thankfulness and dependence on God, who provides our food. Scholars explain the symbolism of the oil and the frankincense in various ways, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

For today: we give God the best of what we have, not what is left over. We can do this with gratitude, time, work, and resources, recognizing that everything comes from him.
exp.1:13:
It says that if someone wanted to bring God the first fruits of their harvest, they were to roast fresh heads of new grain over the fire and crush the kernels. "Grain offering" means a gift of grain presented to God, and the "first fruits" are the first part of the harvest. "To the LORD" means to the LORD.

God speaks to Moses to teach Israel how to bring their grain offerings. The first fruits acknowledged that the land and the harvest came from Him. The text says this offering was not placed on the altar as a pleasing aroma, but a portion was burned as a memorial, together with oil and incense. Scholars explain the symbolism of each element in various ways, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

For today: before you spend what you receive, whether wages, time, or talent, place it first in God's hands with gratitude. Ask yourself how you can honor Him with the first and the best.
exp.26:1:
God tells Moses to speak with the people about special vows. When someone promised to dedicate a person to the LORD, such as themselves or a family member, that promise could be fulfilled by paying a fixed value. The "valuation" was the price or worth assigned to the person.

The passage is spoken by the LORD, and Moses is the one who passes the message on to Israel. We are at the end of the book of Leviticus, where God gives instructions for the life of the people. This chapter sets rules for promises made to God, so that no one would take them lightly and everyone would know how to keep them in an orderly and just way. The verses that follow give the amounts in shekels.

For today: God takes our promises seriously. Before promising Him something, think it over calmly and be sincere. And if you have promised something, seek to keep it faithfully and with joy.
exp.12:24:
This verse describes a burn on the skin that, as it heals, leaves a bright spot. The priest examines it. If the hair in that spot has turned white and the area appears to be deeper than the skin around it, it is a disease that has broken out in the burn, and the person is declared unclean, that is, ceremonially impure. The word "infection" in the verse refers to a sore or diseased area.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priests were to examine skin diseases and protect the health and purity of the community. The Hebrew word translated "leprosy" covered several skin conditions, and we do not know with certainty what all of them were.

For today: God cares for us with order and patience. We can learn to examine wounds calmly, whether of the body or of the heart, not ignoring them, and seeking help in time.
exp.6:21:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that the LORD spoke to Moses again. "Then" marks the next moment in the account, and the words that follow introduce a new message for the people.

Here the LORD speaks, and Moses is the one who receives the word to carry to Israel. Earlier, God had warned about eating the meat of the peace offering while in a state of uncleanness. Now he changes the subject and gives a new instruction about the fat of the animals. This shows that the law came step by step, and that God cared about every detail of the people's life.

For today: God still speaks through his Word, and it is worth listening to it carefully, even on topics that seem small. Before reading the Bible, we can pray: "Speak, Lord, for your servant hears."
exp.13:37:
The priest, after seeing the suspicious spots on the walls, goes outside the doorway of the house, closes it up, and leaves it shut for seven days. A "plague" here means a spot or infection, probably mold or fungus.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel, who would soon live in houses in the promised land.
