No one was punished: the seven days of closing gave time to see whether the spot grew or not. In this way the family and the community were protected, and the decision was made calmly, without haste or assumptions.

For today: when you face a problem you do not fully understand, do not react in a hurry or out of fear. Pause, observe with patience, and seek wise counsel before deciding.
exp.0:0:
This verse says that the LORD called to Moses and spoke to him from the Tent of Meeting. The LORD is the name of God in this verse, and the Tent of Meeting was the sacred tent where God was present among his people, and where the tablets of the law were kept.

Leviticus begins just after the tent was finished, at the end of Exodus. God is the one who speaks, and he addresses Moses so that Moses will pass on to Israel the instructions for how to draw near to God through the offerings. It is God who takes the initiative and calls.

For today: God still speaks and desires a relationship with us. We can set aside a moment each day to listen to him in his Word, remembering that he seeks us first.
exp.21:25:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that God spoke to Moses, and with that it introduces a new group of instructions. The word "said" is the plain form we use today.

The one speaking is the Lord, and Moses is the messenger who must pass his words on to the people. Just before this, God had asked that the animals offered not have any defects. Now he begins to explain other rules about the sacrifices: the age of the animal and respectful treatment toward the young and their mothers.

For today: before deciding how to live and worship, it is worth pausing to listen to God. He is interested not only in what we give him, but also in how we do it. We can set aside a moment each day to read his Word carefully and obey it sincerely.
exp.24:13:
This verse says that when you sell something to a neighbor or buy something from one, you must not take advantage of each other. The other person is not merely a customer to be used, but someone you share a community with, and the verse calls you to deal with them fairly.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, who would soon live in the promised land. In the year of jubilee, each family recovered its land. For that reason, the sale of land was really a lease for a certain number of years. The price had to be fair, according to the harvests that remained until the next jubilee.

Today we can be honest in every deal: telling the truth about what we sell, not hiding defects, and paying or charging a fair price, treating the other person as a brother.
exp.16:11:
God says that none of the Israelites should eat blood, and that no foreigner living among them should eat blood either. The phrase "foreigner living among you" refers to a non-Israelite who lives in the community. The verse makes no distinction between the two groups: the same rule applies to everyone who lives among the people.

Here God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel. He explains that the life of the flesh is in the blood, and that He had given it for the altar, to make atonement or cover sin. Blood was sacred because it represented life, and it was used in the sacrifices. This also kept them from imitating the customs of other peoples.

For today: Christians are not under this law, but we can learn to value life as a gift from God. In addition, the blood of Christ reminds us that our reconciliation with God cost a life given out of love.
exp.26:3:
This verse says that if the person dedicated to God by a vow was an adult woman (between twenty and sixty years old, according to the previous verse), the amount to pay to buy her back was thirty shekels of silver. "Valuation" means the set price or value, and "female" is simply a woman. A shekel was a unit of weight in silver.

God speaks to Moses and tells him to instruct the Israelites on how to fulfill a special vow. When someone promised to dedicate a person to the service of the sanctuary, that person could be bought back by paying a set value. Scholars explain in different ways why the figure for a woman is lower than the figure for a man; some think it relates to the kind of work done in that time, but the text does not make this clear. It was not a judgment about her dignity before God.

For today: God takes the promises we make to him seriously. Before promising him something, let us think carefully, and then faithfully keep what we have said.
exp.3:13:
It says that when the whole community of Israel becomes aware that it has committed a sin, even though it did not know it before, it must bring a young bull as a sin offering to be forgiven. They present it before the Tent of Meeting. "Sin" means falling short or doing wrong; "sin offering" is the sacrifice that covers the guilt; "Tent of Meeting" is the holy tent where God met with his people.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to Israel. Earlier he had already explained what to do if a priest sinned. Now he addresses the sin committed unintentionally by the whole people. It shows that God takes sin seriously, even unintentional sin, and offers a way to be forgiven.

For today: it is not enough to say "I did not know." Let us ask God to show us what we do wrong, and when we discover it, let us acknowledge it with humility, also as a community or church, and turn to Christ, who forgives us.
exp.17:2:
It says that Israel must not follow the practices of Egypt, where they lived for many years, nor those of Canaan, into which God is bringing them. "Lived" refers to the Egypt they stayed in, "bring" means to lead them there, and "practices" refers to established customs and ways of doing things. "Walk in their customs" means to live by their ways.

God speaks to Moses so that he will pass his message on to the people. Before giving laws about moral and sexual conduct, he reminds them who he is: "I am the LORD your God." Their identity as God's people was meant to shape the way they lived, distinct from the cultures around them.

For today: before following what "everyone does," we can ask ourselves whether that pleases God. Our guide is not fashion or social pressure, but the word of the One to whom we belong.
exp.6:24:
This verse forbids eating the fat of the animals that could be presented to the LORD as a food offering. The fat is the part that was burned on the altar as an offering. Anyone who ate it would have to be cut off from his people, an expression that some understand as being removed from the community and others as a punishment from God; the text does not fully clarify which.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct Israel. The fat of those animals belonged to the LORD, since it was burned as the best part of the offering. This law helped the people recognize that what is best belongs to the LORD. Together with the prohibition of blood, it taught respect for what God had set apart as his own.

Today we might ask what the "best" is in our own time, our money, our energy, or our attention, and whether we give it to God first, or only what is left over.
exp.10:6:
The verse says that the pig has a split hoof that is completely divided, but it does not chew the cud, meaning it does not bring its food back up to chew again. For that reason God tells the Israelites to regard it as "unclean for you," a phrase that here means not fit to eat or for worship.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel, newly come out of Egypt. These laws about clean and unclean animals helped them live as a people set apart for God (Leviticus 11:44-45). Scholars explain the reason for each animal in various ways, and the Bible does not detail every reason. It does make clear that this was a call to obey and to be holy.

For today: although Christians are not under these food rules (Mark 7:18-19; Acts 10:15), we can learn to obey God in daily life, asking ourselves which habits show that we belong to him.
exp.25:7:
It says that God would give the Israelites a very great victory over their enemies. Five of them would pursue a hundred, and a hundred would pursue ten thousand. It is a way of speaking that shows God's help is worth far more than the number of soldiers. The phrase "will fall by the sword before you" means their enemies would die in battle, and "pursue" means they would chase them as they fled.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, on Mount Sinai. These are promises of blessing within the covenant: if the people obeyed his commandments, they would have peace, harvests and protection. The numbers are probably language of emphasis, not an exact count.

For today: we do not need more strength, resources or support in order to obey God. If you face a situation today that is beyond you, trust that God can work beyond your limits. Keep doing what is right with faith and humility, without boasting.
exp.12:29:
The passage says that the priest had to examine an infection on the head or chin. If it appeared to be deeper than the skin, and the hair in it was yellow and thin, the person had to be pronounced unclean. This condition is a scaly outbreak, an infectious disease of the head or chin. The word "leprosy" here covered several skin diseases, not only the one we call leprosy today.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. They were rules of health and ritual purity: the priest examined the person calmly, without rushing, and then waited several days before deciding. Scholars agree that being unclean was a ceremonial condition that temporarily set the person apart from the community, and not a judgment about their worth.

For today: before drawing conclusions about someone, look with patience, give time, and seek the facts. In this way we care for the truth and for people.
exp.25:38:
Those who survive will waste away among their enemies because of their own wrongdoing. They will also decay under the sins of their ancestors, which means they will suffer for following the same path their forebears took. "Waste away" here means to fade, to weaken slowly, or to decline.

God speaks through Moses at the end of the book of Leviticus. Before the people enter the promised land, they hear blessings for obedience and warnings for rebellion. This passage speaks of exile as the consequence of breaking the covenant. But the next verse shows an open door: if they confess and humble themselves, God will remember his covenant.

For today: let us not silently repeat the mistakes we inherit. If we recognize our sin and that of our family, and return to God with humility, there is a path to forgiveness and restoration.
exp.11:6:
This verse says that the priest presents the offering before the LORD and makes atonement for the woman who has given birth. With this she is made ceremonially clean from her flow of blood. The phrase "a woman giving birth" in the verse refers to childbirth, and "atonement" is the act of covering or repairing what kept a person from drawing near to God. The verse closes the law about childbirth, whether the child is a male or a female.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. These rules of ritual purity taught that life and nearness to God are sacred. They did not say that giving birth was a sin; the most common interpretation is that this was a ritual state that was resolved through an offering. God also provided an option for the poor.

For today: God makes it possible for us to draw near to Him, and He cares for everyone alike. We can come to Him with confidence, grateful for Christ, and help those who have less.
exp.7:20:
He says that Moses washed the entrails and the legs of the ram with water. Then he burned the entire ram on the altar. It was a burnt offering, meaning an offering that is burned completely. The phrase "a pleasing aroma" describes an offering that is pleasing to God. "A food offering to the LORD" refers to an offering burned on the altar and presented to him. Everything was done just as the LORD had commanded.

Moses is presiding over the ceremony in which Aaron and his sons are set apart as priests. The narrator emphasizes that everything was done just as the LORD had commanded. Before serving the people, the priests had to be consecrated, and this whole offering showed complete surrender to God.

For today: God values sincere and complete devotion, not half-hearted devotion. We can ask ourselves what area of our life we have not yet given to him, and obey him with trust and gratitude.
exp.20:16:
God tells Moses to speak to Aaron. None of Aaron's descendants who has a physical defect may come near to offer the food of their God, meaning the offerings presented to God. The word "approach" in the verse means "come near."

God speaks to Moses and gives rules for the priests, who were to be holy. At that time the priest represented the people before God, and the offerings had to be without defect, as did the person who presented them. The passages that follow clarify that these men could still eat of the holy food (v. 22), though they could not offer it. Interpreters explain the exact reason for this rule in different ways.

Today we do not depend on a human priest, for Christ is our perfect high priest, and all of us can approach God with confidence (Hebrews 4:16). Let us learn to treat God with reverence and to receive everyone with love.
exp.21:6:
This verse says that a priest who had become unclean by touching something defiled had to wash himself with water and wait until the sun went down. Then he was clean again and could eat of the holy offerings. These offerings were his food, since God gave them to the priests for their support. The statement that he "will become clean" means that he was fit to draw near to what is holy.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct Aaron and his sons, the priests. He teaches them that what is holy must be treated with respect. These rules were part of the covenant with Israel. They showed that God is holy and that those who served him had to guard their purity. Scholars explain the meaning of each purity rule in several ways, but here the emphasis is clear: to respect what belongs to God.

For today: before you approach God in prayer or at the Lord's Supper, take a moment to confess to him whatever weighs on you. He promises to forgive and renew those who come to him with sincerity.
exp.13:31:
This verse sums up the rule for a person with a skin disease who was poor and could not afford the full cost of his cleansing. The phrase "cannot afford the cost" means that he did not have the means, and he was permitted to offer a simpler version.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, and through them to Israel. Earlier, Leviticus 14 explains the cleansing ritual for the one who had been healed. Here God adds a provision for the poor: birds in place of more costly animals. Scholars point out that the Hebrew term covers several skin conditions, not only what is today called leprosy.

For today: God does not place fellowship with Him out of reach for anyone because of a lack of money. We can imitate that heart by seeking to ensure that no one in our church or community is excluded because of their financial situation.
exp.10:44:
Here God says that he is the LORD, the one who brought Israel out of Egypt so that he would be their God. For this reason he asks them to be holy, that is, set apart for him, because he himself is holy. The phrase "brought you out of the land of Egypt" makes clear that their freedom came from God's own act of rescue.

God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel, who had just been freed from slavery. He gives them laws about clean and unclean animals. His purpose was to teach them to live differently from the nations around them. Scholars explain the reason for each rule in various ways, but the text emphasizes holiness.

For today: God rescued us so that we would live differently. Today you can choose a habit that does not honor God and ask him for help to leave it, remembering that he loves you and set you free.
exp.12:14:
When the priest sees raw flesh, meaning an open sore or red, tender tissue, on the person who has the skin disease, the priest must pronounce that person unclean. The phrase "skin disease" here is a broad term for several skin conditions, not necessarily the disease we call leprosy today. "Unclean" means ceremonially impure, not necessarily "sinful."

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priest acted as examiner, protected the health and purity of the community in the camp, and also decided when someone could be accepted again. Neighboring texts show that the person could be declared clean once more. The details of each medical case are interpreted in various ways.

For today: the law showed that visible wounds matter. Let us be honest about what needs healing, and accompany with compassion those who suffer, rather than judging them.
exp.15:22:
Aaron, the high priest, returns to the Tent of Meeting and takes off the linen garments he put on before entering the Most Holy Place. He leaves them there. Taking them off simply means that he removes them.

God speaks to Moses about the Day of Atonement. Aaron has already confessed the sins of the people over the goat that was sent away into the wilderness. Now he finishes that part of the rite and prepares to wash and put on his ordinary clothes. Scholars see in the linen garments a symbol of humility and purity, although the text does not give a detailed explanation.

For today: there are sacred moments that call for a special attitude, and there are also moments for returning to daily life. After we draw near to God in prayer or in the congregation, let us go back to our homes and our work carrying humility and gratitude for the forgiveness we have received.
exp.9:15:
Moses searched carefully for the goat of the sin offering and found that it had been burned up. He became angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron's remaining sons. The word "searched" here means he looked closely and asked about it. The sin offering was the offering made to deal with sin.

This happens right after the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, their brothers, who offered fire that God had not authorized. Moses explains God's instructions for the offerings. That meat was to be eaten in the holy place, but it was burned. Moses complains because God's command was not carried out. Later, Aaron gives an answer, and Moses is satisfied. The text does not explain all the details of his reasoning.

For today: obeying God from the heart matters more than going through the motions out of habit. Before reacting, it is wise to listen with humility and patience.
exp.6:23:
The verse says that the fat of an animal found dead or mauled by wild beasts may be used for any other purpose, but it must not be eaten. The word translated as "fat" refers to the animal's fat, and "used for any other purpose" means it could be set aside and put to some other use.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about the offerings. The fat of the animals that were sacrificed was the part reserved for God and was burned on the altar. That is why it was not to be eaten. In addition, an animal that died without being sacrificed was considered unclean. Scholars explain the exact reason in several ways, but the emphasis is on setting apart what belongs to God.

Today we can ask ourselves what the best is that we give to God. He deserves our first place, not the leftovers of our time, attention, or resources. Honoring him with the best is a way of telling him that we love him.
exp.14:0:
This verse is an introduction. It says that the LORD said to Moses and Aaron to give them a message. Here there is not yet a rule; it only announces that an instruction from God is coming.

The one speaking is God, and he addresses Moses, the leader of the people, and Aaron, the priest. This takes place in Leviticus, where God teaches Israel how to live near his presence. The following verses deal with cleanness and ritual uncleanness, and Moses and Aaron were to pass them on to the people.

For today: God is concerned with every detail of his people's life, even the most ordinary and delicate ones. We can come to his Word with confidence and a willingness to listen, knowing that he speaks to us to care for and guide us.
exp.7:17:
This verse tells that Moses presented the ram for the burnt offering, which was an offering burned whole on the altar. Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the animal's head. The wording "presented" means Moses brought the ram forward to the altar. This gesture is usually understood as a way of identifying oneself with the offering.

We are in the ceremony in which Aaron and his sons were set apart as priests. The narrator tells what Moses did following what God had commanded him. Earlier, an animal had been offered for sin; now comes an offering of complete surrender to God.

For today: before serving God, we need to recognize that we do not do so on the strength of our own merits. We can begin the day by giving God our work, our decisions, and our hearts entirely, trusting in his provision.
exp.21:27:
This verse forbids slaughtering an animal and its young on the same day. "Slaughter" here means killing an animal for sacrifice. The verse names an ox or a sheep, and the animal in view is the parent together with its offspring.

God speaks to Moses within the laws about offerings and sacrifices for the priests and the people. Just before this, He commands that a newborn animal must wait seven days before it can be offered. The reason for this rule is not stated. Many believe it teaches respect for life and prevents cruelty, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: let us care with respect for what God has created, even in everyday life. We can treat animals with kindness and not be harsh toward those who depend on us.
exp.10:25:
Leviticus 11:26 says that animals with hooves not completely divided, or that do not chew the cud, are unclean for you. Whoever touches any of them will be unclean. In other words, these animals were not fit to eat or to use in the religious life of the people.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to give laws to Israel, a people just formed, with the tabernacle in their midst. These laws set Israel apart from other nations and taught them that God is holy. Scholars do not agree on the reasons behind each rule: some think of health, others of symbolism or of identity.

Today, as Christians, we are not under these dietary rules (Mark 7:19; Acts 10), but we can learn to live attentive and devoted to God in everyday life: what we eat, touch, and do can be an opportunity to honor him.
exp.18:20:
This verse says that the man who had sinned was to bring a ram to the entrance of the tent of meeting, as his guilt offering to the LORD, to make atonement for his guilt. "Atonement" means covering over or repairing a wrong. The tent of meeting is the holy tent where God met with his people.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct Israel. The case before this one concerns a relationship with a servant who was promised in marriage but was not yet free. The law sets a penalty, but it also provides a way to be forgiven. Some of the legal details of that situation are difficult, and scholars explain them in different ways.

For today: when we fail, God does not want us to hide it, but to acknowledge it with humility. Christians believe that Christ is the final offering for our sin. We can draw near to God with sincerity, ask for forgiveness, and repair the harm we have caused.
exp.3:11:
The passage says the priest had to take the whole bull outside the camp to a clean place, where the ashes from the altar were poured out, and burn it on a wood fire. "Camp" here means the camp of Israel. "Clean" means ceremonially set apart for this purpose. Only the fat was burned on the altar; the rest was burned outside.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about the sin offering for the anointed priest, who had sinned without realizing it. Because his failure affected the whole people, the rite was more solemn. Taking the bull outside showed that sin is a serious matter and must be removed from the midst of the people. Many Christians see here a shadow of Christ, who suffered "outside the gate" (Hebrews 13:11-12).

Today we can learn to take sin seriously, even the sin we commit without meaning to. Let us ask God to show us our faults, and rest thankfully in the knowledge that Christ bore them.
exp.25:40:
It says that if the people turn against God, He will also act against them and bring them into the land of their enemies. There, their uncircumcised hearts, meaning hearts that are stubborn and closed to God, will be humbled, and they will make amends for their wrongdoing. "I acted with hostility toward them" means that God will respond to their resistance.

God speaks, through Moses, at the end of the blessings and warnings of the covenant with Israel. If they disobey, discipline will come. But the punishment is not the last word: it seeks to bring them to acknowledge their guilt. The following text shows that God will remember His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

For today: when we realize that we have failed, let us not hide the mistake or make excuses for ourselves. Humbling ourselves and confessing to God with sincerity opens the door to His forgiveness and to a new beginning.
exp.26:24:
This verse says that every value placed on things dedicated to God must be measured by the official weight known as the sanctuary shekel. That shekel was equal to twenty small units, called gerahs. The gerah was a very small measure of weight. To appraise something means to set a price or value on it.

God speaks to Moses on behalf of the people of Israel. The chapter deals with vows and offerings dedicated to God, and with how to redeem them by paying their value. A fixed and common standard prevented cheating, favoritism, and confusion, because everyone knew exactly how much each thing was worth.

For today: God cares about honesty in what we give and in what we promise. We can examine whether we are fair and clear in our dealings, and whether we sincerely keep what we have promised to God and to others.
exp.22:38:
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, after the people have gathered in the produce of the land, they are to celebrate a feast to the Lord for seven days. The first day will be a day of complete rest, and the eighth day will also be a day of complete rest. The word "after" ties this instruction to the harvest that comes before it, and the word "gathered" describes the crops being brought in. The idea of rest here points to a day set apart from ordinary work, not necessarily the seventh day of the week.

God speaks to Moses so that he will pass these instructions on to Israel. This feast, called the Feast of Tabernacles or of Booths, took place when the harvest was finished. It served to give thanks for God's provision. The verses that follow explain that it also remembered living in booths during the journey through the wilderness.

For today: before asking for more, we can stop to thank God for what He has already given us. A good habit is to set aside time, alone or with family, to name the blessings we have received out loud and to rest in gratitude before Him.
exp.25:16:
If the people turn away from God, He will withdraw His favor. "I will set My face against you" means God would confront them with the consequences of their rebellion. "You will be defeated by your enemies" means losing battles and being overpowered. "Those who hate you will rule over you" means their enemies would dominate them. And "you will flee when no one pursues you" describes a fear so great that they would run even when no one was chasing them.

God speaks through Moses to Israel at Sinai. At the end of the law, He sets before them blessings if they obey and warnings if they despise His covenant. These punishments were not arbitrary: they were meant to lead the people to recognize their error and return to God, as the following verses show, where the discipline increases if they still do not listen.

For today: when fear or insecurity overwhelms us without a clear reason, it is worth asking whether we have drifted away from God. Returning to Him sincerely brings back peace and confidence.
exp.13:19:
This verse says that the priest places on the altar the burnt offering (the offering that was burned whole) and the grain offering (a grain offering with oil). With this he makes atonement, that is, he covers or repairs what stood in the way of fellowship with God, and the person is made clean. "Offering" means gift given to God.

Moses gives these instructions on God's behalf in the book of Leviticus. They describe the ritual by which a person healed of a serious skin disease (rendered as "leprosy," though it is not known with certainty which diseases were included) could return to the community and to worship. This is the final step of a process involving several days and offerings.

For today: cleansing and return to the community are gifts from God, not achievements of our own. We can approach Him with confidence and also receive with love those who have felt excluded.
exp.17:13:
This verse forbids having sexual relations with the wife of your father's brother, that is, with your aunt by marriage. The verse says you must not dishonor your father's brother by approaching his wife for that purpose. The reason is clear: she is the wife of a very close relative, your uncle.

God speaks to Moses so that he will tell the people of Israel. Before they enter Canaan, the Lord gives them rules so that they will live differently from the neighboring nations. These laws protected families, guarded trust within the home, and set clear boundaries.

Today we can learn to respect marriages and the boundaries within the family. Let us take care in how we treat relatives, avoid flirting or situations that harm trust, and honor what God has joined together.
exp.18:7:
It says that whoever eats the peace offering after the permitted time will bear his guilt. Here "guilt" means sin or the responsibility that comes from the wrong. The phrase about profaning what is holy means that he treated as common something set apart for God. The expression about being cut off from his people is understood in several ways: it may mean being removed from the community, or a more serious punishment, and scholars do not fully agree.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. He is explaining how to offer peace sacrifices with respect and order. What was offered to God had to be handled with care, without carelessness or contempt. Right after this, the text moves on to command generosity toward the poor and the foreigner.

For today: God cares about how we approach Him. We can give Him our best, not what is left over, and show that same reverence by being generous to those in need.
exp.14:27:
When a woman is cleansed of her discharge, she must count off seven days, and after that she will be ceremonially clean. Here "clean" does not mean she was sinful. It describes a ritual status, meaning she is set apart for a time and then fit again to take part in the life and worship of Israel.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives these laws to the people who had just come out of Egypt. They were meant to teach that life and health are sacred, and that drawing near to God calls for care. After the seven days, she brought an offering on the eighth day. Scholars explain the meaning of those offerings in several ways.

For today: God is in no hurry with our wounds. Give yourself time to heal, without haste or guilt, and trust that He receives you again with tenderness.
exp.12:53:
If the stain on a garment has not spread, the priest orders the contaminated article to be washed and set apart for another seven days. The stain here means visible contamination or damage, and isolating the item means keeping it aside, not confining a person.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priests were to examine calmly any sign of mildew or corrosion, in order to protect the health and purity of the camp. Scholars debate exactly what kind of mold or fungus was meant; the text simply describes it as contamination in a garment.

For today: do not rush to judge or discard something or someone. God shows patience: it is observed, it is cleaned, and it is looked at again. Before making difficult decisions, take time, seek counsel, and examine the facts carefully.
exp.4:0:
If someone hears a public charge being made about something they have witnessed, and they keep silent instead of coming forward with what they saw or learned, the Bible says they have sinned and will bear the guilt. Here, "testifying" means stating plainly what one knows. "Bearing the iniquity" means being held accountable before God.

God speaks to Moses on behalf of the people of Israel and begins the instructions about the sin offering. Many read this as a witness who stays quiet when a charge is raised or when testimony is needed. The verses that follow show that there is also guilt for wrongs committed without realizing it.

For today: if you know the truth and someone needs you to speak it, as in a case of injustice or abuse, do not hide behind silence. Ask God for courage and wisdom to speak honestly and with respect.
exp.8:5:
Moses tells the people to do exactly what the LORD has commanded, and then they will see the glory of the LORD. The words "so that the glory of the LORD may appear to you" mean that God would be present and visible to them in a special way. "LORD" is the name of God.

Moses speaks to Aaron, the elders, and all Israel, on the eighth day, when Aaron and his sons begin their service as priests. Earlier, they had been commanded to prepare the offerings. The people are already gathered before the tabernacle. Moses explains that obedience prepares the way for God to make himself known. Right away Aaron offers a sacrifice first for his own sin and then for the people.

For today: God delights in our seeking him with humble obedience, not with ideas of our own. We can begin the day by asking ourselves: what has God asked of me in his Word? And we can do it with confidence, knowing that he is faithful to draw near to those who obey him.
exp.26:20:
This verse says that when the year of jubilee comes and the field is released, it does not go back to the person who had dedicated it. It becomes holy, set apart for the Lord, like a field devoted to him, and it becomes the property of the priests. The wording describes the field being released in the jubilee, which means it is set free from its earlier arrangement. The jubilee was the fiftieth year, when land usually returned to the families who first held it.

God gives these instructions to Moses for Israel. The chapter deals with vows made to God. If someone dedicated his field and then sold it without redeeming it, he lost his right to it. The law sought to make sure that vows were taken seriously.

For today: think carefully before promising something to God, and when you do promise, keep it sincerely. What we dedicate to the Lord should not be treated lightly.
exp.13:52:
He tells us that the priest releases the live bird outside the city, into the open fields. By this act atonement is made for the house, that is, what was damaged is covered over and repaired, and the house is declared clean. The phrase "the surface of the field" means the face of the open land. Here "leprosy" was not only a skin disease but also mold or blight on the walls.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives them instructions for the people of Israel. After a house affected by mold was inspected and repaired, this rite declared it clean again. Scholars see in the released bird an image of the stain being carried far away, although the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: God cares about everyday life, even about our homes. You can ask Him to cleanse what is damaged in your house and in your heart, and trust that He knows how to restore and give a new beginning.
exp.7:0:
This verse says that the LORD spoke to Moses. It is a simple phrase that introduces a new command. The word "said" shows that instructions are about to follow.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the one who listens and must obey. In Leviticus 8 the ceremony begins in which Aaron and his sons are set apart as priests. God had already given instructions for this earlier (in Exodus 29), and now He orders that they be carried out with the whole people gathered as witnesses.

For today: God still speaks through His Word, and the first thing He asks of us is that we listen carefully. Before serving Him or doing anything for Him, it is good to stop and read the Bible and pray, so that we obey what He has said and not only what seems right to us.
exp.12:7:
The priest examines the person again. If the rash has kept spreading after he had been pronounced clean, the priest must declare him unclean, that is, ceremonially impure. The phrase "skin disease" here probably covered several conditions, not only the one we call leprosy today.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priest did not act as a doctor, but as a guardian of the purity of the camp, where God dwelt. His examination was patient, with rechecks and a waiting period, before he reached a decision.

For today: let us learn not to judge in haste. Before we give an opinion about someone or about a problem, let us take time, observe carefully, and seek the truth calmly, like someone who wants to care for others and not condemn them.
exp.17:22:
This verse forbids a man or a woman from having sexual relations with an animal. The Berean Standard Bible calls such an act a perversion, a term that describes something that goes against the natural order God designed. The verse also says that the act defiles the person who does it.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, shortly before they enter the land of Canaan. He wanted his people to be different from the neighboring nations, whose practices the text describes as defiling. These laws protected human dignity and the holiness of the people who belonged to God.

Today we can remember that God cares for our dignity and calls us to live out our sexuality with respect and within the limits he set. Before letting ourselves be carried along by the customs of the culture, it is good to ask whether what we do honors God and cares for people.
exp.18:19:
The verse describes a man who has sexual relations with a slave girl who is promised to another man but has not yet been redeemed or given her freedom. The phrase "lies carnally with" describes the act. Being "redeemed" means that a price was paid to free her. The verse says there must be due punishment for both, but they are not to be put to death, because she had not been freed. The text is difficult and is interpreted in several ways, especially the part about the punishment.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, giving them laws to live as a holy people. These rules addressed specific cases in that ancient society, where slavery existed. Even so, the text recognizes that the act is a wrong that calls for making amends: the man must bring a ram as an offering for his guilt and receives forgiveness.

Today we can learn that sexual sin harms others and requires responsibility. If we fail, God offers forgiveness when we acknowledge our guilt with sincerity.
exp.14:20:
What it says: Anyone who touches the bed of a woman who is having her period must wash his clothes, bathe with water, and remain unclean until evening. "Unclean" means ritually impure, not sinful or wicked.

Context: God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives these rules to Israel. They were rules of purity for life near the sanctuary, where God dwelt in the midst of the people. The impurity was temporary and was resolved by washing. Scholars explain their purpose in various ways: caring for reverence toward God, respecting the value of life and blood, or teaching order and health. Not everything is clear.

For today: Although we no longer live under these rules, the passage reminds us to approach God with reverence. We can ask him each day to cleanse our hearts, trusting that Christ purifies us.
exp.22:36:
These are the feasts the LORD appointed, which the people were to announce as sacred assemblies. On these days they brought food offerings to the LORD: burnt offerings and grain offerings, sacrifices and drink offerings, each one on the day set for it.

God Himself speaks to Moses so that he may pass the instructions on to Israel. Leviticus 23 lists the feasts of the year: the Sabbath, the Passover, the firstfruits, Pentecost, the trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the Tabernacles. This verse closes the list. The purpose was to help the people remember, worship, and give thanks to God in an orderly rhythm.

For today: God values the times dedicated to Him. We can set aside fixed moments, such as a day of gathering with the church or a daily time of prayer, to worship and give thanks with intention, not only when we happen to remember.
exp.12:11:
It says that if a skin disease breaks out and spreads over the whole body of the person, from the head to the feet, and the priest can see it, he must examine it carefully. "Spreading" means extending; "skin" is the flesh; "infected" is the person who has the disease; "as far as the priest can see" means as far as the priest can look.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel in the wilderness. The priests were to examine the sick and look after the health and purity of the community. What is surprising is that, according to the next verse, if it covered the whole body and everything had turned white, the priest declared the person clean. Scholars explain that rule in several ways, and there is no single certain answer. Today it is believed that this "leprosy" covered several skin diseases.

Today: before judging someone, look calmly and take in the whole situation, as the priest did, and do not stop at your first impression.
exp.12:5:
In the second examination, the priest looks at the person again. If the sore has faded and has not spread across the skin, he declares the person clean. The word "rash" describes a mild skin irritation. The person washes his clothes and is clean, that is, fit to return to the ordinary life of the community.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. They were rules about skin conditions, and the disease the text calls by a broad name may have covered several different ailments. The priest did not heal anyone: he examined, waited, and decided, protecting the community and avoiding hasty judgments. The details of each diagnosis are understood in various ways.

For today: do not draw quick conclusions about others. God models patience, careful observation, and mercy. Before labeling someone because of a flaw, give them time, look carefully, and seek their restoration.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that no grain offering brought to the Lord was to be made with yeast. It also says that no yeast or honey was to be burned on the altar as an offering. The verse does not use the term for the grain offering, but it clearly refers to offerings presented to the Lord, and the word for "leaven" refers to yeast, which causes dough to rise.

God speaks to Moses and gives Israel instructions for worship. Scholars explain this prohibition in several ways. Many think that yeast was associated with fermentation and decay, and that honey, which can also ferment, had a similar meaning. We do not know the exact reason for certain, because the text does not state it. What is clear is that God wanted a simple and pure offering.

For today: when you give something to God, whether your time, your service, or your money, do it with simplicity and sincerity, without mixing in pride or a desire to look good.
exp.19:1:
This verse forbids anyone from giving their children to Molech, a false god. It says that any Israelite or foreigner living in Israel who did this must be put to death, and that the people of the land were to stone him. The word "children" in the verse refers to one's offspring.

God speaks to Moses to give laws to Israel before they enter Canaan. Many scholars understand that the worship of Molech included the sacrifice of children, though some debate the exact details. God treats this as a most serious crime because it defiled his sanctuary and dishonored his name, and because it destroyed innocent lives.

Today we can ask ourselves what things weigh more in our hearts than God. Nothing should ask us to sacrifice the well-being of our children. Let us care for them with love and teach them to trust in the true God.
exp.14:16:
Leviticus 15:17 says that any clothing or leather on which there is an emission of semen must be washed with water, and it will remain unclean until evening. The "clothing" in the verse is the garment itself, and the "emission" is the discharge; "unclean" means ritually impure, not sinful or dirty through fault.

God gives these instructions to Moses for Israel. They teach the people that life, the body, and closeness to God are serious matters. This impurity was temporary and was resolved through washing and the passing of time. Scholars explain the exact purpose in several ways: order, respect for life, and separation from worship.

For today: God is concerned with every area of life, even the most private ones. We can live with order, cleanliness, and reverence, and remember that Christ truly cleanses us within (1 John 1:9).
exp.10:4:
This verse says the rock badger was not to be eaten. It chews the cud, that is, it brings back its food to chew again, but it does not have a divided hoof. "Unclean" means ceremonially impure, not fit for the people of God. Some think the animal named here is the hyrax, or rock badger, though there is no complete certainty.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, and through them to Israel, shortly after leaving Egypt. These rules about food helped the people live differently from the neighboring nations, because God told them: "Be holy, for I am holy."

Today Christians are not under these food rules; the New Testament makes this clear in Mark 7:19 and Acts 10. But God's desire that his people live set apart for him still stands. Ask yourself: what daily habits show that you belong to God?
exp.22:41:
This verse says that for seven days all the native-born of Israel must live in booths. The phrase "native-born" in this verse refers to those who were born among the people.

This is the Feast of Tabernacles, also called the Feast of Booths, which was celebrated with joy.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes these instructions on to the people. The next verse explains the reason: so that future generations would remember that God made Israel live in booths when He brought them out of Egypt. It was a festival to remember His care during the journey through the wilderness. It was celebrated in the seventh month, after the harvest.

For today: set aside a moment this week to remember with gratitude how God has cared for you in uncertain times. You might write down three examples and thank Him for them in prayer, or share them with someone in your family so they are not forgotten.
exp.25:23:
God says that if his people keep going against him, he will also act against them. "I will strike you sevenfold" means that the punishment will grow much more severe. The number seven stands for something complete or intense, not necessarily an exact count. "Act with hostility" means treating them as enemies rather than as allies.

God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel. This comes at the end of the blessings and curses of the covenant. He had already sent earlier warnings, and here he says that if they do not allow themselves to be corrected, the discipline will increase. His aim was to bring them back to himself.

For today: when you sense that God is correcting you through circumstances or through his Word, do not harden your heart. Listen quickly, acknowledge your error, and return to him, because his discipline seeks to restore you.
exp.3:4:
This verse says that the anointed priest, the priest who had been set apart with oil to serve, was to take some of the blood of the bull that had been sacrificed. He was then to bring it into the Tent of Meeting, the holy tent where God met with his people. The text does not mention the tablets of the law here, so no comment is made about them.

God speaks to Moses and gives instructions about the offerings for sin committed unintentionally. If the one who sinned was the priest, his failure affected the whole people, because he represented them before God. For that reason the ritual was more solemn. The blood showed that sin is serious and that forgiveness has a cost.

For today: let us not minimize sin, especially if we carry spiritual responsibility for others. Christians believe that Christ offered his blood once to forgive us, so we can draw near to God with humility and confidence.
exp.18:2:
What it says: Each person must have a deep respect for their mother and their father, and must also keep God's Sabbaths. The verse is about respect and reverence, not being afraid. The command to "keep" the Sabbaths means to observe them and honor the day of rest. At the end, God reminds the people who is giving the command: "I am the LORD your God."

Context: God speaks to Moses so that he will speak to the whole people of Israel. Just before this, God has said, "Be holy, for I am holy." This verse is one of the first examples of how to live that holiness: in the family and in the time set apart for God. Respect for parents and the Sabbath are named together, and then the rejection of idols follows.

For today: Holiness is lived out in everyday life. You can honor your parents with a phone call, with patience, or with concrete help, and set aside regular time to rest and remember God.
exp.6:26:
This verse forbids eating blood. "If anyone eats blood" means that no one was exempt. The phrase "that person must be cut off from his people" means that such a person would be separated from the community of Israel. Scholars are not sure whether that meant expulsion, direct punishment from God, or another serious penalty.

God speaks to Moses to give Israel instructions about the sacrifices. The prohibition applied to birds and animals, and in all their homes, not only in the sanctuary. Later, Leviticus 17:11 explains that the life is in the blood and that God gave it to make atonement on the altar. In this way, blood was treated as something sacred.

Today we can learn to respect what God calls holy. Christ shed his blood for us, so we can thank him from the heart and live with reverence and gratitude, not taking his forgiveness lightly.
exp.25:27:
He says that God will respond in anger against his people if they keep resisting him. "Walk in fury against you" means that God will turn against them and stop acting in their favor. "Sevenfold" is usually not understood as an exact number, but as a punishment that grows stronger and more complete each time.

God speaks through Moses, at the end of the law of Leviticus. Israel had already received the covenant, with blessings for obedience and warnings for disobedience. This is one step within a series of warnings. God does not act all at once: before this he had given them several chances to return. His goal was that the people would recognize their error and come back to him.

For today: when you feel that God is correcting you or that something is not right, do not harden your heart. Stop, listen to his Word, and ask what you should change. His patience is an invitation to return soon.
exp.24:6:
This verse says that during the sabbath year of the land's rest, whatever the land grew on its own would serve as food for the livestock and the wild animals in the land. The verse names both tame animals and wild ones, so the food was meant for every creature living in the territory. The rest of the year, when the land was not sown or harvested in the usual way, is the time the verse describes.

God speaks to Israel through Moses at Sinai and gives them instructions for life in the promised land. Every seventh year the land rested. In this way, the food was shared with servants, foreigners, and animals, and the people learned to trust God's provision.

For today: God cares for all of his creation. We can practice rest, generosity, and trust, loosening our grip a little on what we produce, and sharing what we have with others.
exp.8:14:
This verse tells that Aaron presented the people's offering. He took the male goat for the people's sin offering, slaughtered it, and offered it for sin, just as he had done with the first one, the calf for his own sin. The sentence explains that the goat was killed and offered for the people's sin, in the same way as the first offering had been.

It is the eighth day, when Aaron and his sons begin their service as priests. Moses had given the instructions on God's behalf. First Aaron offered for himself, and then for the people. This showed that the priests also needed forgiveness. Christians often see in this a shadow of Christ, who is perfect and offered himself only once (Hebrews 7:27).

For today: you do not need to hide your failures or pretend to be perfect. Acknowledge them honestly before God and rest in the forgiveness that Jesus has already won for you.
exp.17:0:
This verse is a simple introduction: God spoke to Moses. The word "Lord" is the name this translation uses for God. What follows are the words Moses was to pass on to the people.

God speaks, and Moses is the messenger. Israel had left Egypt and was heading toward Canaan. God reminds them that they are his people and that they must not copy the customs of either of those places. The chapter deals with sexual and moral conduct that was meant to set Israel apart.

For today: before telling us how to live, God speaks to us with his voice and his authority. We can take time to listen to his Word before deciding what to do, instead of simply going along with what most people do. His guidance flows from a relationship with him.
exp.18:31:
This verse says that people should stand up in the presence of an elderly person and treat them with respect. The phrase "gray hair" in the old version referred to the white hair of old age, and the verse here speaks simply of the elderly. "Honor the aged" means giving them dignified treatment. It then adds "and fear your God," meaning reverence toward God.

God himself speaks to Israel through Moses. In this chapter he teaches them how to live as a people set apart for him. The commands nearby speak of reverence for God and of caring for the most vulnerable, such as the foreigner. Respect for the elderly is part of that same care.

For today: practice respect through concrete actions. Give up your seat, listen with patience, and do not mock someone for their age. In this way you show that you honor people and also honor God.
exp.26:33:
This verse closes the whole book of Leviticus. It says that the laws just read do not come from Moses himself, but from the LORD, who gave them through him to the Israelites on Mount Sinai. The verse says the LORD gave these commandments, which shows they carried his authority. The place was Mount Sinai, where God met with his people after bringing them out of Egypt.

The one speaking here is the narrator, who summarizes and seals the whole book. The earlier chapters dealt with sacrifices, priests, feasts, purity and offerings. The last subject was vows and tithes. With this sentence the reader is reminded that all of this was the will of God for a people who were just beginning to live as his nation.

For today: before deciding how to live, it is wise to ask ourselves what God thinks. We can read his Word not as a burden imposed from outside, but as the guidance of one who knows us and loves us, and obey it with confidence.
exp.10:28:
This verse says that certain small animals that move along the ground were "unclean" for Israel. The mole, the mouse, and the great lizard are named, with the lizards grouped as "any kind" of their type. "Unclean" does not necessarily mean bad, but rather not fit to eat or touch without becoming ceremonially impure. Some Hebrew names of animals are hard to translate exactly.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel, newly come out of Egypt. These laws taught them to distinguish between the clean and the unclean, and to live as a people set apart for God. Touching the dead body of these animals brought impurity until evening, and it was cleansed by washing.

For today: God cares about the details of daily life. Today we seek to live with attention and reverence, knowing that Christ cleanses us within. We can ask him to help us set aside whatever stains our hearts.
exp.3:2:
It says that if the anointed priest, that is, the high priest set apart with oil for his service, sins in a way that brings guilt on the people, he must bring to the LORD a young bull without blemish as a sin offering. "Atonement" means covering guilt and restoring the relationship with God. "Without blemish" means without defect.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about sins committed by mistake, not by rebellion. This is the first case of the sin offerings. Because of his place of responsibility, the priest had to offer the most costly sacrifice. Some understand that his sin made the people he represented guilty.

For today: those who lead or teach others carry greater responsibility, and they should acknowledge their failings with humility. No one stands above the need for forgiveness. For Christians, this points to Christ, the perfect priest who forgives us.
exp.10:1:
God tells Moses and Aaron to say to the Israelites which animals of the land they may eat. "Say to" is the sense of the opening command, and "may eat" marks the start of a list that separates the animals that are allowed from those that are not.

Here the LORD speaks, and He does so through Moses and Aaron. Israel had just begun its life of worship in the tabernacle. God was giving them rules to live as a people set apart for Him. Scholars explain the reason for each animal in various ways, but the text emphasizes holiness (see Lev 11:44).

For today: God is interested in my whole life, even in the everyday. Today I can ask myself whether my habits, such as what I consume and what I do, show that I belong to Him and want to honor Him.
exp.24:9:
This verse commands that the fiftieth year be set apart as holy, belonging to God. Liberty is announced across the whole land for everyone who lives there. The year is called the Jubilee, and each person is to return to their own property and to their clan.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, before they enter the promised land. The Jubilee was announced on the Day of Atonement, after seven cycles of seven years. It kept debts and poverty from leaving families without land forever. Scholars debate how widely it was practiced in Israel's history.

For today: God cares about the freedom and dignity of people. We can forgive a debt, help someone regain their stability, or give someone a second chance.
exp.21:9:
This verse says that no one outside the priest's family may eat from the sacred offering. The reader's wording "no one outside a priest's family" tells us who is meant. A visitor who stayed with the priest, and a hired hand, were also not allowed to eat it.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Aaron and his sons. The offerings were set apart for God, and only those who belonged to the priestly household could eat them. This taught that what is holy is not to be treated lightly. The following passage shows that a servant bought with money and a person born in the household could eat, because they were part of the home.

For today: Treat with reverence what God has set apart, such as prayer, his Word, and fellowship. And remember that in Christ we are no longer outsiders, but part of his family (Ephesians 2:19).
exp.12:3:
If the spot on the skin is white and does not appear to be deeper than the skin, and the hair in it has not turned white, then the priest does not declare anything yet. He isolates the person for seven days to observe. The verse describes an uncertain case, one that needs more time before any judgment is made.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priests were to examine calmly and not decide all at once. The skin conditions in view were likely several different diseases, not only what we today call leprosy. This protected the community and gave a fair process.

For today: before judging a person or a situation, let us take time to observe and wait. God teaches us patience, care, and justice, instead of hasty conclusions.
exp.13:38:
After a week of waiting, the priest returns to inspect the house. His task is to see whether the mildew has spread across the walls. The word for it here refers to a stain or infection on the walls, probably mold or fungus, though exactly what it was is not known with certainty.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel, who would soon live in the land of Canaan. These rules protected the health and purity of the community. Notice that the priest does not decide right away: first he closes the house and waits seven days, giving time to see what happens.

For today: before judging a problem, it is wise to give it time and observe it calmly. But we should also honestly examine our lives, because the small things we do not attend to can grow.
exp.12:17:
It says that if someone had a boil on the skin (an abscess or swelling with pus, also called a festering sore or ulcer) and it healed, the matter is not yet finished. The verse begins an instruction that continues in the following verses: the person must let themselves be examined if something suspicious appears in that same place.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron about diseases of the skin, which the Bible calls "leprosy," though scholars believe it included several conditions and not only the one we know by that name today. The priest made an examination to protect the health of the Israelite community and to care for its purity before God.

For today: a healing does not always mean everything is resolved. Be humble in asking for examination, advice, or help, whether medical, spiritual, or from wise people, and do not hide what still worries you.
exp.18:8:
It says that when the farmer harvests the wheat or barley, he must not cut all the way to the very edge of his field. Nor should he go back to pick up the grain that fell on the ground. The "harvest" is the crop ready to be cut, "your land" is the field that was planted, and "gleanings" means the loose grain left behind after the cutting.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. This chapter teaches how to live as a holy people: "You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy." What follows makes the purpose clear: what was left in the field was for the poor and the foreigner. Holiness includes concrete generosity, not only worship.

Today we can apply this by setting aside a margin of our earnings, whether of time or money, to help others. We can set aside something fixed each month for someone in need, without seeking to squeeze out every last cent.
exp.26:0:
This verse says that the LORD spoke to Moses. The phrase "Then the LORD said to Moses," is a formula that is repeated often in the first five books of the Bible. It marks the beginning of a new instruction. Here there is no command yet, only the introduction to what follows about vows.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the messenger who must pass his words on to the people. Leviticus 27 is the final chapter of the book and deals with vows, that is, promises made to God. The verses that follow explain how to pay a set value to fulfill a vow that involved a person. Many scholars see this chapter as an appendix to the book.

For today: God cares about our promises. Before promising something to him, think it over calmly and be sincere. If you have already promised something, try to keep it with honesty and gratitude.
exp.13:55:
This verse names three kinds of marks on the skin that appear in the list of cases the law was meant to clarify. The first is a swelling; the second is a rash; and the third is a spot. It should be remembered that the word for "leprosy" here refers to several skin diseases, and we do not know with certainty which ones.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron, so that the priests would teach them to the people of Israel. This verse closes a long list of cases. Its purpose was to teach when a person is unclean, and when clean, caring for the health and orderly life of the community.

For today: God is interested in the details of our lives and does not want us to face alone what worries us. We can seek help with humility, whether medical or from our community, and trust that He cares for us.
exp.10:32:
If one of these unclean dead animals falls into a clay pot, everything inside it becomes unclean, and the pot must be broken. "Unclean" means it was not fit for ordinary use or for coming near worship. A "pot" is a container, such as a jar or a bowl.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, and through them to Israel. These laws taught people to distinguish between what is clean and what is unclean, and to live carefully as a people set apart for God. Clay is porous, so it could not be cleaned well. That is why it was broken. Scholars also see reasons of hygiene, though the text emphasizes holiness.

For today: God takes seriously what defiles the heart. Let us ask him to show us which things we must let go of completely, without negotiating with them, and trust that Christ truly cleanses us.
exp.8:7:
Aaron approaches the altar and slaughters the calf as a sin offering for himself. "Slaughters" means he kills the animal by cutting its throat. A "sin offering" is the sacrifice that covers sin and restores the relationship with God. "Approaches" simply means he comes near to the altar.

Moses has ordered that the priesthood, newly set apart, begin its service after seven days of preparation. Before offering anything for the people, Aaron must offer for himself, since he too is a sinner. Everything is done as the LORD commanded, so that God may appear among them.

For today: before pointing out the failings of others or desiring to serve, it is wise to examine our own heart and acknowledge our need for forgiveness. Whoever serves God with humility helps others better.
exp.22:31:
This verse says that the Day of Atonement will be a Sabbath of complete rest for you. The phrase "you shall humble yourselves" means humbling yourselves, and it is commonly understood as fasting and repentance. It says the day is kept "from the evening of the ninth day of the month until the following evening": from the evening of the ninth day until the evening of the tenth day.

God speaks to Moses to give Israel the feasts of the Lord. This day, in the seventh month, was the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur), when forgiveness for sin was sought. For that reason, people were commanded to stop all work and devote the day to God with humility. After this comes the Feast of Tabernacles.

For today: set aside unhurried time to examine your heart, confess your faults to God, and rest in his forgiveness. Christians see in Christ the fulfillment of that atonement.
exp.12:28:
This verse begins a new section of the laws about skin conditions. It speaks of a man or a woman who has an infection on the head or on the chin. The sore is a visible mark on the skin, and the instructions that follow tell the priest how to examine it.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron. These instructions guided the priest in examining carefully anyone with a visible skin condition. The text speaks of a disease that is often called "leprosy," but it is not known for certain whether it was the illness we call that today or several different skin ailments. What is clear is that the aim was to protect the health and order of the community of Israel.

Today we can learn not to judge too quickly. Before forming an opinion about someone, it is wise to look with patience, listen, and care for their dignity, as God cares for everyone.
exp.4:11:
This verse says that the poor person, who could not bring birds, was to bring fine flour to the priest. The priest would take a handful of it as a memorial portion and burn it on the altar atop the food offerings to the LORD, and this was a sin offering. The phrase "memorial portion" means that this handful stood for the whole offering. "Atonement" means covering or cleansing guilt.

God speaks to Moses in the law he gave to Israel. He wanted no one to be left without a way to forgiveness because of a lack of money. The offering had no oil or incense, because it was simple, since it dealt with sin, not with celebration. Here the flour had no blood, and scholars have debated how to understand this; the text only says that God accepted it and granted forgiveness.

Today we can remember that God's forgiveness is not bought and does not depend on what we have. If there is something to confess, come to Him with simplicity and sincerity.
exp.21:29:
This verse says that the meat of the thank offering had to be eaten on the same day it was offered. Nothing could be kept until the next morning.

The passage then sets out the idea of willing giving in this offering: people brought it freely, not because they were forced to.

God himself speaks to Moses so that he will instruct the priests and the people about the offerings. Care was taken that what was set apart for God was handled with reverence. Many believe that the command to eat it that same day taught people to share their gratitude together and without delay, though the text gives no further reasons. It closes by reminding the reader who gives the command, the LORD.

For today: do not put off your thankfulness to God. When you receive something good, give thanks today, sincerely, and share it with others if you can.
exp.6:27:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses again. The words "Then the LORD said to Moses" mark the start of a new instruction, and they signal that something fresh is about to be said.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the messenger who must pass his words on to the people. Earlier, God had given rules about fat and blood. Now he begins to explain how the peace offerings were to be presented, which were offerings of thanksgiving and fellowship with him. This shows that these rules did not come from Moses but from God.

For today: God still speaks through his Word. We can read it with care and respect, without skipping the parts that seem hard, trusting that God wants to teach us how to live close to him.
exp.2:1:
The verse says that the person who brought a peace offering was to lay his hand on the head of the animal and kill it at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. The Tent of Meeting was the sacred tent where God met with his people. Here "to slaughter" means to kill the animal. Then the priests, the sons of Aaron, would splatter the blood on all sides of the altar.

God speaks to Moses from the Tent of Meeting, giving Israel instructions on how to draw near to him. The peace offering expressed fellowship and thankfulness. Laying a hand on the animal is usually understood as identifying oneself with the offering, though scholars explain its meaning with different nuances. The blood showed that life belongs to God.

For today: draw near to God with sincerity and gratitude, knowing that fellowship with him has a cost. Christians see in Christ the complete sacrifice that gives us peace with God.
exp.22:24:
On that special day, the people were not to do any regular work. Instead, they were to present a food offering to the LORD, a sacrifice burned on the altar.

God speaks to Moses so that he may tell Israel. It concerns the first day of the seventh month, a day marked by the blowing of trumpets and a holy assembly. Afterward would come the Day of Atonement. In this way, God set aside times of pause, remembrance, and preparation of the heart.

For today: set aside an unhurried time to stop, pray, and thank God. Setting work aside for a while reminds us that our life does not depend only on what we produce, but on God.
exp.3:33:
This verse says the priest dips his finger into the blood of the animal offered for sin and puts some of it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering, the altar used for the sacrifices. He pours out the rest of the blood at the base of the altar. "Atonement" here means the sacrifice that covers sin and restores the relationship with God.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to Israel. This passage explains what an Israelite had to do when he sinned unintentionally and brought a female lamb. The blood showed that sin is serious and that forgiveness had a cost. Christians often see here a sign that points to Christ, although the text itself speaks of Israel's sacrificial system.

Today we can take sin seriously, without ignoring it or excusing it, and come near to God with confidence, because He offers forgiveness. When you fail, confess it honestly and receive His forgiveness with gratitude.
exp.12:26:
On the seventh day, the priest looks at the spot on the skin again. If it has spread further, he declares the person unclean, meaning ceremonially impure. The verse says the priest "reexamines" him, which means he examines the spot closely once more. The word "diseased infection" in the verse describes a condition that probably covered several skin problems, not only what we today call leprosy.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel. The priest did not decide at once. He waited seven days and watched whether the spot changed. In this way the health and purity of the community were cared for through an orderly and fair process.

Today we can learn not to judge too quickly. Before drawing conclusions about a person or a situation, let us take time, look at the facts, and act with patience and compassion.
exp.2:14:
This verse says that from the animal offered, both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver, were set apart for God. The fat near the loins is the fat along the animal's sides, and the lobe of the liver is the part removed together with the kidneys.

God speaks to Moses, and this is part of the instructions for the peace offering, an offering of fellowship and thanksgiving. The fat was the best part, and it was burned entirely for God. Scholars understand the exact meaning of this detail in various ways, but nearly all of them see in it the idea of giving God what is best and most valuable.

For today: God deserves the best, not the leftovers. Today we can ask ourselves which part of our time, care, and resources we give first, with gratitude and from the heart, and not just what we have left over at the end.
exp.14:29:
The priest offers the two birds the woman brings: one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering. In this way the priest makes atonement for her before the LORD for her unclean discharge, that is, her bleeding outside her normal time. The word "unclean" here refers to ritual impurity, not necessarily personal sin.

God speaks through Moses to Israel. These laws taught that God is holy and lives among his people, in the tabernacle. The sacrifices showed that impurity and death cannot draw near to God without being dealt with. Scholars explain in several ways why a sin offering was required in these cases; the safest view is that it pointed to the general need for purification.

For today: God cares that we approach him with reverence. We do so now by trusting in Christ, whose sacrifice cleanses us completely, and we can pray with confidence and thankfulness.
exp.7:21:
This verse tells that Moses presented a second ram, called "the ram of ordination," the animal used to set the priests apart for God. Aaron and his sons laid their hands on its head. That gesture meant that they identified themselves with the animal, as if offering it in their place.

The passage recounts the ceremony of ordaining the priests. Moses acts following what God commanded him. A bull had already been offered as a sin offering and a ram as a burnt offering. Now, with this second ram, Aaron and his sons are set apart to serve. Scholars explain the exact meaning of laying on hands in several ways, but all agree on the idea of identification.

For today: serving God does not begin with our abilities, but with recognizing that we need to be set apart and cleansed by Him. We can draw near with humility, without presumption.
exp.24:48:
This verse says who may buy back an Israelite who, because of poverty, had to sell himself as a servant to a foreigner. His uncle, his uncle's cousin, or any close relative from his clan may buy him back. To buy back means to pay the price that sets someone free. And if he prospers and gathers the money himself, he may pay for his own freedom.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. These laws about the year of jubilee protected the poor from lifelong slavery. The family had the duty to help, and this relative is called the "kinsman-redeemer." The law does not cancel the payment, but calculates it according to the number of years left until the jubilee.

For today: think about whether there is someone in your family or church who is in debt or in trouble. Perhaps you can help them with money, time, advice, or companionship, without humiliating them.
exp.26:23:
If someone bought a field and dedicated it to God, then in the year of the Jubilee that field did not stay with the temple or with the buyer. It returned to the original owner, the one to whom the land belonged by family inheritance. The phrase "to the one from whom it was bought" names that original owner, and "to dedicate" here means setting something apart for God.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. The land was divided by families and tribes, and the Jubilee, held every fifty years, kept a family from losing its inheritance forever. Even if someone dedicated a field he had bought, he could not dedicate what was not truly his by inheritance. Everything had to respect the rights of the original owner.

For today: when you want to give something to God, do it with what truly belongs to you and with justice. An act of generosity should not override the rights or the well-being of others.
exp.18:21:
This verse says that the priest would offer the ram as a guilt offering and, by doing so, would make atonement before the LORD for the man who had sinned. "Atonement" means covering or repairing a wrong. "Reconciling" means restoring the relationship. The result is clear: he would be forgiven the sin he had committed.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. Before this, the text deals with a case involving a woman who was promised to a servant, and the law sets out a penalty and an offering. Some scholars explain the penalty in several ways, so it is worth reading this carefully. The central point here is that the sin was serious, but God provided a way to be forgiven.

For today: do not hide your fault or minimize it. Acknowledge it before God, seek to repair the harm you can, and trust in his forgiveness. Christians see in Christ the complete sacrifice that makes this forgiveness possible.
exp.23:12:
