This verse is a short phrase that introduces God's answer. "The LORD" is the name of God, and "said to Moses" means that God gave him an instruction directly to settle the case.

The people were in the wilderness. A man, the son of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian father, had spoken against the name of God with contempt, and they had put him under guard. No one decided on their own what to do; they waited for the word of the LORD. What follows is the sentence, given within the laws of Israel at that time.

When we face a conflict or a serious offense, let us not act out of anger or habit. Before deciding, let us calmly seek God's guidance in his Word and in prayer, and let him show us the way.
exp.2:13:
This verse describes part of the peace offering, which was made from a goat. The person bringing the offering had to present to the Lord a food offering, which was the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is on them. "Fat" here means the rich fat of the animal, and a food offering is an offering that is burned on the altar.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel on how to come near to Him. In the verses before, the person laid his hand on the head of the animal, and the priests sprinkled the blood on the altar. The fat was the best part of the animal, and the text says that all the fat belongs to the Lord. It was a way of acknowledging that God deserves the best.

For today: we can ask ourselves whether we give God the best of our time, affection and effort, or only what we have left over. A sincere prayer at the start of the day is a good step.
exp.7:4:
Moses speaks to the whole gathered people and makes clear that what he is about to do is not his own idea. It is what the LORD has commanded.

Moses speaks just before he consecrates Aaron and his sons as priests. He wants everyone to see that the priestly service begins by God's command, not by human ambition, and that the people be witnesses to it.

For today: when we serve God or others, it is good to do so with openness and obedience to what He has said in His Word, not for our own gain. Let us ask ourselves whether what we do springs from His calling and whether we can explain it honestly.
exp.15:14:
This verse describes what the high priest did on the Day of Atonement. He slaughtered the goat of the sin offering that was for the people, carried its blood behind the veil into the most holy place, and sprinkled it against the mercy seat (also called the atonement cover, the lid of the ark) and in front of it, doing with its blood just as he had done with the bull's blood. "Atonement" means covering over or removing sin.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to Aaron. This ritual cleansed the sanctuary from the impurities and rebellions of Israel, because God dwelt in the midst of his people, and his holy presence required purification. First the blood was offered for the priest, and then for the people.

For today: many Christians see here a shadow of Christ, whose blood gives us access to God (Hebrews 9). We can approach God with humility and gratitude, without pretending we have not failed, trusting that his forgiveness is real and costly.
exp.22:4:
The verse says the Passover belongs to the Lord and begins at twilight on the fourteenth day of the first month. The time is the twilight, the period when the sun has set and the light is fading. The name Passover points to a passing over, recalling when God passed over the houses of Israel in Egypt.

God speaks to Moses so that he will tell the people. After the Sabbath, He sets out the yearly feasts. The Passover opens the calendar and is followed by the feast of unleavened bread. God wanted Israel to remember each year that they had been set free.

For today: set aside a regular moment to remember with gratitude how God has rescued you. Christians see in Christ the fulfillment of the Passover, and remembering this leads us to live thankfully.
exp.3:0:
This verse says that the LORD spoke to Moses. The name of God appears in the text as LORD, and the word "said" introduces God's own words, which Moses is to pass on to the people. It is a short phrase that opens a new instruction.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the messenger. In Leviticus, God gives Israel instructions on how to live near Him after the tabernacle was built. Here begins a section about the offerings for sin committed unintentionally, that is, without meaning to or by error. God does not leave the people without a way forward when they fail.

For today: God speaks with clarity and wants us to listen. We can set aside time to read the Bible carefully, willing to let Him show us where we have fallen short, even without realizing it, and to draw near to Him with humility and trust.
exp.17:4:
God tells Israel to keep his statutes (his rules) and his judgments (his fair decisions). The one who does these things will live by them, which means they will have a good life under God's blessing. At the end, God declares, "I am the LORD," reminding them who holds the authority.

God speaks through Moses to the people who had left Egypt and were nearing the land of Canaan. He asks them not to copy the customs of the surrounding nations and to live as a distinct people. Right after this come laws about purity in family relationships. Some understand "will live" to mean a long life in the land; others see it as a full life with God. The New Testament takes up these words again in Romans 10:5 and Galatians 3:12.

For today: do not simply go along with the crowd without thinking. Ask yourself which customs around you clash with the Word of God, and ask him for help to live faithfully before him.
exp.21:19:
This verse says that the Israelites were not to offer animals to God that had physical defects. "Defect" means a flaw or imperfection, and "accepted" means received or pleasing to God. If the animal had a defect, God would not receive it as an offering on their behalf.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Aaron, the priests, and all the people, including the foreigners who lived among them. These rules taught that drawing near to God was a serious matter. Offering the best was a way of showing respect, gratitude, and devotion. The sacrifices pointed to something deeper than the animal itself.

For today: when we give God our time, money, or service, it is worth asking whether we are giving him our best or only what we have left over. It is not about being perfect, but about giving sincerely and wholeheartedly.
exp.24:20:
God promises that in the sixth year he will send a blessing so great that the crop will be enough for three years: the sixth year, the seventh (when no seed is sown), and the eighth, until the new harvest comes in. The land will produce, and there will be plenty to eat until the people are fully satisfied.

God speaks to Israel through Moses. He had commanded them to let the land rest every seventh year. By anticipating the question "what will we eat?", God shows that he understands their fears. It reminds them that the land belongs to him and that they are like travelers who care for it.

For today: when obeying God seems risky, as with resting, giving, or being honest even when it costs us, we can trust that he is faithful. Obedience does not remove our questions, but it teaches us to depend on his care and not only on our own effort.
exp.22:21:
When you harvested the grain from your land, you were not to cut right up to the very edges of your field, and you were not to gather the stalks that had dropped to the ground. Ripe grain is called the harvest, the planted land is called the field, and picking up what falls behind the reapers is called gleaning. Those edges and fallen stalks were to be left for the poor and for the foreign resident.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. This command appears in the middle of the Lord's appointed festivals, right after the feast of Firstfruits, which the verse's surrounding passage connects to the Feast of Weeks. In this way, gratitude for the harvest included generosity toward those in need. God closes by saying, "I am the LORD your God," reminding them that He is the owner of the land and the one who cares for everyone.

Today we can leave a corner of our income or our time without calculating every bit for ourselves. For example, setting aside in advance a portion to help a neighbor, a newcomer, or someone in need.
exp.5:17:
Only the male descendants of Aaron, the priests, were allowed to eat the leftover part of the grain offering. This was to be a permanent rule for all their generations. The offerings burned on the altar are the ones this explanation has in view. The word "touch" means to come into contact with something, and the statement that anything touching the offering "will become holy" means it would be set apart for God. Commentators debate whether this refers to people who touched the offering or to the things that touched it, and the wording allows for either idea.

God speaks to Moses while giving instructions for the offerings in the tabernacle. The priests received no inheritance of land, so God gave them this portion as their provision. They were to eat it in a holy place, because it was something dedicated to God.

For today: what belongs to God deserves respect. We can approach Him with reverence and gratitude, and also support generously those who serve in ministry.
exp.14:11:
This verse says that if a person with a discharge (an abnormal bodily secretion) touched a clay pot, that pot had to be broken. If it was a wooden utensil, it was rinsed with water.

The word "unclean" means not fit to approach worship, not necessarily sinful.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to order the life of the people of Israel in the wilderness. These rules protected health and taught that the presence of God is holy. Clay is porous and could not be cleaned well, so it was broken. Scholars agree on the practical side, although they explain its symbolic meaning in various ways.

For today: God is concerned with everyday life, and holiness includes caring for what we touch and share. Today we can care for cleanliness and protect others, and remember that Christ cleanses us from within.
exp.17:14:
This verse forbids a man from having sexual relations with his daughter-in-law. She is his son's wife, and through marriage she already belongs to the family, which is the reason given for the prohibition.

God speaks to Israel through Moses, shortly before they enter the promised land. He gives them laws so that they will live differently from the neighboring peoples, such as Egypt and Canaan. Several laws in this chapter protect the holiness of the family and the boundaries within the home.

For today: take care of the boundaries in your family. Treat the spouses of your children and of your relatives with respect and purity, and do not allow the family to become a place of abuse or betrayal.
exp.5:21:
The priest who will take Aaron's place, one of Aaron's sons and anointed for that role, is the one to prepare this offering. It is a permanent portion for the LORD, and it must be burned completely.

God speaks to Moses and gives instructions about the offerings. This grain offering, made with oil, was presented every morning and every evening. The priests also needed to offer something to God, and they could not take any of it for themselves. This showed that their service was not for their own benefit.

For today: serve God without seeking personal advantage. Ask yourself whether what you do for others, in the church or at work, comes from a heart that wants to please God and not to be recognized.
exp.2:6:
It says that if someone chooses to offer a lamb as their peace offering, they must present it before the LORD, that is, before the LORD at the place of worship. The phrase "if he is presenting" shows that this offering was voluntary, not required.

God speaks to Moses to teach Israel how to draw near to Him. The peace offering was an offering of fellowship and thanksgiving. Earlier, the case of the cattle was explained; now the lamb is mentioned. Then come the steps: laying a hand on the offering, slaughtering it, and sprinkling the blood on the altar.

For today: God is not interested only in what we give, but in our coming to Him with sincerity. We can offer a prayer of thanksgiving today, without anyone forcing us, simply to stand in His presence with a grateful heart.
exp.6:32:
It says that the son of Aaron who presented the blood and fat of the peace offering received the right thigh of the animal as his portion. The thigh is the upper part of the back leg, near the hip.

The words "peace offering" refer to the offering of fellowship or thanksgiving. The fat, which was burned for God, is the part set apart for the Lord.

God speaks to Moses and gives instructions for Israel. He wanted the people to share their offering with the priests, who had no land of their own and served in the sanctuary. In this way the priests were supported, and the meal before God was lived out as fellowship between God, the priest, and the worshiper.

For today: supporting those who serve in the church with generosity is part of worshiping God. We can ask ourselves how we are caring for those who teach us and walk with us in faith, through prayer, time, or resources.

sum.10: In Leviticus 11, God speaks to Moses and Aaron and tells them which animals the Israelites could eat: those with split hooves that chew the cud, fish with fins and scales, and certain insects. The others were unclean, and touching their dead bodies made a person unclean. God calls them to be holy, because He is holy.
sum.22: In Leviticus 23, God gives Moses the calendar of festivals that Israel was to observe: the weekly Sabbath, Passover, the Festival of Unleavened Bread, the Firstfruits, Pentecost, the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the Festival of Booths. These were times of rest, offering, and thankfulness, and also of remembering the deliverance from Egypt and of caring for the poor.
sum.13: God gives Moses the rules for declaring a person who has been healed of leprosy clean again. The ritual uses two small birds, washing, and offerings on the eighth day, and there is a simpler option for someone who is poor. It also explains what to do about a house that has a "plague": inspect it, remove the stones, replaster it, and then either cleanse it or tear it down if the plague remains.
sum.8: On the eighth day, Moses told Aaron and the people to bring their offerings: a sin offering, burnt offerings, and peace offerings, so that the LORD would appear to them. Aaron offered them just as the LORD had commanded, and he blessed the people. Then the glory of the LORD appeared, a fire came out and consumed the sacrifice, and everyone shouted for joy and fell facedown in worship.
sum.19: God gives Israel laws about holiness, with severe penalties for giving children to Molech, consulting mediums and fortune-tellers, cursing one's parents, and several sexual offenses. He asks them to live apart from the practices of the peoples of Canaan, because He is holy and has set them apart to be His own. In this way they will be able to live in the promised land.
sum.14: God gives Moses and Aaron laws about ritual impurity caused by bodily discharges, both for men and for women. The text specifies washing, waiting periods, and, on the eighth day, offerings of two birds before the priest so that the person may be purified. The purpose was to keep Israel from dying by defiling the tabernacle where God dwelt.
sum.24: God commands that every seven years the land be allowed to rest, and that every fifty years a Jubilee be celebrated, when each family regains its land and enslaved Israelites are set free. Land is not to be sold permanently, because it belongs to God, and the poor must be redeemed and treated with compassion, without interest-taking or harshness.
sum.21: God tells Moses that the priests must take care to remain pure, and that they must not eat of the holy things while they are unclean. Only their own households may eat of those things. He also commands that the animals offered must be without defect, and that his rules be kept, so that his holy name is not profaned, for he is the one who makes them holy.
sum.9: Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, offered "strange fire" to God that he had not commanded, and they died from a fire that came out from the presence of the LORD. Moses told Aaron and his sons not to hold a public mourning, and God commanded them not to drink wine before they served, so that they could distinguish the holy from the common. Aaron explained why he had not eaten the offering, and Moses was satisfied.
sum.18: God calls his people to be holy because he is holy, and he spells this out with practical commands: honor your parents, worship only Jehovah, leave part of the harvest for the poor and the foreigner, be honest and fair, do not take revenge, and love your neighbor as yourself. It also forbids pagan practices and commands that foreigners be treated well.
sum.23: God commands that the lamps of the sanctuary be kept burning at all times, and that twelve loaves of bread be set out before Him every Sabbath. The bread would belong to Aaron and his sons. Then a man blasphemes the Name, and he is stoned. God establishes that justice must be the same for everyone, with the same punishment for the foreigner as for the native-born.
sum.4: Leviticus 5 explains that a person is guilty if they stay silent about what they know as a witness, if they touch something unclean, or if they swear an oath carelessly, even when they do not realize it. The person must confess their sin and bring an offering according to what they can afford, whether an animal, birds, or flour. The law also requires them to make restitution for anything they took from the holy things, and in this way the priest makes atonement and God forgives them.
sum.1: Leviticus 2 explains how to offer a grain offering to God: fine flour mixed with oil and frankincense, whether it was offered raw, baked in an oven, or cooked on a griddle. A portion was burned on the altar, and the rest belonged to the priests. It was not to contain yeast or honey, and it was always seasoned with salt, the "salt of the covenant."
sum.3: God teaches Moses how people can seek forgiveness when they sin unintentionally. The priest, the whole community, a leader, or any individual must bring a sacrifice without defect for their sin. The offerer lays a hand on the animal, its blood is used, and its fat is burned on the altar. The text says that this will bring atonement and forgiveness.
sum.17: God tells Moses that Israel must not copy the customs of Egypt or Canaan, but must follow God's laws instead. It forbids sexual relations with close relatives, adultery, sacrificing children to Molech, and sexual relations between men and with animals. It warns that these practices defiled the land and that anyone who commits them will be cut off from their people.
sum.5: God teaches that whoever deceives, steals, or swears falsely must return what was taken, add a fifth of its value, and bring a ram as a guilt offering, so that they may be forgiven. Then he gives instructions to the priests: the fire on the altar must never go out, and he explains how to handle the grain offerings and the sin offerings, which are most holy.
sum.15: God teaches Moses how Aaron is to enter the Most Holy Place once a year, wearing linen garments and bringing sacrifices, to cleanse the sanctuary and make atonement for the sins of all Israel. One goat is put to death, and another, with the people's sins confessed over its head, is sent out into the wilderness. The people are to humble themselves and rest on that day, every year.
sum.12: God instructs Moses and Aaron on how the priest is to examine spots on the skin, and also mold in clothing and in leather objects. The priest observes, waits seven days, and then decides whether the person or the object is clean or unclean. Anyone declared unclean lives apart, outside the camp.
sum.2: Leviticus 3 describes the peace offering, which could be made with a cow, a sheep, or a goat, always without defect. The person would lay their hand on the animal, and the priests would sprinkle the blood and burn the fat on the altar as an offering to the LORD. At the end, eating fat or blood is forbidden.
sum.0: God called Moses from the tent of meeting and gave him instructions about the burnt offering. The person was to bring an animal without defect, voluntarily, whether a bull, a sheep, a goat, a turtledove, or a young pigeon. The person would lay a hand on the animal, and the priests would offer its blood and burn it on the altar. The text says it was a "pleasing aroma" to the LORD and would serve to make atonement.
sum.7: God commands Moses to set apart Aaron and his sons as priests. Moses washes them, dresses them, anoints them with oil, and offers sacrifices for them, putting blood on their right ear, right thumb, and right big toe. They are to stay seven days at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and they do everything the Lord has commanded.
sum.6: Leviticus 7 explains how the guilt offering and the peace offering were to be made, and what portion belonged to the priests. It also forbids eating fat and blood, and requires that anyone who eats of what has been offered be ceremonially clean. All of this was commanded by Jehovah to Moses at Mount Sinai.
sum.26: God teaches Israel how to fulfill their vows: people, animals, houses, and lands dedicated to Jehovah could be redeemed by paying their value plus an extra fifth. Anything devoted entirely to Jehovah could not be redeemed, and firstborn animals and tithes already belonged to Jehovah.
sum.20: God told Moses that the priests, the sons of Aaron, must live in holiness. They must not make themselves unclean by touching the dead, except for their closest relatives. They must not marry women with a bad reputation or women who have been divorced. The high priest had even stricter rules. Also, no priest with a physical defect could offer God's bread, though he was still allowed to eat from the holy portions.
sum.25: God asks Israel to worship Him alone and to obey Him. He promises rain, good harvests, peace, and His presence among them. If they reject Him, He warns of punishments that grow ever harsher, including famine, war, and exile. But if they humble themselves and confess their sin, God will remember His covenant and will not abandon them completely.
sum.11: God tells Moses that a woman who gives birth becomes ceremonially unclean for a period of time: seven days if she has a boy, and two weeks if she has a girl. After that comes a further period of purification. When it is over, she brings a lamb and a young pigeon or turtledove, or two birds if she is poor, and the priest makes atonement for her.
sum.16: God commands that animals brought for sacrifice be taken to the priest at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and not offered to other gods. He also forbids eating blood, because life is in the blood, and God gave it to make atonement for sins on the altar. Anyone who eats the meat of an animal that died on its own or was torn apart must wash and remain unclean until evening.
